Preface 

THE growing popularity of the one-year course in world history justifies this attempt to meet the exacting demands of such a course. Teachers realize the impossibility of dealing in one year with the detailed narrative that may be handled in a two-year course. Consequently the authors of 

World Civilization have tried to trace in broad outlines the development of civilization rather than the details of the political history of various countries. The thread of a developing and changing civilization — not a summary of rulers and wars has guided them in the selection and treatment of materials. 

The book is organized on the unit plan, with presentations that will aid the student in visualizing the sweep of events and the significance of movements. There are nine units, subdivided into twenty-two chapters. The Table of Contents shows the major parts of the organization. Frequent cross-references, by exact page citations, bind all parts of the narrative together and facilitate reviewing. 

The authors recognize the desirability of a simple vocabulary and have tried to meet the problem in two ways. In the first place, they have avoided many abstract and difficult words and have used those which are within the range of most high-school students. In the second place, recognizing the desirability of enlarging the student's vocabulary, they have carefully defined those words which are most likely to cause difficulty. Efforts have also been made to keep the sentence structure simple and the style clear and direct. 

In the preparation of this text the authors have attempted to meet the recommendations of the various committees of the National Education Association and the American Hisiii

iv 

Preface torical Association. Those parts of former recommendations which appear to be still valid have been heeded. In addition, the authors have taken careful note of the volumes of the current Report of the American Historical Association, particularly of the Conclusions and Recommendations, A Charter for the Social Sciences, and The Nature of the Social Sciences. 

Those topics in history which have been specifically recommended by the Commission will be found in World Civilization.

In addition to supplying the materials for instruction the authors have sought to assist the teacher and student in the process of mastery. The aids to teaching and learning are unusually full and suggestive. They are designed to stimulate and guide the student and assist the teacher. 

These aids deserve special attention, for they have been most carefully prepared. 

1. The "Suggested Glossary" consists of words and phrases to be defined rather than of proper nouns to be identified. The meanings of many of the words are given explicitly in the text; the meanings of others can be inferred from their context; such as remain unknown should be clarified by the use of the dictionary. Teachers have developed a variety of methods for promoting the growth of the pupil's vocabulary. The glossary is designed to assist in selecting the most significant words to be learned. 

2. The "Review Questions" consist of questions to which the text supplies definite answers. While they are factual questions, they nevertheless often involve more than the mere recall of information. They are designed as a challenge to pupils, who can, under the teacher's direction, use them as study-guide questions. 

3. The "Discussion Questions" are those which involve comparisons, contrasts, evaluation, selection, and other processes which call for the use of information. In many instances there are no definite answers to them. Such questions are designed to stimulate discussion, promote suspended judgments, and serve as guides to further reading.

Preface 

V Some of them can easily be made the basis for classroom debates. 

4. The "Projects and Activities" are characterized by the suggestion of some overt activity such as debating, constructing, telling, drawing, writing, reading, or seeing. Resourceful teachers will want to expand the list and adapt those which appear promising to the particular needs of the individual class. 

5. The "Source Readings" are designed to lead to those vitalizing sidelights which go far toward preventing history from becoming a dry subject. No writer, however gifted, can imbue his work with that sense of reality that comes from reading a letter, a diary, or a speech by those whose names cover the pages of history. 

6. The "Selected Bibliographies" are designed primarily for students. An effort has been made to restrict the list to those references especially adapted to the high-school student. More advanced books for teachers and for occasional use by students are listed in the Appendix, with full information as to publisher and cost. 

The Appendix consists of three parts. Appendix A contains a complete list of the books cited in the "Selected Bibliographies." The names of the authors, the titles, the publishers, the dates of publication, and the prices are given. 

It is hoped that this information will be useful to teachers and librarians. Appendix B contains information of special value to teachers, and a list of books, many of which will be useful for both teachers and students. Appendix C contains a list of dates and events. This list will serve as a basis for reviewing, for constructing time lines, and in helping to build the necessary chronological framework. 

This is a new textbook-new in name, form, organization, apparatus, and in much of its content. The authors have, however, made liberal use of previous books by Hutton Webster. Many pictures, maps, and passages have been appropriated, for they have stood the test of classroom requirements. In fact, the incorporation of elements from

vi 

Preface a successful series of textbooks is one of the best guarantees that this new work will likewise meet with the approval of teachers and students. The authors welcome suggestions and criticisms. They are under special obligation to Mr. 

Roman Becker for his extensive criticisms and generous assistance.

HUTTON WEBSTER EDGAR BRUCE WESLEY

Unit I THE DEVELOPMENT OF CULTURE 

How early man adjusted himself to his environment and developed a culture 

(CHAPTERS I-II)

PRESENTATION 

History is the story of men living together and building a civilized society. The beginnings of civilization were humble. 

Early man had to accept his environment as he found it. Slowly through the ages he learned how to kill animals, to build a fire, to make stone tools and weapons, and eventually to use metals. 

Man was thus developing a culture, consisting of what he had achieved as distinct from what nature gave him. (Chapter I) 

While man was developing a culture, he was also spreading over various parts of the earth and developing those characteristics which mark the different races. At the same time he was learning to write, to count, and to keep track of time. Thus he was laying the foundations of civilization. (Chapter II) 

Unit I tells the story of how early man adjusted himself to his environment, developed a culture, and laid the foundations of civilization.

CHAPTER I THE PREHISTORIC AGE 

In every man there is something wherein I may learn of him; and in that I am his pupil. 

1. HISTORY AND CIVILIZATION EMERSON 

History in the day's news. Open today's newspaper or this week's magazine. You cannot read very far without finding yourself deep in history. Why have the communists triumphed in Soviet Russia? Why is the pope called the 

Supreme Pontiff? Why are there so few Protestants in 

South America? Why may another war break out in Europe? Why do the Italians want to restore the ancient

Roman Forum? Why do human beings behave as they do on Hallowe'en? Why are the international athletic contests called the Olympic Games? Why do some people believe that the stars influence their lives? - History alone will answer these questions for you. What, then, is history?

What is history? If history will answer such questions as those which we have just asked, then it must be the story of how things came to be what they are. It must be the story of men living together and working out a society for themselves. It may deal with what was thought or said or done yesterday, a year ago, or thousands of years ago. History, in short, is the narrative of what men have thought and said and done in the process of building today's civilization. 

History deals with social groups. One man by himself cannot build a civilization. Civilization results only when men live in coöperating groups. Consequently, the story of civilization must deal with group life. When individual persons are dealt with in history, it is only because they

The Prehistoric Age are significant members of their groups. Just as biography describes the life of individuals, so history describes the life of social groups such as churches, armies, states or countries, learned societies, trading companies, and villages. 

History, then, is the story of human society rather than the account of individuals. 

History deals with social life. Formerly, history was largely concerned with kings, monarchies, constitutions, debates, diplomacy, and wars. These were and still are important aspects of life, but they are by no means the whole story. Today, history deals with the entire life of a people their houses, furniture, clothing, and food; what occupations they followed; what schools they supported; what beliefs and superstitions they held; what amusements and festivals they enjoyed; what inventions and discoveries they made. Whatever, then, is interesting or important in the everyday life of a people, as well as matters of state, comes within the scope of history. 

Steps toward civilization. This civilization with which history deals has been a long time in the making. Man was first a savage, then a barbarian, and finally a civilized being. The savage is a child of nature. He secures food from plants and wild animals; he knows nothing of metals but makes his tools and weapons of stone, wood, and bone; he wears little or no clothing; and his home is merely a cave, a rock shelter, or a hut of bark. Such primitive folk may still be found in the interior of Africa and Australia. In contrast with the savage, the barbarian has gained some control over nature. Instead of depending upon hunting, he has learned to plant seeds, to tame animals, and to use some metal implements. Some early American Indians and most of the Negroes in Africa may be classified as barbarians. 

Thus the barbarian has taken some steps on the road that leads to civilization. The civilized man is characterized by the extensiveness of his control over his environment. 

What is civilization? We cannot place our finger upon the precise point at which the barbarian becomes a civilized

Early Man 

5 man. The advance from barbarism into civilization is a gradual process. Civilized men know how to control many aspects of their environment. They have learned how to divide their tasks, transport goods, build cities, and organize states. They have perfected a language which enables them to think better than the barbarian. Perhaps the most distinguishing characteristic of civilized man is his ability to write. 

In order to have a civilization, a social group must have developed along many lines. Thus we call the Egyptians and Babylonians civilized when we find them, six thousand years ago, cultivating the soil, laying out roads and canals, working mines, building cities, organizing stable governments, and keeping written records. 

2. EARLY MAN 

The Ice Age. The story of man is bound up with the story of his home, the earth; the development of human culture has been deeply affected by geography and climate. The first traces of man in Europe are associated with a geological period known as the Glacial or Ice Age. Estimates as to when this period began vary considerably, one estimate placing its beginning about 500,000 years ago. During the Ice 

Age an immense ice field formed in the lands encircling the North Pole and gradually moved southward. An icy mass hundreds of feet in thickness covered North America to the valleys of the Ohio and the Missouri, much of northern Asia, Russia, and western Europe to the valleys of the Rhine and Thames. Great glaciers also arose in the Alps, Pyrenees, and 

Caucasus, and descended from these mountains into the plains. Modern Greenland, which is similarly buried in ice, except at the edges, doubtless affords a good picture of what much of the northern hemisphere looked like in glacial times. 

The Ice Age was not, however, one period of uninterrupted cold. There seem to have been advances and retreats of the ice, resulting in three interglacial periods and a final period called postglacial.

The Prehistoric Age 

Europe in the Ice Age. The geography of Europe in the 

Ice Age was unlike what it is today. Considerable areas now beneath the Atlantic Ocean were then dry land. Great 

Britain and Ireland formed part of the Continent, and no 

North Sea separated them from Scandinavia. The Mediterranean basin contained two inland seas. Europe was united RCTIC

Neanderthal man. The first traces of man in Europe are associated with the Ice Age. During the last seventy-five

Early Man 

7 years a number of human fossils, including both skulls and skeletons, have been found in caves and rock shelters, especially in England, France, Belgium, and western Germany. 

Such fossils are believed to indicate the former existence in this part of the world of two different human types. One is called Neanderthal man, the name being derived from the German valley where human relics were discovered as far back as 

1856. About thirty other examples of this type are known.

In appearance Neanderthal man was quite unlike modern man, being only about five feet, three inches in height, thick- 

a. SKULL OF NEANDERTHAL TYPE b. SKULL OF THE CRO-MAGNON TYPE 

set, with heavy jaws, a receding chin, low, retreating forehead, and pronounced eyebrow ridges. He lived during the fourth or last glacial stage, along with the cave bear, cave lion, cave hyæna, and other animals now extinct.

Crô-Magnon man. Thousands of years passed before there appeared in Europe another human type, called Crô-Magnon, from the name of a French cave where five skeletons were unearthed in 1868. Crô-Magnon man, as we know from these and other examples, was tall, with a broad face, a prominent nose, slightly developed eyebrow ridges, welldeveloped chin, and a large brain. His physical and mental development places him close to modern man, though he lived during early postglacial times, when the woolly mammoth, woolly rhinoceros, bison, reindeer, and wild steppe horses still ranged throughout western Europe.

3. THE OLD STONE AGE 

Condition of early man. It is not easy to visualize the condition of the earliest men. They were savages, but more lowly than any now found on the earth. They were naked, fireless, homeless, without tools and weapons, and without any equipment which the other wild animals did not have. 

In fact, the animals had claws and immense teeth, whereas man had only his hands and his brain. In time his superior brain enabled him to triumph over, not only the other animals, but also nature itself to a considerable degree. 

Slowly he began to make discoveries, to invent, and to improve upon his condition, thus taking the first steps in human progress. 

Implements. Man's earliest tools and weapons were those which nature furnished. A branch from a tree served as a spear; a thick stick in his strong arms became a club; while stones picked up at haphazard were thrown as missiles or used as pounders to crack nuts and crush big bones.

Eventually, man discovered that a shaped implement was far more serviceable than an unshaped one, and so he began chipping flints into rude hatchets, knives, spearheads, borers, and the like. Such objects are called palæoliths (old stones), and the period when they were produced is therefore known as the Paleolithic, or Old Stone Age. It seems to have begun in the third interglacial stage and lasted for thousands upon thousands of years. 

Improvement of implements. Great skill is required to chip a flint until it takes a symmetrical form. Practice makes perfect, however, and the Palæolithic Age made noteworthy improvement in manufacturing, not only stone implements, but also those of bone, mammoth ivory, and reindeer horn.

The Prehistoric Age 

Many different kinds of implements, adapted to special uses, were gradually produced. In addition to those already mentioned, we find awls, wedges, saws, drills, chisels, barbed harpoons, and even so neat a device as a spear-thrower. 

Bone and wooden handles were also devised, thus adding immensely to the effectiveness of tools and weapons. 1 2 

PREHISTORIC STONE IMPLEMENTS 

1. Eolith (dawn stone"), a small rough stone, one part shaped as if to be held in the hand, and the other part edged or pointed for cutting. Some eoliths may be natural productions, but others seem to be of human workmanship. 

2. Palæolithic fist hatchet," so called because it was grasped in the hand by the narrow part and was used without a handle. 

3. Neolithic ax head, finely chipped and polished. 

Fire-making. Palæolithic man learned fire-making. Just how, we cannot say. Probably he struck a piece of iron ore with a flint and then allowed the sparks to fall into a bed of dry leaves or moss. Some savages still do this, though more often they produce fire by rubbing two pieces of wood together. The discovery of fire made it possible for man to cook food instead of eating it raw, to smoke meats and thus preserve them indefinitely, to protect himself at night against animal enemies, and to make his cave home more comfortable. Later, the use of fire enabled him to bake clay into pottery and to smelt metals (p. 17), but these inventions were not made in Palæolithic times.

The Old Stone Age 

11 Habitations. The men of the Old Stone Age doubtless passed much of their time in the open, following the game from place to place, and, when night came on, camping out under the stars, or taking shelter under rock ledges and in caves, as some savages do today. Limestone caverns, often very deep and roomy, are especially numerous in western Europe, where they seem to have been occupied by successive generations for many centuries. Huge accumula-

DEPOSITS IN A SWISS CAVE 

The cave of Drachenloch, near Ragatz, Switzerland, contains four layers of relic-bearing deposits. The layers are numbered II, III, IV, and V in the drawing. At A were hearths with charcoal; at B an assemblage of flat stones; and at C an altar on which the skulls of cave bears were piled. Stone and bone implements found in the cave testify to its occupancy by man at a remote epoch, tens of thousands of years ago. tions of ashes and charcoal, stone implements, bones of animals, and sometimes those of man himself frequently cover the floor of a Palæolithic cave to a depth of many feet. These objects are often found covered with deposits formed by lime-burdened water dropping from the roof. 

What was man's home has thus become a museum, only awaiting investigation by a trained student to reveal its story of the past.

Food supply. At the outset Palæolithic man lived on what

The Prehistoric Age nature supplied in the way of wild berries, nuts, roots, herbs, honey, the eggs of wild fowl, shellfish, and grubs,, and on the small animals which he could kill by throwing stones and sticks. As his implements improved and his skill increased, he became a fisher, trapper, and hunter of big game. 

He killed and ate the woolly mammoth, the European bison, the reindeer, and especially the steppe horse, which at one time roamed in great herds over western Europe. The pelts of the slain animals were made into covers and clothing, as we know from the discovery of flint skin scrapers and bone needles.

Art. Some of the Palæolithic men who lived in caves were talented artists. They decorated stone and bone implements with engravings, modeled figures in clay, made stone and ivory statuettes, and covered the walls of their caves with a variety of paintings in red, yellow, brown, and other vivid colors. The subjects are generally animals, though a few representations of the human form have also been found. 

The best Paleolithic pictures are remarkably lifelike, far surpassing the efforts of many modern savages. The men who made them were evidently close observers of animal life. 

PALEOLITHIC SCULPTURE 

A reindeer antler with two of its tines carved in the form of horses' heads, and a third head carved in relief. From the cavern of Mas d'Azil, France.

Religion. The cave dwellers apparently had a rude form of religion. Bodies buried in caves were sometimes surrounded by offerings of food, implements, and ornaments, which must have been intended for the use of the deceased. 

Such care for the dead probably indicates a belief in the soul and in its survival after death.

Age about which little or nothing can be learned with certainty. We can only surmise, from what is known of present-

4. THE NEW STONE AGE 

Entering the New Stone Age. We have seen that man in the Old Stone Age was making discoveries and inventions which bettered his lot and tended to raise him to a higher level of culture. Thus, he had discovered fire, was adding handles to his implements, was using stone scrapers, and was beginning to use the bow and arrow. These improvements did not alter over night his mode of living, but in time they did bring about fundamental and far-reaching changes. 

The appearance of these changes meant that man was entering a new culture epoch. When he invented the grindstone, he may be said to have entered the New Stone Age. 

The grindstone enabled him to improve the quality of his weapons. With a sharp-edged instrument he was enormously better off in his struggle with wild animals. 

Europe in Neolithic times. The New Stone or Neolithic 

Age began in Europe about eight thousand years ago. Europe in this period presented nearly the same outlines as today. Great Britain and Ireland were separated from the 

Continent by the shallow waters of the North Sea, English 

Channel, and Irish Sea. Owing to the sinking of the Mediterranean area, Spain and Italy were no longer joined to Africa by land bridges. The plants which flourished in colder 

Paleolithic times gave place to those characteristic of a temperate climate, and vast forests began to cover what had formerly been treeless steppes. The woolly rhinoceros, woolly mammoth, and cave bear became extinct; the musk sheep and reindeer retreated to Arctic latitudes, while the hippopotamus, elephant, and other big mammals found their way to tropical regions. Only a few of the animals associated

The New Stone Age 

15 with Palæolithic times survived into the Neolithic era; among these were the elk, wild boar, and European bison. 

Neolithic peoples. We do not yet know what became of 

Palæolithic men. They may have become extinct; they may have followed the retreating ice sheet and the retreating reindeer toward the northeast into Siberia and Arctic America; or they may have remained in their old locations and intermingled with the invading Neolithic peoples. These newcomers apparently came from western Asia and northern

Africa, and gradually spread over all Europe. The Neolithic balen rid впотом 

A SWISS LAKE DWELLING (RECONSTRUCTION) 

peoples belonged to the white race. Their blood flows in the veins of modern Europeans.

Neolithic remains. Our knowledge of the Neolithic Age comes, not from deep-lying or sealed-up deposits, such as those in Palæolithic caves, but from remains found on or near the surface of the soil or in rubbish heaps and burial places. 

Along the Baltic coast stretch huge mounds of bones and shells, marking the sites of former camping places. These "kitchen middens," which are merely refuse heaps, are sometimes a thousand feet long, two to three hundred feet wide, and ten feet high; covered with vegetation they look like

The Prehistoric Age natural mounds. Implements of stone, bone, and wood, together with pieces of pottery and other articles of human workmanship, are found in the "kitchen middens." Switzerland affords numerous remains of lake dwellers, who, for protection against their enemies, lived over the water in huts resting on sharpened piles driven into the bottom of the lake. The huts have disappeared, but the mud about the piles contains thousands of objects, including animal bones, seeds of various plants and fruits, implements, shreds of coarse cloth, fragments of pottery, household utensils, and bits of furniture. Neolithic men also erected many stone monuments, either single pillars or groups of pillars inclosing chambers and circles. Single pillars marked a grave, while groups of pillars usually served as sepulchers for the dead. They are rude memorials of far-off times and vanished peoples.

Further steps in human progress. Contrasted with the 

Palæolithic Age, the Neolithic covered only a brief space of time, but it was an age of rapid advance. Neolithic implements, though still of stone, bone, and wood, were greatly improved. The arrowheads (showing that the bow also had been invented) were finely polished, and now that the grindstone had been invented, stone axes could be sharpened. The men of the "kitchen middens" began to make pottery, chiefly for cooking vessels. They also domesticated the dog. The lake dwellers possessed cattle, goats, sheep, and swine, as well as dogs. They also plaited baskets, spun and wove textiles, prepared leather, built boats, used wheeled carts, and, most important of all, cultivated some of the cereals, including wheat, barley, and millet. The new sources of food available enabled Neolithic peoples to abandon the migratory life of hunters and to settle in permanent villages. Their community life must have been well organized, for the erection of lake dwellings and stone monuments required the cooperation of many individuals. In short, Neolithic peoples were not savages; they had passed from savagery to barbarism.

The Age of Metals 

17 Transition to the use of metals. The Neolithic Age was not confined to Europe. It also existed in western Asia, in 

Egypt, in North Africa, and on the islands of Cyprus and 

Crete. The entire basin of the Mediterranean formed a

Neolithic center. Here the transition to the use of metals first occurred. 

5. THE AGE OF METALS 

The metals. Civilization rests on the metals. Stone is not pliable; it is very apt to split in use; and it is ground and polished only with great difficulty. In time men began to seek substitutes for stone in the softer and more easily worked metals - gold, silver, tin, and copper. The widespread use of the softer metals marks the close of the Stone Age and the opening of the Age of Metals. The softer metals are often found in a pure state, not mixed with ore; they can thus be readily extracted and worked cold. The 

American Indians in this way got pure copper from mines near Lake Superior and made it into spearheads, knives, and hatchets, which were modeled after similar stone implements. Other barbarous peoples have likewise worked with the softer metals.

Copper. The Egyptians seem to have been the first people to extract metal from ore by means of heat, a process called smelting. Some of the most ancient graves in Egypt, dating from about 4000 B.C., contain needles and chisels made from smelted copper ore. The Egyptians at a very early period began to mine copper on the peninsula of Sinai. The Babylonians probably obtained copper from the same region. 

Another source of copper was the island of Cyprus, which is rich in that metal. Copper implements gradually spread into Europe, and with their use the Neolithic Age gave way to the Age of Metals. 

Bronze. Copper implements, although vastly superior to stone, were soft and would not keep an edge. Some ancient smith, more ingenious than his fellows, discovered that the

The Prehistoric Age addition of a small quantity of tin to the copper produced the much harder and tougher alloy called bronze. Where this simple but most important discovery took place, we cannot say. Bronze made its appearance in Egypt at least as early as 3000 B.C. and somewhat later in Cyprus, Crete, Asia 

Minor, and on the coasts of Greece. Traders subsequently carried the new alloy throughout the length and breadth of Europe.

Iron. The great durability and hardness of iron must have been noticed by metal workers at an early date. Contrasted with the copper and tin, however, iron is difficult both to mine and smelt; consequently its introduction occurred much later than that of bronze. The Egyptians seem to have made little use of iron before 1500 B.C. They called it the “metal of heaven," a phrase which may indicate that they obtained small quantities of it from meteorites. Although copper and bronze are mentioned forty-four times in the first five books of the Bible, iron is mentioned only thirteen times. The ancient Greeks considered it so valuable that a small lump of iron was one of the chief prizes at athletic games. Western and northern Europe became acquainted with iron only in the last thousand years before Christ. 

6. DAWN OF CIVILIZATION 

Centers of early civilization. Civilization, resting upon the metals, arose only a few thousand years ago in certain isolated areas. The areas in the Old World where civilization sprang up were Egypt, Babylonia (the Tigris-Euphrates valley), northern India, and central China. Those in the 

New World at a much later date were Mexico, Central America, and Peru. The areas mentioned had certain features in common. They were fertile regions, where food could be easily produced, wealth multiplied, and large populations supported by agriculture and trade. They were regions with a favorable climate, where excessive cold did not stunt body and mind or excessive heat sap human energies.

Dawn of Civilization 

19 Some of them were also well-protected regions, surrounded by mountains or deserts, so that access to them by ruder peoples was not easy. Their inhabitants, accordingly, enjoyed opportunities not found elsewhere to develop the arts of civilized life.

Spread of early civilization. Civilization has spread from its original centers until it now covers the greater part of the habitable globe. Uncivilized peoples, who once occupied all the world, have been exterminated or else have been pushed off to remote regions such as the interior of Australia, equatorial Africa, northern Siberia, tropical South America, and the islands of the Pacific. History, from the widest point of view, forms a record of the displacement of savagery and barbarism by civilization. 

The prehistoric age. You will notice that this chapter is entitled The Prehistoric Age. History is largely dependent upon written records for information about what people thought and said and did and as to when events occurred. 

Naturally, then, we cannot have anything like a full history until we reach the period when people could write and keep written records. This long period during which man could not write is called the prehistoric age. From bones, fossils, and other remains we have been able to obtain some idea of the prehistoric period. The account based upon such remains is called prehistory.

The historic age. The historic age in any country begins when the inhabitants keep written records from which it is possible to construct a fairly complete account of their life. 

The historic age, and with it history, therefore begins in different countries at different times. The annals of Egypt go back more than three thousand years before Christ, and those of Babylonia are almost as old. Trustworthy records in China and India do not date farther back than about 1000 B.C., while those of Greece and Rome, although numerous and extensive, do not begin much before the fifth or sixth century B.C. It was only after the opening of the Christian era that most parts of Europe entered the historic age.

The Prehistoric Age 

And it was not until the time of Columbus that the New World came into the light of history. 

Subdivisions of history. The whole historic age may be conveniently divided into three periods, Ancient, Medieval, and Modern. Ancient history begins with Oriental peoples, who were the first to develop the arts of civilization, deals next with the Greeks, and ends with the Romans, who built up an empire embracing much of the civilized world. Medieval history is chiefly concerned with the peoples of eastern and western Europe. It includes a period of about a thousand years from the break-up of the Roman Empire at the end of the fifth century to the discovery of America near the close of the fifteenth century. Modern history covers the last four hundred years and now embraces almost all mankind.

It is no longer a history of Asia or of Europe, but of the world.

CHAPTER II THE SPREAD OF PEOPLES AND CULTURE 

There are birds of many colors red, blue, green, yellow - yet all one bird. There are horses of many colors — brown, black, yellow, white yet all one horse. So, cattle; so all living things — animals, flowers, trees. So men: in this land where once were only Indians are now men of every color white, black, yellow, red - yet all one people.

HIAMOVI, CHIEF AMONG CHEYENNES 

Man is one; civilizations are many.

- A. A. GOLDENWEISER 7. RACES OF MAN 

The world's population. There are nearly two billion people on the earth. Asia has approximately 950 million inhabitants; Europe, 550 million; the Americas, 230 million; and Africa, 150 million. As every one knows, this huge population falls into more or less distinct groups having certain inherited traits of both body and mind. Such a group is a race.

The world's races. Racial distinctions are based on physical traits, especially skin color (black-brown, yellow-reddish, white), head form (narrow, broad, medium), and texture of the hair (woolly, straight, wavy or curly). There are three main races, which together account for at least ninetenths of the world's population. These three races are generally called Negroid, Mongoloid, and Caucasian; the color terms, black, yellow, and white, are also used as convenient, though less accurate, labels for them. Judging from pictures on old monuments, ancient skulls, and the earliest written descriptions that have come down to us, racial traits were as strongly marked five or six thousand years ago as they are now. 22

The Spread of Peoples and Culture 

Distribution of races. When history opens, each of the races occupied quite distinct geographical areas. The Negroid race held most of Africa south of the Sahara, southern

India, and Australia with its adjacent islands. The Mongoloid race occupied most of Asia, whence it spread over the Malay Archipelago, the islands of the Pacific, and the New World. The Caucasian race was limited to Europe, northern Africa, and southwestern Asia. The last four centuries have seen a wonderful expansion of Caucasian peoples, who now form the bulk of the inhabitants of North America, South America, Australia, New Zealand, and part of southern Africa.

Unity of man.

Modern science tends to stress resemblances, rather than differences, between races. The grand divisions of humanity are really blood relations, with a common, though remote, ancestry. Man is now recognized as essentially one in natural endowment. The physical traits separating the races may be numerous, but they do not seem to go deep. The same is true of mental traits. A close similarity certainly exists between the languages, religions, superstitions, arts, and sciences of all mankind. This similarity indicates, therefore, that the races are by nature about 1 The Malays, Polynesians, and American Indians are included among 

Mongoloid peoples.

Human Migrations 

25 equal in intelligence, in morality, and perhaps even in capacity for social progress. Such actual inferiority as may exist is explained as due to the influence of an unfavorable habitat (as in the case of African Negroes) or to isolation (as in the case of Polynesians and American Indians). 

8. HUMAN MIGRATIONS 

The human cradle-land. If man is essentially one, he cannot have had more than one place of origin. He must have had a single cradle-land from which he subsequently made his slow way over the globe. We may never discover its exact whereabouts, though almost certainly it was in the Old World, and possibly in Asia. The vast size, widely varying life conditions, and central position of Asia all suggest that this continent was the birthplace of humanity. Man's movements from a common home doubtless began even before the Ice Age and did not end until after that age had completely passed away.

Dispersal of mankind. Man's tendency to roam was the result of his constant quest for food, his desire for a more genial climate, his love of conquest and plunder, his restlessness, and sometimes the pressure exerted by foes about him. 

Such migratory movements have been possible because of man's ability to adapt himself to varied surroundings. No region is too hot or too cold, too high or too low for him, provided it offers the necessary subsistence, or can by his ingenuity be made to do so.

Prehistoric migrations. Man has been migrating for thousands of years. Human remains unearthed in Europe show that at least two types of people had entered that area during the Stone Age (pp. 7-9). Other parts of the world have also witnessed extensive migrations. The Polynesians, starting from the coast of southeastern Asia, passed from one Pacific island to another over an uncharted ocean. Our Indians probably entered America from Asia by way of Bering Strait and spread eastward and southward until they reached the

The Spread of Peoples and Culture extremity of South America. These and other migrations were made by early man while at a low cultural level, before he possessed metal tools, weapons, and other materials with which to overcome the obstacles offered by seas, deserts, rivers, and mountain ranges, as well as by the wild beasts that endangered his advance.

Historic migrations. History tells of repeated invasions, conquests, and displacements of one people by another. In 

Britain, Romans crowded upon Celts and both had to give way before Anglo-Saxons, Danes, and Normans. On the 

Continent the inroads of Germans and Slavs were followed by those of Huns, Arabs, Mongols, and Turks, who came from Asia during the Middle Ages. Still another example of extensive migration is offered by the Northmen, or Vikings, whose settlements dotted Iceland and southern Greenland. The colonization of America by millions of Europeans forms for us the most significant migratory movement in history.

Fusion of races and peoples. Migrations have necessarily led to contacts between races and peoples and often to racial fusion. Europe has for hundreds of years been a meeting place of peoples, with the result that Italy, France. 

England, and other countries are populated by fused peoples. 

In the United States a population originally English for the most part has received within the past century many millions of emigrants from Continental Europe; the American type thus promises to become a fusion of peoples unlike any one of the contributing races. Latin America, where neither custom nor law raises any barriers to the free intermingling of races, contains all sorts of hybrid stocks, formed by the mixture of Indians, Africans, and Europeans. Thus races are continually migrating and fusing. 

9. LANGUAGES OF MAN 

Race and language. The contact of races and peoples, whether resulting in fusion or not, does often result in the

Languages of Man 

27 substitution of one language for another. The Negroes in the United States now speak English, while those in Latin America speak either Spanish or Portuguese. Latin, carried by the Romans, displaced the earlier languages of Italy, Spain, and Gaul. In short, men may adopt a foreign language and pass it on to their children as they may adopt a foreign religion or custom. Race and language are therefore not synonymous terms.

Hamitic languages. The languages spoken by Caucasians belong, with some exceptions, to one of three families, the Hamitic, the Semitic, and the Indo-European. Least important historically is the Hamitic family, named after Ham, a son of Noah (Genesis, x, 1, 6). Ancient Egyptian was a

Hamitic language, and Hamitic languages are still found in northern and eastern Africa, some of them among peoples who have mixed with Negroes.

Semitic languages. The second family is that of the 

Semitic languages, so called from Shem, another son of Noah (Genesis, x, 1, 22). Semitic-speaking peoples in antiquity included Babylonians, Assyrians, Hebrews, Phoenicians, and Arabs. To these must be added the Abyssinians of eastern Africa. The Semites, as the map on page 23 shows, originally formed a fairly compact group, while today the Semitic-speaking Arabs occupy all of northern Africa, and the Hebrews (Jews) have spread all over the world. 

Indo-European languages. The third family is that of the 

Indo-European languages. This name indicates that they are found in both India and Europe. The peoples using 

Indo-European languages in antiquity formed a widely extended group, which reached from India across Asia and Europe to the British Isles and Scandinavia. Aryans in 

India, Medes and Persians on the plateau of Iran, Greeks and Italians, and the inhabitants of eastern and western Europe spoke related tongues. Their likeness is illustrated by the common words for relationship. Terms such as ‘father,” “mother," "brother," and "daughter" occur with only slight changes in form in nearly all the Indo-European 66

The Spread of Peoples and Culture languages. Thus "father" in Sanskrit (the old Aryan language of India) is pitar, in ancient Persian, pidar, in Greek, patér, in Latin, pater, and in German, Vater. There must have been at one time a single speech from which all the Indo-European languages have descended. They are spoken today by about a third of mankind. 

10. THE EVOLUTION OF WRITING 

Development of writing. Second in importance to language itself was the development of writing. We are so accustomed to both language and writing that we seldom recall that there was once a time when neither of them existed. Language undoubtedly developed first. After a long interval some efforts to record language were made. It is clear that all peoples did not go through the same stages in developing the art of writing, but some typical stages were (1) picture writing, (2) ideographs, and (3) sound writing by means of words, syllables, and letters. (1) Picture writing. Picture writing is the art of drawing pictures in order to convey a message or to record an event. 

The American Indians used picture writing even after the coming of the white man. For example, one Indian wrote a message to his friend. It consisted of a map showing a camp fire at the forks of a river and a number of dead buffaloes some distance beyond. This was his manner of saying that his party had camped at the forks of the river and had succeeded in finding and killing some buffaloes. Mere drawings, carvings, or paintings are not examples of true picture writing; for them to be true picture writing, they must have been made for the purpose of conveying a message. If the cave drawings of Palæolithic man were merely the result of his playful activity during idle hours, the drawings are not picture writing. If, however, they were made to keep a record of hunting expeditions or as messages to the gods, then they are examples of picture writing. True picture writing can be read by a resourceful and imaginative reader

The Evolution of Writing 

29 even though he does not know the language of the author of the pictures. He must, of course, be familiar with the objects depicted. Picture writing belongs essentially to the 

Stone Age. It was, however, as we shall see, an important step in the development of writing, for some pictures of common objects became the basis of the alphabet. (2) Ideographs. Picture writing cannot be used to describe feelings, thoughts, or ideas of a very complex nature. 

The attempt to convey ideas led to the use of pictures, not for the sake of the objects represented, but in order to suggest ideas that were somewhat related to the object. For example, the Chinese conveyed the idea of "bright" by drawing a picture containing the sun and moon. Note that this drawing was not picture writing, because there was no intention of telling something about the sun and moon; the drawing was intended to convey the idea of brightness, and hence was an ideograph. The Egyptians drew a rectangular line around the names of rulers; this inclosure came to signify the idea of "royalty." A wavy line might be used to represent the idea of a large body of water. A picture which conveys an idea instead of merely representing an object is called an ideograph. Ideographs were important in the development of writing because they enlarged the number and kind of messages that were possible. (3) Sound writing. Picture writing and ideographs convey ideas but they do not record the spoken language. A new stage in the development of writing was therefore reached when the picture represented not an actual object or idea, but a sound of the human voice. When men have learned how to represent sounds of the human voice they have discovered the art of recording the spoken language. For this purpose words, syllables, and letters have been employed. (a) Word writing. The most direct way of reducing spoken sounds to written form is to have a sign for each word. In word writing each picture or symbol stands for the sound of an entire word; hence there must be as many signs as there are words in the language. This is the case with

The Spread of Peoples and Culture 

Chinese writing. A dictionary of Chinese contains approximately twenty-five thousand words in good usage, every one represented by a separate written sign. No student ever learns them all, of course. It is enough for ordinary purposes to be familiar with about three thousand signs. 

The mastery of even this number is so laborious a process that reading and writing have never been popularized in China. (b) Syllable writing. A more developed form of sound writing occurs when the signs represent separate syllables instead of entire words. Every language contains words having the same sound but different meanings. For example, in our language, the sound i may be used to mean either "I" or "eye." Again, our word handsome has in it two syllables, each of which if used alone would be a separate word with a completely different meaning. Thus many words can be broken into parts or syllables, and other words when put together become syllables in a new word. A great step forward in the evolution of written language was taken when it was recognized that the thousands of words in the language represented only the recombination of a much smaller number of sounds. The Babylonians had signs for four or five hundred syllables. Syllable writing, though less cumbersome than word writing, still requires the use of a great number of signs, and the same word is not always written in the same signs. The final step in sound writing was the development of letters to form an alphabet. (c) The alphabet. People did not drop picture writing when they learned how to make ideographs; nor did they dispense with ideographs when they learned words and syllables. 

In fact, they kept on using all kinds of combinations. That is why the decipherment of ancient writing presents so many difficulties. The breaking up of words into single sounds led to the devising of letters. The picture used to represent some common word like "flower" might be used as the symbol of the sound "f" wherever it occurred. For example, the word alph meant ox. The picture of an ox then came to

The Evolution of Writing 

31 represent the sound made in pronouncing the first part of the word. The word bet meant house. The picture of a house came to represent the first sound made in pronouncing the word. Thus certain pictures came to stand for single sounds. Since the number of distinct sounds in any language is fairly limited, it is possible to represent them by means of twenty-two, twenty-six, or some small number of symbols, called letters. Other letters were derived in a similar manner as the a and b. When all the common sounds are thus represented, one can put them together in any kind of combination to produce any desired word. The alphabet was truly an epoch-making invention. The people who designed it deserve our lasting gratitude and respect.

CHARACTERS OF THE ALPHABET 

changed it. As early perhaps as the tenth century B.C., the Phoenicians of western Asia were in possession of an alphabet, whose rudiments they probably borrowed from Egypt, Babylonia, or Crete. At all events they adapted it to their own use and spread the knowledge of it all over western Asia. The fact that the Phoenicians carried the alphabet to various peoples caused historians at one time to

The Spread of Peoples and Culture ascribe its invention to them. We now think, however, that they improved and utilized rather than invented it. Their alphabet consisted of twenty-two letters, all consonants. 

When the Greeks received the alphabet, they added the letters which represent the vowels. The Greek form of the alphabet afterward spread to Italy, where the Romans received it, modified some of the letters, and then passed it on to the peoples of western Europe. From them it has reached us.¹

Methods of writing. Different materials for writing were utilized by the Egyptians and Babylonians. The Egyptians traced their hieroglyphic characters upon papyrus with a small brush dipped in ink. Papyrus was a reed which grew plentifully in the Nile marshes. The stem was split into thin strips which were pasted together, pressed, and dried, thus forming a sheet. From papyros, the Greek name of the plant, has come our word "paper." The Babylonians impressed their signs on tablets of soft clay with a sharp-edged instrument. As the edge sank into the clay the mark naturally became wider. These wedge-shaped characters are called cuneiform from the Latin word cuneus, which means wedge. 

The tablets were baked in an oven, a process that has preserved some of their writing. The use of clay as a writing material spread to Palestine, Crete, Assyria, and other regions. 

Written records. As long as all information had to be handed down by word of mouth from one generation to the next a genuine history was impossible. The method of oral transmission was unreliable and often led to false reports, like a piece of village gossip that has been retold many times. 

Written records enabled men widely separated in space and time to share a common knowledge and transmit it to future ages. An exact record was thus made possible, and each generation could profit by the experience of preceding generations.

11. COUNTING AND THE CALENDAR 

Importance of counting. The development of implements, of languages, and of systems of writing formed, as we have just seen, extremely important aspects of the growth of human culture. Another important aspect was the development of counting. Under this term we here include (1) methods of reckoning distances, capacity, weight, time, and objects, and (2) systems of noting or representing this reckoning by means of some kind of signs, such as figures. 

Figures, as well as other systems of notation, are really a kind of language, and methods of reckoning are really methods of thinking. Hence the importance of counting in the history of civilization. 8888 nnni 4434 = 20 Systems of notation. Counting began with calculations on the fingers. Finger counting explains the origin of the

of employing special marks for fives, tens, hundreds, and their multiples, leaving only the units to be indicated by single strokes. Examples are found among the Egyptians and Babylonians. This rather clumsy method has not yet disappeared, for the Roman numerals V, X, C, M, etc., are still in common use. The simpler "Arabic" numerals probably originated in India, where the Arabs found them and introduced them into Europe during the Middle Ages. 

Methods of reckoning. The art of reckoning has likewise a long development. Perhaps the first way was to reckon by means of small objects such as pebbles, beans, or shells.

Traders among the natives of Africa still use such rude

3 5 7 8 counters. The next step was to place them on a counting board, or abacus, which was divided into columns so that in one column the objects represented units, the next tens, and so on. The Roman boy solved his problems in arithmetic by means of the abacus. Chinese merchants are wonderfully expert in its use. The final step in the art of reckoning was to get rid of counters and write down the numbers in ruled columns. For

ROMAN ABACUS OR COUNTING BOARD 

empty columns the sign for "nothing," or zero, was invented. 

Measures of length. The simplest and probably the earliest measures of length were derived from various parts of the human body. Some of our Indian tribes employed the double arm's length, the single arm's length, the hand width, and the finger width. The Aztecs of Mexico used the pace or stride. Greek measures were based on the finger breadth, sixteen of which made the foot. The Romans counted one thousand paces or double steps to the mile. Old English standards, such as the span, the ell, and the hand, all go back to this method of measuring on the body. 

Measures of capacity and weight. Measures of capacity seem to have been first obtained from natural objects of uniform size. The Hebrews had the hen's egg as their unit; the modern Malays employ coconuts as measures; the Chinese use joints of bamboo. In nearly all systems of weight the smallest unit is some actual seed, such as the old English barleycorn, of which twenty-four made a pennyweight. The same natural unit was familiar to the Greeks and Romans. 

Some of our modern standards of weight and capacity can be traced back to those of antiquity; for instance, the pound and ounce, gallon and pint, come from Roman weights and measures.

Counting and the Calendar 

35 99 Calculation of time; the month. It is interesting to trace the beginnings of time reckoning and of that most important institution, the calendar. Some savage peoples distinguish the passage of time only by days and nights. The Eskimos, for example, count by so many "sleeps.' A longer cycle of time was found in the lunar month, the interval between two new moons (about twenty-nine days and twelve hours). 

Most primitive tribes reckon by "moons." The names for moon and month were once the same in nearly all the languages of European peoples, and our term "lunar month" means a period of time reckoned by the interval between two new moons (Latin luna = moon).

The year. Twelve lunar months constitute the lunar year of about three hundred and fifty-four days. In order to adjust the lunar year to the different seasons and make it coincide regularly with them, a thirteenth month was inserted from time to time. Such awkward calendars were used in antiquity by the Babylonians, Jews, and Greeks; in modern times by the Arabs and Chinese.¹ The Egyptians were the only people in the Old World to originate a solar year. It consisted of twelve months, each containing thirty days, with five extra days at the end of the year. This calendar was taken over by the Romans, who added the system of leap years. It has since been adopted by most civilized countries.

The week. The week seems to have arisen simply as a convenient division of the lunar month. The very common ten-day week was probably suggested by the three aspects of the moon in the waxing crescent, the more or less full disk, and the waning crescent. Ten-day periods were familiar to peoples so distant from one another as the Maoris (New Zealanders), the Incas (Peruvians), the Egyptians, and the Greeks. Weeks of eight days were used in antiquity by the Romans.

The seven-day week. The seven-day week arose from the 

1 The Chinese lunar calendar was abandoned for the solar calendar in 

1912 A.D.

The Spread of Peoples and Culture recognition of the four phases of the changing moon - new moon, first quarter, full moon, and last quarter. The Babylonians divided their months into seven-day cycles, the last of which contained more than seven days, since there are more than twenty-eight days in a lunar month. As far as we know the Hebrews were the first to use a seven-day week which does not follow the moon's phases, but runs without interruption through the months and years. The week of seven days named after the sun, moon, and five planets (Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn) was familiar to the Romans as early as the first century A.D. It has since spread to every civilized land, although in our language four of the days are named after Norse instead of Roman deities. It is easy to see which days are named in honor of the sun, moon, and Saturn; the others are named after 

Tiw (who corresponds to Mars), Woden (Mercury), Thor (Jupiter), and Frigg (Venus). 

12. MAN AND CULTURE 

Culture. The historian deals primarily with civilized peoples, in certain definite regions, and during the comparatively brief period that has elapsed since written records began. 

Nevertheless one who is writing a history of mankind must often widen his viewpoint to include uncivilized or partially civilized peoples. They, too, have made some advance in knowledge, arts, morals, and religion, as did Palæolithic and Neolithic men. Even savages and barbarians possess some culture, which is a broader term than civilization and includes all that man has accomplished as distinguished from what nature supplied. Culture consists of material things, such as houses, roads, automobiles, pianos, and books; of institutions, such as laws, etiquette, governments, churches, and fraternities; of ideas, such as democracy, immortality, and truth.

Cultural inheritance. The culture of a particular people may be said to arise and grow from three sources: inherit-

Man and Culture 

37 ance, acculturation, and invention. Each generation inherits the accomplishments of previous generations and adds to them its own. This cultural inheritance consists of a great number of things — language, writing, art, material goods, ideas, institutions, customs, manners, etc. In a glorious sense we are the heirs of all the ages. 

Acculturation. No social group is so isolated that it obtains nothing from the outside. Even a savage tribe may secure such prized commodities as iron, salt, or tobacco by gift, barter, or plunder. Visitors, captives, slaves, and women brought in as wives may introduce new cultural elements. 

Two migrating tribes may settle in the same district, or one tribe may be overrun by another; in either case, there will be cultural interchanges between the two tribes. The trade, travel, and communication of civilized peoples constantly bring about cultural interchange. This process of receiving ideas and customs from other groups is called acculturation. 

Invention. As distinguished from acculturation, invention is the term applied to all improvements in culture which are made by members of the group itself. The invention may be an improved manner of fighting, of planting grain, of governing, of making clothes, or of performing any other activity; in each instance it is a growth of culture. 

The spread of culture. Man has constantly improved his culture. The history of civilization is the story of this developing culture as it grew and spread from land to land. 

Thus our American culture came mainly from the British Isles; British culture came from that of the Continent; 

European culture from that of Rome; Roman culture from that of Greece; and Greek culture from that of the Near 

East, particularly Egypt, Babylonia, and Palestine. The trail then becomes more and more obscure, taking us back to the prehistoric era, where at length we lose it in the mists of the remote past. Similarly, it may be shown that in the 

Far East the countries of China and India have been the great cultural mothers, at whose hearth many Oriental peoples have lighted their own fires. Our study of ancient,

The Spread of Peoples and Culture medieval, and modern history will teach us how true it is that the roots of the present lie deep in the past. race migration Semitic

Unit II THE DAWN OF CIVILIZATION 

How man in some favored regions remade his environment and achieved a civilization 

(CHAPTERS III-IV)

PRESENTATION 

Before the beginning of written records man built a culture but did not achieve a civilization. He adjusted himself to his natural environment, but he did little toward remaking that environment. 

In the East, or Orient, between five and six thousand years ago, man succeeded in doing more than merely adjusting himself to his environment. He succeeded to a considerable extent in remaking his environment by constructing houses, developing inventions, and regulating moisture by means of irrigation. Furthermore, he made written records of his achievements. This tremendous step, by which man passed on to succeeding generations not only his material achievements, but also his intellectual achievements, marks the coming of civilization.

Chapter III tells some of the interesting and important things that we have learned about early peoples and civilizations in the Far Eastern lands of China and India - their government, society, industry, literature, and religion. 

Chapter IV tells how, in the Near Eastern lands, cities arose in the Nile and Tigris-Euphrates valleys, how the cities were combined into kingdoms and the kingdoms into empires- Egyptian, Babylonian, Assyrian — and how at length nearly all the countries of the Near East were brought together in the great Persian realm. The literature, art, religion, industry, and government of these various peoples are also described.

Unit II, in short, tells how man in some favored regions remade his environment and achieved civilization.

CHAPTER III THE FAR EAST IN ANCIENT TIMES 

The higher type of man is universal in his sympathy and free from party bias; the lower type of man is biased and unsympathetic. CONFUCIUS

Victory breeds hatred, for the conquered is ill at ease. 

The tranquil live well at ease, careless of victory and defeat. 

13. LANDS AND PEOPLES OF THE EAST BUDDHA 

The continent of the East. By "the East" we mean the great continent of Asia, which includes such lands as Japan, China, India, Persia, Arabia, and Siberia. Asia comprises almost one-third of the land surface of the globe. On the north, east, and south, the boundaries of Asia are easily traced (see map). On the west and northwest, it is separated from Europe by the Mediterranean Sea, the Black Sea, the Caucasus Mountains, and the Caspian Sea. A few hundred miles to the northeast of the Caspian begin the broad, low Ural Mountains, which stretch away toward the Arctic Ocean and complete the western boundary of Asia. The wide and rugged Caucasus Mountains have been very important as a barrier to migrations. On the other hand, the 

Urals offer few obstacles to movements over them. In the gap between the Caspian and the Urals, the Asiatic steppe merges insensibly into the European plain. Europe has thus always been open to the nomadic tribes of central and northern Asia.

Climatic conditions in Asia. Asia reaches from near the equator to a point halfway between the Arctic Circle and the North Pole. It has therefore some of the hottest regions in 43

The Far East in Ancient Times 

. the world as well as some of the coldest. Every one is familiar with the fact that temperature varies with altitude, and the climate of Asia is profoundly affected by its changing altitude, which ranges from below sea level in the Caspian basin to nearly thirty thousand feet (more than five miles) above sea level on lofty Mount Everest. The mountains of central Asia are so high that moisture-laden clouds cannot cross them, with the result that much of the interior of the continent has little rainfall.

Asia contrasted with Europe. The coast line of Asia is comparatively uniform and unindented, offering fewer opportunities for sea-borne traffic than the deeply indented shores of Europe. The mighty mountains of Asia present barriers to intercourse such as are not afforded by the lower ranges of Europe. Extensive deserts and barren table-lands, which form so characteristic a feature of Asia, are unknown in 

Europe. Asia, in proportion to its size, is not so well supplied as Europe with navigable streams. The climate of Asia is far less mild and equable than that of Europe. The two land masses thus present striking contrasts in their physical features.

Population of Asia. Asia contains about half of the world's population. Yet most of the continent is sparsely settled, for the mountain slopes, the steppes, the deserts, the forests, and the tundras support few inhabitants. The people who do live in these sparsely settled regions subsist chiefly by hunting and herding. The bulk of the population, however, is found in southern and southeastern Asia, where agriculture, not hunting and herding, forms the principal means of livelihood. 

Asiatic races.

All the races of man are found in Asia. 

The Negroid race is represented by the dwarf blacks found in the Malay Peninsula. The Dravidians of southern India also form a large group with Negroid characteristics. 

Members of the Caucasian or white race have occupied northern India, the greater part of western Asia, and Egypt since historic times began. By far the greater number of the

The Far East. We have noticed that most of the population of Asia is centered in the southern and eastern parts of the continent. These populous areas of southern and eastern 

Asia are collectively known as the Far East. In most instances the term is used to include India, China, Japan, and closely adjacent islands.
