CHINESE EMPIRE UNDER THE T'ANG DYNASTY 

China, under the T'ang dynasty (618-907 A.D.), was the largest and most powerful state in the world. The frontiers of the empire reached as far as Persia and the Caspian Sea on the west, and to the Himalaya Mountains and Burma on the south. 

All these together 

China in this sense as well as the populous eastern provinces. contain over four million square miles. is larger than the United States, or Canada, or Brazil. The central eastern provinces embrace only about one-third of

China the total area, but they contain more than nine-tenths of the population and have always formed the real, historic China. 

They are China, properly so called.

Chinese civilization. The annals of China, according to native authorities, began nearly five thousand years ago, but we do not reach firm historical ground until about 1000 B.C. The Chinese have therefore a civilization older than the civilizations of India, Persia, Greece, or Rome, and surpassed in age only by those of Egypt and Babylonia. Their civilization has lasted with little change from the dawn of TIFE ATIBO 

THE GREAT WALL OF CHINA 

The wall was begun in 214 B.C. to protect the northern frontier of China from the inroads of Tatar tribes, and was gradually extended until it reached a length of 1500 miles. It starts from the seashore where the Manchurian and Chinese frontiers meet east of Peking (see map), and extends westward 1500 miles. It consists of two ramparts of brick, resting upon granite foundations. The space within is filled with stones and earth. The breadth of the wall is about 25 feet; its height is between 20 and 30 feet. Watch towers, 40 feet high, occur every 200 yards. In places of strategic importance there are sometimes as many as five huge loops, with miles of country between, so that if one loop were captured the next might still be defended. Many parts of this colossal fortification are even now in good repair. history to the present. Chinese civilization owes little to outside influence, for the Far East lacked that intimate contact between different cultural groups so characteristic of the Near East and Europe. On the other hand Chinese civilization has exerted wide influence upon surrounding

The Far East in Ancient Times areas. The once barbarous inhabitants of Korea, Indo- 

China, and Japan copied the arts and literature, and even to some extent the religion and government of China, while many ruder peoples of central and eastern Asia received from China whatever measure of civilized life they now enjoy. 

Isolation of China. The isolation of Chinese civilization finds at least a partial explanation in geography. On the east China faces the Pacific, a sea which was once a barrier to intercourse, instead of being, as now, a highway of commerce. 

On the southwest, west, and northwest China is separated from the rest of continental Asia by lofty mountain ranges, whose mountain passes were in former days made dangerous for trade and travel by the warlike tribes infesting them. 

The mountains bounding China are buttressed by vast plateaus either semi-arid or completely desert, and arduous even for caravan traffic. The Chinese added to these natural barriers the Great Wall (see note under illustration). 

The Chinese people. The Chinese belong to the Mongoloid or yellow race. They possess the distinctive physical traits of that race: a short stature, a broad head, prominent cheek bones, straight, black hair, and a complexion varying from pale yellow to dark brown. They are also characterized by the so-called Mongolian or "almond" eye.

The pure Mongoloid type, however, has been somewhat modified in China, because for centuries Tibetans, Burmese, Manchus, and other peoples have mingled with the original Chinese. China is the most populous country in the world; its population probably exceeds 400,000,000. 

15. CHINESE SOCIETY AND CULTURE 

The family. In China the family is a peculiarly important institution. It includes not only the father, mother, and children, but also grandparents, grandchildren, uncles, aunts, cousins, and even more distant blood relatives. The sons marry early, usually at about the age of eighteen; they bring their wives into the paternal home and stay there

Chinese Society and Culture 

49 even after they have children of their own. Thus the family expands, until sometimes an entire village is only an enlarged household, or clan. Both the father and the mother receive great deference and respect from their children during life; after death the parents receive ancestral worship. 

Ancestor worship. The worship of ancestors in China must have arisen in prehistoric times, judging from the references to it in the most ancient Chinese literature. An ancestral soul, it is believed, resides particularly in a tablet kept in the family hall or living room. Offerings of food and drink are laid before the tablet from time to time. 

Every spring sacrifices are made at the tombs of the ancestors. The dead, when thus honored and conciliated, are believed to bestow blessings upon descendants, but the religious books declare that a good son ought to sacrifice to his parents without seeking anything from them in return. 

Social classes. The traditional Chinese social system rested upon four classes; namely, scholars, farmers, mechanics, and traders. Practically, however, there were only two classes officials and non-officials. There was no hereditary nobility, except in the case of a few families whose ancestors had greatly served the state, and even they had no special privileges.

Government. The government of China in ancient times, and, indeed, until a few years ago, was a monarchy, in which the emperor had almost unlimited power. His decree was announced as the law of the land. Officials held their positions at his pleasure, and no council, cabinet, or parliament interfered with his power. But the emperor was not supposed to rule for personal gratification. Should he prove to be a tyrant, rebellion against him would be justified. 

Chinese history mentions several occasions when a bad emperor was compelled to resign. Government in China thus rested on a moral basis; there were social obligations and responsibilities which even the emperor could not evade. 

Agriculture. The great majority of Chinese are peasants.

Their holdings are very small, for custom requires that all

The Far East in Ancient Times sons shall inherit substantially equal shares of the father's estate. Consequently there is a process of continual division and subdivision of lands and property. With three acres a family is well off; with ten acres it is wealthy. The Chinese are successful farmers. They have long been familiar with intensive cultivation, scientific fertilizing, and rotation of crops. Irrigation is generally practiced, and extensive dikes are built to drain low-lying lands. In the more thickly populated districts terraces have been constructed on the sides and even to the summits of mountains, which are thus made to yield food for man. All this work goes on with incredible patience and an immense expenditure of human effort. 

Manufactures. The principal manufactures of China are porcelain, silk, and cotton goods. The greater part of the spun silk is used in China, but much raw silk is exported. 

The spinning and weaving of cotton are carried on almost universally. India ink, fans, furniture, lacquer ware, matting, dyes, and varnished tiles are manufactured in various places, while paper, bricks, and earthenware are made in nearly all the provinces. 

Inventions. The Chinese have long been devoted to mechanics and engineering. Examples of this type of industry are their remarkable arched bridges and gateways, their waterwheels and other appliances for irrigation, and the Great Wall and the Grand Canal from Hangchow in the south to Tientsin in the north, a distance of about six hundred and fifty miles. The invention of the mariner's compass has often been attributed to them, but more probably it was introduced into China by the Arabs. The Chinese knew of gunpowder, or an explosive resembling it, in the seventh century A.D. As early as the tenth century A.D. they printed books by taking impressions on paper from wooden blocks. They used coal and gas for heating hundreds of years before Europeans. Wall paper, another Chinese invention, was introduced into Europe by Dutch traders, under the name of "pagoda paper."

Fine arts. The practical character of the Chinese does not

Chinese Society and Culture 

51 prevent their having a genuine appreciation of the beautiful. 

They have excelled in water colors and ink sketches. The 

Chinese painter represents chiefly natural scenes, for human personality does not appeal to him as a subject for his brush. 

In sculpture, however, the Chinese have not excelled, except in bronze. 

Neither have they excelled in architecture.

The main feature of a 

Chinese building is the massive roof, sometimes in double and triple form, decorated with the figures of dragons and other fantastic animals, and often covered ou gouls int und all with brilliant glazed und tiles. Characteristici 

Chinese structures are easy memorial archways, talle pagodas, and graceful p bridges. Literature.

Chinese literature has an unbroken development from distant antiquity down to the present.

Histories, biographies, geographies, and philosophical treatises, to 

A CHINESE PAGODA 

gether with essays, dramas, novels, and poetry, are all represented. The most important literature is contained in the so-called "Classics," which are ancient works edited or compiled by the great teacher Confucius, together with his own productions and those of his disciples. 

Religious beliefs. The mass of Chinese believe that evil

The Far East in Ancient Times spirits populate the country as densely as its human inhabitants and cause accidents, eclipses, earthquakes, disease, and insanity. Some ancient Chinese seem to have believed in one god. He was not regarded as the creator of the universe or of man, but as a personal Supreme Ruler, who rewarded the good and punished the wicked. To this deity every one, from emperor to peasant, offered worship. 

Other gods, such as sun, moon, stars, and earth, were in time recognized, but they were thought of as ministers to the Supreme Ruler. Such ideas persist to the present day among the educated classes of China.

Confucius, 551-478 B.C. The great Chinese sage was Kong- 

Foo-Tze, who was born in what is now the province of Shantung. His name has become familiar to Westerners in its 

Latinized form, Confucius. 

His family, though old and distinguished, lived in straitened circumstances, and Confucius passed his early years in poverty. Nevertheless, he acquired a good education and at the age of twenty-two set up as a public teacher. Pupils resorted to him in increasing numbers, and his reputation grew rapidly. It was during this earlier period of his life that he collected and edited the Chinese "Classics," with which his name has ever since been associated. His later years were taken up with public services, travels in various parts of China, and literary pursuits. Never fully appreciated in life, Confucius became, after death, the center of religious worship. Temples were erected to him in all the CONFUCIUS

A stone carving in the temple of Confucius at K'iu Fu.

Chinese Society and Culture 

53 principal cities, and some people even regarded him as a god.

Confucianism. Confucianism forms a system of morality, not a religion. It emphasizes, particularly, the virtues of filial piety, devotion to ancestors, benevolence toward relatives, propriety of conduct, and reverence for learning. Its noblest expression is the negative form of the Golden Rule: "What you do not want done to yourself do not do to others."

The teachings of Confucius only reflected views current in China for ages before him. This is perhaps the reason why 

Confucianism has not lost its hold upon the popular mind. 

Cultivated Chinese still quote the classical books, and the uneducated masses still repeat the maxims which sum up the worldly wisdom of the philosopher. Confucianism thus continues to inspire the moral code of an entire people. 

Lao Tze and Taoism. Little is known of an older contemporary of Confucius, the famous Lao Tze. He was a highly speculative thinker, who saw in nature the manifestation of a spiritual power. He denounced horse-racing, hunting, and the mad scramble for wealth, and taught that man comes into harmony with the spiritual power by selfeffacement and by the suppression of desire. Doctrines so obscure and mystical could never be understood by the multitude; consequently Taoism, as the teachings of Lao Tze were called, degenerated as it spread among the people. 

Beginning as a system of philosophy, it became a religion with many gods, among whom Lao Tze himself had a prominent place. It accumulated countless saints and protecting spirits with their respective temples, monasteries, priests, and forms of worship. Various superstitions also found a place in popular Taoism.

Chinese Buddhism. Many Chinese became Buddhists (p. 58) as early as the third century B.C. Buddhism long found a bitter opponent in Taoism, but eventually these rival faiths managed to exist peaceably together. Each has borrowed so much from the other that now only an expert can distinguish them. The same persons, in fact,

The Far East in Ancient Times may be followers of Buddha and Lao Tze, as well as of Confucius.

Survival of Chinese civilization. Chinese civilization, as we have seen in the foregoing pages, has an unbroken development through many centuries. Since about the middle of the nineteenth century, however, this vast and populous country, with its ancient society, has witnessed wars, insurrections, revolutions, and invasions. Some of these events will appear as we progress in our story of civilization. They will have an added interest when placed against the background sketched in this chapter. 

16. INDIA 

Position, size, and shape. Compared with the rest of Asia,

India looks small, but actually it is larger than Europe minus Russia. The map of Asia (p. 45) shows India as the middle of three great peninsulas which reach southward from the mainland. India has the form of a triangle with the base resting upon the Himalaya Mountains and the apex projecting far into the Indian Ocean. Its long coast line, however, is so regular that it contains few good harbors. 

Geography and history in India. India is almost surrounded by natural boundaries. In addition to the water boundaries of the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal, it has a land boundary to the north in the stupendous range of the Himalayas. At the eastern and western ends this range sends out offshoots which reach the sea. These offshoots contain passes and open tracts; thus, in spite of the mighty wall of the 

Himalayas, India has been accessible on both its northwestern and northeastern frontiers. And, in fact, all the historic land invasions of India have followed the routes from Persia or central Asia, while in prehistoric times large bodies of immigrants entered India from China. The richest and most densely populated provinces of India are contained in the broad and fertile valleys of her two large rivers, the Indus and the Ganges. South of the Himalayas and the Ganges is

India a large plateau called the Deccan. It is, in general, a broken, rocky region, favorable to the creation of small, independent states. This part of India never came completely under one government until the British conquest. 

Racial types. According to the 1931 census India had a population of over 351,000,000. Among this enormous population several racial types are distinguishable, the two most important being the Dravidians, who occupy the region from Ceylon to the Ganges, and the Indo-Aryans (Hindus), who live in the northern and western parts of the peninsula. The 

Dravidians have doubtless descended from the early inhabitants, while the Hindus have descended from the ancient 

Aryan invaders.

The Aryan invasion. The history of India opens with the coming of the Aryans, from the plateau of Iran, in what is now Persia. They spoke Sanskrit, a language belonging to the Indo-European group (p. 24). They were a hardy, vigorous people, familiar with agriculture, though more given to pastoral pursuits. They had chiefs but no kings, priesthood, or caste system. The Aryans began to enter India from the northwest shortly after 2000 B.C. They occupied the valley of the Indus, and then spread eastward into the plain of the Ganges. There they mingled more or less with the dark-skinned Dravidians, whose land they seized and whom they reduced to slaves and serfs. The caste system arose, the village community developed, and petty tribal chiefs gave way to powerful monarchs. India slowly became an Aryan country.

India and the West. The Aryan invasion was the first of several contacts between India and the West. About the end of the sixth century B.C. Darius the Great, king of 

Persia, annexed the Indus region to his dominions. For nearly two hundred years it was a rich, active, and populous province of the Persian Empire. When Alexander the 

Great conquered Persia he annexed the Indus region to his newly formed empire. The year of Alexander's invasion, 326 B.C., is the first exact date in the history of India. From

The Far East in Ancient Times this time the peninsula began to emerge from obscurity. 

The successors of Alexander exercised some authority in northern India and their courts were centers from which the Greeks influenced Indian art, especially sculpture, and Indian science, especially astronomy. Considerable commerce was carried on between India and the West, both by land routes through central Asia and by water routes leading across the Arabian Sea and up the Persian Gulf and the Red 

Sea (see map, p. 45). Such luxuries as precious stones, ivory, spices, and fine cotton stuffs were thus introduced among Western peoples. India always remained, however, outside the world familiar to the ancient Greeks and Romans. 

17. INDIAN SOCIETY AND CULTURE 

The village community. Today seven-tenths of India's population live by agriculture. The village communities, in which most of them live, consist of landowners or tenants; landless men, working for wages; artisans, such as potters, blacksmiths, carpenters, and cobblers, who receive for their labor a certain share of the harvest; and various public officials. This organization of rural life in economically independent villages closely resembles the manorial life of medieval Europe. Because of the introduction of railways, roads, and other modern improvements, however, the system is beginning to pass away. The village community and the caste system together explain much of the uniformity and conservatism of Indian society. 

Caste. The caste system in India is unique, nothing of the kind being known in any other country. It is a system of dividing people into rigid groups according to color and social standing. The usual Indian names for the castes are varna (color) and jati (birth or descent). There are several thousand castes, the highest of which consists of Brahmans, or priests. The number is constantly growing because old castes are divided and new ones arise. All of them are closely connected with the native religion, and no

Indian Society and Culture 

57 Mohammedan and, of course, no Christian may belong to them.

Rules of caste. One who belongs to a caste must not marry outside it; must not do work of any kind unsanctioned by it; and must not eat or drink with a person of a lower caste, or, as is often the case, with any person of another caste. He must observe the ceremonies customary among his caste fellows in connection with birth, marriage, and death; must abstain from food regarded as impure; must avoid acts considered improper, such as marrying a widow; and finally he must not render services to men of low caste. 

When a member of an upper caste has suffered contact or even proximity with one of a lower caste, he must purify himself as from some evil influence. The person who breaks any of these rules loses caste and becomes an outcast. 

Influence of caste. The caste system, by dividing the people of India into innumerable small groups, tends to prevent the development of any true national feeling among them. It also tends to prevent economic development by restricting each person's wants, occupation, and activities. 

To a Westerner the system seems utterly undemocratic and in every way opposed to the brotherhood of man. The conservative Indian, however, defends the caste, on the grounds that it gives to every man, no matter how humble, a recognized place in society. Were caste to disappear, with it would disappear the strongest force in India working to maintain the traditional moral and social code. 

Hinduism. The native religion of India is called Hinduism. Our earliest knowledge of it comes from some sacred books which were composed after 1000 B.C. These books are called the Vedas and contain hymns, descriptions of forms of worship, charms and spells against evil, and, in fact, the accumulated wisdom of the ancient Hindus. The earliest 

Hindu gods seem to have been personifications of the forces of nature; thus there was a god of the storm, a god of fire, and the earth was called "Mother" Earth. The householder honored these gods through hymns, prayers, offerings, and

The Far East in Ancient Times animal sacrifices. In time arose a special class of religious poets and priests the Brahmans. Under their influence 

HINDU CONCEPTION OF THE EARTH 

The earth as represented by a Brahman. The abode of men is situated between that of the gods above and the infernal regions below. The whole is supported by four elephants on the back of a tortoise, The great the symbol of force and creative power. serpent, shown at the bottom, is the emblem of eternity. the old nature deities declined in importance and other gods made their appearance, the most important being

Brahma (the All- 

Father), Vishnu (the Preserver), and Siva (the 

Destroyer), together with a number of other gods and spirits. Other aspects of Hinduism include a belief in the transmigration of souls (that is, the survival of the same soul in the lives of successive persons or animals), an increase in the number of idols and temples, and the reverence paid to various animals, such as monkeys, serpents, and oxen. The Hindu religion varies from primitive superstition to the most elevated philosophical doctrines from which Westerners have much to learn. 

Gautama Buddha, c560-c477 B.C.¹ During the fifth century B.C. a new religion, Buddhism, arose in India. Its founder, Gautama, was born in the province of Nepal, which lies at the base of the Himalayas. At the age of twenty-nine, he abandoned home, wife, and child and went forth in search of salvation. He learned everything that the 

Brahmans could teach, but their philosophy did not satisfy him. He then became a hermit and for six years he led a life of severe penance. Fasting and other forms of self-

59 mortification were also fruitless; they brought no answer to his questionings. One day, however, as Gautama sat in meditation beneath a tree, the hour of illumination came and he found the truth which neither learning nor selfmortification had taught him. In that moment he became the Buddha, the 

Enlightened. According to

Buddha life involves suffering. The only way to prevent this suffering is by ceasing to exist. As long as one's soul harbors worldly desires it will be reborn. 

Therefore the object of all true Buddhists is selfeffacement; consequently they strive to suppress desires and wants and to practice the most severe. self-control, meditation, and holiness of thought and conduct in order to reach the final goal of Nirvana - the cessation of all personal existence.

Indian Buddhism. Buddha seems not to have opposed the old beliefs of 

Hinduism, for Brahma and other Hindu deities are mentioned in Buddhist scriptures themselves. He did, however, oppose and abolish the cruel practices which were considered meritorious, together with the elaborate sacrifices of animals. 

For Buddha all life was sacred, and hence even animal sacrifice was sinful. Buddha tolerated the caste system for people in general, but he did not allow it to apply to his monks and

The Far East in Ancient Times nuns. All men and women were equal when they entered the holy life. Buddhism, in course of time, became an organized religion with sacred places thronged by pilgrims, with monasteries and temples, and with a cult of saints and relics. 

The human personality of Buddha was lost in the mists of legend and his image became an object of worship. Indian 

Buddhism flourished for more than a thousand years. It began to decline, however, about the middle of the eighth century A.D., and by the thirteenth or fourteenth century it had become practically extinct in India proper, surviving only in 

Nepal and on the island of Ceylon.

Non-Indian Buddhism. The more lasting conquests of 

Buddhism took place outside of India. During the early centuries of the Christian era it entered Burma, Siam, China, Korea, and Japan. It also spread to Tibet, Turkestan, and 

Manchuria, and for a time even penetrated the Malay Archipelago. Practically the entire population of China and 

Japan has been profoundly influenced by Buddhist teachings.

ASHUR-NASIR-PAL II 18. THE REDISCOVERY OF ANCIENT HISTORY 

Our increased information. We have long known something about the peoples of the ancient world. The Bible, Greek and Latin writings, and occasional works in other languages have furnished reasonably accurate and, about some matters, fairly full information. Within recent times, however, the extent and accuracy of our information have been greatly increased. Archæologists have uncovered the ruins of famous cities and interesting buildings. New finds of pottery, tools, and inscriptions are constantly accumulating. And, most important of all, we have learned how to read the two most widely used kinds of ancient writing hieroglyphs and cuneiform.

The Rosetta Stone. The rediscovery of ancient Egypt began with the decipherment of the hieroglyphs. These 62

The Rediscovery of Ancient History 

63 strange fantastic signs, which covered the walls of tombs and temples, were long a puzzle to all inquirers. In 1799 one of Napoleon's soldiers found a large stone slab whose face was covered with inscriptions. Since it was uncovered near the Rosetta mouth of the Nile it has become known as the Rosetta Stone. The inscriptions on it were made during the second century B.C. and contain a decree in honor of 

King Ptolemy, who at that time ruled over Egypt. There are three inscriptions: at the top, hieroglyphs; in the middle, a later and simpler form of Egyptian writing; and at the bottom, Greek. It was naturally supposed that the three inscriptions contained the same message. By comparing the known Greek letters with the unknown hieroglyphs, a resourceful French scholar, named Champollion, was able to decipher the other inscriptions. He thereby secured the key to other hieroglyphic writing, and pyramids, monuments, temples, and tombs, after centuries of silence, were able to tell us their stories.

The Behistun Rock. The decipherment of cuneiform writing formed another remarkable exploit. The key was found in a long historical record which Darius I of Persia caused to be carved high up on the face of a limestone cliff called the Behistun Rock. The inscription, written in cuneiform characters, is in the three principal languages of the king's subjects, namely, Persian, Susian, and Babylonian. It relates how he quelled a rebellion and established himself firmly on the throne. A bas-relief above the inscription tells the same story in pictures. This remarkable document, chiseled in enduring stone, was first examined by an English soldier and scholar, Sir Henry Rawlinson. He scaled the rock and took a cast of the lettering. At that time the old Persian language had been partially deciphered and, by using the proper names in the Persian inscription as a clew, it was possible to translate, first the proper names in the other two languages, and finally the entire record. The Behistun inscription thus furnished a key to the cuneiform writing of the Babylonians.

The tombs of Egypt. The early Egyptian kings raised pyramids for their sepulchers, while many later rulers hollowed out burial chambers in the limestone cliffs bordering the Nile valley. Wealthy persons also built tombs of brick and stone, which still cover the desert near Cairo. The walls of these structures were decorated with sculptures, paintings, and inscriptions. Everything which it was imagined the soul would need in the other world-vessels for food and drink, furniture, jewelry, the soldier's weapons, the workman's tools, the toilet articles of the lady, the playthings of the child was placed in the tombs. Our museums are filled with such objects, thus affording us an intimate view of the life of the ancient Egyptians.

Tel-el-Amarna tablets. Another instance of how our information about ancient Egypt has grown is to be found in the discovery and translation of the Tel-el-Amarna tablets. 

In 1887 some Egyptian workmen found a number of clay bricks inscribed with cuneiform writing. Patient search led to the recovery of about three hundred and fifty of these inscribed tablets. They have since been translated by a 

German scholar, and we now know their contents. They deal with the international affairs of the Egyptian Empire during the fourteenth century B.C. In fact, one may say that the workmen had unlocked the correspondence files of the Egyptian foreign office. Such sensational finds are infrequent, but our information is constantly being increased by the patient labors of many scholars. 

The mounds of Babylonia and Assyria. The immense mounds lining the banks of the Tigris and Euphrates are the remains of extensive palaces, temples, and other public buildings, built usually of sun-dried brick, and raised above the marshy plain upon a lofty terrace. The buildings were onestoried and roofed with huge beams of cedar. These structures and the platforms supporting them gradually decayed, and at length sank down into ruins. They look now like natural hills, for vegetation covers them, and their sides are scarred by the rains of many centuries.

The Land of Egypt 

65 Modern discoveries. The excavation of these ancient tombs, mounds, and other remains in Egypt and Babylonia has gone on with great vigor, especially during recent years. 

Remarkable discoveries have also been made in Palestine, Syria, Asia Minor, and Persia. The knowledge thus gained throws new light upon almost every aspect of Oriental life and thought. 

19. THE LAND OF EGYPT 

The Near East. The smaller of the two historic divisions of Asia is the Near East. It consists of Asia west of the 

Indus River, and historically it also includes Egypt.

The Nile. Egypt owes its existence to the Nile. Rising in the great lakes of east central Africa, it receives many tributaries and enters Upper Egypt a great river. Upper Egypt is a valley five hundred miles long and thirty miles wide. 

The strip of cultivable soil on each side of the river averages, however, only eight miles in width. Not far above modern 

Cairo the hills inclosing the valley fall away, the Nile divides into numerous branches, and the delta of Lower Egypt begins. The sluggish stream passes through a region of mingled swamp and plain, and at length empties into the Mediterranean through three principal mouths. Lower Egypt is a flat, fertile area, which has been created by the constant accumulation of sediment at the mouths of the Nile. 

Egypt a seat of early civilization. In Egypt people could live and thrive. The soil, perhaps the most fertile in the world, produced three crops of grain, flax, and vegetables a year. The clay of the valley and the convenient stone from the mountains near by provided building materials. The hot, dry climate made it possible for the inhabitants to get along with little shelter and clothing. The Nile provided them with a natural highway for domestic trade. Such favoring circumstances enabled the Egyptians to increase in numbers and to settle in populous communities. 

At a time when most of their neighbors were still uncivilized, the Egyptians were building a great civilization.

Egyptian History 67 Prehistoric era in Egypt. The Nile valley was inhabited at a remote period by Neolithic men in the barbarian stage of culture. They made beautiful implements of polished flint, fashioned pottery, built with brick and stone, sailed boats, raised domestic animals, and tilled the soil. In time, they began to smelt copper and to write by means of phonetic signs. Both metallurgy and sound writing arose in Egypt earlier than anywhere else in the world. The Neolithic 

Egyptians probably lived at first in separate tribes, under the rule of chiefs. As civilization advanced, the tribal organization gave way to city-states, that is, to small, independent communities, each one centering about a town or a city. 

The city-states by 4000 B.C. had combined into two kingdoms, one in the Delta, the other in Upper Egypt. 

20. EGYPTIAN HISTORY 

Historical periods. The Egyptians began to keep written records about 3400 B.C. Their history after that date may, for convenience, be divided into three periods: (1) the Old 

Kingdom, c3400-c2500; (2) the Middle Period, c2500- 

1580; (3) the Empire Age, 1580-525 B.C. Only the merest outline of these periods can be given, but even that will furnish a chronological framework, useful for purposes of comparison with Babylonia, Greece, and other early countries. 

The Old Kingdom. The story of the Old Kingdom begins with the union of Upper and Lower Egypt into a single national state. This union was effected under King Menes about 3400 B.C. He was thus the first of that long line of kings, or Pharaohs as they are called in the Bible, who ruled Egypt for nearly three thousand years. During most of the period of the Old Kingdom the capital city was Memphis, at the head of the Nile delta. The union of Upper and Lower 

Egypt enabled the kings to suppress rebellions, extend their boundaries, regulate irrigation, and promote prosperity. 

Under their capable and able leadership Egypt became populous and wealthy.

Pyramid builders. The power and dignity of the Pharaohs of the Old Kingdom is well attested by the pyramids. For centuries the kings had been constructing these magnificent

It contains over two million limestone blocks, each weighing more than two tons, and is 755 feet square at its base and about 450 feet high. According to legend a hundred thousand men labored twenty years to complete this enormous structure. 

It seems certain that a people who could perform such a feat must have been highly civilized. By studying the pyramids modern historians can draw a fairly detailed picture of the life of the ancient Egyptians - their customs, food, dress, tools, inventions, and social organization. 

The Middle Period. As time went on the autocratic powers of the kings were considerably weakened by aristocratic nobles and by the governors in charge of the provinces. The kings also had difficulty in asserting their control over surrounding regions, such as Nubia, Libya, and 

Sinai. Civil wars broke out and the prestige of the Pharaohs was greatly lessened. 

Although some powerful kings who were able to restore the dignity of their office ascended the throne during this time, it HEAD OF MUMMY OF RAMESES II 

was in general a period of confusion. Finally about 1800 B.C. the Hyksos, fierce invaders from western Asia, entered the country by way of the peninsula of Sinai. In addition to

A confused and weakened Egypt was no match for them, and the country, particularly Lower Egypt, fell under foreign control, which lasted for more than two hundred years.

The Empire Age. Upper Egypt never passed completely under the control of the Hyksos. Centering at Thebes, a form of monarchy under native princes was maintained. 

The rebellious governors and nobles realized that even autocratic rule was preferable to foreign domination. The Egyptians, taking a lesson from their enemies, learned to use the improved fighting methods. And finally, led by Ahmose I, the Egyptians expelled the Hyksos and established the new empire at Thebes in 1580 B.C. After the expulsion of the intruders the Egyptians themselves began a career of conquest. The Pharaohs raised great armies, invaded Palestine, Phoenicia, and Syria, and extended their rule beyond the Euphrates. Even the islands of Cyprus and Crete seem to have been under Egyptian influence. The conquered territories paid a tribute of the precious metals and merchandise, while the forced labor of thousands of war captives enabled 

Rameses II (about 1292–1225 B.C.) and other famous Pharaohs to erect great monuments in every part of their realms. 

The ruins of these stupendous structures attest the might and majesty of ancient Egypt. Gradually, however, Egypt declined in warlike energy; her Asiatic possessions fell away; and the country itself in 525 B.C. became a part of the Persian Empire. 

21. EGYPTIAN SOCIETY AND CULTURE 

Social classes. Ancient Egypt had no caste system, but there were, as in all countries, several more or less distinct classes. Those in Egypt consisted of officials, priests, farmers, slaves, artisans, traders, and professional men, such as physicians and scribes. There was no class of hereditary nobles, but officials and wealthy persons formed an aristocratic group.

The king and his helpers. At the top of the social order stood the king, who was considered as the earthly representative of the gods. Temples were erected to him and offerings were made to his sacred majesty. He had many duties.

Egyptian Society and Culture 

71 He was commander, judge, and high priest, all in one. In time of war, he led his troops and faced the perils of the battlefield. During intervals of peace, he held frequent audiences with his courtiers, hearing complaints, settling disputes, and issuing commands. The king was also occupied with a constant round of sacrifices, prayers, and processions, which could not be omitted without exciting the anger of the gods. Next to the king was a host of officials, ranging from the viceroy of Thebes, who acted for the king during his absence, to the obscure magistrate of a frontier town. 

The king had a council of advisers who supervised the various departments, such as taxation, irrigation, and public buildings. There were thousands of scribes and clerks. Faithful officials were rewarded by advancement; consequently the kings were usually served by an efficient corps of helpers. 

Administration of law. Royal government was administered in the provinces by appointees of the king, and there was a whole system of local and superior courts. Criminal law was crudely administered. Witnesses were tortured and magic was employed in determining the guilt of the accused. 

Fortunately, however, the penalties were not extremely severe, death being inflicted for only a few crimes, such as murder and stealing from temples. Laws relating to property and individual rights were much more highly developed than criminal law. Except in time of war, life was fairly safe, property was reasonably secure, and people were protected in their occupations. There were law books (unfortunately lost) and definite rules relating to contracts, loans, leases, mortgages, partnership, marriage, and the family. The legal position of woman was high; she had full rights of ownership and inheritance and could engage in business on her own account.

Priests and religion. The priests constituted an influential group. They stood high in popular estimation, and in some periods they even performed political duties. Their principal concern, however, was the care of temples and the propagation of their religion. Nature worship, so common

among savage and barbarous peoples, survived in Egypt. 

The sun formed an object of particular adoration and was represented by several deities. Animals also played an important part in their religion. The jackal, bull, ram, hawk, crocodile, snake, and scarab received the utmost reverence because they were thought to be the symbols of various gods. The most popular divinities were Osiris, god of the dead; Horus, god of the rising sun; Isis, goddess of life;

Set, god of evil; and Amon, Re, and Aton, successively gods of the sun. Belief in one supreme god is called monotheism. Some Egyptians reached the idea of a single supreme being, but in general the mass of people could not grasp or understand so lofty a conception.

The future life. The Egyptians, like their neighbors, believed that man has a soul which survives the death of 14

They thought it essential, however, to preserve the body from destruction, so that it might remain to the end of time a home for the soul. Hence arose the practice of embalming. The embalmed body (mummy) was placed in the grave, which the Egyptians called an "eternal dwelling."

Egyptian Society and Culture 

73 At a later period they thought of the future as a place of rewards and punishments, where the soul underwent the ordeal of a last judgment. Before the throne of Osiris, King of the Dead, a man's heart was weighed in the scales of judgment. If the soul could truthfully say that it had observed the moral law, it was admitted to the happy land where it became one with Osiris. If, however, the scales turned against the soul, it was cast to waiting monsters. 

Farming. The land in Egypt was owned largely by the king and other wealthy persons. It was divided into great estates rather than small farms. The work was done by peasants and slaves, who led a dreary, monotonous existence. 

Their labors are pictured in great variety and detail on Egyptian monuments. We see the peasant as he breaks up ul. DDD 

PLOWING AND SOWING IN ANCIENT EGYPT 

The picture shows from left to right a scribe, two plowmen, one holding the plow and one driving the oxen, a man with a hoe, who breaks up the clods left by the plow, and a sower scattering seed from a bag. the earth with a hoe or plows a shallow furrow with a sharppointed stick. We see the sheep being driven across sown fields to trample the seed into the moist soil. We watch the patient laborers as with sickles they gather in the harvest and then with heavy flails separate the chaff from the grain. 

Although their methods were crude, the farmers raised large crops. Wheat and barley were the principal grains. Vegetables and fruits grew in great abundance. Cattle, sheep, goats, and pigs were raised, and oxen and asses were the principal work animals. The horse was introduced during the period of the Hyksos (p. 69), but it was used chiefly by the army.

Industry. Blacksmiths, carpenters, stone-cutters, weavers, potters, glass blowers, and workers in ivory, silver, and gold were found in every city. The creations of these ancient craftsmen often exhibit remarkable skill. Egyptian linens were so wonderfully fine and transparent as to merit the name of "woven air." Egyptian glass, with its lines of different hues, was much prized. Fine vases, linen, jewelry, and papyrus were produced in great quantities for exporting. 

Commerce. A highly developed country like Egypt naturally had an extensive domestic trade, and its foreign trade, in spite of obstacles, was considerable. The Egyptians, pioneers in so many fields of human activity, are believed to have made the first seagoing ships. As early as the thirtieth century B.C., they began to venture out into the eastern Mediterranean and to carry on a thriving trade with both Cyprus and Crete, which lay almost opposite the mouths of the Nile. The ships of the Pharaohs also sailed up and down the entire length of the Red Sea, bringing ebony and cinnamon from the east coast of Africa. Ivory, gold, and ostrich feathers were imported from Nubia, and from Syria came fish, wine, and incense. During early times goods were simply exchanged; eventually the Egyptians used small pieces of gold, each of which was equal to the value of a cow. It was necessary to weigh the metal whenever a purchase was made. A common picture on the Egyptian monuments is that of the weigher with his scales. 

Literature. Next to historical inscriptions the most interesting type of Egyptian literature is that which deals with religion. Hymns and magic sayings have been found in great numbers. The best known work is the Book of the 

Dead, a collection of hymns, prayers, and magical phrases to be recited by the soul on its journey beyond the grave. A chapter from this work usually covered the inner side of the mummy case. In addition to historical and religious writings, a number of poems, folk songs, and tales have been preserved.

Houses and architecture. Aristocratic families lived in

Egyptian Society and Culture 

75 large, well-built houses made of wooden frames covered over with brick. The latticed windows with their colored curtains gave the houses an air of charm. Well-planted gardens and orchards supplied abundant food, and numerous servants gave attentive respect to the wishes of their masters. The poor people lived in one-room houses made of mud-brick. 

In the cities the houses had only a single wall between them. 

Narrow alleys marked off blocks of such hovels. Even the dwellings of the nobles did not embody the full knowledge of architecture possessed by the Egyptians. The characteristic works of Egyptian architecture were the tombs of the kings and the temples of the gods. These structures, even in their ruins, leave upon the observer an impression of peculiar massiveness, solidity, and grandeur. They seem built for eternity.

Engineering. The art of stone masonry arose in Egypt earlier than anywhere else in the world. It soon produced the Great Pyramid, the largest stone structure ever erected in ancient or (until recently) in modern times. The Egyptians were also the first people who learned how to raise buildings with vast halls, the roofs of which were supported by rows of columns (colonnades). An upper story, or clerestory, containing windows, made it possible to light the interior of these halls. The column, the colonnade, and the clerestory, as architectural devices, were adopted by Greek and Roman builders, from whom they descended to medieval and modern Europe.

Science. Conspicuous advance took place in the exact sciences. A very old Egyptian manuscript contains arithmetical problems with fractions as well as whole numbers, and geometrical formulas for computing the capacity of storehouses and the area of fields. The Egyptians also knew something of astronomy. By 4000 B.C. they had given up reckoning time by lunar months (the interval between two new moons) and had formed a solar calendar consisting of twelve thirty-day months, with five extra days at the end of the year. This calendar, improved by the insertion of

leap years, has come down to us (p. 35). In medicine the 

Egyptians made some progress. An old medical treatise which has been preserved distinguishes various diseases and notes their symptoms. The curious characters by which druggists indicate grains and drams are of Egyptian origin. 

Education. Such schools as existed in Egypt were attached to the temples and were conducted by priests or scribes. 

Reading and writing formed the chief subjects of study.

The schoolbooks, which have survived in great numbers, contain model letters and petitions and wise sayings calcumelated to inspire the pupils. A pupil who learned to read and write might become a scribe. 

When a man wished to send a letter, he had a scribe write it, signing it himself by affixing his seal. When he received a letter, he usually employed a scribe to read it to him.

The scribes also compiled and sents a scribe with pen and papyrus roll copied the papyrus rolls which constituted the Egyptian books. Only the well-to-do could afford to secure an education. The common people remained grossly ignorant, and they were therefore slow to abandon time-honored superstitions and reluctant to adopt new customs even when better than the old. Consequently civilization in Egypt seemed unable to rise above its established level.

Explorations on the site of Babylon have been conducted by the German Oriental Society. Large parts of the temple area, as well as sections of the royal palaces, have been uncovered. The soil which the Tigris and Euphrates bring down every year fills up the Persian Gulf at the rate of about three miles a century. Their delta was therefore much less extensive five or six thousand years ago than it is today. In ancient times it was a plain about one hundred and seventy miles long and forty miles wide. Formerly known as the land

SEAL OF SARGON I 

of Shinar, it is best known to us by the name Babylonia, after Babylon, which became its leading city and capital. 

Babylonia a seat of early civilization. The plain of Babylonia was once wonderfully fertile. The alluvial soil, when properly irrigated, yielded abundant harvests of wheat, barley, and millet. The fruit of the date palm provided a nutritious food. Workable clay was abundant. Molded into brick and afterward dried in the sun, it became adobe, the cheapest building material imaginable. Nature, indeed, had done much for Babylonia. We can understand, therefore, why prehistoric peoples were attracted to this region of the Near East, and why it became the seat of another early civilization. 

Four empires. The ancient history of the Tigris-Euphrates valley may be divided into four periods, each centering around the history of an empire: (1) Babylonia, c2600c1700 B.C.; (2) the Kassite domination, c1700-c1100 B.c.; (3) Assyria, c1100-612 B.C.; (4) the Second Babylonian 

Empire, 612-539 B.C.

Babylonia. The valley of the Tigris-Euphrates was easily accessible to hunting tribes from the mountains and to nomads from the steppes. Their inroads and migrations into the fertile plain of the two rivers form a constant feature of

Babylonian history. The earliest inhabitants of the lower valley about whom we know anything were the Sumerians, who entered the country about 4000 B.C. They gradually settled down to an agricultural life and formed a number of independent city-states, each with its king and its patron god. After the Sumerians came Semitic-speaking people from northern Arabia. Under a leader named Sargon (c2700 B.C.) the Semites subdued the Sumerians and began to adopt their civilization. Sargon united all the city-states into a kingdom. He also carried his victorious arms as far

The Kassite domination. About 1700 B.C. an Indo-Euro pean people from east of the Zagros Mountains invaded and conquered Babylonia. They were barbarians, but they slowly learned some of the arts of civilization from their sub-

79 jects. They also eventually accepted the Babylonian religion. The Kassites introduced the horse into Babylonia, just as the Hyksos were doing in Egypt at about the same time. Under the Kassites, Babylonia made little progress, and they in turn fell before the stronger power of Assyria. 

Assyria. The Assyrian Empire had its center on the upper 

Tigris, well to the east of the Euphrates. Equipped with horses, chariots, and iron weapons, the Assyrians began a series of conquests which made their name the terror of the AA 

TRANSPORT OF AN ASSYRIAN COLOSSUS 

A slab from a gallery of Sennacherib's palace at Nineveh. The immense block is being pulled forward by slaves, who work under the lash. ancient world. With savage ferocity and cruelty they burned, killed, and mutilated their captives. In 722 B.C., under Sargon II they captured Samaria, the capital of the Kingdom of Israel, and carried its inhabitants into captivity. 

Sargon's son, Sennacherib, tried to conquer the Kingdom of Judah and did succeed in shutting up King Hezekiah "like a caged bird in his royal city of Jerusalem." A pestilence smote the Assyrians and they withdrew from the siege.

Assyria's cruel and harsh rule raised up many enemies. Its resources had been exhausted in wars, and, when its subject peoples revolted, the weakness of Assyria became apparent. The Medes of Persia and the Kassites of Babylonia united to destroy it. After a terrible siege the great capital of Nineveh was taken by storm (612 B.C.), and the last king of Assyria, with his courtiers and slaves, fell before the vengeance of his enemies.

Second Babylonian Empire. Upon the fall of Nineveh, Babylonia once more seized leadership. Its most famous king during its revived period was Nebuchadnezzar, who waged several successful wars of conquest. Perhaps his best known exploit was the capture of Jerusalem in 586 B.C.

Its temple and palace were destroyed, and its inhabitants slaughtered or carried into captivity. Babylonia, however, was unable to maintain its conquest. A powerful alliance of Medes and Persians was formed, and in 539 B.C., after a spectacular siege, Babylon was captured and the empire came to an end. 

23. BABYLONIAN AND ASSYRIAN CULTURE 

Social classes. The upper class of Babylonia consisted of officials, priests, nobles, and wealthy merchants. The lower class was composed of small farmers, artisans, and shop keepers. The third class was made up of slaves, who had certain rights, such as owning property and marrying freemen. The distinction between classes was sharper and more rigid than in Egypt. Severer penalties were prescribed by law for slaves and poor freemen than for the upper class. 

Government. Independent city-states flourished in Babylonia until the time of Sargon, who united the Sumerians and the Semitic invaders. The monarch then became supreme. 

A host of tax collectors and inspectors carried out the royal will. In Assyria the powers of the king were exceedingly great, being limited only by the fear of a revolt of the army. 

Perhaps the most definite check upon the powers of the Baby-

Babylonian and Assyrian Culture 

81 lonian kings was the system of written laws, for even a king cannot conveniently violate his written pledge. 

Babylonian law. The Babylonians were a very legalminded people. When a man sold his wheat, bought a slave, married a wife, or made a will, the transaction was duly noted on a contract tablet. He then stamped his seal on the soft clay of the tablet. Every one who owned property had to have a seal. A contract tablet was protected from defacement 1918ve by being placed in a hollow clay an case, or envelope.

Hammurabi's code of laws. A recent discovery has provided us with almost the complete text of the laws which Hammurabi, the 

Babylonian king, ordered engraved on stone monuments and set up in the chief cities of his realm. Hammurabi's code shows, in general, a keen sense of justice. A man who tries to bribe a witness or a judge is to be severely punished. A farmer who is careless with his dikes and allows the water to run through and flood his neighbor's land must restore the value of the grain he has damaged. The owner of a vicious ox which has gored a man must pay a heavy fine, provided he knew the disposition of the animal and had not blunted its horns. On the other

A shaft of stone, nearly 8 feet high, contains the code of Hammurabi. The monument was found on the site of Susa in 1901-1902. It is engraved in 44 columns and over 3600 lines. A relief at the top shows the Babylonian king receiving the laws from the sun god, who is seated at the right. Flames rising from the god's shoulders indicate his solar character. hand, the code contains some rude features, especially the reliance upon retaliation - "eye for eye, tooth for tooth" as the punishment of injuries. For instance, a son who struck his father was to have his hands cut off. The nature

of the punishment depended, moreover, on the rank of the aggrieved party. A person who had caused the loss of a gentleman's" eye was to have his own plucked out; but if the injury was done to a poor man, the culprit had only to pay a fine. Hammurabi's code thus presents a vivid picture of Babylonian society twenty-one centuries before Christ. 

Agriculture. The earliest records of Babylonia mention canals and irrigation ditches. The cost of constructing and maintaining such a system was considerable; consequently most of the land was owned by the king, priests, nobles, and wealthy merchants. The farms were worked by slaves under the direction of overseers or by peasant tenants. Wheat, barley, and dates were the principal crops. Great numbers of sheep were raised in order to supply wool, which was one of the principal exports.

Industry. The Babylonians were primarily an agricultural people. As time went on, however, they turned more of their attention to industry and commerce. In fact, they became such persistent traders that one historian has referred to them as a nation of hucksters. In addition to agricultural products, they made woolen and linen garments, cut stones, tapestries, and leather goods. The craftsmen who engaged in industry made annual contracts with their masters and received food and a small wage in return for their labor. 

Commerce. The cities of the Tigris-Euphrates valley were admirably situated for commerce, by both sea and land. 

The shortest way by water from India skirted the southern coast of Iran and, passing up the Persian Gulf, gained the valley of the two rivers. There were also overland roads for caravan trade from India and China. These converged at 

Babylon and Nineveh and then spread westward to Asia 

Minor, Syria, Phoenicia, Palestine, and Egypt. All these routes were arteries of commerce from prehistoric times. 

Many of them are in use even today. 

Architecture. The architecture of the Tigris-Euphrates peoples differed entirely from that of the Egyptians, because brick, rather than stone, formed the chief building material.

Babylonian and Assyrian Culture 

83 In Babylonia the most characteristic structure was the temple. It was a solid square tower, rising in stages (usually seven) to the top, where the shrine of the deity stood. The different stages were connected by a winding ascent. These tower-temples must have been very conspicuous objects.

In Assyria the most characteristic structure was the palace. 

The sun-dried bricks, of which both temples and palaces were composed, lacked the durability of stone and have long since dissolved into shapeless mounds. 

Religion. Like the Egyptians, the peoples of the Tigris 

Euphrates valley practiced nature worship. They had a number of gods who personified the various aspects of nature. Their chief gods were 

Bel or, as he was eventually called, Marduk, god of the earth; Ea, god of the prac waters; and Anu, god of the heavens. The most popular Assyrian god was Asur, god of military prowess and empire. The 

Babylonians also believed themselves to vea A be constantly surrounded by a host of evil spirits, who caused insanity, sickness, ac-won cidents, and death. To cope with them the He

Divination. The Babylonians had many ways of predicting the future. Soothsayers divined from dreams and from the casting of lots. Omens of prosperity or misfortune were also drawn from the appearance of the entrails of animals slain in sacrifice. A sheep's liver was commonly used for this purpose. Divination by the liver was studied for centuries in the temple schools of Babylonia. The practice afterward spread to the Greeks and Romans.

Astrology. Astrology received much attention in Babylonia. The five planets then recognized, as well as comets and eclipses, were thought to exercise an influence for good or evil on the life of man. Babylonian astrology passed to western lands and became popular in much of Europe. 

People who try to read their fate in the stars are really practicing an art of Babylonian origin. 

Education and libraries. Schools in which children learned how to read and write were in existence in Babylonia at an early date. Some of the copy books of children who went to school four thousand years ago have been preserved. 

Like us, they copied moral sayings and did sums in arithmetic. Bills of lading were attached to the bales of goods which were shipped out of and into Babylonia. Fragments of these attached bills, written in cuneiform characters on clay tablets, have been found by the thousands, thus attesting to the fact that writing was a common art. Some kings, at both Babylon and Nineveh, collected libraries. The last of the great Assyrian kings collected an immense number of books; thirty thousand of the tablets which he brought together are now in the British Museum. 

Literature. Parts of two famous Babylonian epics have been preserved on clay tablets found in the royal library at Nineveh. The epic of the Creation tells how the god Marduk overcame a terrible dragon, the symbol of primeval chaos, and thus established order in the universe. With half of the body of the dead dragon he made a covering for the heavens and set therein the stars. He then caused the new moon to shine and made it the ruler of the night. His last work was the creation of man, in order that the service and worship of the gods might be established forever. The second epic contains an account of a Deluge, sent by the gods to punish sinful man. The rain fell for six days and nights and covered the entire earth. All people were drowned, except the Babylonian Noah, his family, and his relatives, who safely rode the waters in a boat. This ancient narrative closely resembles the Biblical story in Genesis.

A cross-section of history. In studying history it is very easy to fall into the error of thinking that only one country existed at a time. Perhaps many students assume that 

Egypt rose, had its day, and passed off the scene, followed by Babylonia, whose history ran a similar course. The notion that history consists of the story of the rise and fall of successive countries is very appealing because it is so simple. 

As a matter of fact, Egypt, Assyria, Persia, Greece, and Rome did have a successive prominence, but their histories overlap

Their overlapping shows that several countries existed at the same time. and several peoples were disputing the ownership of Palestine. Thus many states were in existence in 1500 B.C., and so it was at any other date that may be selected in either ancient or modern times. We try merely to trace the main outlines of the most important countries. Of necessity we

must consider them one at a time, but that method should not lead us into the error of thinking that only one country existed at a time. This caution may help in studying the peoples, not only of Syria, Phoenicia, and Palestine, but those of all other countries.

The great highway of nations. The region between the 

Mediterranean and the deserts of Arabia contained in antiquity three small countries: Syria, Phoenicia, and Palestine.

Their situation put them on the great highway of the Near East, and through them ran the caravan routes connecting the Nile and the Euphrates. The inhabitants spoke Semitic languages and probably came from northern Arabia. They are known as Aramæans, Phoenicians, and Hebrews. None of these peoples ever played a leading part in the history of the Near East, but each made important contributions to civilization.

The Aramæans. The Aramæans of Syria were keen business men, who bought and sold throughout western Asia. 

Their language thus became widely spread and in time took the place of Hebrew as the ordinary speech in Palestine. 

Some parts of the Old Testament are written in Aramaic. 

The chief center of the Aramæans was Damascus, one of the oldest cities in the world and still a thriving place. 

The Phoenicians. The Phoenicians occupied a narrow stretch of coast, about one hundred and twenty miles in length and seldom more than twelve miles in width, between the Lebanon Mountains and the sea. This tiny land could not support a large population by farming; so the Phonicians became a nation of sailors. They found in the cedars of Lebanon a soft, white wood for shipbuilding, and in the Egyptian vessels which had been entering their harbors for centuries a model for their own craft. The great Phoenician cities of Sidon and Tyre established colonies throughout the

Mediterranean and had an extensive commerce with almost every region of the ancient world. 

Phoenician trade routes. Starting from Tyre and Sidon, the Phoenicians soon extended their trade routes to Cyprus

Syria, Phoenicia, and Palestine 

87 and Crete, then to the islands of the Ægean, and in some cases even as far as the Black Sea. When they were finally driven from these regions by the rising power of the Greek states, they sailed farther westward and established trading posts in Sicily, Sardinia, North Africa, and Spain. They also passed through the Strait of Gibraltar into the stormy Atlantic and visited the coasts of western Europe and Africa.

Tin, which was especially valuable because of its use in making bronze, seems also to have been brought from southwestern Britain (Cornwall), where mines of this metal are still productive. From Africa came ivory, ostrich feathers, and gold; from Arabia came incense, perfumes, and costly spices. These commodities found a ready sale throughout the Near East. Still other products were imported directly into Phoenicia to provide raw materials for her flourishing manufactures. The fine carpets and glassware, the artistic works in silver and bronze, and the beautiful purple cloths

produced in the factories of Tyre and Sidon were exported to every part of the known world. 

Phoenician settlements. The Phoenicians established set tlements wherever they went (see map, p. 113). Most of these were merely trading posts which contained warehouses for the storage of goods. Here the shy natives came to barter their raw materials for the finished products cloths, tools, weapons, wine, and oil — which the strangers from the East had brought with them. Phoenician settlements sometimes grew into large and flourishing cities. 

Gades in southern Spain, which was the most distant of their colonies, survives to this day as Cadiz, one of the oldest cities in Europe. Carthage, founded in northern Africa by colonists from Tyre, became the commercial mistress of the western Mediterranean. Carthaginian history, as we shall learn, has many points of contact with that of the Greeks and Romans.

Importance of the Hebrews. From the standpoint of importance the Hebrews deserve much space, but their history from Abraham to the birth of Jesus is well known through the teachings of the churches. Their great contributions to literature and religion have affected all subsequent peoples. 

Few documents have exerted a greater influence than the Old Testament with its Mosaic Code, the highest expression of ancient morality and ethics. The Hebrews were the only ancient people who developed a clear conception of one God; they were, therefore, the first monotheists. 

Origin of the Hebrews. The western part of Palestine, more familiarly known as Canaan, was the home of the Hebrews. Their story is found in the Old Testament, especially in the two books called Genesis and Exodus. We learn how Abraham journeyed from "Ur of the Chaldees," a very ancient city on the desert edge of Babylonia, and took up his abode in Canaan; how his grandson Jacob (or Israel), when a sore famine troubled the land, went down into Egypt with all his family and settled on the rich plains of the Delta; how there his descendants dwelt in peace for

Syria, Phoenicia, and Palestine 

89 many generations, gaining great possessions and multiplying exceedingly; how, when the Egyptians began to vex them with grievous burdens, the Israelites united under the leadership of Moses and escaped to the peninsula of Sinai; and how they wandered for forty years in the "Wilderness" until ready to enter once more the "Promised Land" of Canaan.

Hebrews in Canaan. The history of the Hebrews begins with their settlement in Canaan. According to the Biblical account, they crossed the Jordan under the leader Joshua and after a struggle with the inhabitants made good their footing in the new home. The thorough conquest of Canaan proved to be no easy task. At first the twelve Hebrew tribes formed only a loose and weak confederacy without a common head. 

To resist their enemies with success, it was necessary to have a king who could bring all the tribes under his firm, wellordered rule.

The Hebrew kingdom. Toward the close of the eleventh century B.C. the Hebrew tribes united into one kingdom, under a ruler named Saul. His reign was filled with constant struggles against the warlike Philistines, who occupied the southwestern coast of Palestine. David, Saul's successor, overthrew the Philistine power. For a capital city 

David selected the ancient fortress of Jerusalem, which henceforth became for the Hebrews the center of their national life. The reign of David's son, Solomon (about 955925 B.C.), formed the most glorious period in Hebrew history.

Solomon's authority reached from the peninsula of Sinai northward to the Lebanon Mountains and the Euphrates. 

He married an Egyptian princess, a daughter of the reigning 

Pharaoh. He joined with a king of Tyre in trading expeditions on the Red Sea and Indian Ocean. The Tyrian ruler also supplied him with skilled Phoenician workmen, who built at Jerusalem a splendid Temple for the worship of Jehovah.

Division of the Hebrew kingdom. The greatness of the 

Hebrew monarchy did not endure. The people were not ready to bear the burdens which their government imposed

upon them. They objected to the standing army, to the forced labor on public buildings, and especially to the heavy taxes. The ten northern tribes seceded shortly after Solomon's death and established the independent kingdom of Israel, with its capital at Samaria. The two southern tribes, Judah and Benjamin, formed the kingdom of Judah and remained loyal to the successors of Solomon. These two small states were constantly attacked by their powerful neighbors. 

The Assyrians finally conquered Israel and the Babylonians conquered Judah.

THE PERSIAN EMPIRE ABOUT 500 B.C. 

60° The Persian Empire at its greatest extent under Darius I (521-485 B.C.) embraced an enormous area. Its eastern and western frontiers were nearly 3000 miles apart, or considerably more than the distance between New York and San Francisco. Darius divided his dominions into provinces, about twenty in number, and connected them by military roads for the dispatch of troops and supplies. The Royal Road from Susa, the Persian capital, to Sardis in Lydia was about 1600 miles in length. Government couriers, using relays of fresh horses, could cover this distance in about a week.

History and Culture of the Persian Empire 

91 pean speech. Cyrus the Great (553-529 B.C.) united the

Medes and Persians under his sway and then conquered the kingdom of Lydia in Asia Minor. He is also remembered for his kindness in allowing the Hebrew captives to return to their native land. Cyrus's son, Cambyses, conquered Egypt in 525 B.C. and governed it as a part of his realm. The next ruler, Darius I (521-485 B.C.), added northwestern India, together with some territory in Europe. He describes himself in an inscription as "the great king, king of kings, king of countries, king of all men.' 

Organization of the empire. Darius I was not only a great conqueror; he was also an able organizer and administrator. 

The Persians had conquered many peoples unlike in race, language, customs, and religion. Darius did not try to weld 

ROCK SEPULCHERS OF THE PERSIAN KINGS 

The tombs of seven Persian kings are cut in the face of a cliff a few miles from the ruins of the royal city of Persepolis. Above the colonnade in each tomb front is a representation of the king worshiping the god Ahura Mazda. The tombs still contain the massive stone coffins in which Darius I, Xerxes, and their successors were buried. them into unity. As long as his subjects paid tribute and furnished soldiers, they were allowed to manage their affairs with little interference. The entire empire, excluding Persia proper, was divided into about twenty provinces, each with

governors (satraps) to collect taxes and command the provincial armies. Darius also provided special agents whose business it was to travel throughout the empire and investigate the conduct of the royal officials. It became a proverb that "the king has many eyes and many ears." As a further means of holding his dominions together, Darius laid out military roads for the dispatch of troops and supplies. 

Persians and Greeks. Under Darius I and his son Xerxes, the Persians came, as we shall see (p. 119), into contact with the Greeks. The power of Persia was somewhat lessened by this conflict, but the empire continued in existence until the invasion of Asia by Alexander the Great in 333 B.C. (p. 136). 

Persian civilization. The Persians were the heirs of Babylonian and Assyrian culture. They used cuneiform writing and imitated Assyrian architecture, sculpture, and military tactics. In the organization of their empire they probably were superior to the Assyrians. The Persians absorbed civilization, but not only for themselves; by forcibly uniting different peoples under one government they broke down isolation and spread civilization. 

The royal court. The Persian king lived far removed from the common eye in the recesses of a lordly palace. When he gave audience to his nobles, he sat on a gold and ivory throne. 

When he traveled, even on military expeditions, he carried with him costly furniture, gold and silver dishes, and gorgeous robes. Hundreds of servants, bodyguards, and officials were about him. All who approached his person prostrated themselves in the dust.

Religion. In religion the Persians approached monotheism. 

The great prophet, Zoroaster, taught that Ahura Mazda, the heaven-deity, is the maker and upholder of the universe. He is a god of light and order, of truth and purity. Against him stands Ahriman, the personification of darkness and evil. 

These rival powers are engaged in a ceaseless struggle. Man, by doing right and avoiding wrong, by loving truth and hating falsehood, can help make Good triumph over Evil.

Ahura Mazda in the end will overcome Ahriman and will

93 reign supreme over a righteous world. Zoroastrianism still survives in some parts of Persia, although that country is now chiefly Mohammedan, and among the Parsees (Persians) of India. 

26. THE NEAR EAST AND EUROPE Origin of civilization. Our study of the Near East in antiquity has been confined chiefly to the Nile and 

Tigris-Euphrates valleys. The Egyp tians and the Babylonians originated civilization during the thousand years between 4000 and 3000 B.C., while all the rest of the world continued either in Neolithic barbarism or Palæolithic savagery. In Egypt and Babylonia men first developed out of the tribal state and began to form cities, states, kingdoms, and empires; here they first passed from hunting, fishing, and herding to the cultivation of the soil, manufacturing, and commerce; here first arose metallurgy, architecture, phonetic writing, mathematics, astronomy, medicine, and many other arts and sciences indispensable to the His head is surmounted by a higher life of mankind. Unit III GREEK CIVILIZATION 

How the Greeks achieved a greater civilization than previous peoples 

(CHAPTERS V-VI)

PRESENTATION 

The rising civilization in the Nile and the Tigris-Euphrates valleys was slowly transmitted to Europe, which henceforth became the center of the world's history. 

On account of its coast line, climate, resources, and people, Europe — particularly the Mediterranean basin was well suited to become a center of civilization. European civilization first appeared in the eastern Mediterranean, where the Greeks achieved a greater civilization than previous peoples. The stages of civilization centering in 

Greece are called Ægean, Homeric, Hellenic, and finally Hellenistic. 

The Greeks founded numerous city-states which became centers of commerce, politics, and culture. From these city-states colonists went out to Italy, the Black Sea region, and other areas, carrying with them their Greek speech, customs, and manners. On the mainland the city-states of Sparta and Athens rose to prominence and led the Greeks in a long struggle against Persia, thus saving Europe from domination by Asia. Following this struggle, Athens founded an empire. But the city-states quarreled and warred with one another until they were finally overcome by the Macedonian Greeks under Philip II. Philip's son, Alexander the Great, led the armies of the Greek city-states in a conquest of the Persian Empire. The conquests of Alexander and his successors led to a merging of the civilization of the Greeks with that of the Orient, thus producing the Hellenistic civilization; it dominated the Mediterranean until the rise of the Romans. (Chapter V) 

The Greeks have left such an impression upon all later civilization that the details of their dress, houses, home life, education, and social life are matters of interest. In our buildings and art we are still copying Greek models. The writings of the Greeks have come down to us, bringing a priceless heritage of philosophy, science, art, and literature. Herein lies "the glory that was Greece." (Chapter VI)
