27. THE EUROPEAN SETTING B. I. WHEELER 

Predominance of Europe in history. Although the earliest recorded history deals with the East, for the last twenty-five centuries history has centered in the West, that is, in Europe. 

Modern industry and commerce, modern systems of government, modern art, literature, and science throughout the world are largely the creation of Europeans or of people of 

European origin. Within the last four hundred years they have occupied and populated America and Australia and have brought under their control the largest part of Asia, nearly the whole of Africa, and the islands of all the seas. 

They have introduced into these remote regions their languages, laws, customs, and religion, until today the greater part of the world is subject to European influence. 

Area of Europe. Considering its great influence, Europe is surprisingly small; in fact, it is, with the exception of Australia, the smallest of the continents. Geographically it is not a continent but a peninsula of Asia. Map makers usually place the dividing line between Europe and Asia at the Ural 

Mountains, the Caspian Sea, and the Caucasus Mountains. 99

Greece

Europe has less than half the area of North America, less than one-third that of Africa, and a little more than one-fifth that of Asia. It includes about one-fifteenth of the land surface of the earth.

Physical Europe. The geographical advantages enjoyed by Europe account, in part, for its historic importance. The sea penetrates deeply into the continent, forming numerous bays and harbors and giving to it a longer coast line than Africa and South America combined. Europe is well supplied with rivers which are navigable for long distances. Another feature of European geography is the great extent of fertile lowlands. Finally, the mountains of Europe are well provided with passes, which afford convenient routes of communication from one country to another. 

Climatic Europe. Nearly all Europe lies in the northern half of the North Temperate Zone, that is, within those latitudes most favorable to the development of civilization. 

Nowhere, except beyond the Arctic Circle, does extreme cold stunt body and mind, and nowhere does excessive heat sap human energies. The climate is moderated by the Gulf 

Stream, an ocean current which moves northeast from the Gulf of Mexico, warming the winds which blow over parts of western and northern Europe. The absence of mountains on the west and the deeply penetrating waters of the North and Baltic Seas still further facilitate the movement of these tempering winds, which bring abundant rainfall to many parts of the continent. Consequently, it is the only continent without extensive deserts.

Northern and southern Europe. The Pyrenees, Alps, and 

Balkans, stretching across Europe from the Atlantic Ocean to the Black Sea, have formed an historical dividing line, as well as a geographical barrier between northern and southern Europe. Twenty-five centuries ago the European peoples dwelling north of these mountains were still barbarians. We hear little of them in ancient times, except as their occasional migrations brought them into contact with the civilized Græco-Latin peoples on the shores of the Mediterranean.

28. THE MEDITERRANEAN BASIN 

Characteristics of the Mediterranean basin. Europe, we have just noted, furnished the general setting for the development of civilization during the past twenty-five centuries; and that part of Europe known as the Mediterranean basin was the more specific scene for the first great European civilizations. The Mediterranean is the most extensive inland sea in the world. Its length east and west is about twentytwo hundred miles, and its breadth varies from four to six hundred miles. It washes the shores of three continents- 

Europe, Asia, and Africa. Nevertheless, its basin is relatively isolated, being confined within a mountain wall on the north and an almost impassable desert on the south. The climate of the basin falls halfway between tropical and temperate conditions. The rainfall is, on the whole, scanty, with the result that the vine and the olive, which offer considerable resistance to drouth, are very important products. 

A highway of nations. The Mediterranean was well suited for early commerce because of its long and contracted shape, indented northern shore, and numerous islands. Mariners seldom had to proceed far from land and good harbors. Since the Strait of Gibraltar shuts out the great waves of the Atlantic, its storms, although frequent and fierce, are usually brief. Freedom from high tides also facilitates navigation. 

Such advantages made the Mediterranean from a remote period an avenue by which everything that the older Eastern world had to offer could be passed on to the younger West. 

The various European peoples themselves were also able to exchange their products and communicate their ideas and customs along this "highway of nations."

The Egean Sea. Projecting northward from the eastern 

Mediterranean is the Ægean Sea. It is almost surrounded by land. Only narrow passages lead northward to the Black

Sea, while on the south the long and narrow island of Crete lies like a huge breakwater. Hundreds of smaller islands dot the surface of the Ægean, so many and so close together that

The Ægean Age 

103 they have always served as "stepping stones" between 

Greece and Asia Minor.

Influence of geographical conditions. Greek history illustrates in three ways the influence of geographical conditions on the life of a people. In the first place, mountain ranges cut 

Greece into many small areas, separated from one another by natural ramparts. No place in Greece is more than fifty miles from a mountain range. Isolated from one another, the 

Greeks never learned how to unite into one nation under a single government but stubbornly maintained their own local independence. In the second place, the near presence of the sea enabled the Greeks to become sailors and led them to devote much energy to foreign commerce. They early felt, in consequence, the stimulating effects of intercourse with other peoples. And in the third place, the location of Greece at the threshold of Asia, with its best harbors and most numerous islands on the eastern coast, enabled the country to receive and profit by the culture of the Orient. Greece faced the civilized East. 

29. THE AEGEAN AGE 

Ægean civilization. Until a comparatively recent date we knew nothing of a remarkable civilization which was ancient when the Greeks arrived. Its existence has been revealed by modern excavations. This civilization centered in the island of Crete and spread by commerce and colonization to the nearby islands, the coast of Asia Minor, and the shores of Greece. One may speak, therefore, of an Ægean civilization, since it came in time to prevail so widely in this part of the Mediterranean basin.

Schliemann's excavations at Troy. The man who did most to reveal this civilization was a wealthy German merchant named Heinrich Schliemann. An enthusiastic lover of

Homer, he believed that the stories of the Trojan War related in the Iliad were not just fancies but real facts. In 

1870 he started to test his beliefs by excavations at a hill

Greece called Hissarlik, on the northwestern coast of Asia Minor. 

Tradition had always identified this hill as the site of ancient Troy. Schliemann's discoveries and those of later explorers proved that on the same site at Hissarlik at least nine successive cities had come into existence, flourished, and passed away. The sixth city in order from the bottom was probably the one of which Homer sang. It had powerful walls defended by towers, well-fortified gates, and palaces of stone. 

The marks of fire throughout the ruins indicate that the city must have been destroyed by a great conflagration. 

Schliemann's excavations at Mycena and Tiryns. The remarkable disclosures at Troy encouraged Schliemann to excavate other Homeric sites. At Mycenæ he laid bare a number of rock-hewn graves, containing the skeletons of men, women, and children. The faces of the dead had been covered with thin masks of gold, and their bodies had been decked with gold diadems, bracelets, and pendants. The other funeral offerings included gold rings, silver vases, and a variety of bronze weapons. It is clear that these were the graves of wealthy and powerful rulers. At Tiryns, near

Mycenae, Schliemann uncovered the ruins of an extensive structure with gateways, open courts, and closed apartments. 

It contained separate quarters for men and women, a series of storerooms for provisions, and such a modern convenience as a bathroom with pipes and drains. 

Evans's excavations at Cnossus. Excavations in Crete have been equally important and fully as spectacular. 

Shortly after 1900 Sir Arthur Evans began his work at Cnossus, the ancient capital of the Cretans. He found the remains of an enormous palace, with numerous courts, passages, and rooms, in which it is difficult not to lose one's way. 

Here is the royal council chamber with the throne on which the king once sat. Here are the royal storerooms, still filled with huge earthenware jars for the storage of provisions. A great number of brilliant pictures hunting scenes, landscapes, portraits of men and women-cover the palace walls. At one of the main entrances the visitor sees a row of

The Ægean Age

Ægean civilization. These discoveries in the Ægean area enable us to place another venerable center of civilized life by the side of Babylonia and Egypt. As early as 3000 B.C. the inhabitants of the Ægean were giving up the use of stone tools and weapons for those of metal. Copper and then

Greece bronze came into general use, as is shown by the excavations. 

The five centuries between 1600 and 1100 B.C. seem to have

The Ægean peoples were no longer wandering hunters or herdsmen, but settled farmers. 

They lived in villages and cities, where the frowning fortress of the chief or king looked down on the humble dwellings of common men. The monarch was doubtless a despot, whose subjects and slaves toiled to build the great palaces and tombs. If life was hard and cheerless for them, it must have been pleasant enough for court ladies and gentlemen, who occupied luxurious apartments, wore fine clothing and jewelry, and enjoyed such exhibitions as bull-leaping and the contests of pugilists.

Ægean art. Ægean architects raised imposing palaces of hewn and squared stone. 

The one at Cnossus in Crete and the stronghold at Tiryns were equipped with tile other in her lap. The water-pipes, bathrooms, and other modern date of the picture is conveniences. Ægean artists made wall paintings, plaster reliefs, fine carvings in stone, and porcelain vases decorated with plant and animal forms. They carved ivory, engraved gems, and inlaid metals. It was doubtless from their Ægean forerunners that the Greeks derived some of their artistic genius. about 1400 B.C.

Ægean writing. The Ægeans had a highly developed system of writing. The explorations in Crete show that its inhabitants had passed from picture writing to sound writing. 

The palace at Cnossus contained several thousand clay tablets with inscriptions in a language as yet unread. About seventy characters were in common use. They probably denote syllables and indicate a decided advance over both 

Egyptian and Babylonian scripts.

Crete was mistress of the seas, and her merchants controlled the trade of the Mediterranean long before the Phœnicians (p. 86).

Downfall of Ægean civilization. Ægean civilization was confined mainly to seafaring peoples; consequently it did not extend very far into Europe. Even the interior of Greece remained the home of barbarous tribes, who had not yet learned to build cities, to create beautiful works of art, or to traffic on the seas. Possibly it was these barbarians who, about 1100 B.C., destroyed the palace at Cnossus and brought about the downfall of Ægean civilization. 

30. THE GREEKS 

Invaders of Greece. Long before the downfall of Ægean civilization various tribes of barbarians moved southward into the Greek peninsula. These invaders were tall, lightcomplexioned, fair-haired, and blue-eyed, as are the inhabitants of northern Europe today. Physically they offered a sharp contrast to the short-statured and dark-skinned Ægean peoples. These invaders lived a nomadic life as hunters and herdsmen. When the grasslands became insufficient for the support of their sheep and cattle, they began to move gradually southward into the Danube valley and thence through the many passes of the Balkans into Greece. They did not stop even at the southern limits of Greece but crossed to Crete and other Ægean islands and to the western shore of 

Asia Minor.

Formation of the Greek people. The principal tribes which invaded Greece were the Achæans, the Dorians, and the Ionians. Armed with iron weapons, they gained a speedy victory over the bronze-using natives. The invaders probably in

Greece some instances exterminated or enslaved the natives; more often, perhaps, they settled peacefully among them. As successive tribes invaded the peninsula they intermingled with one another and with the conquered natives. The result of this intermingling was the Greek people. It must not be supposed, however, that this fusion erased all characteristics of the original tribes. In fact, there was a surprising persistence of differences. These tribal differences, together with the isolation caused by geographic features, account to some extent for the lack of unity among the Greeks. 

The Homeric Age. Several hundred years elapsed between the end of the Ægean civilization and the beginning of historic times in the Greek world, about 750 B.C. This period is called the Homeric Age because our information about it comes primarily from the Iliad and the Odyssey. The former tells the story of a Greek expedition led by Agamemnon, king of Mycenæ, against Troy; the latter relates the wanderings of the Greek hero Odysseus on his return from Troy.

These two poems were probably composed in Ionia, and were attributed by the Greeks to a blind bard named Homer. 

Many modern scholars, however, regard them as the work of several generations of poets. 

Culture in the Homeric Age. The Iliad and the Odyssey show how rude was the culture of the Homeric Age, as compared with the splendid Ægean civilization which it displaced. 

The Greeks at this time had not wholly abandoned the life of shepherds for that of farmers. Wealth still consisted chiefly of flocks and herds. Nearly every freeman, however, owned a little plot of land on which he cultivated grain and cared for his orchard and vineyard. Though iron was used for weapons and farm implements, bronze continued to be the commoner and cheaper metal. Coined money was unknown; consequently there was little commerce. People depended upon Phoenician merchants for articles which they could not themselves produce. There were no skilled workmen, or architects, or artists such as flourished in the earlier Ægean Age. Social life was very simple. Princes tended

Early Greek Religion 

109 flocks and built houses; princesses carried water and washed clothes. Agamemnon, Odysseus, and other heroes were not ashamed to be their own butchers and cooks. Warfare was constant and cruel. Piracy ranked as an honorable occupation. Murders were frequent. The murderer had to dread, not a public trial and punishment, but rather the private vengeance of the kinsmen of the victim. On the other hand, both the Iliad and the Odyssey contain many charming descriptions of family life and portray heroes with many admirable traits. 

31. EARLY GREEK RELIGION 

Greek deities. The Homeric Greeks and their successors worshiped various gods and goddesses. Twelve of the most important deities formed a select council, which was supposed to meet on snow-crowned Mount Olympus in northern

Thessaly. The head of this council was Zeus, "father of gods and men," as Homer calls him. He gathered the clouds in storms and hurled the thunderbolt. His brother, Poseidon, ruled the sea. His wife, Hera, presided over the life of women and especially over the sacred rites of marriage. His son, Apollo, a god of light, who warded off darkness and evil, became the ideal of manly beauty and the patron of music, poetry, and the healing art. Athena, a goddess who sprang full-grown from the forehead of Zeus, embodied the ideal of wisdom and all womanly virtues. Some of the deities seem to have been simply personifications of natural phenomena. 

In another sense they were really magnified men and women with human passions and appetites, but endowed with more than human power and with the gift of immortality. 

Ideas of the future life. Greek ideas of the future life were dismal to an extreme. All men, it was thought, went down after death to Hades and passed there a shadowy, joyless existence. Thus the Greeks did not conceive, as we do, a future life in which the good are rewarded and the evil are punished.

Greece

Oracles. The Greeks believed that communications from the gods were received at certain places called oracles. The oldest of Greek oracles was that of Zeus at Dodona in Epirus. 

Here the priests professed to read the divine will in the rustling leaves of an oak tree sacred to 

Zeus. At Delphi the god Apollo was supposed to speak through a prophetess. The words which she uttered when "possessed" by the deity were interpreted by the attendant priests and delivered to inquirers. The fame of the Delphic oracle spread throughout Greece and reached foreign lands. 

Every year great numbers of people visited Delphi. Statesmen wished to learn the fate of their political schemes; ambassadors sent by kings and cities asked advice as to weighty matters of peace and war; and colonists sought directions as to the best country in which to settle. The oracle lasted for over a thousand years. It was still original by Myron, a sculp- honored at the close of the fourth century A.D., when a Roman emperor, after the adoption of Christianity, silenced it forever. Jeon www

The Olympian games. At an early period the Greeks manifested a great love for athletics. Their most famous athletic festivals were those in honor of Zeus at Olympia in the city-state of Elis. The Olympian games took place every fourth year,¹ in midsummer, and lasted for five days. A sacred truce was proclaimed for an entire month, so that the thousands of spectators from every part of the Greek world might arrive 1 The first recorded celebration of the games occurred in 776 B.C., and from this year all Greek dates were reckoned.

The Greek City-States 

111 and depart in safety. No one was allowed to participate in the games unless he was of Greek blood and free from crime. 

The games began with contests in running. There was a short dash through the stadium (about 210 yards), a quartermile race, and a longer race of two or three miles. Other contests included the broad jump, hurling the discus, throwing the javelin, wrestling, boxing, horse races, and chariot races.

Influence of the Olympian games. The Olympian games were religious in character, because the display of manly strength was thought to be a spectacle most pleasing to the gods. The winning athlete received a wreath of wild olive at

Olympia, and at home he enjoyed the gifts and reverence of his fellow citizens. The thousands of visitors at the festival gave to it the character of a great fair, where merchants set up their shops and sold their wares. Poets recited their lines, orators delivered their speeches before admiring audiences, and artists exhibited their masterpieces. Heralds read treaties recently framed between Greek cities, in order to have them widely known. The Olympian games thus did much to preserve a sense of fellowship among Greek communities. 

32. THE GREEK CITY-STATES 

The city-state. Following the Homeric Age, the Greeks slowly built up the city-states for which they have become noted in history. A Greek city included not only the area within its walls, but also the surrounding district where many citizens lived. Since these Greek cities with their surrounding districts were independent and self-governing, they are very aptly called city-states. They could declare war, conclude treaties, and make alliances. Such city-states were not large. Athens, at the climax of her power, may have had a quarter of a million inhabitants; Thebes, Argos, and

Corinth, the next largest places, probably had between fifty and one hundred thousand; Sparta probably had less than

Greece fifty thousand. These figures include all classes of the population-citizens, slaves, and resident foreigners. 

The citizens. The citizens of a Greek city-state formed a very compact and patriotic group. They believed themselves to be descended from a common ancestor and they shared a common worship of the god or hero to whom they looked for protection. These ties of religion and supposed kinship made citizenship a unique privilege which a person enjoyed only by birth and which he lost upon removing to another city-state. 

Thus, outside his own city-state he was only a foreigner lacking legal rights — a man without a country. 

Government of the city-state. From the Iliad and the 

Odyssey we obtain some idea of how the city-state was governed. The government consisted of three parts, the king, the council, and the assembly. The king, "the shepherd of the people," as Homer calls him, did not possess absolute power as in Egypt or Persia; he was more or less controlled by a council of nobles. This council helped him in judgment and sacrifice, followed him to war, and occupied the principal offices. Both king and nobles were obliged to consult the common people, who formed the assembly. It acted on matters of great importance, such as making war. The citizens were summoned to meet in the market place, where they shouted their assent or disapproved by silence when proposals were laid before them. The assembly became more important as political institutions developed among the Greeks. 

Political changes in the city-state. The Greek city-states were constantly experimenting with different forms of government. In some of them, for example, Thebes and Corinth, the nobles became strong enough to abolish the kingship altogether. Monarchy, the rule of one, thus gave way to aristocracy, the rule of the nobles. In Sparta and Argos the kings were not driven out, but their authority was much lessened. 

Some city-states came under the control of usurpers, whom the Greeks called "tyrants." A tyrant was a man who gained supreme power by force or guile and governed autocratically. 

Still other city-states, of which Athens formed the most con-

33. EXPANSION OF THE GREEKS Age of colonization. Following the Homeric Age the 

Greeks continued to increase in numbers. The surplus population needed to find an outlet. Beginning about 750 B.C. the city-states began to plant colonies along the shores of the 

Mediterranean and of the Black Sea. The great age of colonization covered the period from 750 to 500 B.C. 

Motives for colonization. Trade was one motive for colonization. The Greeks, like the Phoenicians, were able to realize large profits by exchanging their manufactured goods for the food and raw materials of other countries. Land hunger was another motive. The poor soil of Greece could not support many inhabitants, and, as population increased, emigration offered the only means of relieving the pressure of numbers. 

A third motive was political and social unrest. The citystates at this period contained many men of adventurous disposition, who were ready to seek in foreign lands a refuge from the oppression of nobles or tyrants. They hoped to find abroad more freedom than they had at home. 

Nature of colonization. A Greek colony was not simply a trading post; it was a center of Greek life. The colonists continued to be Greeks in language, customs, and religion; they called themselves "men away from home." Mother city and daughter colony traded with each other and in time of danger helped each other. The sacred fire carried from the public hearth of the old community to the new settlement formed a symbol of the close ties binding them together. 

Colonies in the North and Northeast. The Greeks established many colonies along the coast of the northern Ægean and on both sides of the passages leading into the Black Sea. Among these settlements was Byzantium, upon the site of Constantinople (now called Istanbul). The colonies

Expansion of the Greeks 115 which fringed the Black Sea were centers for the supply of fish, wood, grain, meats, wool, and slaves. The large profits to be gained by trade made the Greeks willing to live in what was then a wild and inhospitable region. 

AN ATHENIAN TRIREME 

Bas-relief found on the Acropolis of Athens. Dates from about 400 B.C. The part of the relief preserved shows the waist of the vessel, with the uppermost of the three banks of rowers. Only the oars of the two lower banks are seen. 

Colonies in the West. The Greeks could feel more at home in southern Italy, where the genial climate, clear air, and sparkling sea recalled their native land. They made so many settlements in this region that it came to be known as Great Greece (Magna Græcia). Among the important cities in southern Italy were Cumæ, Tarentum, Regium, and Messina. The most important colony in Sicily was Syracuse, founded by the city-state of Corinth. The Greeks were unable to occupy all Sicily because the Carthaginians had already established colonies in the western part of the island. 

Other Mediterranean colonies. The Carthaginians also prevented the Greeks from gaining much of a foothold in Corsica and Sardinia and on the coast of Spain. The Greeks did settle, however, at Massilia (Marseilles) at the mouth of the Rhône. In Egypt the principal Greek colony was Naucratis, in the delta of the Nile. Other colonies were located on the southern coast of Asia Minor and in northern Africa, west of the mouth of the Nile. 

Results of colonization. Greek colonial expansion formed one of the most significant movements in ancient history,

Greece because it spread Greek culture over so many lands. To distinguish themselves from the foreigners, or "barbarians,” about them, the Greeks began to give themselves the common name of Hellenes. Hellas, their country, came to include all the territory possessed by Hellenic peoples. The 

Greeks, henceforth, were no longer confined within the narrow limits of the Ægean. Colonization laid the basis for the spread of the rich civilization which the Greeks were about to achieve. 

34. SPARTA AND ATHENS 

Rise of Sparta. Before the colonization period was over, some of the city-states had shown marked characteristics of leadership. The two most prominent city-states were Sparta and Athens. In the southern part of the Peloponnesus (the southern peninsula of Greece) was Sparta, which had been settled by the Dorian invaders. About 900 B.C. Sparta was a flourishing city-state, much like other Greek city-states. 

Not being on the seacoast, it maintained itself largely by agriculture. The necessity of extending its area led it into conflict with neighboring cities, and Sparta slowly developed its most marked characteristic — its militarism. By 500 B.C. its power extended over most of the Peloponnesus. Their concentration upon conquest and agriculture kept the Spartans from developing industry and commerce. Neither did they make any significant contributions to art, literature, or philosophy. 

Government of Sparta. The Spartan government was a monarchy in form, but since there were always two kings reigning at once, neither could become very powerful. The real management of affairs was in the hands of five men, called ephors, who were elected every year by the citizens. 

The ephors accompanied the kings in war and directed their actions; guided the deliberations of the council of nobles and public assembly; superintended the education of children; and exercised a paternal oversight of everybody.

Sparta and Athens 117 Life in Sparta. Spartan education had a single purposeto produce obedient citizens who would be good soldiers. 

A sound body formed the first essential. A Spartan father was required to submit his son, soon after birth, to an inspection by the elders of his tribe. If they found the child puny or ill-shaped, they ordered it to be left on the mountain side, to perish from exposure. At the age of seven, a boy was taken from his parents' home and placed in a military school. Here he was trained in marching, sham fighting, and gymnastics. 

He learned to sing warlike songs and in conversation to express himself in the fewest possible words. 

Above all, he learned to endure hardship without complaint. He went barefoot and wore only a single garment, winter and summer. He slept on a bed of rushes. Every year he and his comrades had to submit to a public flogging, and the hero was the lad who could bear the torture longest without giving a sign of pain. The youth became a warrior on reaching twenty years of age. He did not live at home, but passed his time in barracks, as a member of a military mess to which he contributed his proper share of food, wine, and money. At the age of thirty the Spartan became a full citizen and a member of the popular assembly. He was then compelled to marry in order to raise children for the state. Marriage did not free him from attendance at the public meals, the drill ground, and the gymnasium. A Spartan, in fact, enjoyed little home life until his sixtieth year, when he became an elder and retired from actual service. 

All the period of manhood was thus claimed by the strict, harsh discipline of a soldier's career. As a sarcastic Athenian once remarked, "A Spartan's life is so unpleasant that it is no wonder he throws it away lightly in battle."

Athens as a city-state. Very different was life at Athens, the city-state that grew up in the district of Attica in central Greece. The inhabitants of the Attic towns and villages gave up their separate governments and became members of the one city-state of Athens. Henceforth a man was an 

Athenian citizen, no matter in what part of Attica he lived.

Greece

Draco's code. The kings of Athens in time lost their power to the nobles, whose rule bore harshly on the common people. 

Then arose in succession three lawgivers, who did much to advance democracy at Athens. Draco provided the Athenians with a written body of laws, to replace the unwritten customs which the judges (who were all nobles) interpreted so as to favor their own class. Draco's code was very severe, the penalty for most offenses, even the smallest theft, being death. The Athenians used to declare that the code had been written "not in ink, but in blood."

Reforms of Solon. Solon, who followed 

Draco, improved the condition of the Attic peasants by canceling the debts which they owed their landlords, by restoring to freedom all those who had been enslaved for debt, and by limiting the amount of land which a noble might henceforth own. He also encouraged industry and trade by attracting to Attica skilled workingmen from abroad. Finally, he admitted even the poorest citizens to the popular assembly, where they could vote for magistrates and take part in public affairs. Solon thus gave the common people a greater share in the government and fostered the democratic movement at Athens. His name has come down to us as a synonym for a wise legislator. 

Clisthenes. After Solon, Athens was ruled for half a century by tyrants, but these were finally driven out. A third lawgiver, named 

Clisthenes, now appeared on the scene. He carried further the democratic movement begun by Draco and Solon and gave to the Athenians the stable government under which they lived for nearly two man.

Persia Attacks the Greek City-States 

119 centuries. Clisthenes is said, also, to have established the practice known as ostracism. Every year, if necessary, the people might by their votes declare any prominent man dangerous to the state and banish (ostracize) him for ten years.

Democratic Athens. The city-state of Athens thus stood in marked contrast to Sparta. Athens, by 500 B.C., had rid itself of kings and tyrants, had overthrown the power of the nobles, and had created the first really democratic government in antiquity. We shall describe later the Athenian democracy (p. 126) and set forth, also, some of the contributions of the Athenian genius to the artistic and intellectual life of mankind. 

35. PERSIA ATTACKS THE GREEK CITY-STATES 

The Persian menace. The growth of the Persian Empire (p. 90) was a threat to Greek independence. Cyrus the Great had conquered Asia Minor and thus became the overlord of the Ionian Greeks on the eastern side of the Ægean. Cambyses, by conquering Egypt and Cyprus, had brought still more Greeks within the limits of the Persian Empire. When 

Darius I ascended the throne, he determined to extend Persian control to the Danube River. He accordingly sent an expedition against the warlike Scythians on the lower Danube. In connection with the Scythian expedition the Persians gained control of the wild tribes of Macedonia and Thrace, and of the Greek settlements about the western end of the Black Sea. Thus the Persians were slowly annexing territories inhabited by Greeks and were forming a chain of encircling states.

The Ionian revolt, 499-493 B.C. Not long after the Persian expedition against the Scythians, the Ionian cities of Asia Minor revolted against Persia. The Ionians sought the help of Sparta, the chief military state of Greece. The 

Spartans refused to take part in the war, but the Athenians, who realized the menace to Greece from the Persian advance,

Greece aided their Ionian kinsmen with both ships and soldiers. 

The allied forces captured and destroyed Sardis, the chief city of the Persians in Asia Minor. The rest of the Asiatic 

Greeks now joined the Ionians, and even Thrace threw off the Persian yoke. These successes, however, were only temporary. The revolting cities, unable to hold out against the vast resources possessed by the Persian king, again fell one by one into his hands.

First Persian expedition. Darius soon made ready to reassert Persian supremacy in the Balkan peninsula and to punish Athens for her share in the Ionian revolt. A large army, commanded by Mardonius, the son-in-law of the 

Persian monarch, soon reconquered Thrace and received the submission of Macedonia. But the Persian fleet, on which the army depended for supplies, was wrecked off the promontory of Mount Athos, and the attempt to punish Athens failed. 

Second Persian expedition. The partial failure of the first Persian expedition only aroused Darius to renewed exertions. Two years later another fleet, bearing perhaps twenty thousand soldiers, set out from Ionia to Greece. It sailed straight across the Ægean and landed on the plain of 

Marathon, twenty-six miles from Athens.

Battle of Marathon, 490 B.C. The situation of the Athe nians seemed desperate. They had scarcely ten thousand men with whom to face an army at least twice as large and hitherto invincible. The Spartans promised support, but delayed sending troops at the critical moment. Nevertheless, the Athenians decided to take the offensive. Their able general, Miltiades, believed that the Persians, however numerous, were no match for heavy-armed Greek soldiers. 

The Athenians crossed the plain at the quickstep and in the face of a shower of arrows drove the Persians to their ships. 

The Persians then sailed for home, with their errand of vengeance unfulfilled. 

Third Persian expedition. Ten years after Marathon

The Greek soldiers, with their long spears, huge shields, and heavy swords, were completely successful. These two engagements practically ended The victorious Greeks. The Persian wars were much more than a military struggle between an empire and a people. 

They were a struggle between East and West; between 

Oriental despotism and Occidental democracy. Had Persia won, the fresh, vigorous Western civilization then being developed by Athens and other Greek states would have been submerged, perhaps for ages, under the influx of Eastern ideas and customs. The Greek victory saved Europe for better things. It was a victory for human freedom. 

36. THE RISE OF ATHENS 

Greatness of Athens. The repulse of Persia brought honor and leadership to Athens. The interval of seventy-five years between the close of the Persian wars in 479 B.C. and the end of the Peloponnesian wars in 404 B.C. (p. 131) was the great period of Athenian ascendancy. During this period the city produced great statesmen, built up an empire, established democracy, developed commerce, and became the intellectual and artistic center of the world. Even when wars brought

Greece its material greatness to an end, it still maintained its artistic and intellectual leadership.

Athenian leaders. Following the Persian wars, Themistocles remained the outstanding figure in Athens. He rebuilt the walls around Athens and included a large area wherein the people could find safety in case of attack. The port of 

Piræus was repaired and enlarged in order to handle the growing commerce of Athens. Aristides, who next assumed the leadership, formed the Delian League to guarantee continued protection against Persia. The next leader, Cimon, extended the power and influence of the league. The greatest Athenian leader, however, was Pericles. So marked was his influence upon Greece that the period of his leadership (461–429 B.C.) is often called the Age of Pericles. He was not only a political and military genius, but an orator, a builder, and a promoter of art, poetry, and culture in general. 

Let us see how Athens developed under these leaders. 

The Delian League. In order to remove the danger of another attack from Persia, the Athenians formed a defensive league with the Greeks in Asia Minor and on the Ægean islands. It included, finally, over two hundred city-states. 

Some of the wealthier ones agreed to provide ships and crews for the allied fleet. All the other members made their contributions in money, allowing Athens to build and equip the ships. Athenian officials collected the revenues, which were placed for protection in the temple of Apollo on the is land of Delos hence the name, Delian League. 

Athens founds an empire. The Delian League formed the most promising step which the Greeks had yet taken in the direction of federal government. It might have developed into a United States of Greece, but the Athenians preferred to convert it into an empire. They used the naval force that had been formed by the contributions of the league as a means of bringing its members into dependence on Athens. 

The Delian communities were compelled to accept governments like those of Athens, to endure the presence of Athenian garrisons in their midst, to furnish soldiers for Athenian

Greece armies, and to pay an annual tribute. Even the common treasury of the league was transferred from Delos to Athens. 

What had started out as a voluntary association of free and independent states thus ended by becoming, to all intents and purposes, an Athenian Empire. The map on the preceding page shows how extensive it was about the middle of the fifth century B.C.

Athenian democracy. Of all the contributions of Athens perhaps the greatest one is the ideal of democracy. The 

Athenians had tried kings, nobles, and tyrants, and they came to the conclusion that no citizen was good enough to govern another citizen. They therefore tried democracy. 

Under this system every citizen, whether rich or poor, whether a noble or a commoner, had an opportunity to hold office, to serve in the courts, and to take part in legislation. 

Hence the Athenian popular assembly and courts were open to all respectable citizens. (It must be remembered, however, that by no means all of the inhabitants of Athens were citizens.) The offices, also, were made very numerousfourteen hundred in all so that they might be distributed as widely as possible. Most of them were annual, and some could not be held twice by the same person. Election to office was usually by lot. This arrangement did away with favoritism and allowed the poor man a chance in politics, as well as the man of wealth or noble birth. 

The Assembly. The center of Athenian democracy was the Assembly. All citizens who had reached twenty years of age were members. The number present at a meeting rarely exceeded more than five thousand, because most of the citizens lived outside the walls in the country districts of Attica. Forty regular meetings were held every year. These took place on the slopes of the hill called the Pnyx. A speaker before the Assembly faced a difficult audience. It was ready to yell its disapproval of his advice, to mock him if he mispronounced a word, or to drown his voice with shouts and whistles. The debates naturally became a training school for orators. Whatever the decision of the Assembly, it was final. This great popular gathering settled questions of war and peace, sent out military and naval expeditions, authorized public expenditures, and had general control over the affairs of Athens and her dependencies. 

The Ten Generals. The Assembly was assisted in the conduct of public business by many officers and magistrates, among whom the Ten Generals held the leading place.

No representative system. Democracy, then, reached its height in ancient Athens. The people ruled, and they ruled

Greece directly. Every citizen had some active part in politics. 

Such a system worked well in the management of a small city-state like Athens. It proved to be less successful in the government of an empire. The subject communities of the 

Delian League were unrepresented at Athens. They had no one to speak for them in the Assembly or before the popular courts. Their interests, therefore, were always put below those of the Athenians. We shall notice the same absence of a representative system in republican Rome (p. 192). 

Industrial Athens. Athens contained many skilled workmen, for the city was an important manufacturing center. 

THE OLIVE HARVEST 

The average rate of wages was low. 

In spite of cheap food and modest requirements for clothing and shelter, it must have been difficult for the artisan to earn a comfortable living. Outside of Athens, in the country districts of Attica, lived the peasants, whose farms pro- Painting on a Greek wine jar of duced the olives, grapes, and figs for which Attica was famous. the sixth century B.C. 

Honey was another important product.

Commercial Athens. Athens now formed the chief commercial city of the Greek world. "The fruits of the whole earth," said Pericles, "flow in upon us; so that we enjoy the goods of other countries as freely as of our own." Exports of wine and olive oil, pottery, metal wares, and objects of art were sent out from Piræus to every region of the Mediterranean. The imports from the Black Sea region, Thrace, and the Ægean included such commodities as salt, dried fish, wool, timber, hides, and, above all, great quantities of wheat. 

Athens was able to feed all her people only by bringing in food from abroad. To make sure that in time of war there should be no interruption of food supplies, the Athenians built the so-called Long Walls between the city and its port of Piræus. Henceforth they felt secure from attack as long as their navy ruled the Ægean.

The Rise of Athens 

129 Artistic Athens. The wealth which the Athenians accumulated by trade and industry, together with the tribute paid by the Delian League, enabled them to adorn their city with beautiful buildings, sculptures, and other works of art. The finest monuments arose on the Acropolis, the hill overlooking Athens. Access to this steep rock was gained through a superb entrance gate, or Propylæa, constructed to resemble the front of a temple with columns and pediment. A huge bronze statue of the goddess Athena, by the sculptor Phidias, stood just beyond the Propylæa.

On the crest of the Acropolis were two temples. The smaller one was named after Erechtheus, a legendary Athenian king; the larger one, called the Parthenon, was dedicated to Athena. Because of its perfection of construction and admirable proportions, it is justly regarded as an architectural masterpiece.

Athens, the "School of Hellas."

Athens at this time was the heart of Greek intellectual life. The greatest poets, historians, philosophers, and orators of Greece were 

Athenians, either by birth or by residence. There is, therefore, no exaggeration in the proud words which Pericles applied to Athens in the fifth century B.C. "Our city," he said, "is equally admirable in peace and in war. We are lovers of the beautiful, yet simple in our tastes, and we cultivate the mind without loss of manliness. Wealth we employ, not for talk and ostentation, but when there is a real use for it. To acknowledge poverty with us is no disgrace; the true disgrace is in doing nothing to avoid it. 

An Athenian citizen does not neglect the state because he takes care of his own household; and even those of us who are engaged in business have a very fair idea of politics.

Greece

We alone regard a man who shows no interest in public affairs, not as a harmless, but as a useless, character..

In short, Athens is the school of Hellas." 

Slavery. It must not be forgotten that even this noble city exhibited some of the defects which characterized every community in ancient Greece. In the first place, Athenian civilization owed much to the existence of slavery. The number of slaves was so great and their labor so cheap that we may think of them as taking the place of modern machines. Slaves did most of the work on large estates owned by wealthy men, toiled in mines and quarries, and served as oarsmen on ships. The system of slavery enabled many an Athenian to lead a life of leisure, but it made manual labor seem ignoble and tended to prevent the rise of the poorer citizens to positions of responsibility and trust. 

Class rule. In the second place, not all the freemen of 

Athens to say nothing of the slaves - were citizens. The law restricted citizenship to those freemen who were the sons of an Athenian father (himself a citizen) and an Athenian mother. Foreign merchants and artisans living in Athens could not vote, could not buy land in Attica, and could not legally marry Athenian women. 

37. WARS AMONG THE CITY-STATES 

Lack of harmony. The Persian wars brought about a temporary unity of purpose among some of the Greek citystates. The Delian League was also a unifying force. 

As soon as the Persian menace had passed, however, the city-states resumed their old quarrels. A common blood, language, and religion, which ordinarily promote unity, failed to unite the Greeks. The larger and stronger city-states would not let the smaller ones remain independent. This tendency to dominate and annex was the fatal defect in the system of small, self-governing city-states. 

Athens against Sparta. The two leading opponents among the city-states were Athens and Sparta. Athens, supreme

Wars among the City-States 

131 upon the sea, and Sparta, the chief military power in the Peloponnesus, were rivals for the leadership of Greece. When 

Athens tried to become also a military power, Sparta declared war. The struggle continued at intervals for about fifteen years. Finally, in 445 B.C., a treaty was made by which Athens recognized Sparta's supremacy on land, and Sparta recognized the Athenian Empire and Athenian control of the sea. Near the end of the Age of Pericles the smoldering fires of distrust and jealousy again flamed into open conflict. "And at that time the youth of Sparta and Athens were numerous; they had never seen war, and were therefore very willing to take up arms.' 99 Peloponnesian War. This second Peloponnesian war arose out of a dispute between Athens and Corinth, an ally of Sparta, and, next to Athens, the chief commercial power in Greece. Athens had already won the Ægean trade from 

Corinth and was now reaching out for her Italian and Sicilian trade. The Athenians even went so far as to interfere in a quarrel between Corinth and one of her colonies. This interference aroused the resentment of the Corinthians, who appealed to Sparta for aid.

First stage of the war. The first stage of the war was indecisive. A strong Peloponnesian force invaded Attica, and the people congregated within the Long Walls. A terrible plague, whose spread was facilitated by the crowded conditions within the city, broke out, and about one-third of the population died. Among the dead was the matchless leader, Pericles. Thus, almost at the outset of the struggle, the Athenians were deprived of the only leader under whom they had any great chance for success. Athens had difficulty in keeping her allies in line and failed to gain any decisive advantage. In 421 B.C. a truce was made between 

Sparta and Athens. Unfortunately each had made entangling agreements with certain allies, who failed to observe the truce; consequently it lasted for only a few years. 

Last stage of the war. In 415 B.C. Athens sent a great expedition to Sicily to capture Syracuse, an ally of Corinth

Greece and Sparta. The expedition consisted of over three hundred vessels and 27,000 men. The Athenians "were absolutely annihilated - both army and fleet — and of the many thousands who went away only a handful ever saw their homes again." Athens never recovered from this terrible blow. The Spartans quickly renewed the contest, now with the highest hopes of success. The Athenians had to guard their city against the invader night and day; their slaves deserted to the enemy; and they themselves could do no farming except under the protection of the walls of the city. 

For supplies they had to depend entirely on their ships. 

Nevertheless, the Athenians kept up the struggle for nearly ten years. Finally, the Spartans overcame the Athenian fleet near Ægospotami on the Dardanelles. On the night that the news of this terrible disaster reached Athens no man slept. 

They knew that the end had come, for the treasury was empty, the able-bodied men had perished, and the fleet was gone. The Spartans pressed in upon the city, and famine added the finishing touch. The terms were harsh. Athens had to destroy its Long Walls, raze its fortifications at Piræus, surrender the rest of its ships, give up its empire, and, perhaps bitterest of all, acknowledge the supremacy of Sparta.

Further struggles. Sparta's victory over Athens enabled it to assume the leadership of Greece. The city-states soon found that they had exchanged the mild and enlightened sway of Athens for the brutal despotism of Sparta. The revolt of Thebes, a city-state in central Greece, under its great general, Epaminondas, turned into a glorious victory on the battlefield of Leuctra in 371 B.C. For a brief time

Thebes became supreme, but it also raised up enemies. 

Even Athens joined its old enemy Sparta to bring about the downfall of Thebes, an event that was accomplished by the battle of Mantinea in 362 B.C. The long years of fighting had exhausted the city-states. They had demonstrated their inability either to unite or to respect one another's independence. Their conflicts had thus prepared the way for a con-

The Rise of Macedonia 

133 quering people from the north who were strong enough to impose their will upon the city-states. 

38. THE RISE OF MACEDONIA 

The Macedonians. North of Thessaly was a rough region inhabited by the Macedonians, distant cousins of the Greeks. 

By commerce and war they had been brought within the circle of Greek influence. Their kings had also cultivated 

Greek customs and manners. Macedonia had the advantage of being a united state under a single ruler. The lack of harmony among the city-states gave Macedonia its opportunity, and, when Philip II became its king in 359 B.C., he determined to conquer and unite the Greeks. 

Philip II, 359-336 B.C. Philip II was one of the most remarkable men of antiquity. He was not a stranger to the land which he purposed to conquer. Part of his boyhood had been passed as a hostage at Thebes, where he learned the art of war as the Greeks had perfected it and also gained an insight into Greek politics. The distracted condition of 

Greece offered Philip an opportunity to secure for Macedonia the position of supremacy which neither Athens, Sparta, nor Thebes had been able to hold. He seized the opportunity. 

Philip's army. Philip created a standing army of professional soldiers and improved their methods of fighting. 

Hitherto, battles had been fought mainly by soldiers massed in rows, thus forming a phalanx. Philip retained the phalanx, only he deepened it and gave to the rear men longer spears. The business of the phalanx was to keep the front of the opposing army engaged, while horsemen rode into the enemy's flanks. This reliance on masses of cavalry to win a victory was something new in warfare. Another novel feature consisted in the use on the battlefield of catapults, a kind of artillery able to throw darts and huge stones into the enemy's ranks. All these different arms working together made a war machine which was the most formidable in the ancient world until the days of the Roman legion.

Greece expo adi 

Demosthenes. Philip's conquests in northern Greece excited mixed feelings at Athens, Thebes, and Sparta. He had many influential friends in these cities, some paid agents, but others honest men who favored Macedonian headship as the only means of uniting Greece. Those opposed to Philip found their foremost representative in the famous Athenian orator, Demosthenes. He loved Athens with passionate devotion, and Athens, he urged, should become the leader of Greece in a second war for independence. 

His stirring speeches against Philip have given us the word "philippic," meaning a spirited speech directed against some person. bate tols 1000 erf 720 of boc

Battle of Chæronea, 338 B.C. The stirring appeals of Demosthenes met little response, until Philip entered central Greece at the head of his army. 

Athens, Thebes, and some Peloponnesian states then formed a defensive alliance against him. The decisive battle took place at Charonea, in Boeotia. On that fatal field the well-drilled and seasoned troops of Macedonia, led by a master of the art of war, overcame the citizen-soldiers of Greece. The victory made Philip master of all the Greek states, except Sparta, which still preserved its liberty. It was the victory of an absolute monarchy over free, selfpressive of the orator's governing commonwealths. The citystates had had their day. They never again became first-rate powers in history.

39. ALEXANDER THE GREAT BUILDS AN EMPIRE 

The youthful Alexander.

He had Aristotle, the most learned man in Greece, for his tutor. This great teacher inspired him with a lifelong admiration for Greek civilization.

300 500 XeIA ander destroyed an empire which had held the Near East in subjection for two centuries. The myriads of the Persian king, under their numerous leaders, could not break the solid, unified phalanx of the well-drilled Greeks. 

Battle of Issus, 333 B.C. With his small but well-drilled army, Alexander set out from his capital at Pella and crossed into Asia Minor near the site of Troy. As you will note on the map above he passed through Sardis, Ephesus, and the southern part of Asia Minor. Wherever he met Persian troops he defeated them and soon drove the enemy from the western and southern parts of that peninsula. Meanwhile, Darius III, king of Persia, had assembled a large army and had advanced to the narrow plain of Issus, between the Syrian Mountains and the Mediterranean. Superiority in numbers counted for nothing in such cramped quarters. Alexander perceived this, and struck with all his force. After a stubborn resistance the Persians gave way, turned, and fled. The battle now became a massacre, and

The Macedonians poured in and Tyre fell before the onslaught. The great emporium of the Near East became a heap of ruins. 

Alexander in Egypt. From Tyre Alexander led his victorious troops southward through Palestine into Egypt. The 

Persian officials there offered little resistance, and the Egyp-

Greece tians themselves welcomed Alexander as a deliverer. He entered Memphis in triumph and then sailed down the Nile to its western mouth. Here he laid the foundations of the city of Alexandria, which replaced Tyre as a commercial metropolis. 

Battle of Arbela, 331 B.C. Alexander next turned eastward, crossed the Euphrates and Tigris, and near the old Assyrian town of Arbela again defeated the army of the Great King. The battle of Arbela decided the fate of the 

Persian Empire. Alexander had only to gather the fruits of victory. Babylon surrendered to him without a struggle, and Susa, the Persian capital, fell into his hands.

Alexander in Iran and India. Alexander had now overrun all the Persian territories except distant Iran and India. 

These regions were peopled by warlike tribes of a very different stamp from the effeminate Persians. Alexander might well have left them undisturbed, but he could never rest while there were still conquests to be made. Long marches and many battles were required to subdue the tribes about the Caspian and the inhabitants of the countries now known as Afghanistan and Russian Turkestan. Alexander next led his soldiers into the valley of the Indus and quickly added northwestern India to the Macedonian possessions. 

He then planned to press forward to the conquest of the Ganges valley, but his troops refused to go farther. They had had their fill of war. 

The return to Babylon. Alexander was of too adventurous a disposition to return by the way he had come. He built a fleet on the Indus and had it accompany the army down the river to its mouth. Alexander himself led the army by a long and toilsome march, through desert wastes, to Babylon.

That city became the capital of his empire. 

Death of Alexander, 323 B.C. The reign of Alexander was now nearly over. In 323 B.C., while planning expeditions against the Arabs, Carthage, and the Italian states, he suddenly sickened and died. He was not quite thirty-three years of age.

Alexander the Great Builds an Empire 

139 The Greeks in the Orient. The immediate result of Alexander's conquests was the disappearance of the barriers which had so long shut in the Oriental world. The Near 

East, until his day, was an almost unknown land. It now lay open to the spread of Greek civilization. In the wake of the Macedonian armies followed Greek philosophers and scientists, Greek architects and artists, Greek colonists, merchants, and artisans. Everywhere into that huge, inert, unprogressive Oriental world came the active and enterprising men of Greece. They brought their arts and culture and became the teachers of those whom they had called “barbarians."

Fusion of East and West. The ultimate result of Alexander's conquests was the fusion of East and West. He realized that his new empire must contain a place for Oriental, as well as for Greek and Macedonian, subjects. 

He welcomed Persian nobles to his court and placed them in positions of trust and honor. He organized the government of his provinces on a system which resembled that of Darius I (p. 91). He trained thousands of Persian soldiers to replace the worn-out veterans in his armies. He encouraged by liberal dowries mixed marriages between Macedonians and Orientals and himself wedded the daughter of the last Persian king. To hold his dominions together and provide centers of intercourse, he founded no less than seventy cities in Egypt, western Asia, central Asia, and India. Such measures as these show that Alexander had a mind of wide, cosmopolitan sympathies.

After Alexander. With Alexander the Great the history of Greece begins to merge into the history of the ancient world. We now follow, not the development of a single people, but the gradual spread of Greek customs and ideas and, in turn, their modification by contact with those of the Near East. Purely Greek, or Hellenic, culture became in this way Hellenistic culture.

40. THE HELLENISTIC AGE 

Nature of the Hellenistic Age. The Achæan, Dorian, and 

Ionian barbarians from the north had entered Greece and developed a civilization equaled by no peoples before them. 

Through colonization they had spread Greek culture. And finally when they were themselves conquered they proceeded to transmit their civilization to their conquerors and to all the peoples of the Near East. This third stage constituted the Hellenistic (as distinguished from the Hellenic) Age. It covered the period from the battle of Charonea in 338 B.C. to the conquest of Greece by Rome. 107

LIGHTHOUSE OF ALEXANDRIA (RESTORED) 

The island of Pharos, in the harbor of Alexandria, contained a lighthouse built about 

280 B.C.

It rose in three diminishing stages, the first being square, the second octagonal, and the third round, to a height of nearly four hundred feet. On the apex stood a statue. 

The lighthouse was considered by the ancients one of the "Seven Wonders" of the world. 

It collapsed (as the result of repeated earthquakes) in 1326 A.D. The minarets of Moslem mosques and spires of Christian churches are both derived from this famous structure. 

Hellenistic kingdoms. The empire created by Alexander did not survive him. It broke up almost immediately into a number of Hellenistic kingdoms, including Macedonia, Syria,

The Hellenistic Age 

141 and Egypt. They were ruled by dynasties descended from 

Alexander's generals. These three states remained independent, though with shifting boundaries, until the era of 

Roman expansion in the Near East.

Hellenistic cities. Alexander's successors continued citybuilding on a still more extensive scale. The Hellenistic cities, unlike Greek city-states, did not enjoy independence. 

They formed a part of the kingdom in which they lay, and paid tribute, or taxes, to its ruler. The new cities also contrasted in appearance with those of Greece. They had broad streets, well paved and sometimes lighted at night, a good water supply, baths, theaters, gymnasiums, and parks. The upper classes, whether Greeks or "barbarians," spoke Greek, read Greek, and wrote in Greek. A large part of the civilized world now had for the first time a common language. 

Commerce between East and West. Some Hellenistic cities were only garrison posts in the heart of remote provinces or along the frontier. Many more, such as Alexandria in Egypt, Seleucia in Babylonia, Antioch in Syria, and Rhodes on the island of that name, were thriving business centers, through which Asiatic products reached Greece. Kings, nobles, and rich men now began to build palaces, to keep up large households with many servants, and to possess fine furniture, carpets, tapestries, gold and silver vessels, and beautiful works of art. The standard of living was thus raised by the introduction of luxuries to which the old Greeks had been strangers. 

Intellectual relations between East and West. Greece and the Near East exchanged ideas as well as commodities. 

What the Greeks had accomplished in art, literature, philosophy, and science became familiar to the Egyptians, Babylonians, and other peoples. They, in turn, introduced the 

Greeks to their achievements in the realm of thought. 

Alexandria. This commercial and intellectual mingling took place on many frontiers, but Alexandria in Egypt furnishes a splendid example of its specific effects. Alexandria was the foremost Hellenistic center because of its

Greece unrivaled site for commerce with Asia, Europe, and the rest of Africa. The inhabitants included not only Egyptians, Greeks, and Macedonians, but also Jews, Syrians, Babylonians, and other Orientals. The population increased rapidly, and by the time of Christ Alexandria ranked in size next to imperial Rome.

Alexandrian culture. The Macedonian rulers of Egypt made Alexandria their capital and did everything to adorn it with imposing public buildings and masterpieces of Greek art. Learning flourished at Alexandria. The city possessed in the royal Museum, or Temple of the Muses, a genuine university, with lecture halls, botanical and zoölogical gardens, an astronomical observatory, and a great library. The collection of books, in the form of papyrus or parchment (sheepskin) manuscripts, finally amounted to over five hundred thousand rolls, containing almost everything that had been written in antiquity. The learned men at Alexandria translated into Greek various productions of Oriental literature, including the Hebrew Old Testament. Much progress took place in mathematics, astronomy, physics, geography, anatomy, medicine, and other branches of knowledge. 

The Ætolian and Achæan Leagues. During the period following Alexander the Greek city-states began to realize that the freedom they prized so much could only be secured by a close union. Consequently they formed leagues, the most outstanding of which were the Ætolian League in central Greece and the Achæan League in the Peloponnesus. The latter was the more important. Its business lay in the hands of an assembly or congress, where each city, whether large or small, had one vote. The assembly, meeting twice a year, chose a general, or president, levied taxes, raised armies, and conducted all foreign affairs. The cities, in local matters, continued to enjoy their old independence. This organization shows that the Achæan League was more than a mere alliance of city-states. It formed the first genuine federation that the world had ever seen, and its example was repeatedly cited by the American statesmen who helped to frame our

The Hellenistic Age 

143 Constitution. The attempt to unify Greece came too late. 

Sparta refused to enter the Achæan League, and Athens failed to join the Ætolian League. Without these two powerful states, neither association could achieve lasting success. 

Cosmopolitanism. The Greeks who emigrated in such numbers to Egypt and western Asia lost citizenship at Athens, Sparta, or Thebes. They surrendered local attachments and prejudices, which had so long divided them, to become "cosmopolitans," or citizens of the world. They likewise lost old feelings of antagonism toward non-Greeks. 

Henceforth the distinction between Greek and barbarian gradually faded away, and mankind became ever more unified in sympathies and aspirations. This Græco-Oriental world of city-states, federations, and kingdoms about the eastern Mediterranean was now to come in contact with the great power which had been arising in the western Mediterranean Rome.

EPHEBIC OATH This chapter. The previous chapter explained the geographic setting of Greece and traced the story of its political life. The political story gives us a framework of events, enabling us to place the people and their contributions in time and place. We now know that the fifth century B.C. was the period of greatest political activity. It was also a period of great activity in art, literature, science, and philosophy. This intellectual activity did not cease with the loss of independence by the Greeks, but continued for several centuries, far into the Roman period. Chapter VI presents a picture of Greek life and summarizes the achievements of the greatest artists, writers, and philosophers. It shows that the Greeks were in some ways strikingly modern. We can see our problems and our thoughts in another setting. 

41. CLOTHING AND HOUSES 

Tunic and mantle. The mild Mediterranean climate permitted the Greeks to wear a simple and scanty costume. It did not change with the whims of fashion but remained almost the same for centuries. Male attire consisted of the tunic and mantle. The tunic was an undergarment of wool or linen, without sleeves. When the wearer was busy in an occupation that required freedom of movement, the tunic 146

Clothing and Houses 

147 was drawn up tightly about the body and held fast by a belt or girdle. Over this undergarment was thrown a large woolen mantle, so wrapped about the figure as to leave free only the right shoulder and head. In the house a man wore only his tunic; out of doors and on the street he usually wore the mantle over it. The dress of women was much the same as that of men, but with greater variety in shape, draping, color, and ornamentation. 

Coverings for head and feet. The use of head-coverings, among both men and women, was much less common than with us today. In rainy weather the mantle could be pulled up so as to cover both head and face. Broad-brimmed hats were worn on a journey or out in the country, as a protection against the summer sun. Veils sometimes formed a part of women's costume, especially for young girls and brides who appeared in public. People often wore sandals indoors and leather shoes outdoors, but coverings for the feet were not regarded as essential to a decent appearance in public. 

Greek customs in dress suggest to us that the Greeks liked simplicity and dignified usefulness.

The house. The same liking for simplicity and usefulness shows in the way the Greek built his house. It stood close to the street line. The exterior was plain and simple to an extreme. The owner was satisfied if his mansion shut out the noise and dust of the highway. He built it, therefore, about one or more open courts, which took the place of windows supplying light and air. Except for the doorway, the front of the house presented a bare, blank surface, relieved only by narrow slits or lattices in the wall of the upper story. The street side of the house wall received a coating of whitewash or of fine marble stucco. The roof of the house was covered with clay tiles. This style of domestic architecture is still common in Mediterranean lands.

Furniture. The Greek house had little furniture. Chairs, tables, lamps, and couches or beds for sleeping and for reclining at meals constituted the usual furniture. These had, however, an elegance of form which modern cabinet-

makers seek in vain to rival. The furnishings of the house presented a daily lesson in good taste. 

42. HOME LIFE 

Children. Greek boys and girls, until the age of seven, remained under the general oversight of their mothers. Most households were able to afford a slave woman or a foreigner to shoulder the chief responsibility in caring for the children. 

In most Greek city-states, when a boy reached his eighth year he was placed under the care of a slave called a pedagogue. It was the duty of this pedagogue to teach the boy good manners, to prevent him from falling into bad companionship, and to attend him everywhere - to and from school, on the playground, and in the house. 

Seclusion of girls. The boy's sister, meanwhile, remained in seclusion at home. She learned the usual duties of household management, but she enjoyed no such advantages in the way of careful schooling as did her brother. An Athenian girl was closely guarded by her parents. If, on rare occasions, she went outside the house to witness some religious festival, to visit a temple, or to attend a funeral, she was always accompanied by an older woman as a chaperon. 

It sometimes happened that an Athenian youth did not see his future wife until the wedding day. The young man's father had most to do with the selection of a wife. He tried to secure for his son the daughter of some friend who possessed rank and property equal to his own. If he found a suitable match, the parents of the two parties entered into a contract which, among other things, usually stated how large a dowry the bride's father was to settle on his daughter. 

Inferior position of women. Marriage did not usually bring the young woman freedom. In Homeric times women seem to have occupied a high social position, on an equality with the men. At Sparta women were highly respected, and the girls received gymnastic training. In many of the citystates, however, and particularly in Athens, the wife, during

Home Life 

149 the early years of marriage, was more or less of a prisoner. 

She could not go out except by permission. She took no part in the feasts and entertainments which her husband gave. 

She lived a life of confinement in that quarter of the house assigned to the women for their special abode. An Athenian wife, moreover, had no legal rights. If her husband illtreated her, she found it difficult to secure a separation. In case of a divorce, the father kept possession of the children. 

The inferior position of women at Athens affords a marked contrast to the general refinement of life and manners. 

Daily life. The ancient Greek citizen, though he loved play and feasting, was no sluggard. He got up at sunrise, or even before, washed his face and hands, put on his scanty garments, and was soon ready for the street. Before leaving the house he broke his fast with a few mouthfuls of bread dipped in wine. Then he left the house to ride into the country and visit his estates or to call on his friends in the city. 

At noon he returned home to enjoy a light meal and a rest during the heat. As the day grew cooler, he went out again and visited a gymnasium. He returned home by sunset for the principal meal of the day. If he had no guests, he shared this repast with his wife and children. The ordinary fare was very much what it is now in Greece bread, olives, figs, cheese, with a little meat as an occasional luxury. As a substitute for sugar, the Athenian used honey; olive oil took the place of butter; and snow served instead of ice for cooling water or wine. A wealthy man might add to these simple articles of diet a few dainties, such as fruits, nuts, and cakes. At the end of the meal the diners refreshed themselves with wine mixed with water. The Greeks seem to have been usually as temperate in their drink as they were frugal in their food. The remainder of the evening would be devoted to conversation and music and possibly a little reading. As a rule they went early to bed. The lighting arrangements of an ancient house were not such as to encourage late hours; besides, as we have said, the practice was to rise very early of a morning.

43. EDUCATION 

Private schools. It is plain, from what has been thus far said, that men were much more important than women in the life of most Greek city-states. We need not be surprised, therefore, to learn that education was for boys and not for girls. Public opinion insisted that all male citizens should be educated. The Greeks were thus the first people to realize the importance of an educated citizenry. There was no system of free or common schools, but Athens and other cities contained many private schools, open to boys of all classes on the payment of moderate fees. No matter how poor his parents, a Greek boy could gain at least an elementary education. This consisted of training in gymnastics, music, and grammar.

Gymnastics. The gymnastic exercises were taken in the palestra, an open stretch of ground on the outskirts of the city. A teacher was on hand to give instruction in the various sports of running, boxing, jumping, wrestling, discus hurling, and javelin throwing. The participants in these sports usually wore little or no clothing. Before the contests they rubbed their bodies with oil, and afterward they cleaned themselves with a scraper. The palestra was often situated near a stream in which the youths could swim and dive. These daily exercises in the open air tended to develop fine athletes.

Music. Music, the second important branch of Greek education, was intended to fit the young men for pleasant social intercourse. They learned to play the seven-stringed lyre and to sing to their own accompaniment. The instruction was not intended to produce great musicians. It was enough if it enabled a man to take his part in the music and singing on social occasions and to furnish amusement. 

It was also thought that music, by its beauty and harmony, purified the thoughts and strengthened the moral nature.

Grammar. Grammar, the third branch of education, in-

Education 151 cluded instruction in writing and the reading of the national literature. The Greeks never thought of making foreign languages a subject of study. They were content with the thorough mastery of their own tongue. The boy began by tracing his letters with a stylus on wax-coated wooden tablets which rested on his knees. When he had learned to write and to read, the schoolmaster took up with him the works of the great poet Homer, the Fables of Æsop, and other literary compositions. The student learned by heart much of the poetry so well that he always remembered it. Not a few 

Greeks, it is said, could recite the whole of Homer's Iliad and Odyssey. By means of such studies, which the Greeks included under the general name of grammar, the Greek youth learned to admire the heroic and skillful deeds of his ancestors and to use his own language with a keen sense of the meanings of words and the force of sentences.

A "liberal" education. The system of slavery in Greece freed many citizens from the need of working with their hands or of engaging in trade or industry. To spend all of one's time and energy in money-making was felt to be unworthy of a free-born Greek. A life devoted entirely to business, said the Greek thinkers, injures the body, enfeebles the mind, and leaves no leisure to engage in public affairs. The 

Greeks therefore cared little for manual or industrial training. On the other hand, unlike many Americans, they did not think of education as mainly the learning of what is in books. They thought of education as a means of cultivating the self and of preparing for citizenship. Their educational system aimed, therefore, to produce the sound mind in the sound body. The typical Greek, especially at Athens, valued knowledge for its own sake, appreciated intelligent and witty conversation, and found much pleasure in the drama, music, poetry, and the fine arts. Thus there developed the Greek ideal of the education befitting a freeman, of a truly "liberal" education. This ideal became a part of later thinking about education and has lasted among us to the present day. It is not unusual to hear people nowadays arguing whether edu-

cation should be "liberal" or "practical." The Greek ideal was that of a liberal education. 

44. SOCIAL LIFE 

Town society. It is clear by now that if we went back to live in some of the old Greek city-states, we should not find ourselves complete strangers. In some of them, we should find people living an interesting and attractive life.
