THE THEATER AT EPIDAURUS 

The theater at Epidaurus in Argolis was built about the middle of the fourth century B.C. 

The auditorium, holding about 15,000 spectators, is well preserved, as is also the circle of the orchestra bordered by a line of white stones. 

Religious festivals. Holidays in connection with religious ceremonies were another important part of Greek social life. (1) The Olympic festivals, with their games and throngs of people, have been already described (p. 110). (2) Almost as important was the Great Panathenæa, held at Athens every fourth year. It was a holiday time, when slaves enjoyed many indulgences and women came out from their seclusion.

Social Life 

155 The men and women of Athens sought to honor their patron goddess, Athena, by sacrifices, feasts, and processions, and by athletic and poetic contests. (3) Near Athens, in the little town of Eleusis, there grew up another celebration, which finally became a Panhellenic festival, open to all Greeks, women as well as men, slaves as well as freemen. This great festival was the annual celebration of the Eleusinian Mysteries. These "mysteries" consisted of secret ceremonies or rites connected with the worship of Demeter, goddess of vegetation and of the life of nature. The celebration of the 

Eleusinian Mysteries lasted nine days. When those who were to be initiated into the mysteries or secret rites had been worked up to a state of religious excitement, they entered a brilliantly lighted hall and witnessed a play dealing with the legend of Demeter. The purpose of this play seems to have been to show them a kind of living picture of life in the next world and to hold out to them the promise of a blessed lot in another existence. As an Athenian orator said, "Those who have shared this initiation possess sweeter hopes about death and about the whole of life." (4) Less religious than the celebration of the Eleusinian Mysteries were the festivals in honor of the god Dionysus. These took place in midwinter and spring, in various cities, especially in Athens. The populace gathered in the local theater, and for three days they watched, from morning till night, the performance of both tragedies and comedies. On each day the citizens voted a prize to the poet whose play had pleased them best. Some of these dramas have been preserved until our own day and have, because of their excellence, made the authors famous.

The theater. Greek plays were performed out of doors in the bright sunlight, in an amphitheater built on a hillside. 

At the bottom of the amphitheater was a circle, called the orchestra or the dancing ring. The stage was a long, elevated platform closing in one end of the amphitheater. Greek theaters had practically no scenery; the spectator had to imagine for himself the setting of the play. The actors were

men, and usually numbered not more than three; each actor was therefore obliged to play several different rôles in the same performance. All wore elaborate costumes, and the actors in a tragedy were made to appear larger than human by means of masks, padding, and thick-soled boots, or buskins. 

From a distant seat on the hillside, the actors down on the stage must have looked like majestic statues. In the orchestra circle was 

Estationed a chorus, which numbered fifteen men for tragedy and twenty-four for comedy.

Between the incidents or scenes of the play, this chorus chanted hymns or performed elaborate dances; sometimes the chorus recited a poem pointing out to the audience that the story of the play taught a lesson as to the consequences of evil conduct. The theater held an important place in the social life of most Greek cities, and was a partial substitute for our pulpit and press. It brought all the citizens together to see reenacted on the stage some thrilling event from the past in which the gods had either helped the Greeks out of disaster or punished them for evil doing; thus patriotism, morals, and religion were taught. The plays helped to form political opinion by showing some of the public officials in a favorable light and others in an unfavorable one.

45. PHILOSOPHY 

The first philosophers. The preceding description of Greek social life contains several hints of the important place of philosophy and philosophers in the lives of the more cultivated Greeks. Back in the sixth century B.C., long before the Persian wars, a few thinkers in Greece began to inquire into the mysteries of nature. They were not content with the explanations given by poets like Homer, who declared

Philosophy 157 that gods caused the thunderstorms, the eclipses, the changes from night to day, and the succession of seasons. On the contrary, said these first bold thinkers, such happenings in nature must have a perfectly natural cause, there must be some reason why they happen. The men who spoke thus must be called the first philosophers. They made some true guesses and many false ones. By sincerely trying, however, to understand the reason why things happened, instead of simply repeating mythological explanations of natural happenings, these men were the beginners of both philosophy and science.

The sophists. Shortly after the Persian wars, there arose in Greece another class of thinkers, who declared it a waste of time to study the material or physical universe. If men wanted to be wise, said these thinkers, they should study man and his affairs; the knowledge thus gained would be true wisdom. So these men traveled throughout Greece, gathering young men about them and lecturing for pay on subjects of daily human concern. Many of them were brilliant thinkers who helped to spread more reasonable ideas about politics, morals, and religion. In time, they became known as sophists, probably from the Greek word sophos, meaning wise. The sophists were for about a hundred years the most prominent and popular teachers and philosophers in Greece. They made a specialty of teaching young citizens how to hold their own in an argument by means of shrewd reasoning and clever speaking. Such teaching was important in some of the cities where each person had to plead his own case before the great citizen-juries. Young persons so trained, however, often disturbed conservative people by asking them questions that they could not answer. Soon these sophists and their pupils seemed to be questioning everybody and everything. 

They asked if justice was possible, and if men were capable of governing themselves. They asked whether the gods really did live, and whether they had power over the lives of men. 

Soon the older men in the Greek cities were worried. It seemed to them that the sophists and their pupils were not

only a nuisance, but a menace to law and order. It must be admitted that many of the sophists were not genuine lovers of wisdom but only talkers and questioners who tried to deceive people by arguments which they did not themselves believe. The name of sophist thus came to be used disrespectfully. It was applied to any one who tried to win an 

SOCRATES 

British Museum, London argument by tricky and deceitful reasoning. We still use the word sophist with that meaning, and when we think anybody's line of reasoning is only a clever attempt to deceive us we call it sophistry.

Socrates. The sophists were numerous in Athens about the time of the Peloponnesian wars (431-404 B.C.).

During those years the philosopher Socrates began to teach in Athens. 

He is one of the most picturesque characters in all history. Judging from the stone bust which has survived from the ruins of ancient sculpture, Socrates was not handsome; he had a bulky figure, and a round face, with deep-set eyes, and a large, broad nose. Yet even the stone reveals, upon closer inspection, a kindliness and a simplicity that explain in part why he was loved by his followers. Early in life he had given up his father's occupation of sculptor and taken to the more congenial one of philosopher. In time, his name spread throughout Greece, and in Athens he became a public figure, loved by many but heartily disliked by others. 

A marble statuette from 

Egypt; reduced copy of a fourth-century original.

Socrates and the sophists. Among those who had reason to dislike Socrates were the sophists. He did not altogether approve of them. For one thing, he did not believe in accepting, as they did, pay for teaching. We are not surprised,

Philosophy 159 therefore, to learn that he had to live in the most frugal manner possible and that his wife and children often felt the pinch of poverty. Socrates also thought that many of the sophists boasted too much about their wisdom and thus caused their pupils to be conceited. He thought it was a bad thing for any one to think himself wise. So he would not allow himself to be called a sophist or wise man; instead, he was content to be known only as a lover-of-wisdom, or, to use the Greek word, a philosopher (from two Greek words, philos, meaning friend or lover, and sophos, the meaning of which we have already noted). A philosopher, then, according to 

Socrates, is literally a lover of wisdom, some one who never becomes satisfied that he is wise, but is always modestly and humbly inquiring and seeking to find out wisdom or truth. 

Know thyself. Socrates did not differ entirely, however, from the sophists. Both Socrates and the sophists considered knowledge about the stars or about thunderstorms largely useless. They asserted that in order for man to be wise, what he really needed to know was what he meant by such things as justice and injustice, courage and cowardice, the state and statesmanship, honor, virtue, and patriotism. 

Socrates thought that if you could get men to find out what they meant when they spoke of such things, you could at least set them on the road to wisdom. Know thyself was the motto of Socrates.

The Socratic method. Socrates's method of getting men to discover what they meant when they spoke of justice, courage, virtue, and other ideas has become famous. Barefoot and clad in an old rumpled tunic, Socrates walked through the streets of Athens and loitered in the market place. He was sure, before long, to meet some self-important official or some thoughtless youth who had just come bursting with knowledge and conceit from one of the popular sophist teachers. Socrates fell into conversation with him, questioning the man as to what he meant by some word he had used for example, "justice," "virtue," "good," or 

---

"bad." Socrates led the man to see that he had never carefully considered the meanings of the words he used, that his thought was confused and uncertain. If the man did not leave in anger, Socrates then tried to get him to start thinking more carefully about what he really did mean. The 

Socratic method is the use of questions to stimulate thought and conclusions.

Death of Socrates. The Socratic method not only stirred up thought; it also stirred up many enemies for Socrates. 

Then, as now, men did not like to be made uncomfortable by having to examine their ideas critically. When Socrates was seventy years old, he was publicly accused of denying the existence of the gods (impiety) and of corrupting the minds of the city's youth. When brought to trial, he claimed that his conscience, which he considered the voice of God, prompted him to teach. Had he adopted a conciliatory tone with his fellow citizens, he might have been let off, but this he refused to do. He declared that, if allowed to live, he would continue to go through the city, saying to this or that person whom he met, "O my friend, why do you care so much about laying up the greatest amount of money and honor and reputation, and so little about wisdom and truth and the improvement of the soul?". Consequently, he was condemned to drink the poison hemlock. Refusing to plead for a pardon or to take advantage of a chance to flee, he drained the cup which brought him death — and fame as one of civilization's earliest martyrs to freedom of thought. Plato. For information about the ideas and opinions of 

Socrates we have to go to the writings of his pupils, for he himself left no writings. The greatest of his pupils was 

Plato, a wealthy aristocrat. In the neighborhood of Plato's estate was a public pleasure-ground, called the Academy, which was adorned with walks, groves, and fountains. In this public park Plato often strolled with his pupils while he taught them, and when he died (347 B.C.), at the ripe age of eighty-one, he left his fortune to maintain a school in the Academy. This school became known as the Academy.

Philosophy 161 It continued for over eight hundred years, and we still use the name academy for certain kinds of schools. 

Plato's Dialogues. Plato left a number of writings in which he explained what he and others thought about such matters as government, education, religion, virtue, and justice. Each of these writings is in the form of an imaginary conversation or dialogue between several persons who are reasoning together on some topic. Plato's writings are therefore known collectively as the Dialogues. In most of them, Plato makes his old teacher, Socrates, the chief speaker. 

Three beautiful dialogues present a touching picture of the last days of Socrates. Another dialogue, called the Republic, describes an ideal society or state in which there is perfect justice because only the wisest men are rulers and every one in the state is doing the work for which he is best fitted by birth, breeding, and character. Plato did not believe that a society so perfect would ever exist on this earth; he did believe, though, that good men should always keep in their minds the picture or idea of such a society and try to make their country as much like the ideal as possible. Throughout his writings Plato emphasized the importance and power the ideas we have, rather than the wealth and material things we own. He also stressed the desirability of a man's always striving for perfection in thought and deed. "We ought," he said, "to become like God, as far as this is possible." of Aristotle. Among Plato's pupils in the Academy was one who was so eager for knowledge and so capable in acquiring it that Plato called him "the mind of the school." The pupil thus honored was Aristotle (384-322 B.C.), a Macedonian who had come to Athens in order to study under Plato. 

When Aristotle was a little over forty years old, King Philip of Macedonia (p. 135) invited him to return to his native state and take charge of the education of Philip's son, Alexander, later to be known as Alexander the Great. After 

Aristotle's royal pupil became king, Aristotle returned to

Athens, and there, in the garden and gymnasium of the Lyceum, he founded a school which was called the Lyceum.

He continued as head of it until Alexander died (323 B.C.); then an uprising of the Athenians against the Macedonians caused Aristotle to flee for his life. He died the following year, an old man in exile. 

Aristotle's achievement. Aristotle seems to have taken all knowledge for his province. He gathered the constitutions of over a hundred and fifty Greek city-states, drew from them some general principles of politics, and then composed a treatise, called the Politics, on the principles of politics and government. He examined the acts and beliefs of men, tried to formulate from them theories as to what was excellence in human conduct, and then composed a treatise called the Ethics. He studied carefully the many dramas of which the Greeks were so fond, and then wrote a book (called the Poetics) pointing out the difference between a good play and a poor play. Aristotle also did important work in botany and zoölogy. He studied collections of strange plants and animals from the Mediterranean and the lands to the east, and then wrote careful descriptions of the anatomy and habits of both plants and animals. It is said that Alexander's soldiers collected many specimens for Aristotle. Perhaps the supreme achievement of Aristotle was his creation of the science of logic, or the principles of correct reasoning as distinguished from faulty reasoning. The foregoing are only some of the great achievements of Aristotle. Apparently his two great aims were (1) to collect as many observable facts as possible and then (2) to systematize these into reliable theory. He was thus not only a philosopher, but also a scientist. Indeed, it is difficult to decide how one shall classify him. In the twenty-two centuries since his death, his achievements have been repeatedly the inspiration of both great scientists and great philosophers.

Epicureanism. Another school near Athens, in the century following Aristotle, was "the garden of Epicurus," where Epicurus taught that pleasure is the sole good in life, and pain the sole evil. Nowadays, when we call a man an

Epicurean, we think of him as a person who believes in the

Science 163 free indulgence of every appetite and passion without regard to any higher principles. But Epicurus himself taught no such doctrine. He meant by pleasure not so much the passing enjoyments of the hour as the permanent happiness of a lifetime, not so much the enjoyment of bodily luxury as the satisfaction of the mind. Indeed, he believed that in order to be happy men must lead a simple life, and that to do so they must keep themselves untroubled by useless luxuries or ambitions. He also believed that to be happy men must be virtuous, for virtue will bring more real satisfaction than vice.

Stoicism. A contemporary of Epicurus was Zeno, who taught a very different theory of how to live wisely. The theories of Zeno and his followers have since become known as Stoicism. The Stoics argued that the right way to live was to accept whatever happenings seemed to be the consequence of natural law. Thus, if man must suffer pain and lose his dear ones in death, he should not show himself rebellious against nature's law by grieving unduly; his reason should show him that these things must be. The Stoics stressed the importance of reason as a guide to conduct, and the untrustworthiness of the feelings. They practiced self-denial, despised the pomps and vanities of the world, and tried to rise above such emotions as grief, fear, hope, and joy. They held that nothing external to man - riches or fame or power really counts. The slave or peasant who bore with fortitude all the ills of life might be more virtuous, and therefore happier, than a king. These inspiring doctrines gained many adherents among the Romans, and through them Stoicism became a real moral force in ancient society. 

46. SCIENCE 

Philosophy and science. If you go into a public library today you will find the books separated into sections. One section will be called Poetry, another Philosophy, and another Science. If you go to a college you will find that there is one department of science, another of literature, another of

history, and still another of philosophy. This extensive organization of knowledge into separate departments is one of the late developments in the history of mankind. There was a time when no such separation had been made between the various parts or aspects of human knowledge. The 

Greeks did not recognize the distinction we now make between philosophy and science. 

Greek philosophy and science. Early Greek philosophers might also be called scientists, since they studied nature and tried to explain her operations in a natural manner. Even some of the later philosophers contributed to scientific knowledge. Democritus, a contemporary of Socrates, thought of all material things as being made up of ever-moving atoms, so small that their size cannot be diminished. Plato and his followers did useful work in mathematics and astronomy. 

Aristotle's careful descriptions of animals entitle him to be called a zoölogist. His pupil, Theophrastus, who succeeded him in the headship of the school in the Lyceum, made a thoroughgoing classification of the known plants, and thus ranks as a botanist.

Mathematics. The Greeks never accomplished much in arithmetic, because their way of writing numbers and counting was even clumsier than the Roman method with which we are still familiar. Geometry, however, had a marked development. Euclid, who lived at Alexandria about 300 B.C., composed a geometry textbook known as the Elements. Its theorems are still the basis of modern works on the subject. 

Another mathematician founded trigonometry. Archimedes of Syracuse, who had once studied at Alexandria, was the most eminent mathematician of antiquity. He worked out many theorems, especially in regard to the sphere, the cone, the cylinder, and other figures. One of his achievements was the calculation of the value of π (pi), the ratio of the circumference of a circle to its diameter. 

Physics. Archimedes likewise made many discoveries in physical science, including specific gravity and the law of floating bodies. He also studied the principles of the lever

Science 165 and the pulley. "Give me a fulcrum on which to rest,” he said, "and I will move the earth." What Archimedes and his successors learned about engineering and mechanical devices was taken over by the Romans, who put this theoretical knowledge to practical use in building. 

Astronomy. The Greek achievement in astronomy was impressive. One scientist of the third century B.C. discovered that the sun is many times larger than the moon and that the latter shines by the sun's reflected light. He also roughly estimated the distance between these two heavenly bodies. Another astronomer counted more than a thousand stars and grouped them into constellations, determined the length of the solar year within a few minutes of the correct time, and devised the modern method of fixing the location of places by means of their latitude and longitude. Greek astronomy was put into final shape by Ptolemy of Alexandria, who lived in the second century A.D. He taught that the earth was the center of the universe. His Almagest remained the standard treatise on astronomy throughout the Middle Ages.

Medicine and anatomy. In the fifth century B.C. Hippocrates, by freeing the art of healing from superstition, gained the title “father of medicine." His high ideals as to medical practice were embodied in the "Hippocratic Oath," which is still recited by graduates of our medical schools. Medicine and anatomy received much attention at Alexandria, where there were dissecting rooms, charts, and models for the study of the human body. Surgical operations, sometimes of a major type, were performed, and unconsciousness was produced by the use of various drugs. Greek scientists discovered that the brain is the center of the nervous system, that nerves exist to transmit the sensations and impulses, and that the blood is borne in streams to every part of the body. 

Classical knowledge of medicine and anatomy was gathered up and systematized in the writings of Galen of Pergamum (born about 130 A.D.). He remained the supreme authority in these fields for more than a thousand years thereafter.

Geography. The Carthaginians and early Greeks made several important voyages of exploration and discovery. Accounts of these voyages together with other geographical information were collected by Eratosthenes, a librarian of Alexandria who lived in the third century B.C. By observing the shadows cast by the sun at two different places in Egypt seven hundred miles apart, Eratosthenes was able to estimate the circumference of the earth at 28,000 miles, a remarkably close estimate. The astronomer Ptolemy was also an eminent geographer. His famous map of the world presented the geographical knowledge of the ancients and was apparently still in use at the time of Columbus. After Ptolemy no important additions were made to geographical learning until late in the Middle Ages.

Ancient and modern science contrasted. The Greeks in scientific study seem to have gone about as far as it was possible to go without the aid of elaborate apparatus. They had no real telescopes or microscopes, no mariner's compass or chronometer, no very delicate balances, and nothing comparable to our laboratories for physics, chemistry, and other sciences. Modern scientists are perhaps not better thinkers than were those of antiquity, but they have far better instruments for research and can make careful experiments whereas the ancients had to rely upon shrewd guesses. It should be noticed, also, that the Greeks did little toward linking up their pure science with its applications to the practical arts. For the great inventions which have done and are still doing so much to transform our lives we must wait until modern times. 

47. ART 

Architecture. The traveler in Greece today finds many ruins of ancient buildings from which he can get some idea of the leading characteristics of Greek architecture. The building materials were limestone and white marble. The blocks of stone were not bound together by cement, but by metal clamps which held them in a firm grip. It was usual to color

Art the ornamental parts of a temple and the open spaces that served as a background for sculpture. The Greeks did not rely upon the arch as a means of covering large areas with a

The Greek temple. The temple formed the chief structure in a Greek city. It was a rectangular building, provided with doors, but without windows, and surrounded by a single or double row of columns. The architrave, a plain band of massive stones, reached from one column to another. Then came the frieze, adorned with sculptured reliefs, then the horizontal cornice, and at the ends of the building the triangular pedi-

ments formed by the sloping roof. The pediments were sometimes decorated with statues. Since the temple did not serve as a meeting place for worshipers, but only as a sanctuary for the deity, its interior usually had little ornamentation. 48. LITERATURE 

Survival of Greek literature. The ancient Greeks have long since passed away, their city-states have been broken up, their temples are in ruins, and most of their statues and paintings have vanished. But their books, or copies of them, are still on our shelves, translated even into our own language, and read by thousands of our contemporaries. The life and thought of the Greeks have survived through their songs and poems, their plays (tragedies and comedies), their histories and biographies, and their treatises on animals, plants, politics, and the laws of correct thinking (logic). 

Epic poetry. The earliest poetry of the Greeks was inseparable from music. Wandering minstrels sang at feasts in the palaces of kings and accompanied their lays with the music of the clear-toned lyre. At a later time the singer gave up the lyre and depended for effect solely on the poetic power of his narrative. Such minstrel-songs were finally combined into long poems, called epics, which told the story of some famous event in the past. The most famous epics are the 

Iliad and the Odyssey, works which the Greeks attributed to 

Homer (p. 108).

Lyric poetry. In addition to the long poems which told some heroic story, the Greeks also composed many short poems for the purpose of expressing personal feelings. These poems were called lyrics. The love poems of the poetess

Sappho, who lived on the island of Lesbos, were celebrated in antiquity, but only fragments have survived. The greatest

Greek lyric poet was Pindar, who lived in Thebes. We still possess forty-four of his odes, which were written in honor of victorious athletes at the Olympic and other national games. His fame spread throughout Greece, and it is said that, when Alexander was suppressing rebellion in Thebes, he gave orders to spare the house in which Pindar had lived.

Dramatic poetry. We have already seen that Greek citizens were fond of the theater. Their dramas were written in poetic form, and might be either tragedies or comedies. The three great masters of the tragic drama were schylus, Sophocles, and Euripides. All of them lived and wrote in 

Athens during the splendid half-century between the Persian and the Peloponnesian wars. The greatest Athenian writer of comedies was Aristophanes. In some of his dramas he attacks the demagogues who were prominent in Athenian politics, while in others he ridicules the philosophers, makes fun of the ordinary citizen's delight in serving on juries, and criticizes those responsible for the unfortunate expedition to Sicily (p. 131).

History. Herodotus, who lived about the middle of the fifth century B.C., is often called the "father of history."

Though a native of Asia Minor, he spent some of the best years of his life at Athens. He traveled widely in the Greek world and in the Near East, as a preparation for his great task of writing an account of the rise of the Oriental nations and the struggle between Greece and Persia. Herodotus's history is filled with incidents and gossip which make his narrative charming, but he did not diligently sift truth from fable. Thucydides, an Athenian who lived during the Peloponnesian War, became the historian of that contest. He is generally ranked as the first historian who tried to tell just what happened as distinct from hearsay and legend.

Biography. The greatest Greek biographies were written as late as the first century of our era, by Plutarch. By that time, Greece was a province of the Roman Empire. Plutarch, in his book, first relates the life of an eminent Greek;

Literature 171 then of a famous Roman who in some way resembled him; and ends the account with a short comparison of the two men. Plutarch's book of biographies is appropriately called the Parallel Lives. It has for centuries been a popular work. 

The Greek genius. Our debt to the Greeks is above all an intellectual one, due to their preëminence in such fields as literature and philosophy, science, and art. In Greece, it has been said, men first learned to be truly human; to develop the body, to train the mind, to purify and refine the spirit. The 

Greeks were marked off from their predecessors in the Orient by a great love of speculation and discussion, by an eager curiosity which led them to search out the cause of things, by a wonderful feeling for the beautiful, and by a desire to live their lives in accordance with reason. No other people has surpassed or even equaled them in these respects.

CORINTH 

Excavations on the site of Corinth, conducted since 1896 by the American School of Classical Studies, have uncovered the ancient market place (Agora), a theater, the main street leading from the harbor, and the fountain of Pirene, which provided the inhabitants with an inexhaustible supply of water. Unit IV ROMAN CIVILIZATION 

How the Romans became rulers of the Mediterranean world and founded civilization in western Europe 

(CHAPTERS VII-VIII)

PRESENTATION 

In Italy the hardy Romans rose to supremacy and slowly extended their sway throughout the whole peninsula. While developing an energetic state, the Romans also developed a strong, practical character, new customs, and a new system of government. Meanwhile, across the Mediterranean, on the shores of northern Africa, arose the commercial state of Carthage. Expanding Rome clashed with and triumphed over Carthage. Rome then extended its sway throughout the eastern and the western Mediterranean. Slowly the effects of ruling a wide area reacted upon the Roman republic. 

Through a series of great leaders such as Marius, Pompey, Cæsar, and Augustus it was transformed into an empire. Under able emperors, Rome's boundaries were extended, but at the same time internal conflicts and weaknesses were sapping the vitality of the empire. It split into two parts, an eastern and a western. The western half lay exposed to the barbarians who were soon to put an end to Roman supremacy. (Chapter VII) 

Great The Romans reached so high a cultural level that their life and thought influenced profoundly the less advanced and even barbarous peoples of Europe. Thus classical civilization was transmitted from its Mediterranean center to western Europe; the Romans had most to do with this westward movement of civilization. builders, great governors, and great lawgivers, the Romans set their abiding mark on much of the civilization that we have inherited. 

Their language has survived not only in the remains of Latin literature, but also in thousands of words of modern languages. The 

Roman sense of justice embodied itself in a series of laws which have formed the pattern of all subsequent law. Herein lies "the grandeur that was Rome." (Chapter VIII)

49. ITALY AND SICILY --JUSTINIAN 

It

Italy. The Italian peninsula is long and narrow. measures nearly seven hundred miles from the Alps to the sea but is only about one hundred miles across, except in the north, where it is much broader. The Apennine Mountains form the backbone of Italy. Branching off from the Alpine chain at the Gulf of Genoa, they cross the peninsula in an easterly direction almost to the Adriatic. Then they turn sharply to the southeast and parallel the coast for a considerable distance. The plains of central Italy, in consequence, are all on the western slope of the mountains. In southern Italy the Apennines swerve to the southwest and penetrate the "toe" of the peninsula.

Divisions of Italy. Italy may be divided into a northern, a central, and a southern section. Northern Italy contains the important region known in ancient times as Cisalpine Gaul. 

This is a level plain two hundred miles in length, watered by the Po, which the Romans called the "king of rivers,” because of its length and many tributary streams. Central 177

Rome Italy, lying south of the Apennines, includes seven districts, of which the three on the western coast - Etruria, Latium, and Campania - were most conspicuous in ancient history. 

Southern Italy, because of its warm climate and deeply indented coast, early attracted many Greek colonists. Their colonies here came to be known as Magna Græcia, or Great 

Greece (p. 115).

Sicily. The triangular-shaped island of Sicily is separated from Italy by the Strait of Messina, a channel which, at the narrowest part, is only two miles wide. Lying in the center of the Mediterranean and in the direct route of merchants and colonists from every direction, Sicily has always been a meeting place of nations. Greeks, Carthaginians, and 

Romans contended in antiquity for the possession of this beautiful island.

Influence of geographical conditions. Geographical condi tions exerted the same profound influence on Italian history as on that of Greece (p. 103). In the first place, the peninsula of Italy is not cut up by a tangle of mountains into many small districts. It was therefore easier for the Italians than for the Greeks to establish one large and united state. In the second place, Italy has comparatively few good harbors, but possesses upland pastures and rich lowland plains. The 

Italian peoples consequently developed cattle raising and agriculture much earlier than commerce. And in the third place, the location of Italy, with its best harbors and most numerous islands on the western side, for a long time brought the peninsula into closer relations with the western islands and the coasts of Gaul, Spain, and North Africa than with the countries bordering on the eastern shores of the Mediterranean. As Greece faced the civilized nations of the East, so 

Italy fronted the barbarous tribes of the West. 

50. ITALIAN PEOPLES 

Etruscans. The earliest civilization in Italy was brought by the Etruscans. They came by sea, perhaps from Asia

Italian Peoples 

179 Minor, and as early as 900 B.C. founded a strong state on the west coast of Italy in the region called after them Etruria (modern Tuscany). The Etruscan dominions in time extended along the coast from the Bay of Naples to the Gulf of Genoa and inland to the Po valley as far as the Alps. These 

Etruscans are a mysterious people; indeed no one has been able to read their language. They were skillful workers in bronze, iron, and gold, and they built cities with massive walls, arched gates, paved streets, and underground drains. 

A great part of Etruscan civilization was ultimately absorbed in that of Rome.

Greeks. After 750 B.C. Greek colonies began to be planted in southern and southwestern Italy. These were all on or near the sea, from the Gulf of Taranto to Campania. The 

Greeks never penetrated deeply into the peninsula. Room was therefore left for the native Italians, under the leadership of Rome, to build up their own power in the peninsula. 

Italians. The Italians were an Indo-European people who spoke a language related both to Greek and to the Celtic tongues of western Europe. They entered the Italian peninsula through the numerous Alpine passes. Wave after wave of these northerners flowed southward, until the greater part of Italy came into their possession. We must assume that the invaders, having overcome all armed opposition, mingled more or less with the earlier inhabitants of Italy. There is every reason to believe that the historic Italians, like the historic Greeks, were a mixed people. 

Latins. The Italians who settled in the central, eastern, and southern parts of the peninsula were highlanders. The western Italians, or Latins, were lowlanders, who dwelt in Latium, originally a flat plain extending south of the Tiber River between the mountains and the sea. The Latins, as they increased in number, gave up tribal life and established little city-states, like those of Greece. The need of defense against their Etruscan neighbors across the Tiber and against the Italian tribes of highlanders in the adjacent mountains bound the Latin tribes together. They united

Rome at a very early period in the Latin League. The chief city in this league was Rome.

THE VICINITY OF ROME 

Anagni (Anagnia)

The Gallic invasion. The enemies of the Etruscans turned out to be also enemies of the Romans. They were the Gauls, a people of Celtic speech, who lived in central and western Europe. These barbarians, whose huge bulk and enormous weapons struck terror to the hearts of their adversaries, poured through the Alpine passes and ravaged far and wide.

Rome

Having defeated the Etruscans, they pressed on toward Rome. At the Allia River, only a few miles from the city, they annihilated a Roman army. The city was panicstricken. No one thought of defending the walls. Some of the citizens withdrew to the citadel on the Capitoline Hill, while others, having hastily removed the sacred fire, fled to neighboring towns. The Gauls plundered and burned Rome but could not capture the citadel. Finally, we are told, the 

Romans induced them to withdraw by the payment of a heavy ransom. Another tale, more favorable to Roman pride, declares that as the gold was being counted out a fresh Roman army appeared and forced the Gauls to retire without booty. 

Rome supreme in Latium, 338 B.C. The Gallic tide receded as swiftly as it had come, and Rome rose from her ashes mightier than ever. About half a century later she was able to subdue her former allies, the Latins. Rome now ruled in 

Latium and southern Etruria and had begun to extend her sway over Campania. She was ready to contest the supremacy of the peninsula with the one Italian people able to meet her on equal terms - the Samnites. 

Rome supreme in central Italy, 290 B.C. Romans and 

Samnites were well matched in numbers, courage, and military skill. Nearly half a century of hard fighting was required before Rome gained the upper hand. The close of the Samnite wars found her supreme in central Italy. Her authority was recognized from the upper Apennines almost to the foot of the peninsula.

Rome supreme in southern Italy, 264 B.C. The wealthy 

Greek cities of southern Italy offered a tempting prize to Roman greed. Many of them before long received Roman garrisons and accepted the rule of the great Latin republic. 

Tarentum, however, the most important of the Greek cities, held jealously to her independence. Unable single-handed to face the Romans, Tarentum turned to Greece for aid. She called on Pyrrhus, king of Epirus, the finest soldier of his age. 

Pyrrhus led twenty-five thousand mercenary soldiers into Italy, an army almost as large as Alexander's. The Romans

Rome could not break the bristling ranks of the Greek phalanx, and they shrank back in terror before the huge war elephants which Pyrrhus had brought with him. The invader won the first battle, but lost many of his best troops. He then offered peace on condition that the Romans should give up their possessions in southern Italy. The Senate returned the proud reply that Rome would not treat with the enemy while he stood on Italian soil. A second battle was so bitterly contested that Pyrrhus declared, “Another such victory, and I am lost." Weary of the struggle, Pyrrhus now crossed over to Sicily to aid his countrymen against the Carthaginians. 

The rapid progress of the Roman arms called him back, only to meet a crushing defeat. Pyrrhus then withdrew in disgust to Greece; Tarentum fell; and Rome soon established her control over southern Italy.

Roman Italy. Rome now ruled from the Strait of Messina northward to the Arno and Rubicon rivers. All the peoples of this part of the Italian peninsula acknowledged her sway. 

It should be noticed, however, that as yet Rome governed only the central and southern parts of what is the modern kingdom of Italy. The Gauls held the Po valley, while most of Sicily and Sardinia remained in possession of the Carthaginians. 

52. EARLY ROMAN LIFE 

The ideal Roman. The early Romans were celebrated for their patriotism, their simplicity of living, and ther conservative, old-fashioned ways. They worked hard on their little farms, fought bravely in their legions, and kept up with careful piety all the ceremonies of their religion. The ideal 

Roman was a Cincinnatus or a Curius Dentatus. When 

Rome was in grave peril, Cincinnatus left his farm to assume the dictatorship. Curius, the conqueror of the Samnites and of Pyrrhus, had celebrated three triumphs, but he still lived modestly in a cottage on a four-acre plot, which he tilled with his own hands. To him came envoys from the 

Samnites, offering rich bribes. "Go tell the Samnites,” he

Early Roman Life 

185 answered, "that Curius counts it glory, not to possess wealth, but to rule those who do." Such men as these, despite their many faults, soon made the little city-state by the Tiber great among the nations.

Roman characteristics. These early Romans were a hardy breed, abstemious in food and drink, iron-willed, vigorous, and strong. Before everything else, they were dutiful citizens and true patriots.

Such were the sturdy men who on their farms in Latium formed the backbone of the Roman state. Their character has set its mark on history for all time. 

EARLY ROMAN BAR MONEY 

A bar of bronze having the value of an ox, whose figure is stamped upon it. 

Dates from the fourth century B.C.

The Roman family. The family formed the unit of Roman society. Its most notable feature was the unlimited authority of the father. In his house he reigned an absolute king. 

His wife had no legal rights: he could sell her into slavery or divorce her at will. Nevertheless, no ancient people honored women more highly than the Romans. A Roman wife was the mistress of the home, as her husband was its master. 

Though her education was not carried far, we often find the Roman matron taking a lively interest in public affairs, and aiding her husband in both politics and business. It was the women, as well as the men, who helped to make Rome great among the nations. Over his sons and his unmarried daughters the Roman father ruled supreme as over his wife. 

He brought up his children to be sober, silent, modest in their bearing, and, above all, obedient. Their misdeeds he might punish with penalties as severe as banishment, slavery, or death. The father's great authority ceased only with his death. Then his sons, in turn, became lords over their families.

Economic conditions. Agriculture was the chief occupation of the early Roman people. "When our forefathers,"

Rome said an ancient writer, "would praise a worthy man, they praised him as a good farmer and a good landlord; and they believed that praise could go no further." Roman farmers raised large crops of grain -the staple product of ancient 

Italy. Cattle breeding, also, must have been an important pursuit, since in early times prices were estimated in oxen and sheep. No great inequalities of wealth existed. Few citizens were very rich; few were very poor. The members of each household made

53. ROMAN RELIGION 

Worship of ancestors. The Romans regarded their dead ancestors as still members of the family. The living and the dead were thus bound together by the closest ties. Ancestor worship greatly strengthened the father's authority, for it made him the chief priest of the household. It also made marriage a sacred duty, so that a man might have children to accord him and his forefathers all honors after death.

Household deities. Roman gods and goddesses were closely connected with daily activities in the home. The ancient 

Roman house consisted of one large room, the atrium, where all members of the family lived together. It was entered by a single door, which was sacred to Janus. On the hearth, opposite the doorway, the housewife prepared the meals. 

The fire that ever blazed upon it gave warmth and nourishment to the inmates. Here, according to the Romans,

Roman Religion 

187 dwelt Vesta, the spirit of the kindling flame. The cupboard where the food was kept for future use came under the charge of the Penates, who blessed the family store. The house as a whole had its protecting spirits, called Lares. 

Janus and Vesta. The early Roman state was only an enlarged family, and hence the religion of the state was modeled upon that of the family. Some of the divinities, such as Janus and Vesta, were taken over with little change from the family worship. The entrance to the 

Forum formed a shrine of Janus. The door, or gateway, stood open in time of war, but shut when Rome was at

At the south end of the Forum stood the round temple of Vesta, containing the sacred hearth of the city. 

Here Vesta was served by six virgins of free birth, who dwelt in a kind of convent close by. It was their duty to keep the fire always blazing on the altar. If by accident the fire went out, it must be relighted from a "pure flame,' either by striking a spark with flint or by rubbing together two dry sticks. Such methods of kindling fire were those familiar to the prehistoric Romans.

Rome

Jupiter and Mars. The Romans worshiped various gods connected with their lives as farmers, shepherds, and warriors. The chief divinity was Jupiter, who ruled the heavens and sent rain and sunshine to nourish the crops.

The war god Mars reflected the military character of the Romans. March, the first month of the old Roman year, was named in his honor.

Divination. The Romans took many precautions, before beginning any enterprise, to find out what was the will of the gods and how divine favor might first be gained. 

They did not have oracles, but they paid much attention to omens of all sorts. A sudden flash of lightning, an eclipse of the sun, a blazing comet, or an earthquake shock was an omen which indicated the disapproval of the gods.

The Romans learned from their 

Etruscan neighbors how to predict the future by examining the entrails of animal victims. They also borrowed from the Etruscans the practice of looking for signs in the number, flight, and actions 2

Importance of Roman religion. This old Roman faith was something very different from what we understand by religion. It had little direct influence on morality. 

It did not promise rewards or threaten punishments in a future world. Roman religion busied itself with the everyday life of man. Just as the household was bound together

Roman Government 

189 by the tie of common worship, so all the citizens were united in a common reverence for the deities that guarded the state. The religion of Rome made and held together a nation. 

54. ROMAN GOVERNMENT 

A threefold system. While Rome was developing into a powerful city-state, it was also evolving a system of government that would fit the changing situation. Early Rome had a threefold government like that of Homeric Greece (p. 112). The king had wide powers: he was commander-in-chief, supreme judge, and head of the state religion. A council of elders (Latin senes, "old men") made up the Senate, which assisted the king in governing. The popular assembly, whenever summoned by the king, voted on important measures.

COTACIUO-CEVOL P 

OPPIANO JEI VIR CURULE CHAIR AND FASCES 

A consul sat on the much

The consuls. After the establishment of the republic in 509 B.C. the king's place was taken by two magistrates called con- curule suls. They enjoyed equal honor and authority. Unless both agreed, nothing could be done. They thus served as a check upon each other, as was the case with the two Spartan kings (p. 116). chair, which resembled our camp chair. The fasces were bundles of rods with an ax in each bundle, symbolizing the consul's power to flog and behead offenders.

These marks of authority were borrowed by the Romans from the Etruscans. 

The dictator. When grave danger threatened the state and unity of action seemed necessary, the Romans sometimes appointed a dictator. The consuls gave up their authority to him and the people put their property and lives entirely at his disposal. The dictator's term of office might not exceed six months, but during this time he had all the power formerly wielded by the kings.

Patricians and plebeians. The Roman city-state seems to have been divided, during the regal age, between an

Rome aristocracy and a commons. The nobles were called patricians (Latin patres, "fathers"), and the common people were known as plebeians (Latin plebs, "the crowd"). The patricians occupied a privileged position, since they alone sat in the Senate and served as magistrates, judges, and priests. The plebeians thus found themselves excluded from much of the political, legal, and religious life of Rome. 

The tribunes. The oppressive sway of the patricians resulted in great unrest at Rome, and after the establishment of the republic the plebeians began to agitate for reforms. They soon compelled the patricians to allow them to have officers of their own, called tribunes, as a means of protection. Any tribune could veto, that is, forbid, the act of a magistrate which seemed to bear harshly on a citizen. To make sure that a tribune's orders would be respected, his person was made sacred, and a solemn curse was pronounced upon the man who injured him or interrupted him in the performance of his duties. 

The Twelve Tables, 451-449 B.C. Before 451 B.C. the 

Romans did not have written laws. They had simply unwritten customs, which, as in Athens before Draco's legislation (p. 118), were interpreted by patrician judges. The plebeians demanded that the customs be set down in writing - be made laws so that every one might know them and secure justice in the courts. A commission was finally appointed to prepare a code. The laws were engraved on twelve bronze tablets and set up in the Forum. Some sentences from these Twelve Tables have come down to us in rude, unpolished Latin. They mark the beginning of Rome's legal system.

Plebeian office-holding. It would take too long to tell how the plebeians broke down the patrician monopoly of office-holding. The result was that in time they became eligible to the consulships and other magistracies, to seats in the Senate, and even to the priesthoods. Henceforth all citizens, whether patricians or plebeians, enjoyed the same rights at Rome.

Italy under Roman Rule 191 Magistrates. Rome had many officials. Besides the two consuls and an occasional dictator there were the ten tribunes, the prætors, who served as judges, and the quæstors, or keepers of the treasury. The two censors were also very important officers. It was their business to make an enumeration or census of the citizens and to assess property for taxation. Their office grew steadily in significance, especially after the censors began to exercise an oversight of the private life of the Romans. They could expel a senator from his seat for immorality and deprive any citizen of his vote. 

We are told that they punished a man for neglecting his farm, another for having kissed his wife in the presence of his daughter, and another for spending too much money on a kinsman's funeral. The censors thus came to sit in judgment on the virtue of all Roman citizens. 

The Senate. The authority of the magistrates, including both consuls and tribunes, was much limited by the Senate. 

It contained about three hundred members, who held office for life. Vacancies in it were filled, as a rule, by persons who had previously held one of the higher magistracies. All weighty matters came before it for decision. It conducted war, received ambassadors from foreign countries, made alliances, administered conquered territories, and, in short, formed the real governing body of the republic. The Senate was not unworthy of its high position. During the centuries when Rome was winning dominion over Italy and throughout the Mediterranean basin, the Senate conducted public affairs with foresight, energy, and success. An admiring foreigner once called it "an assembly of kings." 

55. ITALY UNDER ROMAN RULE 

Roman citizenship. As Rome extended her rule in Italy, she bestowed citizenship upon the conquered peoples. It formed a great gift, for a Roman citizen enjoyed many privileges. He could hold and exchange property under the protection of Roman law; could contract a valid marriage which

Rome made his children citizens; and could vote in the popular assemblies at Rome and hold public office there. This extension of the citizenship to those who formerly had been enemies was something quite new in history, and it was the great secret of Rome's success as a governing power. 

No representative system. Rome was a city-state, and her rule over Italy formed in the fullest sense the rule of a city. She was unfamiliar with the principle of representative government. Citizens who lived outside of Rome could not send representatives to discuss and resolve in their behalf. They had to visit in person the capital city when they wished to exercise their political rights. Few persons, of course, would trudge on foot or ride on horseback many miles to Rome in order to cast their votes or stand for office. The elections, moreover, were not all held on one day as with us, but consuls, prætors, and other magistrates were elected on separate days, while meetings of the assemblies might be held in any part of the year. A country peasant who really tried to fulfill his duties as a citizen would have had little time for anything else. In practice, therefore, the city populace of Rome had the controlling voice in ordinary legislation. The Romans were never able to remedy this grave defect in their political system. 

A ROMAN STANDARD 

BEARER 

Bonn Museum

From a gravestone of the first century A.D. The standard consists of a spear crowned with a wreath, below which is a crossbar bearing pendant acorns. 

Then follow, in order, a metal disk, Jupiter's eagle standing on a thunderbolt, a crescent moon, an amulet, and a large tassel. "Friends and allies" of Rome. The conquered tribes and cities of Italy which did not receive Roman citizenship at this period were not treated as complete subjects. Rome called them, rather, her "friends and allies." They lost the

Rome and Carthage 193 right of declaring war on one another, of making treaties, and of coining money. Rome otherwise left them to govern themselves, never imposing tribute on them and only requiring them to furnish soldiers for the Roman armies in time of war.

Latin colonies. The Romans established what were called 

Latin colonies in various parts of Italy. The colonists, usually veteran soldiers or poor plebeians who wanted farms, surrendered Roman citizenship. When the list of colonists was made up, they all marched forth in military array to take possession of their land and build their city. Having sprung from Rome, they usually remained faithful to her interests. 

The colonies thus formed permanent settlements to keep the conquered peoples loyal and at the same time to spread the Latin language, law, and culture throughout Italy. There were, ultimately, thirty-five of these Latin colonies. They were united with one another and with Rome by an extensive system of roads (p. 237), which are traced on the map on page 183. 

56. ROME AND CARTHAGE 

The Punic wars. The conquest of Italy made Rome one of the five leading states of the Mediterranean world. In the East there were the kingdoms of Macedonia, Syria, and Egypt. In the West there were Carthage and Rome, once in friendly alliance, but now to become the bitterest foes. 

Rome had scarcely reached the headship of united Italy before she was involved in a life-and-death struggle with this rival power. The three wars between them are known as the Punic (that is, Phoenician) wars; they are the most famous contests that ancient history records. 

Commercial empire of Carthage. More than a century before the traditional date at which Rome rose upon her seven hills, Phoenician colonists laid the foundations of Carthage. The city bordered on rich farming land and had the largest harbor of North Africa. By the middle of the

Rome third century B.C. the Carthaginians had formed an imposing commercial empire. Their African dominions included the strip of coast from the Greek city of Cyrene westward to the Strait of Gibraltar. Their settlements lined the shores 

THE BUILDING OF CARTHAGE Vatican Library, Rome

The western half of the 

Mediterranean had become almost a Carthaginian lake. The wealth of Carthage enabled her to raise armies of mercenary soldiers and to build warships which in size, number, and equipment surpassed those of any other Mediterranean state. 

Mistress of a wide realm, strong both by land and poems. masons squaring blocks. Notice the large wheel for lifting the blocks.

It shows a smithy with workers and sea, Carthage was now to prove herself Rome's most dangerous foe.

First Punic War, 264-241 B.C. The First Punic War, which lasted more than twenty years, was a contest for the control of Sicily. The Carthaginians wished to extend their rule over all that island, which from its situation seems to belong almost as much to Africa as to Italy. The Romans, now supreme in the Italian peninsula, also cast envious eyes on

Sicily. They believed, too, that the conquest of Sicily by the Carthaginians would soon be followed by the invasion of southern Italy. By the very nature of the situation the war was fought principally on the sea. The Romans were not a seafaring people and so the Carthaginians naturally had an initial advantage. With characteristic energy, however, the 

Romans built fleet after fleet until they mastered the art of naval warfare. Finally they won a complete victory over the enemy. According to the terms of the treaty Carthage

Rome and Carthage 195 was forced to give up all claims to Sicily, and that island became a Roman province.

The interval of preparation. The peace amounted to no more than an armed truce. The decisive conflict, which should determine whether Rome or Carthage was to rule the western Mediterranean, was yet to come.

Scale of Miles 950 100 200 300 10 15 30 quering the Gauls in the Po valley. The Roman power now extended over northern Italy to the foot of the Alps. Carthage, meanwhile, created a new empire in Spain, as far north as the Ebro River. Spain at this time was a rich, though undeveloped, country. The produce of its silver mines filled the Carthaginian treasury, and its hardy tribes made excellent soldiers for the Carthaginian army. The Punic city thus had both means and men for another struggle with Rome. 

Hannibal. The Second Punic War began in 218 B.C. It is often called the Hannibalic War because the great Cartha-

Rome ginian leader, Hannibal, was its outstanding figure. As a youth he had been with his father during the Punic conquest of Spain. He knew how to follow as well as to lead. He learned to endure danger, toil, and fatigue. At the opening of the second struggle with Rome he was not quite twentyseven years of age. Bold and energetic, he became the idol of his men and the hero of his country. 

Hannibal's invasion of Italy. The Romans planned to conduct the war in Spain and Africa, at a distance from their own shores. Hannibal's bold movements took them by surprise. The young Carthaginian general had determined to fight in Italy. Since Roman fleets now controlled the western 

Mediterranean, it was necessary for him to lead his army, with its supplies, equipment, horses, and war elephants, from Spain through the defiles of the Pyrenees, across the wide, deep Rhône River, through the snow-covered passes of the Alps, and down their steeper southern slopes into the valley of the Po. When, after a five months' march, he stood on the soil of Italy, Hannibal had scarcely twenty-five thousand troops with which to meet the armies of Rome - a power that, given time, could muster to her defense more than half a million disciplined soldiers. 

First victories of Hannibal. The Romans were surprised by the boldness and rapidity of Hannibal's movements. The first battles were complete victories for the Carthaginians and opened the road to Rome, but Hannibal did not want to shatter his army in an assault on the strong walls of that city. 

His real object was to bring the Italians over to his side, to ruin Rome through the revolts of her allies. He now learned, apparently for the first time, that Italy was studded with Latin colonies (p. 193), each a miniature Rome, each prepared to resist to the bitter end. Not a single city opened its gates to the invader.

A dictatorship. The Roman Senate faced the crisis with characteristic energy. New forces were raised and intrusted to a dictator, Quintus Fabius. He refused to meet Hannibal in a pitched battle, but doggedly followed his footsteps,

Rome and Carthage 197 meanwhile drilling his soldiers to become a match for the Carthaginian veterans. This strategy was little to the taste of the Roman populace, who nicknamed Fabius Cunctator, “the Laggard." However, it gave Rome a breathing space, until her preparations to crush the invader should be completed. 

Battle of Cannæ, 216 B.C. After the term of Fabius as dictator had expired, new consuls were chosen. They commanded the largest army Rome had ever put in the field. 

The opposing forces met at Cannæ. The Carthaginians, counting allies and fresh troops, numbered less than fifty thousand men; the Romans had more than eighty thousand troops. Hannibal's sole superiority lay in his cavalry, which was posted on the wings, with the infantry occupying the space between. The Roman soldiers, having pierced the enemy's lines, found themselves exposed on both flanks to the African infantry and taken in the rear by Hannibal's splendid cavalry. The lost battle ended in a hideous butchery. One of the consuls died fighting bravely to the last; the other escaped from the field and with the wreck of his army fled to Rome. A Punic commander who survived such a disaster would have perished on the cross; the Roman commander received the thanks of the Senate "for not despairing of the republic."

After Cannæ. The battle of Cannæ marks the summit of Hannibal's career. He maintained himself in Italy for thirteen years thereafter, but the Romans, taught by bitter experience, refused another engagement with their foe. Hannibal's army was too small and too poorly equipped with siege engines for a successful attack on Rome. His brother, Hasdrubal, led strong reënforcements from Spain to Italy, but these were caught and destroyed before they could effect a junction with Hannibal's troops. Meanwhile the brilliant 

Roman commander, Publius Scipio, drove the Carthaginians from Spain and invaded Africa. Hannibal was summoned from Italy to face this new adversary. He came, and on the field of Zama (202 B.C.) met his first and only defeat. Scipio, the victor, received the proud surname, Africanus.

Rome 

Carthage surrenders, 201 B.C. Exhausted Carthage could now do no more than sue for peace on any terms that Rome was willing to grant. In the hour of defeat, she still trusted her great soldier, and it was Hannibal who conducted the final negotiations. The conditions of peace were severe 

"PUBLIUS SCIPIO AFRICANUS" 

Naples Museum enough. The Carthaginians gave up Spain and all their ships except ten triremes. 

They were saddled with a huge indemnity and bound to engage in no war without the consent of Rome. Carthage thus became a vassal state. 

Third Punic War, 149-146 B.C. Carthage had been humbled, but not destroyed. She still enjoyed the advantages of her magnificent situation and continued to be a competitor for the trade of the western Mediterranean. Rome watched anxiously the revival of the Punic city and at length determined to blot it out of existence. A Roman army landed in Africa, and the Carthaginians were ordered to remove ten miles from the sea. It was a sentence of death to a people who lived almost entirely by maritime trade. In despair they took up arms again and for three years resisted the Romans. The city was finally captured and burned, and its site dedicated to the infernal gods. 

Such was the end of the most formidable rival Rome ever met in her career of conquest. The territory of Carthage was now annexed to Rome and organized as a province, named Africa.

57. THE BEGINNINGS OF EMPIRE 

Empires. The conquest of Sicily gave Rome its first overseas territory. Perhaps it would be profitable to review examples of some empires which have been described. Early 

Egypt was a kingdom, but as soon as it extended its control

The Beginnings of Empire 

199 into Palestine and Syria it became an empire. Assyria and 

Persia became empires when they reached out and got control of peoples of different races, languages, and religions. 

These empires had kings or emperors at their head. The countries were thus imperial in government as well as in extent of territory. Athens, although a democracy in government, controlled an empire of overseas islands and citystates. Now Rome, a republic in government, began to build an empire. Could it control great areas and remain a republic, or would its government also become imperial? 

Sicily and Spain. The first test of Roman ability to govern an empire occurred in Sicily. Fortunately it was inhabited by civilized and peace-loving people, who accepted Roman rule as docilely as they had accepted Greek and Carthaginian control. On the other hand, Spain gave the Romans some hard fighting. The wild Spanish tribes loved their liberty and long kept up a desperate struggle for independence. 

Eventually, the entire Spanish peninsula, except the inaccessible mountain district in the northwest, became Roman territory. Many colonists settled in Spain; traders and speculators flocked to the seaports; even the legionaries, quartered there for long periods, married Spanish wives and made their homes in the peninsula. Rome thus continued in 

Spain the process of Romanization which she had begun in Italy (p. 182). She was to repeat this process in Gaul and 

Britain. Her way was prepared by the sword, but after the sword came civilization.

Rome and Macedonia. While Rome was subduing the 

West, she was also extending her influence over the peoples of the East. Roman interference in the affairs of Macedonia found an excuse in the attempt of that country, during the Second Punic War, to give aid to Hannibal. Macedonia was finally made into a dependent ally of Rome. Thus disappeared a great power, which Philip had founded and which Alexander had led to the conquest of the world. 

Rome and Greece. Having overcome Macedonia, Rome proclaimed Greece a free state. This "freedom" really meant

Rome subjection, as was amply proved when some of the Greek cities rose in revolt against Roman domination. The heavy hand of Roman vengeance descended on Corinth, then one of the most beautiful cities of the world. In 146 B.C., the same year in which the destruction of Carthage occurred, Corinth was sacked and burned to the ground. The fall of 

Corinth may be said to mark the final extinction of Greek liberty. Though the cities and states of Greece were allowed to rule themselves, they paid tribute and thus acknowledged the supremacy of Rome. A century later, Greece became in name, as well as in fact, a province of the Roman Empire. 

Rome and Syria. Rome, in the meantime, was drawn into a conflict with the kingdom of Syria. That Asiatic power proved to be no more capable than Macedonia of checking the Roman advance. The Syrian king had to give up the greater part of his possessions in Asia Minor. The western part of the peninsula, together with the Greek cities on the coast, was formed in 133 B.C. into the province of Asia. 

Political situation in 133 B.C. Roman supremacy over the 

Mediterranean world was now all but complete. In 264 B.C. 

Rome had been only one of the five great Mediterranean states (p. 193). In 133 B.C. no other power existed to match its strength with that of Rome. To her had fallen in the 

West the heritage of Carthage, in the East the heritage of Alexander. Rome had built up this mighty empire at a terrible cost in blood and treasure. Let us see what use she was to make of it. 

58. EFFECTS OF FOREIGN CONQUESTS 

Provinces. Rome's dealings with her new dependencies overseas did not follow the methods that had proved so successful in Italy. The Italian peoples had received liberal treatment. Rome regarded them as allies and in many instances conferred upon them Roman citizenship. It did not seem possible to extend this wise policy to regions beyond the borders of Italy. Rome adopted, instead, much the

Effects of Foreign Conquests 

201 same system of imperial rule that had been followed by Persia and by Athens. The conquered territories were made into provinces. Their inhabitants were disarmed, were obliged to pay tribute, and in all their affairs had to accept the control of Roman officials.

The provincial system. The proper management of conquered territories is always a difficult problem for the bestintentioned state. It cannot be truly said that even Rome's intentions were praiseworthy. There was little desire to rule for the good of the subject peoples. A Roman governor exercised almost absolute sway over his province. He usually looked upon it as a source of personal gain and did everything possible during his year of office to enrich himself at the expense of the inhabitants. They could complain of the governor's conduct to the Senate, which had appointed him, but their injuries stood little chance of being redressed by senatorial courts quite ignorant of provincial affairs and notoriously open to bribery. The provincials also suffered terribly from the extortions of the tax collectors (publicans), who wrung all they could from the people, paid the Roman government its stipulated amount, and then kept the remainder for themselves. They were so grasping that their name became a byword for all that was greedy. One finds in the New 

Testament "publicans" and "sinners" mentioned side by side.

Growth of luxury. The wealth that now poured into Rome from every side promoted the growth of luxurious tastes. 

Newly rich Romans developed a relish for all sorts of reckless display. They built fine houses adorned with statues, costly paintings, and furnishings. They surrounded themselves with troops of slaves. Instead of plain linen clothes, they wore garments of silk and gold. At their banquets they spread embroidered carpets, purple coverings, and dishes of gilt plate. Pomp and splendor replaced the rude simplicity of earlier times.

Disappearance of the peasantry. The rich were becoming richer, but it seems that the poor were also becoming poorer.

Rome After Rome became mistress of the Mediterranean, her markets were flooded with the cheap wheat raised in those granaries of the ancient world, Sicily, North Africa, and 

Egypt. The price of wheat fell so low that Roman peasants could not raise enough to support their families and pay their taxes. They had to sell out, often at a ruinous sacrifice, to wealthy persons who turned many small farms into extensive sheep pastures, cattle ranches, vineyards, and olive orchards. These great estates were worked by gangs of slaves from Carthage, Spain, Macedonia, Greece, and
