59. THE DECLINE OF THE REPUBLIC 

The Gracchi. It was not long before efforts began at 

Rome to remedy some of the evils which were undermining Roman society. The first persons to undertake the work of reform were the two brothers, Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus, each in turn. The Gracchi belonged to the highest nobility of Rome. Their father had filled a consulship and a censorship and had celebrated triumphs. Cornelia, their mother, was a daughter of Scipio Africanus, the conqueror of Hannibal. A fine type of the Roman matron, she called her boys her "jewels," more precious than gold, and brought them up to love their country better than their own lives.

Tiberius Gracchus. Tiberius, the elder brother, was only thirty years old when, in 133 B.C., he became a tribune of the people and began his brief career in politics. Tiberius now brought forward a measure intended to revive the drooping agriculture of Italy. He proposed that some of the public lands of Rome, then largely occupied by wealthy men, who alone had the capital to work them with cattle and slaves, should be reclaimed by the state, divided into small tracts, and given to landless citizens. This proposal aroused a hornet's nest about the reformer's ears. Rich people had occupied the public lands so long that they had come to look upon them as really their own. The great landowners in the Senate got another tribune, devoted to their interests, to place his veto on the measure. The impatient Tiberius now

Rome took a false step. Though a magistrate could not legally be removed from office, Tiberius had the offending tribune deposed and thus secured the desired legislation. This action further angered the aristocrats, who threatened to impeach him as soon as his term expired. To avoid impeachment

Tiberius sought reëlection to the tribunate for the following year. This, again, was contrary to law, which did not permit any one to hold office for two successive terms. On the day appointed for the election, while voting was in progress, a crowd of senators burst into the Forum and killed Tiberius, besides many of his followers. Both sides had now begun to disregard the law. Force and bloodshed, henceforth, were to decide political disputes.

Gaius Gracchus. Nine years after the death of Tiberius 

Gracchus, his brother Gaius also became a tribune. Gaius soon secured the passage of a law permitting the sale of grain from public storehouses to Roman citizens at about half the market price. The law made Gaius popular with the poorer classes, but it increased, rather than lessened, the number of paupers. Gaius showed much more statesmanship in his other measures. He encouraged the emigration of landless men from Italy to the provinces and tried to reform the government of the provinces. He even proposed to be- . stow the right of voting in the assemblies at Rome upon the inhabitants of the Latin colonies (p. 193). This effort to extend Roman citizenship cost Gaius his popularity. It aroused the jealousy of the city mob, which believed that the enrollment of new citizens would mean the loss of its privileges. There would not be so many free shows and so much cheap grain. The people therefore rejected the measure. 

They even failed to reëlect Gaius to the tribunate, though a law had been recently passed permitting a man to hold the position of tribune year after year. The Senate took advantage of the situation to declare Gaius a public enemy. 

Another bloody tumult broke out in which several thousand of his followers perished. Gaius himself committed suicide. 

The senatorial aristocracy. Civil strife at Rome had so

The Decline of the Republic 

205 far left the aristocrats at the head of affairs. They still controlled the Senate, and the Senate still governed Rome. But that body had degenerated. The senators were no longer such able and patriotic men as those who had piloted the state while Rome was gaining world dominion (p. 191). They now thought less of the republic than of their own interests. 

Hence, as we have just seen, they blocked every effort of the Gracchi to improve the condition of the poorer citizens in Italy or of the provincials outside of Italy. Their growing incompetence and corruption, both at home and abroad, made the people more anxious than ever for a leader against the senatorial aristocracy. 

A troubled period. Events of a serious nature were occurring. From the north came German tribes, who had annihilated large Roman armies and were demanding permission to settle in Italy (113-102 B.C.). In Africa Jugurtha, the king of Numidia, had not only rebelled, but had bribed 

Roman senators and consuls (107 B.C.). Throughout Italy the Italian allies were demanding Roman citizenship and started the Social War (90-88 B.C.). In southern Italy a band of slaves, led by the gladiator Spartacus, started the 

War of the Gladiators (73-71 B.C.). A Roman senator, 

Catiline, formed a series of conspiracies to overthrow the government (66-62 B.C.). The times called for a united government and for great leaders. A succession of able but untrustworthy men came to the front.

New leaders. The popular party, which opposed the aristocratic Senate, found a new leader in Marius, who was not an official but a general. He had won his reputation by subduing Jugurtha and by defeating the German tribes who were overrunning northern Italy. The senatorial party also found a new leader in the aristocratic and capable Sulla. He too had won a military reputation. By putting down the rebellious allies who fought the Social War he became the hero of the senatorial party. The war was won, however, only after Rome had granted citizenship to nearly all the Italian towns. It was, nevertheless, a hollow victory, for

Rome the citizens could exercise their rights only by going to Rome. 

This situation left the populace of Rome still in control. 

Rivalry of Marius and Sulla. Marius and Sulla were rivals not only in war but also in politics. The one was the champion of the democrats, the other, of the aristocrats. 

The rivalry between them finally led to civil war, with its attendant bloodshed. Sulla triumphed, thus becoming supreme in the state. Rome now came under the rule of one man, for the first time since the expulsion of the kings (p. 181). 

Sulla used his position of "Perpetual Dictator" only to pass a series of laws intended to intrench the Senate in power. He then retired to private life and died soon afterward (78 B.C.). 

End of senatorial rule. Sulla's attempts to preserve the republic by maintaining all the powers of the Senate were doomed to failure. Many of the senators were incompetent and corrupt. Ambitious generals who had gained fame in foreign wars returned with their victorious legions to seize control of the home government. Strife between classesrich against poor, aristocrats against commoners offered every opportunity for unscrupulous leaders to mount to power by championing the cause of influential and self-seeking groups.

Cicero. Not all the senators, however, tamely stood by while the Roman state moved toward rule by demagogues and dictators. Perhaps the noblest of those who wished to preserve the republic was Cicero. He had come to Rome a youth without wealth or family influence, and had made his way into Roman society by his social and conversational powers and by his capacity for friendship. His mind had been carefully trained under the influence of Greek culture; he had traveled and studied in Greece; and throughout life he loved to steal away from the tumult of the Forum and the law courts and enjoy the companionship of his books. Though the proud nobles were inclined to look down on him, Cicero's splendid eloquence soon gave him prominence at Rome. He was sincerely attached to the republican government and desired to restore the good old days when the Senate repre-

He believed that Rome might yet go back to the ideal of a free commonwealth and that Roman citizens would never accept the slave's ideal of a good but absolute master. 

Impeachment of Verres, 70 B.C. Cicero rose to prominence through his prosecution of Verres, a thieving governor of 

Sicily. Verres had powerful friends among the nobles at

Rome and counted on his influence and wealth to escape punishment. He openly boasted that he had plunder enough to live in luxury, even though he had to surrender two-thirds of it as fees to his lawyers and bribes to the jury. Verres had not reckoned, however, with the brilliant young Cicero, who hurried to Sicily and there collected such an overwhelming mass of evidence that the bare statement of the facts was enough to convict the corrupt governor. Verres went into exile, while Cicero became the foremost lawyer of Rome. 

Seven years later he was elected consul. 

Conspiracy of Catiline, 63 B.C. During his consulship 

Cicero did a public service by exposing the conspiracy of Catiline. Lucius Catiline, a young noble of ability, but bankrupt in character and purse, organized a conspiracy to seize Rome, murder the magistrates, and plunder the rich. He gathered about himself outlaws, slaves, landless peasants, and bankrupts. In a series of speeches before the astounded 

Senate, Cicero exposed Catiline's plans. Catiline then fled to his camp in Etruria and shortly afterward perished in battle, together with three thousand of his followers. Cicero now gained fresh popularity and honor. "If you saved the republic abroad," he said to Pompey, upon the latter's return from the East, "I have saved it at home." 

Pompey and Crassus. Neither Cicero nor Pompey, however, succeeded in saving the republic permanently. Pompey, in fact, finally assisted in destroying it. When he returned from the East in 60 B.C., he was a famous man. 

He had just added Syria and Palestine to the Roman dominions and had conquered Mithridates the Great, a king in Asia Minor, who had fought and defeated Roman armies for

Rome nearly twenty years. He had also, in the course of his career, crushed rebellions in Sicily, Spain, and Italy. He had swept the pirates from the Mediterranean. This very fame caused the Senate to fear his return, and since he had not brought his legions with him, it dared to treat him with disdain. It hesitated to vote him honors or to ratify his arrangements in the 

East. In this predicament Pompey turned for help to his former associate Crassus.

Both had been generals under Sulla and both had served as consuls a few years earlier. Crassus had amassed a colossal fortune in real estate, silver mines, and slaves. He had, besides, won military renown by victory in the War of the Gladiators, a revolt of slaves, outlaws, and ruined peasants. Money and military fame were in these corrupt times the means to political power. Pompey and Crassus formed a political partnership. Into this partnership they took Crassus's friend,

Gaius Julius Cæsar. These three formed what we would call a political ring and what the Romans called the First 

Triumvirate. Why did the veteran politicians and warriors, Pompey and Crassus, admit Cæsar to their partnership? 

POMPEY 

An original marble bust at Copenhagen; probably an authentic portrait. 

60. JULIUS CÆSAR The Rise of Cæsar. Gaius Julius Cæsar belonged by birth to the proud patrician family of the Julii. As a young man he threw himself whole-heartedly into the exciting game of politics as played in the capital city. He won the ear of the multitude by fiery harangues, bribes of money, and gifts of food and public shows. Notwithstanding his aristocratic birth, he identified himself with the popular party, depending for political power on his influence with the city mob rather than on his friends in the Senate. After spending a

Julius Cæsar 209 66 private fortune in currying favor with the populace, he was 'financed" by the millionaire Crassus. When the First

Triumvirate was formed, he was forty years old. Though he had not yet celebrated a military triumph or been a consul, he had held public office, taken part in military affairs, and become an influential politician. Pompey, the military hero, and Crassus, the man of wealth, could use this rising leader, and he could use them. They managed to secure his election as one of the consuls for the year 59 B.C. In return, Cæsar secured the passage of laws which favored Crassus's friends, gave public lands to Pompey's veterans, and ratified Pompey's arrangements in the East. 

Cæsar conquers Gaul, 58-50 B.C. Cæsar did not, meanwhile, forget his ambitions for himself. The careers of 

Marius, Sulla, and Pompey taught him that the road to power at Rome lay through a military command, which would furnish an army devoted to his personal fortunes. Accordingly, after serving a year as consul, he obtained the appointment as governor of Gaul on both sides of the Alps (Cisalpine and Transalpine Gaul). The next eight years were devoted to his remarkable campaigns against the barbarous inhabitants of western Europe. The story of these campaigns has been told by Cæsar himself in his Commentaries, which have become a text for studying Latin in our schools. Cæsar overcame the Gallic tribes in one battle after another, twice bridged the Rhine and invaded Germany, made two military expeditions to Britain, and brought within the Roman dominions all the territory bounded by the Pyrenees, the Alps, the Rhine, and the Atlantic Ocean. 

Cæsar's conquest of Gaul widened the map of the civilized world from the Mediterranean basin to the shores of the Atlantic. Gaul soon received and speedily adopted the 

Latin language, Roman law, and the customs and religion of Rome. 

Cæsar marches on Rome, 49 B.C. The glory that Cæsar gained among the Romans by his conquest of Gaul is indicated by Cicero's exclamation, "Let the Alps sink. The gods

Rome raised them to shelter Italy from the barbarians, but now they are no longer needed." Cæsar was at last the equal of 

Pompey; the situation at Rome soon forced these two leaders into open enmity. Crassus was dead, and Pompey had become identified with the senatorial party. As we have seen, 主持​茶 ​nidhiw non

JULIUS CAESAR

Museum of Art the weak Senate feared successful generals. It had found out, however, that Pompey was its defender. It had therefore allowed him to remain in Rome and had made him sole consul. But the rising general in Gaul, the Senate feared. Consequently it ordered him, in 

49 B.C., to lay down his command. No compromise was possible for 

Cæsar. He had either to submit or to cham- pion his own cause with an army disciplined by eight years of fighting and devoted to his interests. Since it was illegal to lead a provincial army into Italy, such an action would mean war against the republic. Cæsar boldly chose to lead his troops to Rome. As he crossed the Rubicon, the little stream that marked the boundary between Cisalpine Gaul and Italy, he exclaimed, "The die is cast." The civil war that followed ended in the defeat and death of Pompey, the overthrow of the senatorial party, and the complete supremacy of Cæsar. He returned to Rome to receive from

Julius Cæsar 211 the servile Senate the title of "Father of his Country" (Pater Patriæ) and to enjoy the power his sword had won. 

Cæsar's reforms at Rome and in Italy. Cæsar used his power wisely and well. No sooner was internal peace assured than, with restless energy, he entered on a series of far-reaching reforms. His measures sought to remove the economic and social evils which a century of discord had made so manifest. By restricting the monthly distribution of grain to those actually in need, he tried to discourage the public charity which was making the capital city a paradise for the idle and the shiftless. By establishing great colonies beyond the sea, notably on the sites of Carthage and Corinth, he sought to provide farms for the landless citizens of Italy. 

Other measures were intended to bring about a revival of Italian agriculture. Cæsar's active mind even found time to draw up a program.for great public works at home and abroad, for a census of the population and resources of the Roman world, for the improvement of the coinage, and for the reformation of the calendar. 

Cæsar's reforms in the provinces. Cæsar's reforms in the provinces were also epoch-making. He reduced taxes, lessened the burden of collecting them, and took into his own hands the selection of provincial magistrates. He set about breaking down the barriers between Rome and her provinces, so that the distinction between the conquerors and the conquered would be wiped out. To accomplish this purpose, he granted Roman citizenship to communities in Gaul and Sicily, appointed non-Italians to the Senate, and enlisted non- 

Italians in the legions.

Cæsar's position and power. The achievement of these extensive reforms required a strong government. Cæsar was the government. Though he abolished none of the old republican forms, he gathered nearly all the power into his own hands. The Senate became simply his advisory council; the assemblies became his submissive agents; and the consuls, prætors, and tribunes became his pliant tools. He was made dictator for life and held the offices of consul, censor,

Rome and pontifex maximus (high priest). He was also given the title of imperator, with which soldiers customarily saluted a victorious general. He did not accept the title of king, but some believed that he wished that title also. He did not need it. The laurel wreath, the triumphal dress, the conqueror's scepter- all proclaimed the autocrat.

Cæsar's assassination, 44 B.C. Cæsar did not long enjoy supreme power. His foes were enraged, and even some of his friends alarmed. A conspiracy was formed against him by a group of envious and irreconcilable nobles, who believed that he intended to hand down his authority to his heir. The ringleaders in this conspiracy were two supposed friends of Cæsar, namely, Brutus and Cassius. Brutus had served with Cæsar in the Gallic campaigns; Cassius had been a supporter of

Pompey, but Cæsar had pardoned him and given him office. 

In March, 44 B.C., on the very day that the Senate was to discuss a bill giving Cæsar the title of king, the conspirators stabbed him to death in the Senate House. He fell at the foot of Pompey's statue, pierced with no less than twentythree wounds. But Rome had not thereby been helped; as 

Cicero himself said, hearing the news, "The tyrant is dead; the tyranny still lives." 

61. TRANSITION TO EMPIRE 

Octavius appears on the scene. The murderers of Cæsar thought that all Rome would applaud them as the saviors of the republic. But the senatorial party was lukewarm, and the populace mourned Cæsar as a lost friend. The conspirators soon found themselves in great peril. Brutus and

Cassius withdrew to the eastern provinces, leaving Mark 

Antony, Cæsar's friend, to rule Rome. Before long, Cæsar's adopted son and heir, Octavius, appeared on the scene. He was later famous as Augustus, but when he arrived in Rome he was a youth of nineteen who had just returned from studying in Greece. He won the favor of the populace by agreeing to pay Cæsar's legacies to them; he won the

Transition to Empire 

213 Senate by siding with it against Antony. He was already popular with the legions. Men now began to talk of Octavius as the destined restorer of the republic. 

Second Triumvirate, 43 B.C. Octavius, however, had other designs. Like Cæsar, he formed a political ring to promote his fortunes. This ring consisted of Octavius himself, his former antagonist, Antony, and one of Cæsar's officers, Lepidus. At the head of forty-three legions, they marched on 

Rome and forced a hastily gathered assembly to vote them full authority to reorganize the government. Since this government consisted of three men, it is known as a triumvirate, and each member of it had the office of triumvir. One of the first acts of this Second Triumvirate was to wage war against Brutus and Cassius, the last defenders of the republic. 

Octavius and Antony, with their legions, crossed over to the eastern provinces. At Philippi, in 42 B.C., they dispersed the troops of Brutus and Cassius, who, to save themselves from capture, committed suicide. The Second Triumvirate now held the Roman world in its hands. Soon Lepidus was brushed aside by his stronger colleagues, who then divided between themselves the Roman world. Antony took the 

East, with Alexandria as his capital; Octavius took the West, with Rome as his capital. But, as we shall see, this arrangement did not last long. 

Octavius triumphs. Octavius ruled his half of the empire with moderation and success, and year by year became more popular with all classes. Men congratulated themselves upon the return of peace and prosperity under a second Cæsar. 

Things did not go so well, however, in the eastern half of the empire. Soon the Romans were startled by tidings that 

Antony had fallen under the sway of Cleopatra, queen of Egypt, and had restored to her certain Roman provinces which had once been Egyptian possessions. Antony's conduct aroused such public indignation at Rome that the Senate deprived him of the powers which he had as triumvir and declared war on Cleopatra. Octavius led the Roman forces against Antony and Cleopatra. He met their fleet off the

Rome coast of Greece and defeated them in a naval battle in the 

Bay of Actium, 31 B.C. Cleopatra and Antony fled, and Octavius pursued them into Egypt, where the ill-fated couple perished by their own hands. The death of Antony left

Octavius sole survivor of the Second Triumvirate and master of the Roman world.

The first Roman emperor. The triumph of Octavius was a fortunate event. It made possible the return of constitutional government, which had been suspended since the assassination of Cæsar in 44 B.C.; it ended the long period of recurring anarchy which had begun in 88 B.C., when the rivalry of Marius and Sulla brought civil war and bloodshed to Rome. The final step toward orderly government was taken in 27 B.C., when Octavius resigned as triumvir and received from the Senate the title Augustus, by which he will henceforth be designated. The word Augustus is nearly equivalent in our language to "His Sacred Majesty." Thus the Senate was, in effect, declaring him emperor, a word derived from imperator, whose origin we have already noted. Henceforth 

Rome became an empire in form, as well as in territorial extent. 

62. THE EARLY EMPIRE 

The Augustan Age. The emperor Augustus turned with unwearied devotion to the task of ruling wisely and well his vast dominions. He followed the example of Julius Cæsar in his insistence on just government of the provincials. In 

Italy he put down brigandage, repaired the public highways, and planted many colonies in unsettled districts. In Rome he established a regular police service, organized the supply of grain and water, and continued, on a larger scale than ever, the public games. His public works were so numerous that he could boast he had "found Rome of brick and left it of marble." He was also a generous patron of literature, and some of the most famous Latin authors gave splendor to his reign (p. 238). He restored numerous temples that had fallen

The Early Empire 

215 into decay, revived the ancient sacrifices, and celebrated once more the festivals that had been neglected. Upon his death in 14 A.D. the Senate voted him divine honors and enrolled his name among the gods. Temples rose in every province to the deified Augustus, and altars smoked with sacrifices to him. 

Emperor worship spread rapidly over the ancient world and helped to unite all classes in allegiance to the new government.

Successors of Augustus. 

For more than half a century following the death of Augustus, his place was filled by four emperors who claimed kinship with him and Julius Cæsar. 

The first of these was 

Tiberius, a general who had fought on the German frontier during the reign of Augustus. He was tactless, unsocial, and economical. Nevertheless he ruled so conscientiously that emperor set up as a memorial to himself and

Claudius, who ascended the throne in 41 A.D., was a man of broad political vision, which may be traced to the fact that he was a scholar.

Rome very careful whom he appointed to govern them. When he appointed a provincial governor he is said to have remarked, "Do not thank me; I do you no favor but call you to share with me the responsibility of governing. I shall thank you if you will perform your duty well." During Claudius's reign Britain was made a Roman province (p. 201). Claudius's successor, Nero, was a seventeen-year-old boy. For several years he was guided in his governing by his tutor Seneca, an able man. But under the evil influence of his mother and the court he degenerated into a pleasure seeker and a tyrant. He murdered his brother, his mother, and his wife. The Senate finally declared him a public enemy, and, when the soldiers came to seize him, he committed suicide.

Burning of Rome, 64 A.D. During Nero's reign half of 

Rome was burned to the ground by a great fire which raged for a week. A new Rome speedily arose. It was a much finer city than the old, with wide, straight streets instead of narrow alleys, and houses of good stone in place of wooden hovels. Except for the loss of the temples and public buildings, the fire was a blessing in disguise. 

Threatened anarchy. After the death of Nero no one could legally claim the vacant throne. The imperial guard and the legions on the frontiers, profiting by the disorder and uncertainty, placed their own candidates in the field. The throne was finally secured by an able general, Vespasian. 

Capture of Jerusalem, 70 A.D. The Jews, ever since Pompey's campaigns in the Near East (p. 207), had been subject to Rome, and Palestine had formed a part of the province of Syria. During Vespasian's reign a Jewish revolt was crushed and Jerusalem, after a terrible siege of six months, was captured by the emperor's son, Titus. It is said that one million 

Jews perished during the siege and that one hundred thousand were sold into slavery. The Holy City was destroyed and a Roman camp was pitched upon the spot. We may still see in Rome the triumphal arch erected by Titus to commemorate his victory. 

The Good Emperors. Near the end of the first century

The Early Empire 

219 A.D. began the reigns of the five Good Emperors. Three of these are especially noteworthy Trajan, Hadrian, and 

Marcus Aurelius. Under their just and beneficent government the empire reached its greatest prosperity. Trajan enlarged the Roman world to the widest limits it was ever to reach. (See map between pp. 215 and 218.) Hadrian aban- 

THE MAUSOLEUM OF HADRIAN 

This huge structure is on the right bank of the Tiber and opposite what was once the Campus Martius. It was begun by Hadrian in 136 as a tomb for himself and his successors. 

During the Middle Ages it was turned into a castle, which the popes used as a fortress. 

The building rests on a vast square base, above which rises a cylindrical colonnaded story and a conical roof. A second story has disappeared, together with the marble facing of the tomb and the many statues which ornamented it. The present name, "Castle of the 

Angel" (Castel' Sant' Angelo), arose from the legend that the archangel Michael, when a great plague raged in Rome during the sixth century, had been seen above the building sheathing his fiery sword as a sign that the wrath of the Lord was satisfied. A statue of the archangel now crowns the monument. The bridge across the Tiber was also built by Hadrian. doned some of these conquests, and on other frontiers he built fortresses and walls. In the provinces he raised baths, aqueducts, theaters, and temples. The last of the Good 

Emperors, Marcus Aurelius, was a thinker and a student, but he enjoyed little opportunity for meditation. His reign was filled with an almost uninterrupted series of campaigns, many of them against the Germans on the Danube and the Rhine. These wars revealed the weakness of the frontiers and the rapidly growing strength of the barbarians outside

Rome the empire. Wars were still going on when Marcus Aurelius died of fever in his camp at Vienna. He must have felt, as he closed his eyes forever, that the age of peace and prosperity was drawing to a close and that evil days were now in store for Rome.

Pax Romana. Over two hundred years passed between the battle of Actium in 31 B.C. and the death of Aurelius in 

180 A.D. For the Roman Empire, this long period was a time of settled government and internal tranquillity. With one 

ROMANS DESTROYING A GERMAN VILLAGE Relief on the Column of Marcus Aurelius, Rome exception, following the death of Nero, there had been an orderly succession to the throne. Disturbances of a serious nature occurred only on the frontiers and in the city of Rome. 

But the clash of arms on the distant frontiers scarcely disturbed the serenity of the Roman world, and the doings and misdoings of the ruling classes at Rome exerted little influence outside the capital city. Rome itself might be disturbed by conspiracy and bloodshed, but Italy and the provinces kept their prosperity. This period of over two hundred years has become famous in history as the longest period of peace the world has ever known. It was made possible by a

The Later Empire 

221 strong government that enforced its will upon the members of the empire. The long peace thus secured has been called the Pax Romana, or the Roman Peace. 

63. THE LATER EMPIRE 

A period of decline. The period called the Later Empire covers the two hundred and fifteen years from the death of the emperor Marcus Aurelius to the division of the Roman world at the death of Theodosius I in 395. It formed, in general, a period of decline. The very existence of the empire was threatened, from within and from without. The Roman armies on the frontiers often set up their favorite leaders as contestants for the throne, thus provoking civil war. Ambitious governors of distant provinces sometimes revolted against a weak or unpopular emperor and tried to establish independent states. The Germans took advantage of the unsettled condition of affairs to make constant inroads on the northern frontier. In the East the Persians endeavored to recover from Roman hands provinces which had once belonged to the old Persian realm. During much of this troubled period emperor after emperor followed in quick succession to reign for a time and then to perish in some sudden insurrection. Within a single year (237-238) six rulers were chosen, worshiped, and then murdered by their troops. 

Weaknesses in the imperial system. Early in this period of decline serious weaknesses in the imperial system became apparent. In the first place, the empire was unwieldy. 

There were the distant frontiers on the Rhine, Danube, and Euphrates to be guarded; there were all the provinces to be governed. A single ruler, no matter how able and energetic, had more than he could do. In the second place, the succession to the imperial throne was uncertain. Sometimes an emperor named his successor, sometimes the Senate elected him, and sometimes the swords of the legionaries decided the succession. Such an unsettled state of affairs led to civil strife which threatened to wreck the empire.

Rome 

Reign of Diocletian, 284–305. A hundred years after the death of Marcus Aurelius the government seemed to be on the verge of collapse. The crisis brought forth a strong, ambitious man, Diocletian, who had entered the army as a common soldier, risen to high command, and fought his way to the throne. Resolutely he set himself to the task of remaking the Roman government. He selected a trusted lieutenant named Maximian to share equally with himself both the duties and the honors of emperor. Diocletian chose to rule the East and left Maximian to rule the West. 

Diocletian then centralized authority by arranging for a regular gradation of officials, reaching from the lowest to the highest. Each of the hundred and one provinces contained several magistrates responsible to the governor of the province. The provinces were grouped into thirteen dioceses, each of which was in charge of a vicar. The thirteen dioceses were grouped into four prefectures, each of which was in charge of a prefect. Over this series or hierarchy of officials the emperors, with the title of Dominus (Lord), ruled supreme. They were treated as gods, and everything that touched their persons was sacred. They wore a diadem of pearls and gorgeous robes of silk and gold, like those of

Asiatic monarchs (p. 92). They filled their palaces with a crowd of fawning, flattering nobles, and busied themselves with an endless round of stately and impressive ceremonials. 

It was the aim of Diocletian to display the unbounded power of a Roman emperor.

Reign of Constantine, 324-337. Diocletian's reforms did not end the disputes about the succession. Finally, in 324, after another civil war, Constantine emerged as the sole master of the Roman world. His reign was made memorable by two events of lasting importance. In the first place, he recognized Christianity as one of the religions of the empire and thus paved the way for the triumph of that faith over the ancient paganism (p. 256). In the second place, he established a new capital for the Roman world at Byzantium on the Bosporus. Soon it was called, in honor of its founder,

The Later Empire 

223 Constantinople. It was to be not simply a new seat of government but a distinctively Christian capital. Such it remained throughout the Middle Ages (p. 296). 

The two Roman Empires. After the death of Constantine the eastern and western halves of the empire tended more and more to grow apart. By 395 there came to be in fact, if not in name, a Roman Empire in the East and a Roman Empire in the West. The dividing line between them is 10 50 London avis Mutotras Saxons Vandols

The Roman Empire in the East managed to endure for over a thousand years until its final overthrow by the Turks in 1453 (p. 315). "Classical" civilization. We have now gained some idea of the civilization built up by Græco-Romans around the shores of the Mediterranean during the thousand years between 500 B.C. and 500 A.D. Their civilization is called

Rome "classical," a word which comes to us from the Latin and still has a general reference to anything of the first rank or of supreme excellence. The Greeks and Romans reached so high a cultural level that they could not fail to influence profoundly the less advanced and even barbarous peoples of Europe, who have grown into the leading nations of today. There was a transmission of classical civilization from its Mediterranean center to western Europe, just as, in earlier times, many civilizing elements passed from the 

Near East to the Greeks.

CHAPTER VIII ROMAN LIFE AND THOUGHT 

these 

Remember thou, O Roman, to rule the nations with thy sway shall be thine arts to crown Peace with Law, to spare the humbled, and to tame in war the proud. 

- VIRGIL Other aspects of Roman history. The history of the 

Romans is more than a record of what they did as warriors, rulers, and builders of states and empires. It includes a description of their private and community life, and an account of their accomplishments in literature, philosophy, science, and the arts. 

64. CLOTHING AND HOUSES What the Romans wore. The mild Mediterranean cli mate permitted the Romans as well as the Greeks to wear a simple, scanty costume. The toga, corresponding to the 

Greek mantle, formed the public dress of the citizens. It was a heavy, woolen robe, white in color, enveloping the entire figure and reaching to the feet. Roman boys wore a toga with a crimson border. On reaching their majority they exchanged it for a pure white toga. Women's clothing was very similar to that of the men, but often of finer texture and more varied in color. Head coverings were seldom worn, except in rainy or stormy weather. Footwear consisted of sandals and shoes; soldiers wore boots. Most persons in the house wore only sandals. 

How we learned about Roman houses. A great misfortune that overtook two Roman cities has enabled us to learn many details about Roman houses. At the foot of Mount Vesuvius, near Naples, were the two cities, Pompeii and Hercu- 227

Roman Life and Thought laneum. Mount Vesuvius was a volcano which had been inactive for centuries. In the year 79 it broke forth in a mighty eruption and covered Pompeii with cinders, small stones, and ashes to an average depth of eighteen to twenty feet. 

Herculaneum was overwhelmed by the same volcanic deposits, but these, being drenched with water, hardened into a sort of rock, which ranges from forty to more than one hundred feet in thickness. The unfortunate cities were completely entombed, and in time their very location was forgotten. The site of Pompeii was accidentally discovered in 1748. Since that date numerous excavations have laid bare a large part of that ancient city, with its streets, shops, baths, temples, and theaters. At Herculaneum recent excavations have uncovered many household articles. In these ancient cities the visitor gains a vivid impression of Roman life during the first century of our era. CAVEC

The atrium. The excavations at Pompeii afford a very good idea of a Roman house, especially of its interior arrangements. A small vestibule opened from the street into a narrow passage closed at the farther end by a heavy oaken door. A dog was sometimes kept chained in this hallway; in Pompeii there is a picture of one worked in mosaic on the floor, with the warning beneath it, "Beware of the dog."

Having made known his presence by using the knocker, the guest was ushered into the reception room, or atrium. This was a large apartment covered with a roof, except for a hole in the center admitting light and air. A marble basin underneath caught the rain water which came through the opening. The atrium represents the single room of the early 

Roman house without windows or chimney.

65. DAILY LIFE AT ROME 

Morning round of a Roman noble. A Roman of the higher class rose at an early hour and after a light breakfast attended to his private business with the help of his steward and manager. He then took his place in the atrium to meet the crowd of dependents who came to pay their respects to their patron

Daily Life at Rome 

231 and to receive their usual morning alms — either food or sufficient money to buy a modest dinner. Having greeted his visitors and perhaps helped them in legal or business matters, the noble entered his litter and was carried down to the Forum. Here he might attend the law courts to plead a case for himself or for his clients. If he were a member of the 

Senate, he would take part in the deliberations of that body. 

At eleven o'clock, when the ordinary duties of the morning were over, he would return home to eat his luncheon and enjoy the midday rest, or siesta. The practice of having a nap in the heat of the day became so general that at noon the streets of a Roman city were practically deserted. 

The afternoon exercise and bath. After an hour of refreshing sleep it was time for the regular exercise out of doors in the Campus Martius or indoors at one of the large city baths. Many houses of wealthy nobles also contained special rooms fitted up for gymnastic exercises, especially for the game of handball. Then came one of the chief pleasures of a Roman's existence — the daily bath. It was taken ordinarily in one of the public bathing establishments. A 

Roman bath was a luxurious affair. After undressing, the bathers entered a warm anteroom and sat for a time on benches, in order to perspire freely. This was a precaution against the danger of passing too suddenly into the hot bath, which was taken in a large tank of water sunk in the middle of the floor. Then came an exhilarating cold plunge and anointment with perfumed oil. The bathers afterwards rested on the couches with which the resort was supplied and passed the time in reading or conversation until the dinner hour. 

Evening meal. The evening meal with the Romans, as with the Greeks, was the principal one of the day. It was usually a social function. The Romans borrowed from the 

Greeks the custom of ending a banquet with music and conversation (p. 149).

Roman Life and Thought 66. ROMAN AMUSEMENTS 

Dramatic shows. The average Roman citizen could not endure to sit all day on the hard stone benches of an outdoor theater watching the tragic dramas that held a Greek audience enthralled. Only the lighter comedies, adaptations from Greek originals, were really popular at Rome. Pantomimes formed the staple amusement of the Roman theater. 

In these performances a single dancer, by movement and 

THE CIRCUS MAXIMUS (RESTORATION) 

gestures, represented mythological scenes and love stories; a chorus accompanied him with songs. There were also vaudeville entertainments by jugglers, rope-dancers, acrobats, and clowns, to amuse a people who found no pleasure in the refined productions of the Greek stage. 

Chariot races. The "games of the circus" took place at 

Rome chiefly in the Circus Maximus. Chariot races furnished the principal attraction. Four horses were usually harnessed to a chariot, though sometimes the drivers showed their skill by handling as many as six or seven horses. The contestants whirled seven times around the low wall which divided the race course. The shortness of the stretches and

Roman Amusements 

233 the sharp turns about the wall must have prevented the attainment of great speed. A race, nevertheless, was a most exciting sport. What we should call "fouling" was permitted and even encouraged. The driver might turn his team against another or might try to upset a rival's car. 

It was a very tame contest that did not have its accompaniment of broken chariots, fallen horses, and killed or injured drivers. One event followed another during the day, until the approach of darkness compelled the spectators to turn homewards.

Animal shows. The Circus Maximus was often used for a variety of animal shows. Fierce wild beasts, brought 'from every quarter of the empire, were turned loose to slaughter one another or to tear to pieces condemned crimi- There were also contests between savage animals and Such amusements did something to satisfy the lust for blood in the Roman populace a lust which was more completely satisfied by the combats of gladiators (Latin gladius, "sword"). nals. men.

Gladiatorial shows. Exhibitions of gladiators probably started from the early practice of sacrificing prisoners or slaves at the funeral of their master. The custom then arose of allowing the victims a chance for their lives by having them fight one another, the conquerors being spared for future battles. It was only a step from this to keeping trained slaves as gladiators. Gladiatorial shows were freely given by aspiring politicians who wished to curry favor with the populace. The number of such exhibitions increased greatly during the imperial age. The emperor Trajan, for example, in celebrating one of his victories exhibited no less than ten thousand men within a space of four months. 'Bread and the games of the circus." Gladiatorial combats, chariot races, and dramatic shows were free performances. They became the chief pleasure of life for the lower classes in the Roman city. The days of their celebration were public holidays, which in the fourth century A.D. numbered no less than one hundred and seventy-five. The once

67. THE CITIES 

Growth of cities. The peace and prosperity which the 

Roman world enjoyed during the first two centuries of our era fostered the growth of cities. Rome was the largest of these, her population being estimated at over a million. 

Numerous other cities rose to magnificence. Every city was a miniature Rome, with its forum and senate house, its temples, theaters, and baths, its circus for racing, and its amphitheater for gladiatorial combats. Most of the cities enjoyed an abundant supply of water, and some had good sewer systems and well-paved, though narrow, streets. The excavations at Pompeii have revealed to us the appearance

Commerce and Industry 235 of one of these ancient cities. What we find at Pompeii was repeated in hundreds of places from the Danube to the Nile, from Britain to Arabia. 

City politics. The cities of Roman origin, especially those in the western provinces, copied the municipal system of Rome. 

Each had a council, or senate, and a popular assembly which chose the magistrates. Many of the inscriptions found on the walls of Pompeii show that local politics excited the keenest interest. One inscription reads, "Vote for Gaius

Julius Polybius, he provides fine bread"; another reads, "Vote for Bruttius Balbus, he will manage the city treasury well." Public officials provided banquets, imposing festivals, wild beast hunts, and bloody contests of gladiators like those of Rome.

Support of the cities. The cities were not supported by direct taxes levied on the citizens. Some municipal revenues were derived from mines, quarries, and other public property. Private individuals, however, bore a large share of the expenditures for pavements, buildings, education, feasts, and games. Heavy contributions for such purposes were expected from all who held the honor of a magistracy. A law was even passed forbidding a candidate to promise great benefactions to the voters, unless, after election, he carried them out. Wealthy men were glad to win the applause of their fellows by splendid donations. Many of the emperors also made gifts for civic purposes. 

68. COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY 

Promotion of commerce. The first two centuries of our era also formed the golden age of Roman commerce. Augustus and his successors kept the seas free from pirates, built lighthouses and improved harbors, policed the highways, and made travel by land both speedy and safe. An imperial currency replaced the various national coinages, and free trade flourished between the cities and provinces of the 

Roman world.

Roman Life and Thought 

Rome as a commercial center. The importation and disposal of foreign goods at Rome furnished employment for many thousands of traders. There were great wholesale merchants in whose warehouses were stored grain and all kinds of merchandise. There were also many retail shopkeepers. They might be sometimes the slaves or freedmen of a wealthy noble, who supplied them with capital but himself kept in the background. Sometimes they were men of free 140

Albertinum, Dresden

A tomb relief of the imperial age, from Rome. The inside of the shop is shown, with the butcher at work and with his wife writing accounts. birth. The feeling that petty trade was unworthy of a citizen, though strong in republican days, tended to disappear under the empire.

Life of the working classes. Free workingmen throughout the Roman world seem to have led a fairly comfortable existence. They were not forced to labor for long hours in grimy, unwholesome factories. Slums existed, but no sweatshops. If wages were low, so also was the cost of living. 

Wine, oil, and wheat flour were cheap. The public baths stood open to every one who could pay a trifling fee. Numerous holidays, celebrated with games and shows, brightened existence. On the other hand, the slaves were often condemned to bare, hard, hopeless lives.

Commerce and Industry 

237 Landholding. The class of small farmers well-nigh disappeared from Italy during the latter days of the republic. 

During the imperial age most of the land continued to be owned by a few wealthy men, who worked it with slave labor or else rented it out to the former peasant owners. 

The latter thus became tenants, depending on their landlords for tools and stock and paying to them a percentage of the crops as rent. Many tenants were not much better off 

A ROMAN VILLA 

During the imperial age, Italy, from the Bay of Naples to the foot of the Alps, was dotted with elegant residences, having flower gardens, game preserves, fishponds, and artificial lakes. The above picture is drawn from a wall painting found at Pompeii. than slaves, for the law often compelled them to work for their masters a certain number of days each year without recompense and also forbade them to leave their farms in search of employment elsewhere. Such compulsory tenants are called "serfs." This system of landholding had long prevailed in the Near East and in North Africa under the Carthaginians. The Romans extended the system to Spain, Gaul, Britain, and other provinces, and it afterward became general throughout western Europe during the Middle Ages. 

Roads. An effective system of communication and transportation was necessary to keep the commerce and government of the Roman Empire functioning. The first great road, known as the Appian Way, was carried as far as

Roman Life and Thought 

Capua and was later extended to Brindisi on the Adriatic Sea, whence travelers embarked for Greece. Other trunk lines were soon built in Italy, and from them a network of smaller highways penetrated every part of the peninsula.

The principal trunk lines began at the gates of Rome and radiated thence to every quarter of the empire. Along these highways sped the couriers of the Cæsars, carrying dispatches and making, by means of relays of horses, as much as one hundred and fifty miles a day. They resounded to the tramp of the legionaries passing to their stations on the distant frontier. Travelers by foot, horseback, or litter journeyed on them from land to land, employing the maps which described routes and distances. 

Traders used the roads for the transport of merchandise and so they became important arteries of commerce. Roman roads were the railways of antiquity. 

69. EDUCATION 

Home training. In the early days of Rome the boy received only home training, which aimed to fix good habits rather than to impart knowledge. The father took his son into the fields to learn the work of the farmer, and into the Forum to learn the duties of a citizen. Since every Roman was bred for the soldier's life, the boy was taught the use of arms, as well as such manly exercises as riding and swimming. 

He also acquired from his father's tuition some knowledge of reading, writing, and arithmetic.

Elementary schools. When elementary schools became popular, their instruction more and more took the place of the father's teachings. A boy began his school days at about the age of seven. He learned to read, to write with a stylus on wax tablets, and to cipher by means of the reckoning board, or abacus (p. 34). He received a little instruction in singing and memorized proverbs and maxims, besides the laws of the Twelve Tables (p. 190). His studying went on under the watchful eyes of a harsh schoolmaster, who did not

Education 239 hesitate to use the rod. A Roman poet tells us that if a boy missed a single syllable in his reading, he was soon black and blue all over "striped just like his nurse's cloak." 

Grammar schools. After Rome began to come into close contact with Greece the curriculum was enlarged by the study of literature. The Romans were the first people who made the learning of a foreign tongue an essential part of a liberal education. Schools now arose in which the Greek language and literature formed the chief subject of instruction. As Latin literature developed, its productions were also studied. Cicero's orations and the poems of Virgil and 

Horace were in common use as texts for study. In these grammar schools Roman boys completed their ordinary education. By this time they would have become of age (usually between the fourteenth and seventeenth years) and would be ready to assume the duties of citizenship.

Rhetoric schools. The rhetoric schools lay outside the regular educational system. They were conducted by Greek, and occasionally by Roman, teachers. These institutions were like our colleges in providing an advanced course for young men who had already finished their elementary studies. The instruction given in them had to do chiefly with the art of prose composition and the practice of public speaking. Their work became very popular at Rome, for oratory was one of the main avenues to distinction open to a young man of ability and ambition. 

Travel and study abroad. Persons of wealth or noble birth might continue the training of the rhetoric schools by a university course at a Greek city, such as Athens, Alexandria, or Rhodes. Here the Roman youth would listen to lectures on philosophy delivered by the deep thinkers whom Greece still produced, and would profit by the treasures of art and science preserved in those ancient capitals. Many famous 

Romans thus passed several years abroad in graduate study. 

During the imperial age real universities also arose in the West, particularly in Gaul and Spain, and attracted students from all parts of the empire.

Roman Life and Thought 70. LATIN LITERATURE 

The record of Roman thought. As we have seen, much of our knowledge of Roman civilization has been obtained from the remains of Roman statues and buildings, especially in such cities as Rome and the rediscovered Pompeii. From the 

Roman writings that have come down to us, we know how the Romans felt and thought. During the Middle Ages, when 

Greek literature was either neglected or forgotten in western Europe, Latin literature was still read and enjoyed. It has come down from the Middle Ages to us. 

Cicero and Cæsar. The famous statesman Cicero ranks also as an eminent author. He created a style for Latin prose which has been admired and imitated by literary men even to our own day. Cicero's qualities as an author are shown in his Orations and in the numerous Epistles which he wrote to friends and correspondents in all parts of the Roman world. They are models of what good letters ought to be, the expression of the writer's real thoughts and feelings. Another eminent statesman, Julius Cæsar, won success in literature. His Commentaries on the Gallic and 

Civil wars, though brief and in most parts rather dull, are highly praised for their simple, concise style. 

Virgil and Horace. Latin literature reached its golden age in the reign of Augustus. The most famous poet of this period was Virgil. The Eneid, which he undertook at the suggestion of Augustus, is his best known work. This poem is a narrative of the adventures of the Trojan hero Æneas, but its real theme is the growth of Rome under the fostering care of the gods. The Æneid is the only ancient epic worthy of comparison with the Iliad and the Odyssey. Another member of the Augustan circle was Virgil's friend and fellow worker, Horace. He reproduced in Latin verse the forms and sometimes even the ideas of Greek poets, but what he borrowed he made his own by the added beauty which he gave to it. He is most famous for his Odes. 

Livy and Tacitus. The most famous prose writer of the

Roman Art 

241 Augustan period was Livy. His history of Rome, beginning with Romulus and extending to Augustus, traced the rise and growth of the Roman state during eight centuries of triumphal progress. It did in prose what Virgil's Eneid had done in poetry. The other great Roman historian is 

Tacitus. He wrote during the period of the Good Emperors (p. 218). The crowning labor of his life was a history of 

Rome from about 14 A.D. to 96 A.D. He tells us little about the provinces but a great deal about the emperors and 

Roman politics.

The arch was employed at first mainly for gates, drainage sewers, aqueducts, and bridges, but later it was used in the construction of vast buildings with enormous domes. The principle of the dome

Roman Life and Thought has been employed in some of the finest creations of ancient and modern architecture. 

The use of concrete. For many of their buildings the 

Romans made use of concrete. Its chief ingredient was a sand found in great abundance near Rome and elsewhere in Italy. When mixed with lime it formed a very strong cement. 

This material was poured in a fluid state into timber casings, where it quickly set and hardened. Buildings of concrete were usually faced with brick, which in turn might be covered with thin slabs of marble.

Temples and basilicas. Roman temples are mostly copies from the Greek. In comparison with their originals they lack grace and refinement.

Aqueducts. Perhaps the most imposing, and certainly among the most useful, of Roman structures were the aqueducts for bringing water to the city. There were sixtyeight in Italy and the provinces. No less than fourteen supplied the capital city with water. The aqueducts usually

243 ran under the surface of the ground, as do our water pipes. 

They were carried on arches across depressions and valleys. These structures were intended simply as engineering 

A ROMAN AQUEDUCT 

The bridge called the Pont du Gard near Nîmes in southern France was built in the late first century B.C. or in the early first century A.D. It spans two hilltops nearly a thousand feet apart and carries an aqueduct with three tiers of arches at a height of 100 feet above the river Gard. Public baths. The abundant water supply furnished by the aqueducts was connected with a system of great public baths. Scarcely a town or village throughout the empire lacked one or more such buildings. Those at Rome were constructed on a scale of magnificence of which we can form but a slight conception from the ruins now in existence. In addition to many elaborate arrangements for the bathers, the baths included lounging and reading rooms, libraries, gymnasiums, and even museums and galleries of art. 

Triumphal arches and columns. A very characteristic example of Roman building is found in the triumphal arches.

Their sides were adorned with bas-reliefs, which pictured

Roman Life and Thought the principal scenes of a successful campaign. Memorial structures, called columns of victory, were also set up in Rome and other cities. Both arch and column have been frequently imitated by modern architects. 

ARCH OF CONSTANTINE 

Erected at Rome in 315 A.D. It consists of a central gateway and two smaller arches flanked by detached columns in the Corinthian style. There are four large statues in front of the upper story and numerous sculptures in relief. 

Circuses, theaters, and amphitheaters. The palaces of 

Roman emperors and nobles, together with their luxurious country houses, or villas, have all disappeared. A like fate has befallen the enormous circuses, such as the Circus Maximus at Rome and the Hippodrome at Constantinople. The 

Roman theaters that still survive reproduce, in most respects, the familiar outlines of the Greek structures. In the amphitheaters, where animal shows and gladiatorial combats were exhibited, we have a genuinely Roman invention; the gigantic Colosseum, which still survives in Rome, is an example of an amphitheater. 

Roman sculpture. Roman sculpture owed much to Greek models. However, the portrait statues and bas-reliefs show originality and illustrate the tendency of the Romans toward realism in art. The sculptor tried to represent an historic

Roman Law 

245 person as he really looked or an historic event, for example, a battle or a triumphal procession, as it actually happened. 

The portrait statues of Roman emperors and statesmen impress us at once with a sense of reality. 

Roman painting. Our knowledge of Roman painting is almost wholly confined to the wall paintings found at Rome, Herculaneum, and Pompeii. What has survived consists mostly of scenes from classical mythology. The coloring is very rich, and the peculiar shade of red used is known today by the name of "Pompeian red." The practice of wall painting (murals) passed over from the Romans to later European artists, who have employed it in the frescoes of medieval and modern churches. 

72. ROMAN LAW Growth of Roman law. The code of the Twelve Tables, framed by the Romans almost at the beginning of the republic, was too harsh, technical, and brief to meet the needs of a growing state. The Romans gradually improved their legal system after they began to rule over conquered territories and to become familiar with the customs of foreign peoples. 

Roman law in this way took on an exact, impartial, liberal, and humane character. It protected the child against a father's tyranny and wives against ill-treatment by their husbands. It provided that a master who killed a slave should be punished as a murderer, and even taught that all men are originally free by nature and therefore that slavery is contrary to natural right. Justice it defined as "the steady and abiding purpose to give to every man that which is his own."

The Code of Justinian. The extension of Roman citizen ship to the provincials carried this better law throughout the empire. During the reign of Justinian (527-565 A.D.) all the sources of Roman law were collected and put into scientific form. The result was the famous code called the Corpus 

Juris Civilis, the "Body of Civil Law." It passed from

Roman Life and Thought ancient Rome to modern Europe, becoming the foundation of the legal systems of Italy, Spain, France, Germany, and other continental countries. Even the Common Law of 

England, which has been adopted by the United States, owes some of its principles to the Corpus Juris Civilis. The law of Rome, because of this widespread influence, is justly regarded as one of her most important gifts to the world. toga

Unit V 

MEDIEVAL CIVILIZATION 

How civilization faltered, became Christian, and slowly regained its pace 

(CHAPTERS IX-XI)

PRESENTATION 

In the preceding unit we brought the story of our civilization down to the splitting of the Roman Empire into an eastern and a western division. In Unit V we shall treat of the thousand and more years that followed, a period known as the Middle Ages. We shall notice the following developments.

Christianity rises, slowly wins the empire, and builds up a strong organization. But barbarians are already crossing the frontiers of the empire; soon they overrun it and bring on a Dark Age. In time they come under the influence of Christianity and of what remains of classical civilization. (Chapter IX) 

Then the Franks revive the idea of an inclusive empire, but there occur fresh inroads of barbarians, those of the Northmen leading to the foundation of new states. Out of the general confusion arises an arrangement of society called feudalism, which is a step toward recovery. Also, amidst this confusion the Christian church in the 

West rises to leadership in spiritual and often in political affairs. 

Meanwhile, in the East, the Byzantine Empire preserves Græco- Roman civilization, but Mohammedan Arabs develop a civilization and a religion which threaten Christianity. The Crusades bring the Christians of western Europe into contact with their more cultivated fellow Christians in the East and with the Mohammedan Arabs in Asia Minor and the Holy Land; the Crusades thus still further speed the recovery of civilization. As cities and commerce revive, feudalism declines and kings grow more powerful, and national states arise. (Chapter X) 

By the later Middle Ages the darkness that followed the barbarian invasions had begun to lift. The later Middle Ages were for western 

Europe a period of developing government, increasing knowledge, and progress in many fields of human activity. New cities, with a thriving industry and commerce, came into being. The various national or vernacular languages of Europe began to take their present form, and both poetry and prose were written in them. 

Architecture revived and flowered in majestic cathedrals. Great universities arose all over western Europe. This rich, many-sided culture naturally owed much to the classical civilization which preceded it, but it was in many respects a new civilization, and to it the name medieval is given. It underlies the civilization of our own day. (Chapter XI)

JAMES BRYCE 73. RISE AND SPREAD OF CHRISTIANITY 

Jesus. While the emperor Augustus was reigning over his mighty empire, there was born, in a far-away province on the fringe of the Roman world, a child who was destined to build an empire of another kind- and more lasting. 

The child Jesus, as is told in the New Testament, was born of humble Jewish parents in the little town of Bethlehem in Judæa. He spent most of his short life in the village of 

Nazareth in Galilee; he is therefore variously called Jesus of Nazareth, the Nazarene, and the Galilean. When about thirty years of age, Jesus began to teach and preach throughout Galilee and Judæa. He soon attracted many followers from among the common people. Twelve of these he chose as his disciples, who kept him company and went about with him from place to place. Jesus invited men to become members of a new kingdom. He warned them that his kingdom was not of this world, but that it existed in the hearts of men who repented of their sins and wished to do the will of God. After about three years of teaching and preaching, Jesus died on the cross on a hill overlooking

Jerusalem in about the year 29 A.D. (Owing to ancient errors in the calendar, the date of Jesus's birth is called 4 B.C.) 

Christianity among the Jews. Jesus had lived to preach 251

Transition from Classical Civilization his gospel for only three years, but he had left behind him his disciples. At first they were stricken with sorrow and dismay by his crucifixion. When, however, they were convinced of the resurrection of their

THE GOOD SHEPHERD AND THE SHEEP 

A wall painting in the catacombs of St. 

Callixtus, Rome. Whom does the shepherd symbolize? master, they were fired with a new devotion and enthusiasm. They now said that 

Jesus was not only a great prophet whose coming had been foretold in the Jewish scriptures, but that he was a divine being, the Son of 

God, who had been raised from the dead and taken up into heaven. They remained in Jerusalem for several years, preaching and making converts. The 

Jewish leaders at Jerusalem, however, still continued their opposition, and many of the Christians withdrew to Samaria, Damascus, and Antioch, where there were large Jewish communities among which they continued to teach and preach.

The Apostle Paul. Among those who were reached by this preaching was Saul of Tarsus, later known as the 

Apostle Paul. Though born a Jew, he received Greek training in the schools of Tarsus, a city in Asia Minor. He was then sent to Jerusalem to receive careful instruction in the Jewish scriptures. He became a zealous defender of the 

Jewish faith and helped to persecute the Christians. fact, he was on his way to Damascus to help in the work of exterminating Christians, when he had a vision, which he describes as follows in the Book of Acts: 

In as I made my journey, and was come nigh unto Damascus about noon, suddenly there shone from heaven à great light round about me.

Rise and Spread of Christianity 

253 

And I fell unto the ground, and heard a voice saying unto me, Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me? 

And I answered, Who art thou, Lord? And he said unto me, I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom thou persecutest.

After this vision, Paul showed as much zeal in promoting Christianity as he had formerly shown in opposing it. He turned his attention to extending Christianity among the Gentiles (non-Jews), and is hence known as the Apostle to the Gentiles. For more than twenty years, sometimes alone and sometimes with companions, he traveled throughout Asia Minor, Macedonia, Greece, and the islands of the eastern Mediterranean, preaching and establishing churches. He encouraged these struggling young churches by writing them a series of letters (epistles). 

Christianity among the Gentiles. Christianity spread steadily among the Gentiles throughout the Roman world. 

At the close of the first century there were Christian churches throughout Asia Minor and even a few in Italy. The second century saw the establishment of churches in almost every province of the Roman Empire. "We are but of yesterday," says a Christian writer of those days, “yet we have filled all your places of resort cities, islands, fortresses, towns, markets, the camp itself, the tribes, town councils, the palace, the senate, and the forum. We have left to you only the temples of your gods." Two hundred years later there were missionaries along the Rhine, on the Danube frontier, and in distant Britain. It is important to notice these missionary activities among the Germans, for, as we shall see, many of them were already Christians before they entered the Roman Empire.

Conditions favoring the spread of Christianity. Several factors contributed to the success of this gigantic missionary enterprise. Considerable credit must be given to the early

Christian missionaries for the energy and fervor with which they preached the new gospel. Nevertheless, circumstances themselves were favorable for the rapid spread of a new religion. For one thing, barriers to intercourse among

Transition from Classical Civilization peoples were removed by the unity of government brought about by the Roman Empire. The early missionaries, such as 

Paul himself, were often Roman citizens who enjoyed the protection of the Roman law and profited by the ease of travel and communication which the imperial rule had made possible. Since Greek and Latin were widely used throughout the empire, Christian writers and speakers could reach most of the people through one or the other of these languages. Finally, Christianity had a special appeal for those who enjoyed few of the benefits of classical civilization -the poor, the sick, and the downtrodden.

Appeal of Christianity. The new religion had many appealing aspects. In the first place, to the oppressed and unfortunate of this world it held out the hope of a blessed state in a life after death. In the second place, it stressed the great principle of love. In the words of Jesus, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. 

This is the first and great commandment. 

And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself.

This teaching meant that slave and master were brothers, that all men were equal in the sight of God, and that benevolence to the poor and the sick was a duty. In the third place, Christianity, like Judaism, emphasized prayer, through which the humblest believer could obtain peace and comfort through direct communion with God. In the fourth place, when the scriptures were written, they furnished a definite guide which gave believers the assurance that they knew the will of God. 

74. OPPOSITION TO CHRISTIANITY 

Popular hostility to Christians. Though the new religion had a great appeal for many, it aroused among others disapproval and even fear. They regarded its followers as very unsociable persons. The Christians never appeared at public

Opposition to Christianity 255 feasts and entertainments because such occasions often involved the worship of pagan gods. They would not join in the amusements of the circus or the amphitheater, for they disapproved of the cruelty involved in gladiatorial combats. 

They refused to send their children to the established schools. 

Such people puzzled the ordinary citizen. It is not surprising, therefore, that the Christians were called "haters of mankind." Furthermore, the Christians aroused fear among the superstitious. Christians were accused of feasting on children and of being magicians who caused all sorts of disasters. It was not difficult, therefore, to excite the vicious crowds of the large cities to riots and disorders in which many followers of the new religion suffered wounds and death. As a Christian writer said, "If the Tiber rises, if the Nile does not rise, if the heavens give no rain, if there is an earthquake, famine, or pestilence, straightway the cry is, 'The Christians to the lion.""

Governmental hostility to Christians. Popular hostility does not account for all of the opposition which the early Christians had to endure. The government itself regarded them as a menace. The Christians denounced the pagan religion as sinful and idolatrous; they refused to worship the emperor by burning incense before his statue, which stood in every town; and they refused to serve in the army or to swear by the pagan gods in the law courts. It is therefore not surprising that the Roman government viewed them as disloyal and passed laws against them. 

Persecution of the Christians. Various emperors authorized persecutions of the Christians. Nero did so in order to escape the charge that he himself had set fire to Rome. One emperor did so because the Christians had failed to pay certain taxes. Even some of the Good Emperors, like Marcus

Aurelius, felt that it was necessary for the public good to persecute the Christians. The persecution beginning under 

Diocletian (p. 222) in 303 was the last and most severe.

It continued, with some interruptions, for eight years. Only 

Gaul and Britain seem to have escaped its ravages. The

Transition from Classical Civilization government began by burning the holy books of the Christians, by destroying their churches, and by taking away their property. Members of the hated faith lost their privileges as full Roman citizens. Then sterner measures followed. The prisons were crowded with Christians. Some were thrown to wild animals in the arena, stretched on the rack, or burned over a slow fire. Many Christians welcomed the torture and death which they believed would gain for them a heavenly crown. The word martyr is applied to those who thus paid the extreme penalty of death for their faith. 

75. TRIUMPH OF CHRISTIANITY 

Official toleration of Christians. While the Christians were being thus persecuted, they were, in fact, on the verge of triumph. In 311 Galerius, the ruler of the Eastern Empire, published an edict permitting the Christians to rebuild their churches and worship undisturbed. Two years later Constantine and his colleague, Licinius, issued the so-called "Edict of Milan," which proclaimed freedom to every one to worship God according to the religion of his own choice. 

This edict placed the Christian faith on an equality with paganism. Constantine himself accepted Christianity and favored its followers throughout his reign. He surrounded himself with Christian bishops, freed the clergy from taxation, and spent large sums in building churches. 

The first great church council. As Christianity expanded and enrolled many followers from various parts of the known world, uncertainties and differences as to beliefs naturally appeared. The principal dispute was over the nature of Christ. A priest named Arius maintained that Christ the Son, having been created by God the Father, was necessarily inferior to Him. This doctrine of the secondary nature of Christ was called Arianism. Another priest, named 

Athanasius, opposed this view. He maintained that Christ was not a created being, but was in all respects equal to God. 

In order to secure uniformity of belief on this and other
