MODERN JERUSALEM 

Jerusalem stands on a rocky plateau, about 2500 feet above the Mediterranean and 3800 feet above the Dead Sea. The site is largely shut in by mountains. The view is of the city looking eastward from the Mount of Olives and showing the massive fortifications, which, in their present form, date from the 16th century A.D. The older parts of Jerusalem, within the walls, are built upon a vast accumulation of rubbish (in places 100 feet deep), the remains of former cities on the site. The newer parts of Jerusalem lie outside the walls. In the foreground appears the Temple area, now occupied by the so-called Mosque of Omar and other Moslem structures.

Development of the Christian Church 

257 disputed points, so that the Church would be strengthened, Constantine called an assembly, or council, of bishops to meet at the town of Nicæa, in Asia Minor, not far from Constantinople. The council met in 325. It was composed of more than three hundred bishops or their representatives. 

It was the first general council of the Church. The principal work of the council was the settling of the dispute between Arius and Athanasius. The council accepted the arguments of Athanasius and condemned Arius as a heretic. Beliefs, or doctrines, that the Church has condemned as false are known as heresies, and persons who teach them are called heretics. The council then formulated a statement of fundamental beliefs, which is known as the Nicene Creed. 

Christianity becomes the state religion. Less than sixty years after the Council of Nicæa Christianity advanced from the position of the favored religion to that of official state religion. In the year 392 the emperor Theodosius proclaimed Christianity the only legal religion of the empire. 

Sacrifices to the pagan gods were forbidden, the temples were closed, and their property was taken away. Those strongholds of the old paganism, the Delphic oracle, the Olympic games, and the Eleusinian mysteries, were abolished. The ancient worship of ancestors was prohibited. 

The household beliefs and ceremonies survived for a long time afterward, especially in country districts, but paganism as a religious force disappeared by the end of the fourth century. Henceforth, also, Christians who taught doctrines that were condemned by the Church as false were guilty not only of a sin against the Church but of a crime against the state. From the fourth century onward, therefore, European history tells of the trial and punishment of heretics. 

76. DEVELOPMENT OF THE CHRISTIAN CHURCH 

Christian communities. While Christianity was spreading throughout the Roman world, its adherents were forming themselves into groups. These groups met, not in syna-

Transition from Classical Civilization gogues, as did the Jews, but in private houses; at Rome they sometimes went down into the catacombs, which were underground tunnels for the burial of the dead. Wherever they met, they sang hymns, listened to readings from the Holy Scriptures, and partook of a sacrificial meal in memory of the last supper of Jesus with the Twelve Apostles. This was known as the Lord's Supper, or the Eucharist. Certain officers, called presbyters or priests (from a Greek word meaning "elders"), were chosen to conduct the services and instruct the converts. The chief priest received the name of bishop, which comes from a Greek word meaning an “overseer" or "guardian." There were also deacons, who visited the sick and relieved the wants of the poor. Every Christian community thus formed a little brotherhood of earnest men and women, united by common beliefs and common hopes. 

The bishops. The increase in the number of converts and the multiplication of churches led in time to a more elaborate organization, with the bishops of the chief cities as the principal officers. The bishops kept in touch with one another by visits and letters and together formed a governing board for all the churches in a given district or province. 

In each district one of the bishops was made an archbishop and had the duty of presiding over the other bishops. The bishops of the five great cities of Jerusalem, Antioch, Alexandria, Constantinople, and Rome were given the title of patriarch (still another Greek word, meaning the "chief” or "father of a family"); these patriarchs had authority over the archbishops. A church with this organization of bishops is called an episcopal church. By the third century, the 

Christian Church was episcopal in form—that is, had a rule by bishops.

The Bible. Christian worship, as we have noted, consisted partly of reading from a collection of sacred writings called the Scriptures or, later, the Bible. These writings may be grouped into two large divisions, one of which is called the New Testament. It contains four accounts of the life of Jesus. These are called the gospels and are ascribed

Development of the Christian Church 

259 to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, who were apostles, or early followers of Jesus. The New Testament also contains an account of the struggles of the early apostles. This account is appropriately known as the Acts of the Apostles. 

Still another part of the New Testament is made up of epistles (letters) to the various churches, written by Paul and other apostles. Thus the New Testament took form and slowly became the accepted statement of Christian doctrines. 

The other large division of the Bible is called, in contrast to the New, the Old Testament. Many parts of it were ancient even in the time of Jesus. It contains the old Jewish 

Scriptures, with which Jesus and his disciples were familiar and which they sometimes quoted. These old writings were collected and accepted by Christians as being a part of their sacred writings. In its completed form, the Old Testament consists of thirty-nine parts, or "books," which may be classified as historical, poetical, or prophetic. Finally both the Old and the New Testaments were completed and accepted as the authoritative statement, or Bible, of the 

Christian Church.

The Church. The different local churches maintained friendly relations with one another in order to preserve a united front against the forces of paganism. They thus came to regard themselves as members of a larger whole, namely, the Church, which included all Christian believers throughout the world. This all-embracing Church appeared, henceforth, as a great and powerful organization, with fixed laws, with a graded series of officers, and with councils or gatherings to promote its unity and strength. 

The Catholic Church. To this Church was applied the word catholic, a Greek word meaning "universal" or "general." The Church was catholic in two senses. In the first place, it included all local Christian churches in one unified organization. In the second place, it represented a religion that was, in contrast to the pagan and Jewish faiths, for all peoples and all nations.

Monks. The monks constituted a group that aided in pro-

Transition from Classical Civilization moting Christianity. About the middle of the third century, while the Christians were still being persecuted, a wealthy young convert named Paul (not 'the Apostle Paul) fled for safety into the Egyptian desert. There he lived in a cave sheltered by a tree, with a stream of water close by. He led the life of a monk - that is, a life of solitude devoted to meditation and prayer. The fame of his example spread, and others imitated him. An able monk named Pachomius organized some of these scattered monks into a new institution, namely, the monastery. The monks in a monastery still lived in cells, but coöperated in work and worship. 

Pachomius's plans were copied by Basil, who founded monasteries throughout the eastern Roman Empire. The plan of Pachomius was likewise copied by others, who carried it to Italy, whence the plan spread over the western empire. 

In the West, the aim of the monks came to be not merely to lead a life of seclusion and prayer, but actively to promote Christianity. Even the remotely located monasteries became frontier posts of civilization, and the monks were a powerful factor in the conversion of the Germans. 

St. Benedict. The monastic system in the western empire looked to St. Benedict as its organizer. While yet a young man, St. Benedict had sought to escape from the vice about him by retiring to a cave in the Sabine hills near Rome. He lived here for three years as a hermit, shutting himself off from all human intercourse, wearing a hair shirt, and rolling in beds of thistles to subdue "the flesh." St. Benedict's experience of the hermit's life convinced him that there was a surer and better road to religious peace of mind. His fame as a holy man had attracted to him many disciples, and these he now began to group in monastic communities under his own supervision. St. Benedict's most important monastery was at Monte Cassino, midway between Rome and Naples. 

It became the capital of monasticism in the West. 

Rule of St. Benedict, 529. To control the monks of Monte

Cassino, St. Benedict framed a Rule, or constitution, which was modeled in some respects upon the earlier Rule of St.

The Barbarians 

261 Basil. The monks formed a sort of corporation, presided over by an abbot, who held office for life. Every candidate for admission took the vow of obedience to the abbot. Any man, rich or poor, noble or peasant, might enter the monastery after a year's probation; having once joined, however, he must remain a monk for the rest of his days. The monks were to live under strict discipline. They could not own any property; they could not go beyond the monastery walls without the abbot's consent; and the amount of their food and clothing was determined for them by the abbot. 

Christianity transmits classical civilization. The foregoing story of the rise and triumph of Christianity shows it often in conflict with classical civilization. But when the story is carefully read, it also shows the Christian Church depending upon classical civilization and absorbing many of its features. Men trained in Greek philosophy brought their skill in reasoning to the service of the Church and thus preserved some of the classical heritage in philosophy. From the Roman government the Church borrowed many features of its organization. Church architects embodied and preserved many features of classical architecture. In these various ways, then, the Church may be regarded as an avenue along which much of classical civilization was passed to the barbarians, who, by the end of the fourth century, were already overrunning the Roman Empire and engulfing 

Europe in a Dark Age. 

77. THE BARBARIANS 

The barbarians. The people who overran the Roman Empire are called barbarians. The word barbarian (p. 143) is not used to cast scorn upon these peoples; it is used only to indicate the stage of culture which they had reached. From beyond the frontiers of the Roman Empire, they moved into the areas of Italy, France, Spain, England, and other European countries, and became a basic stock of present-day populations. They slowly ceased to be barbarians and be-

Transition from Classical Civilization came civilized peoples. Centuries later, from the countries of Europe, thousands of their descendants spread to America. 

Thus these barbarians became the bearers of civilization. 

This fact justifies our interest in them and their progress. 

Three groups of barbarians. The Roman Empire was almost surrounded by restless hordes of wandering peoples. 

Within the empire and along its frontier in Europe, these peoples were collectively called either Goths, or Teutons, or Germans. Of these three terms, we shall use the word 

Germans. It designates a number of tribes, such as the Ostrogoths, Visigoths, Vandals, Burgundians, Angles, Saxons, and Jutes. These tribes, as we shall see, overran the empire and became the successors of the Romans. The Germans were not, however, the only barbarians. To the east of the 

Germans, in what is now Russia, lived another group of tribes which were collectively called Slavs. They were constantly pressing upon the Germans and eventually overran parts of the eastern Roman Empire; in fact, they eventually settled throughout eastern and southeastern Europe. To the east of the Slavs was still another group of nomads called Huns. They were of the Mongoloid, or yellow, race. 

They were continually pressing in upon both the Slavs and Germans. Thus we see that the Roman Empire was beset by hordes of wandering barbarians, eager to possess the fertile lands of the empire. These many barbarian tribes we have classified into three great groups - Huns, Slavs, and Germans.

The Germans. The most important and numerous tribes were those whom we have called Germans. They inhabited the region from the Rhine eastward to the Vistula, and from the Danube northward to the Baltic Sea. (See map, p. 265.)

Our earliest written notice of them is found in the Commentaries by Julius Cæsar, who twice invaded their country (p. 209). Somewhat later the Roman historian Tacitus wrote a little book called Germania, which gives an account of the people as they were before coming under the influence of Rome and Christianity. Tacitus speaks of their towering

The Barbarians 263 stature, fierce blue eyes, and blond or ruddy hair. These physical traits made them seem especially terrible to the smaller and darker Romans. He mentions their love of warfare, the fury of their onset in battle, and the contempt which they had for wounds and even death itself. When not fighting, they passed much of their time in the chase, and still more time in sleep and gluttonous feasts. They were so passionately fond of gambling that, when a man's wealth was gone, he would even stake his liberty on a single game. 

Tacitus also dwells on certain attractive qualities possessed by these northern barbarians. They were hospitable to the stranger, they respected their sworn word, and they loved liberty and hated restraint. Their chiefs, we are told, ruled rather by persuasion than by authority. Above all, the Germans had a pure family life. "Almost alone among barbarians," writes Tacitus, "they are content with one wife. 

No one in Germany laughs at vice, nor is it the fashion to corrupt and be corrupted. Good habits are here more effectual than good laws elsewhere.” 

Reasons for the Germanic invasions. The Germanic invasions came about in a very natural way. In the first place, the Germans had the barbarians' love of fighting and lust for booty. In the second place, the problem of subsistence (livelihood) became urgent. The country of the 

Germans consisted of dense forests, extensive marshes, and sandy plains. In winter it lay buried under snow and ice, and in summer it was enveloped in clouds and mists. The 

German barbarians did not know how to utilize even the productive areas. They had no vineyards, orchards, or gardens, but only scattered patches of cultivated ground and a few herds of stunted cattle. When the soil, as the 

Germans then understood how to use it, could no longer sustain increasing numbers, the inhabitants had the alternative of migrating or starving. In the third place, from their contacts with the Romans, the Germans had learned of a region to the south which had a favorable climate, settled homes, and a wealthy civilization. Finally, the process of

Transition from Classical Civilization entering the empire had already been started. Some Germans had been brought into the empire as slaves. Friendly tribes had sometimes been admitted to unoccupied lands within the empire. Great numbers of Germans had been hired as soldiers in the imperial army. All these Germans already within the empire set an example for their kinsmen of the north to follow.

German tribes and confederations. An examination of the map on page 265 will show the position of the chief German tribes and confederations on the eve of the great invasions. The Ostrogoths (East Goths) lived north of the 

Black Sea, between the Don and Dniester rivers. Their kinsmen, the Visigoths (West Goths), occupied the country now called Rumania, north of the lower Danube. The 

Vandals dwelt in the plains of Austria and Hungary and along the Oder River. The Burgundians inhabited what is now southern Germany. The Franks held lands on both sides of the lower Rhine, partly in western Germany and partly in northern Gaul. The Saxons, Angles, and Jutes had settled along the coast of the North Sea as far as the extremity of the present Denmark. There were many other tribes and confederations in the interior of Europe, but those just mentioned took the leading part in the invasions of the fourth and fifth centuries. 

78. THE BARBARIANS BREAK THE FRONTIER BARRIERS 

The Huns press the Germans into the empire. The Huns were a wild, nomadic people in central Asia. Roman writers describe their olive skins, little, turned-up noses, black, beady eyes, and generally ferocious appearance. They spent most of their time on horseback, sweeping over the country like a whirlwind and leaving destruction and death in their wake. Entering Europe north of the Caspian Sea, the Huns quickly subdued the Östrogoths and forced them to join in an attack upon their kinsmen, the Visigoths. Roman authorities to allow them to cross that river and place its broad waters between them and their terrible foes. 

Their prayer was granted. Day and night the Visigoths poured across the Danube, some on board ships and rafts, others in canoes made of the hollowed trunks of trees. 

Their entire nation men, women, and children- stood at length on Roman soil.

The Visigoths overrun the empire. These Visigoth immigrants soon became dissatisfied with the treatment they received at the hands of Roman officials, who robbed them of their possessions, withheld the promised supplies of food, and even tried to murder their leaders at a banquet. At length the Visigoths revolted. In the battle of Adrianople in 378 they defeated the Roman legions and slew the Roman emperor. The defeat at Adrianople was one of the decisive battles in the history of the world. It meant that the barbarians had come into the empire to stay. It meant that the Danube barrier was broken once for all. 

Swarms of Ostrogoths, as well as Visigoths, overran the provinces south of the Danube. For a time the Visigoths were pacified by emperor Theodosius, but, after his death in 395, their leader Alaric determined that the Visigoths should be masters. Under his leadership they overran Greece, and turned to invade Italy. In 410 Rome found the Visigoths within her gates. For three days and nights the city was given up to pillage. Alaric, who was a Christian, ordered his followers to respect the churches and to refrain from bloodshed. The city did not suffer greatly, but the moral effect of the disaster was immense. Rome, the eternal, the unconquerable, had been conquered. After the sack of Rome, the Visigoths made their way into southern Gaul and Spain. They were soon driven from Gaul by the Franks, but they continued in control of Spain for three hundred years. They gradually intermingled with other inhabitants, and thus furnished one strain out of which the modern 

Spanish people have grown.

Burgundians, Vandals, and Franks overrun Gaul. When

The Barbarians Break the Frontier Barriers 

267 the Visigoths invaded Italy the Roman legions were recalled from the northern and western frontiers to oppose them. Taking advantage of the absence of the legions, a great company of Germans crossed the Rhine and swept almost unopposed through Gaul. Some of these peoples carved out kingdoms for themselves from the ruins of the empire. The Burgundians settled on the upper Rhine and in the fertile valley of the Rhône in eastern Gaul. After less than a century of independence, they were conquered by the Franks. Their name survives, however, in Burgundy, a territory now included in France. The Vandals, after crossing through Gaul, settled in Spain. But they did not stay there many years. As we have seen, the Visigoths also moved into Spain, arriving shortly after the Vandals. 

Several years of war between the Vandals and Visigoths followed. Then in 429 the remnant of the Vandal nation, numbering about 80,000 persons, crossed into Africa. (Note their route on the map, p. 265.) There the Vandals desolated its fertile fields and seized the prosperous city of Carthage.

They made themselves masters of Roman Africa. While the Visigoths were finding a home in the districts north and south of the Pyrenees Mountains, the Burgundians in the Rhône valley, and the Vandals in Africa, the Franks began to spread over northern Gaul. They contented themselves with a gradual advance into Roman territory. It was not until near the close of the fifth century that they overthrew the Roman power in northern Gaul and began to form the Frankish kingdom out of which has grown modern France, the land of the Franks.

Angles, Saxons, and Jutes invade Britain. The troubled years of the fifth century saw also the beginning of the Germanic conquest of the island of Britain. The withdrawal of the Roman legions left the Britons defenseless against attacks by savage tribes from the north and west; also the eastern coasts were exposed to raids by Saxon pirates. The 

Britons in their extremity adopted the old Roman practice of getting the Germans to fight for them. Bands of Jutes

Transition from Classical Civilization were invited over from Denmark in 449. The Jutes forced back the tribes from the north and west and then settled down on the island as conquerors. They were followed by the Angles and Saxons, who subdued nearly all that part of Britain which Rome had previously conquered. The Angles and Saxons in this way became ancestors of the English people.

The Huns scourge the empire. We have already seen how the Huns pushed the Visigoths across the Danube. The 

Huns themselves then pressed on into central Europe and

Under their leader 

Attila, they built up a great military power obeyed by many barbarous peoples from the 

Caspian Sea to the 

Rhine. From his rude capital on the Danube, Attila led expeditions of plunder and destruction. Germans and Romans alike called him the "Scourge of God." In 451 he led his hosts, said to number half a million men, across the Rhine. Many cities, with their yet active Roman life, were visited by the Huns with fire and sword. Romans and Germans united against the common foe. Visigoths, under their native king, hastened from Spain; Burgundians and Franks joined their ranks; and to these forces was added the last Roman army in the West. Opposed to them Attila had his Huns, the conquered Ostrogoths, and many other barbarian peoples. 

The Huns are turned back. The opposing forces met near Châlons on the Marne River. The battle of Châlons in 451 has been well called a struggle of the nations; it was one of the fiercest conflicts recorded in history. Thousands perished on both sides, but so many of Attila's men

The Fall of Rome 

269 fell that he dared not risk a fresh encounter on the following day. He drew his shattered forces together and retreated beyond the Rhine. The battle of Châlons had saved western 

Europe from the devastation of the Huns. In the following year Attila captured and plundered northern Italy. When he threatened Rome, the bishop (Pope Leo I) persuaded him to spare the city. Attila withdrew from Italy and died within a year. The great confederacy which he had formed broke up at once. The German subjects gained their freedom, and the Huns themselves either withdrew to their Asiatic wilds or mingled with the peoples whom they had conquered. Europe was saved from the "Scourge of God."

The Vandals plunder Rome. Rome escaped a visitation by the Huns only to fall a victim to the Vandals. We have already seen that the Vandals established a kingdom in northern Africa, with Carthage as its capital. From there they put out in their long, light vessels, swept the western Mediterranean, and raided many a populous city on the coast. Their inroads were so terrible that the word vandalism has come to mean the aimless and wanton destruction of property. Their ships appeared at the mouth of the 

Tiber River in 455. The Romans offered no resistance, but once more Leo went out with his clergy to meet the invader and intercede for the city. The Vandals promised only to spare the lives of the inhabitants and not to destroy the public buildings. For fourteen days they stripped Rome of her wealth. Besides shiploads of booty, the Vandals took away thousands of Romans as slaves, including the widow and two daughters of an emperor. The sack of Rome by the Vandals in the year 455 reduced the imperial throne to a mere plaything of the army and its contending factions. 

79. THE FALL OF ROME 

The fall of Rome. Soon after the sack of Rome by the 

Vandals the imperial throne was seized by the Germans. 

In 476 they deposed the boy emperor, Romulus Augustulus,

Transition from Classical Civilization whose name curiously enough recalls both Romulus, the legendary founder of Rome, and Augustus, the first Roman emperor. After 476 there was no longer any Roman emperor ruling in western Europe. Barbarian kingdoms had been set up in Italy, Africa, Spain, Gaul, and Britain. This outcome is often labeled the "fall of Rome," and the year 476 is chosen as a convenient date at which to close the history of the ancient world. 

Nature of the fall of Rome. To speak of the “fall” of

Rome suggests the idea of a violent catastrophe which suddenly plunged the empire into ruin. As the foregoing pages have shown, however, the breakdown of the imperial government was a gradual process, lasting several hundred years. 

Just as Rome was not built in a day, so it did not fall in a day. It was a long time falling. Nor had all of the empire fallen by the end of the fifth century. The barbarians never made much impression on that part of its territory lying in eastern Europe. Here the empire, with a capital at Constantinople, survived for centuries and upheld the Roman tradition of law and order. The eastern empire did not entirely disappear until the year 1453, when Constantinople was captured by the Ottoman Turks. But a glance at the map on page 265 will show that by 476 the greater part of Europe was already within the barbarian kingdoms. 

Finding causes for Rome's fall. The student of government will point out that Rome made many mistakes in governing her provinces, in levying taxes, and in choosing emperors. The student of military history will point out that 

Rome employed mercenaries and lost the idea of a patriotic citizen army. The student of morals will point out that 

Romans became immoral, cruel, and selfish. The student of land problems will point out that a few rich men gained control of all the desirable land and forced the tenant farmers to move to the city. In short, there was not just one cause; many factors operated together to cause the empire to crumble. One must guard, therefore, against accepting too easy an explanation for a complex event like the gradual

Transition from Classical Civilization collapse of the Roman Empire. When we select for special note the political and economic weaknesses of the empire, we do not explain all of the causes. 

Political weaknesses of the empire. The empire embraced too wide a territory for its efficient management. It was so big as to be unwieldy. Second, the empire contained too many diverse peoples for its real unification. There existed between them no unity of language, religion, and customs enabling them to work together for common ends. Third, the empire made no provision for local self-government. 

As time went on, nearly all power was concentrated in the hands of the emperor and his officials. He assessed the taxes, framed edicts having the force of laws, and acted as the supreme judge. The old Græco-Roman ideal of democracy, which had meant so much for civilization, was destroyed by the imperial system. The inhabitants of the empire looked to their all-powerful ruler to protect them; when he failed to do so, they could not, or would not, protect themselves. The barbarians entered the empire to find a spiritless people, who seldom opposed, and indeed often welcomed, their coming.

Economic weaknesses of the empire. During the third and fourth centuries the population of the empire actually decreased, partly because of an increased death rate, due to the prevalence of malaria and plagues, but chiefly as the result of a decreased birth rate. Men and women, finding it more and more difficult to make a living, did not marry; or, if they married, they had few children, perhaps none at all. The custom of infanticide was likewise very common, especially among the poorer classes. The empire suffered from want of men to serve as soldiers in the armies, as artisans in the workshops, and as peasants on the farms. It is no wonder, therefore, that in province after province large tracts of land went out of cultivation, that the cities decayed, and that there was a general "slump" in commerce, manufacturing, and other forms of business enterprise. "Hard times" settled on the Roman world.

The Fall of Rome 

273 

The Germans some- 

The fall of classical civilization. times destroyed cities and killed or enslaved the inhabitants. 

Even when they settled peaceably within the empire, they appropriated a large part of the farming land and set up their own tribal governments. They allowed aqueducts, bridges, and roads to go without repairs, and theaters, baths, and other public buildings to sink into ruins. Being devoted chiefly to agriculture, they permitted both industry and commerce to languish. Lacking any appreciation of education, they failed to keep up schools, universities, and libraries. Classical civilization had been declining before the 

Germans came. The invasions hastened the decline, with the result that large parts of western Europe sank into semibarbarism.

Civilization continues. It required hundreds of years to restore the high level of culture which the Romans had established. Even in periods of decay, however, there are usually forces which operate for the continuance of civilization. In the wreck of the ancient world there were two such forces. One of them was the Christian Church. The other, strangely enough, was the people who did so much to destroy Rome, namely, the Germans. They had the capacity and the willingness to learn from those whom they had conquered. 

Their fusion with the Romans was helped by the previous settlement within the empire of so many German soldiers, colonists, and slaves. Fusion was also promoted by the fact that some of the principal peoples, including the Visigoths, Ostrogoths, Vandals, and Burgundians, were already Christians at the time of their invasions; other peoples, including the Franks and the Anglo-Saxons, afterward adopted Christianity. These new inhabitants of the empire accepted what they understood of Græco-Roman culture, and then imparted to the enfeebled provincials their fresh blood, youthful minds, and vigorous, progressive life. The fusion of Germans and 

Romans, with the accompanying spread of Christianity, formed the basis of civilization in the Middle Ages.

MOHAMMED 80. ATTEMPTS TO RESTORE THE EMPIRE 

The problems confronting the Middle Ages. The same year that was used to mark the fall of Rome, 476, may also serve to mark the beginning of a new era in the world's civilization. This new era covers the thousand years between antiquity and modern times. It is known as the Middle 

Ages. The decline of classical civilization and the invasions of the barbarians had set civilization so far back that the period following the fall of Rome is called the Dark Age.

The problems confronting the peoples of western Europe in the Middle Ages were, therefore, the reëstablishment of orderly government and the rebuilding of a lost culture. 

The most pressing need was for a government which could restore and maintain order. Of the various German invaders, the Franks came closest to supplying this need. 

Rise of the Franks. We have already seen that the Franks spread over northern Gaul and established there a kingdom (p. 267). In 486, just ten years after the fall of Rome, they conquered the only fragment of the Roman Empire remaining in Gaul. They then proceeded to annex the territories of their German neighbors. They built up in this way a great 

Frankish state. 276

Attempts to Restore the Empire 277 The Franks become Christians. The Franks were still heathen when they entered upon this career of conquest. 

But their leader Clovis had married a Burgundian princess who was a devout Christian. The story is told that Clovis, when hard pressed by his foes in a battle, vowed that if his wife's God gave him victory he would become a Christian. 

The Franks won, and Clovis had himself and three thousand warriors baptized as Christians. By this act Clovis secured the loyalty of his Christian subjects in Gaul and won the favor of the Roman Church. The friendship between the popes and the Frankish rulers afterward ripened into a close alliance.

Beginnings of a new empire. The successors of Clovis were for more than two hundred and fifty years the strongest rulers in western Europe. The annals of their reigns form an unpleasant catalogue of bloody wars, horrible murders, and deeds of treachery without number. Nevertheless, some of these rulers were strong men, under whose direction the Frankish territory continued to expand, until it included nearly all of what is now France, Belgium, and Holland, besides a considerable part of Germany. The Franks built up in this way the largest and most permanent of all the barbarian states founded in western Europe. They further increased the prestige of their kingdom by beating back the Moslem Arabs at the battle of Tours, in 732, thus helping to save Europe for Christianity (p. 308).

Charlemagne. Thus far the Franks had established a strong kingdom; their king Charlemagne made it an empire. 

He reigned for nearly half a century (768-814) and set his stamp on all later European history. His character and personality are familiar to us from a brief biography written by his secretary. According to him, Charlemagne was a tall, square-shouldered, strongly built man, with bright, keen eyes, and an expression at once cheerful and dignified. Riding, hunting, and swimming were his favorite sports. He was simple in his tastes and temperate in food and drink. Except when in Rome, he wore the old Frankish costume, with high-

laced boots, linen tunic, blue cloak, and sword girt at his side. 

He was a clear, fluent speaker, could use Latin as readily as his native tongue, and understood Greek when it was spoken. "He also tried to learn to write and often kept his tablets and writing book under the pillow of his couch, that, when he had

France, Belgium, Holland, Switzerland, Austria, western 

Germany, northern Italy and northern Spain, besides a part of Czechoslovakia and Jugoslavia. This was truly a gigantic realm, and it was under the sway of one man. 

Charlemagne is crowned emperor, 800. It seemed fitting that such a ruler should become the successor of the Roman emperors. On Christmas Day, 800, the pope, in old St.

Peter's Church at Rome, placed on Charlemagne's head a golden crown, while all the people cried out, "Long life and victory to Charles Augustus, the great and pacific emperor, crowned by God." This ceremony seemed to bring to life again the empire which had ceased when Romulus Augustulus was deposed in 476 (p. 269). Of course, this German emperor differed sharply from the old Roman emperors, who regularly spoke Latin, administered Roman law, and regarded the Germans as their most dangerous foes. Furthermore, his empire was largely a new creation, the result of an alliance between the kingdom of the Franks and the Roman Church. 

The new empire united the political and military power of the king to the spiritual power of the Church, and thus strengthened the forces of civilization against the barbarism of the uncivilized tribes. 

Civilizing work of Charlemagne. Charlemagne did his best to establish systematic government throughout his wide domains. He divided them into districts, over each of which he appointed a special officer. He appointed other officials to travel from district to district, bearing the orders of their royal master and making sure that these orders were promptly obeyed. Charlemagne also made other efforts to revive civilization in western Europe from the low state into which it had fallen during the period of the barbarian invasions. We still possess a number of his laws issued for the promotion of education. He founded schools in the monasteries and cathedrals, where not only the clergy but also the common people might receive some training. He formed his whole court into a palace school, in which learned men from Italy, Spain, and England gave instruction to his own children and those of his

More Invasions 281 

The Northmen nobles. He had the manuscripts of Latin authors collected and copied, so that the knowledge preserved in books should not be forgotten. All this civilizing work, together with the peace and order which he maintained throughout a wide territory, made his reign the most brilliant period of the early Middle Ages.

A setback. After Charlemagne died, in 814, his empire slowly went to pieces. It had never been firmly established, and no emperor appeared with Charlemagne's genius for directing the processes of recivilizing western Europe. His son was a weak ruler, and Charlemagne's three grandsons quarreled among themselves. By the Treaty of Verdun, in 

843, they divided the empire into three parts, thus destroying its unity and strength. One grandson took the west; his kingdom later became France. Another took the east, which later became Germany. The third grandson took northern Italy and a strip of land lying between the kingdoms of his two brothers. This strip of land, extending from the 

Alps to the North Sea, has since often been a bone of contention between France and Germany. 

The imperial idea lives on. The idea of one inclusive empire, however, was not lost. About one hundred and fifty years after Charlemagne's death, an able German ruler called Otto the Great led his armies across the Alps, went to Rome, and had the pope crown him as Roman emperor. Otto's dominions were considerably smaller than Charlemagne's, including only Germany and north Italy. Nevertheless, Otto and his successors, by claiming to be the heirs of Charlemagne, Constantine, and Augustus Cæsar, kept alive the imperial idea for more than eight hundred years. It did not disappear from European politics until the opening of the nineteenth century. 

81. MORE INVASIONS THE NORTHMEN 

The Northmen. About the time of Charlemagne, there began the last wave of that great Germanic movement which

had previously flooded western Europe and overwhelmed the Roman Empire. The new barbarian invaders were the 

Northmen. Most of them lived in what is now Norway, Sweden, and Denmark. According to their own writings, called sagas, they were a restless, warlike people. The sagas also reveal other characteristics of the Northmen: a cruelty which made them a terror to their foes; an almost barbaric love of gay clothing and ornament; and even a feeling for the Tartogr

A VIKING SHIP 

A Viking chieftain, after his days of sea-roving had ended, was sometimes buried in his ship, over which a grave-chamber, covered with earth, would be erected. Several such burial ships have been discovered. The Gokstad vessel, shown in the illustration, is of oak, twenty-eight feet long and sixteen feet broad in the center. It has seats for sixteen pairs of rowers, a mast for a single sail, and a rudder on the right or starboard side. The gunwale was decorated with a series of shields, painted alternately black and gold. romantic beauty of their northern home, with its snow-clad mountains, dark forests of pine, sparkling waterfalls, and deep, blue fiords. At the time the Northmen began their invasions, they were untouched by classical civilization or the Christian religion. 

Raids and settlements of the Northmen. The Northmen started out as raiders but often settled down as colonists. 

They fell upon the coasts of western Europe. They also found it easy to ascend the rivers in their shallow boats and

More Invasions - The Northmen 

283 reach places far inland. These pirate crews of the Northmen who plundered the coasts and inlets were known as Vikings. 

Their attacks inspired such terror that a special prayer was inserted in the church services: "From the fury of the Northmen, good Lord, deliver us." The raids of the Northmen took place at first only in summer, but before long the Northmen began to winter in the lands which they visited. Their fleets became larger year by year, and their attacks changed from mere forays of pirates to well-organized expeditions of conquest and colonization. The map on page 287 shows their extensive discoveries and settlements, together with the dates when these were made. 

Northmen push westward. Among the places which the 

Northmen visited and settled was the far-away island of Iceland. The group of Northmen who settled it were from Norway and hence are called Norwegians. They transferred to 

Iceland the language, literature, and customs of Norway. 

An Icelander, Eric the Red, led an expedition to Greenland. 

He called the country by that name, not because it was green, but because, as he said, "there is nothing like a good name to attract settlers." Leif Ericsson, his son, voyaged still farther westward, and about the year 1000 he visited the coast of North America. They did not, however, follow up their explorations by lasting settlements. All memory of the far western lands faded before long from the minds of men. The curtain fell on the New World, not to rise again until the time of Columbus. 

Danes invade England. Another group of Northmen, the 

Danes, made expeditions to England, where they found some of their own kinsmen already established. These kinsmen were the Germanic tribes - Angles, Saxons, and Jutes who had settled in England during the fifth century (p. 267). 

Early in the ninth century King Egbert united the various Anglo-Saxon kingdoms under one government. His work of unification was made more difficult by bands of Danish Vikings who made occasional forays on the English coast. 

Alfred and the Danes. After Egbert's death, the real

Danish invasion of England began. The Danes came in large numbers, made permanent settlements, and soon controlled all England north of the Thames. Eventually, however, they were defeated by King Alfred, grandson of Egbert. 

The Danes agreed to accept Christianity and to divide the country with the Anglo-Saxon inhabitants. Alfred then turned to the task of ruling and building up again his wellnigh ruined country. 

Civilizing work of Alfred. When Alfred died in 901, after thirty years' rule, he had won for himself a place in history along with Charlemagne as one of the leaders in bringing Europe out of the Dark Ages. Alfred's first care was to organize a fighting force always ready to repel invasions and an efficient fleet to patrol the coast. He had the laws of the 

Anglo-Saxons collected and reduced to writing, tried to rebuild the ruined churches and monasteries, and labored to revive education among the English folk. His court at Winchester became a literary center where learned men wrote and taught. The king himself mastered Latin, in order that he might translate Latin books into the English tongue. 

Through the mists of ten centuries his figure still looms large. 

It is the figure of a brave, patient, and modest man, wearing himself out in the service of his people. 

Northmen invade France. About the time the Danish 

Northmen started their invasions of England, another group of Northmen began to invade and plunder northern France. 

They first appeared on the French coast toward the end of Charlemagne's reign. After that ruler's death the wars of his grandsons left the empire defenseless, and the Northmen in consequence redoubled their attacks. They sailed far up the rivers of France to plunder and murder. Paris, then a small but important city, more than once suffered at their hands. The destruction by the Northmen of many monasteries was a loss to civilization, for the monastic establishments at this time were the chief centers of learning and culture (p. 351). 

From Northman to Norman. One of Charlemagne's suc-

Rollo and his men then settled in the region granted them. 

They soon became thoroughly French in language and culture. It was amazing to see how quickly the descendants of wild sea-rovers made their new home a Christian land, noted for its churches, monasteries, and schools. The change in the mode of life of these Northmen is symbolized by the change of their name to Normans, the word Nor-man being a softened form of North-man. The district ceded to them in northern France became known as Normandy. Its ruler in 1066 was William, duke of Normandy.

With a large fleet bearing several thousand archers, foot soldiers, and horsemen, he crossed the Channel and landed in England. At first he met no resistance. Harold, who had been chosen king, was far away in the north fighting against the Northmen. After defeating them, he hurried southward to face Duke William and the Normans. The two armies met near Hastings. All

day they fought. The stout English infantry, behind their wall of shields, threw back one charge after another of the Norman knights. Again and again Duke William rallied his men and led them where the foe was thickest. At last, with the approach of evening, Harold was killed by an arrow; his household guard died about him; and the rest of the English took to flight. William pitched his camp on the field of victory, and “sat down to eat and drink among the dead." 

The battle of Hastings settled the fate of England. Following up his victory with relentless energy, William pressed on to London. That city, now practically the capital of the country, opened its gates to him. On Christmas Day, 1066, in Westminster Abbey, the duke of Normandy was crowned king of England. Norman merchants and artisans followed 

Norman soldiers to England and became an important element of the English population. 

Normans conquer Sicily and southern Italy. During the eleventh century the Normans found still another region in which to display their energy and daring. They turned southward to the Mediterranean and created in Sicily and southern Italy a Norman state known as the kingdom of the Two Sicilies. From this convenient location these daring adventurers were able to join, a little later, the crusaders who undertook to recover the Holy Land (p. 313). The Normans themselves governed the Two Sicilies for only about one hundred and fifty years, but under other rulers the kingdom of the Two Sicilies lasted until the middle of the nineteenth century, when the present kingdom of Italy came into existence.

Review. The Northmen spread into so many lands that it is worth while, before leaving them, to summarize their movements. The Northmen set out from the region which we now call the Scandinavian peninsula. Some of them sailed westward across the sea and peopled the island of Iceland; later, Northmen from that island pushed still farther westward, to Greenland and to the American continent. 

Another group of Northmen, the Danes, invaded England,

82. GOVERNMENT BY FEUDALISM 

Feudalism rises out of disorder. While the Franks were building up their kingdom and the Northmen were spreading over various lands, a new arrangement of society was taking place. This new arrangement had its origin in the troubled times of the barbarian invasions. As the barbarians overran the Roman Empire, law and security gave way to chaos and insecurity. In many areas there were no officers of the law, no courts - in fact, no government to which people could turn. In this extremity they sought help from one another. 

Tenants and small farmers turned for protection to powerful landowners. The tenants and small farmers agreed to work for and serve under the powerful landowner, who promised them in return security and protection. The powerful landowner thereby became their lord. This arrangement, by which a man gave up a small holding and some degree of freedom in return for security and protection, is known as feudalism.

Rise of the feudal lord. Thus under feudalism local lords had the powers that we customarily think of as belonging only to the king. But during the Dark Age it was really impossible for a king to govern with a strong hand. The absence of good roads or of other easy means of communication made it difficult, in case of revolts or invasions, for him to

Government by Feudalism 

289 move troops quickly from one district to another.. Even had good roads existed, the lack of ready money would have prevented him from maintaining a strong army devoted to his interests. Moreover, the king's subjects, as yet not welded into a nation, felt toward him no sentiments of loyalty and affection. They cared far less for their king, of whom they knew little, than for their local lords, who dwelt near them. 

The decline of the king's authority meant that the chief functions of government came to be more and more performed by the nobles, who were the great landowners, or lords, of the kingdom. They were practically independent of the king. 

Under an unusual ruler like Charlemagne, these powerful lords were subjected to royal authority, but after the break-up of his empire, they reasserted their independence. By the middle of the ninth century the local lords exercised the prerogatives of government the of feudalism had arage rived. 

Aspects of feudalism. Since feudalism was a form of government, it naturally affected fundamentally many aspects of life, just as a monarchy or a republic does. (1) Feudalism provided for the ownership and inheritance of land - or what is known as land tenure. (2) It provided a system of local government. (3) It provided for carrying on the economic activities necessary for sustaining life. (4) It provided a military organization. (5) Most important of all, it determined the development of social classes. A fuller treatment of these various aspects of feudalism follows. 

Land tenure under feudalism. Feudalism provided for the ownership and inheritance of land. Owing to the decay of commerce and industry, land had become, in the early Middle Ages, practically the only form of wealth. The king, who was theoretically the owner of the soil, would pay his officials for their services by recognizing them as lords over certain areas of land. In the same way, one who had received large estates would parcel them out among his followers as a reward for their support. Sometimes an unscrupulous noble increased his holdings by seizing the lands

of his neighbors and compelling them to become his tenants. 

Often, too, as we have seen, those who owned land in their own right surrendered the title to a noble, who then became their protector. Thus practically no one owned his land absolutely; both lords and tenants held it conditionally. An estate in land which a person held of a superior lord was called a fief. When the holder of a fief (estate) died, his oldest son inherited it. If a man had no legal heir, the fief went back to the lord.

The feudal pyramid. The supreme landlord was the king, who was supposed to hold his land from God; below the king stood the greater lords (dukes, marquises, counts, barons), with large estates; and below them came the lesser lords, or knights, whose possessions were considered to be too small for further subdivision. Thus landowners may be thought of as forming a pyramid, from the humblest knight up to the king. Each person in this pyramid was called the vassal of his superior lord. Every holder of land was in theory, though not always in fact, the vassal of some superior lord. 

The vassal's obligations to his lord. The vassal owed various services to his lord. In time of war he did garrison duty at the lord's castle and joined him in military expeditions. In peace, the vassal helped his lord by enforcing justice in his own domain and attended him on ceremonial occasions. The vassal was also required, under certain circumstances, to make money payments. When he inherited a fief, he had to pay his lord a sum, usually equivalent to one year's revenue from the estate. If a vassal sold his fief, the lord, before giving his consent to the transaction, received a large sum from the purchaser. There were three other instances in which the vassal had to make money payments: (1) for the ransom of the lord in case he was made prisoner of war; (2) to meet the expenses connected with the knighting of the lord's oldest son; (3) to provide a dowry for the lord's oldest daughter. These exceptional payments were called aids. 

The lord's obligations to his vassal. The vassal, in return

Government by Feudalism 

291 for his services and payments, looked to the lord for the protection of life and property. The lord agreed to secure him in the enjoyment of his fief, to guard him against his enemies, and to see that in all matters he received just treatment. 

Thus the lord as well as the vassal assumed certain obligations.

Homage and investiture. The agreement between a lord and his vassal was solemnized by formal ceremonies. One who wanted to become "a lord's man" (that is, become a vassal and hold a fief) went through the ceremony of homage from Latin homo = man. He came bareheaded and unarmed into the lord's presence, knelt down, placed his hands between those of the lord, and promised henceforth to be his man. The lord then kissed him and raised him to his feet. 

The vassal placed his hands upon the Bible or upon sacred relics and swore to remain faithful to his lord. Then took place the ceremony of investiture by which the vassal was given formal possession of his fief. The lord gave the vassal some object - a stick, a clod of earth, a lance, or a glove in token of the vassal's possession of the fief. Henceforth, lord and vassal were bound to each other by mutual obligations.

Local government under feudalism. In addition to providing a system of land tenure, feudalism provided for local government. The feudal lord lived on a landed estate, or manor, surrounded by dependents over whom he exercised the rights of a petty sovereign. He could tax them; he could require them to give him military assistance; he could try them in his courts; he even enjoyed the privilege of declaring war, making treaties, and coining money. 

Economic activities under feudalism. Feudalism also provided for carrying on economic activities necessary for sustaining life. A lord's manor was a self-sufficing economic unit. Within its hundreds of acres it contained a mill, a blacksmith shop, bake ovens, a general workshop, and even an entire village of workers. The pastures, fields, and woods supplied the raw materials which could, by patient toil, be

transformed into usable goods. Thus feudalism, by favoring the growth of these self-sufficing units, determined the economic organization of the times. 

Military organization under feudalism. Feudalism also provided the framework of an army. If the United States were to declare war tomorrow, all those who entered military service would become members of a national army directly under the control of the national government. Such centralization was unknown in the days of feudalism. If a feudal king had a war on his hands, he relied upon a small number of great nobles, who were his vassals, to furnish groups of warriors. The great nobles, in turn, depended upon lesser lords to supply warriors, and the humblest lord gathered his knights and went to fight for his immediate overlord. Thus a feudal army was made up of relatively independent units. In this way, the feudal pyramid of landlords (p. 290) provided a method of equipping, raising, and leading an army.

Social classes under feudalism. In feudal times, people were grouped according to station and rank. At the top of the social scale were the great nobles, who lived in fortified castles and were practically independent princes. Lesser lords ranked according to their holdings and power, and so on down the scale to the humblest vassal knight. At the bottom of the social scale were the peasants who worked on the manors and in general led a life of drudgery and toil. 

Feudalism a natural development. Feudalism in Europe was not a unique development. Parallels to it may be found in other parts of the world. Whenever the state becomes incapable of protecting life and property, powerful men in each locality will themselves undertake this duty; they will assume the burden of their own defense and of those weaker men who seek their aid. Such was the situation in ancient 

Egypt for several hundred years, in medieval Persia, and in modern Japan until about two generations ago. In Europe, also, feudalism was a natural development that took place when centralized authority broke down. The absence of

The Byzantine Empire 

293 government called it into existence, and with the rise of strong national governments (p. 316), it tended, as we shall see, to disappear.

Extent of European feudalism. European feudalism arose and flourished in the countries which had formed Charlemagne's empire, that is, in France, Germany, and northern 

Italy. It also spread to Bohemia, Hungary, Poland, and the

Christian states of Spain. Toward the close of the eleventh century the Normans transplanted it into England, southern Italy, and Sicily. During the twelfth and thirteenth centuries the crusaders introduced it into the kingdoms which they founded in the Near East. Still later, in the fourteenth century, the Scandinavian countries became acquainted with feudalism. 

83. THE BYZANTINE EMPIRE 

The Byzantine Empire. Western Europe during the early 

Middle Ages presented a scene of violence and confusion while the German peoples were settling in their new homes. 

A different picture was presented in eastern Europe. Here the Roman Empire survived and continued to uphold, for nearly a thousand years after the deposition of Romulus Augustulus, the Roman tradition of law and order. After 

476 it became more and more Greek in character, owing to the loss of the western provinces in the fifth century and then of Syria and Egypt in the seventh century. The eastern empire is known as the Byzantine Empire because its capital, Constantinople, was once called Byzantium, although the term is most appropriately applied to the empire in still later times when its possessions were reduced to Constantinople and the territory in the neighborhood of that city.

Byzantine commerce and industry. The merchant ships of Constantinople carried on much of the commerce of the 

Mediterranean and the Black Sea. The products of Byzan tine industry were exchanged at that city for the spices, drugs, and precious stones of the East. Byzantine wares also found

their way into Italy and France and, by way of the Russian rivers, reached the heart of eastern Europe. Russia, in turn, furnished Constantinople with honey, wax, fur, wool, grain, and slaves. A traveler of the twelfth century well described the city as a metropolis "common to all the world, without distinction of country or religion." 

Byzantine art. Many of the emperors at Constantinople were great builders. Byzantine architecture became a leading form of art. Its most striking feature is the dome, which replaced the flat, wooden roof used in the churches of Italy. 

The exterior of a Byzantine church is plain and unimposing, but the interior is adorned on a magnificent scale. The eyes of the worshipers are dazzled by the walls faced with marble slabs of various colors, by the columns of polished marble, jasper, and porphyry, and by the brilliant mosaic pictures of gilded glass. The entire impression is one of richness and splendor. Byzantine artists, though not very good painters and sculptors, excelled in decorative art. Their carvings in wood and ivory and their work in metal, together with their embroideries, enamels, miniatures, and mosaics, enjoyed a high reputation in medieval Europe. 

Byzantine scholarship. The libraries and museums of 

Constantinople preserved classical learning. The wisest men of the day resided in that city, where they taught philosophy, law, medicine, and science to thousands of pupils. Byzantine students did not make many new discoveries, preferring to compile huge encyclopedias from the books which antiquity had handed down to them. Eastern Europe thus cherished the productions of classical learning until the time came when western Europe was ready to receive them and profit by them. 

The Greek Church. The break-up of the Roman Empire brought about the separation of Eastern and Western Christianity. The two churches remained in formal unity until 

1054, when disputes between them on points of doctrine led to their final rupture. They have never united. The missionary zeal of the Greek Church resulted in the conversion of the barbarians who entered southeastern Europe during the

The Byzantine Empire 

295 early Middle Ages. At the present time, most of the Christian inhabitants of the Balkan peninsula, including Greeks, Jugoslavs, Bulgarians, and Rumanians, belong to the Greek

Church. Its greatest victory was the conversion of the Russians, toward the close of the tenth century. The Russian ruler, having made up his mind to embrace Christianity, appointed commissioners who visited both Rome and Constantinople. The commissioners reported in favor of the Greek

The numerous peoples whom the Greek Church converted to Christianity received at the same time the use of letters and some knowledge of Roman law and methods of government. Constantinople was to them, henceforth, such a center of religion and culture as Rome was to the Germans. 

Constantinople. The heart of Byzantine civilization was 

Constantinople. It was the largest, most populous, and most

wealthy city in medieval Europe. When London, Paris, and Venice were small and mean towns, visitors to Constantinople found paved and lighted streets, parks, public baths, hospitals, theaters, schools, libraries, museums, beautiful churches, and magnificent palaces. The renown of Constantinople penetrated even into barbarian lands. The Northmen called it the "Great City"; the Russians knew it as the "City of the Cæsars." Both names did not lack appropriateness, but its own people best described it as the "City guarded by God."

Importance of the Byzantine Empire. For over eleven hundred years, from 330 to 1453 — that is, from the time that Constantine made Constantinople his capital until the invading Turks captured the city -the Byzantine Empire maintained the traditions of classical civilization, formed the missionary center for Christianity in eastern Europe, and stood as a bulwark against the barbarians - Germans, Huns, Slavs, and Arabs. 

84. RISE OF THE PAPACY 

The Roman Church as a 'mother church." Rome, the largest and most flourishing city in the empire and the seat of the imperial government, naturally became the center from which Christianity spread over the western provinces. Many of the first Christian communities planted in Spain, Gaul, and Africa owed their start to the missionary zeal of the popes. As a “mother church," Rome enjoyed a superior position among the churches of the West. 

Independence of the Roman Church. The development of the Roman Church was also fostered by its independence. 

The bishop of Rome was the only patriarch (p. 258) in the 

West, and as such he ranked above the bishops of the other western churches. Furthermore, the removal of the capital from Rome to Constantinople helped to free the Roman bishop from the close oversight of the imperial government. 

He was able, henceforth, to promote the interests of the

Exterior Interior

SANCTA SOPHIA, CONSTANTINOPLE 

Built by Justinian and dedicated on Christmas Day, 538 A.D. The main building is roofed over by a great central dome, 105 feet in diameter and 184 feet in height. After the Ottoman Turks turned the church into a mosque, a minaret was erected at each of the four exterior angles. The outside of Sancta Sophia is somewhat disappointing, but the interior, with its walls and columns of polished marble, granite, and porphyry, is magnificent. The crystal balustrades, pulpits, and large metal disks are Turkish.

CHOIR OF WESTMINSTER ABBEY 

The church formerly attached to the Benedictine abbey of St. Peter in Westminster was built in the 13th century, upon the site of an earlier church raised by Edward the Confessor in the 11th century. Since the Norman Conquest all but one of the English sovereigns have been crowned here, and until the time of George III, it served as their last resting place. The abbey is now England's Hall of Fame, where many of her distinguished statesmen, warriers, poets, artists, and scientists are buried.

Rise of the Papacy 

297 church under his control without much interference on the part of the emperor at Constantinople. 66 The Roman Church as defender of the faith." The development of the Roman Church was aided by its attitude on disputed questions of belief. While Christendom in the 

East was torn by theological disputes, the Church of Rome stood firmly by the Nicene Creed (p. 256). After Arianism and other heresies were finally condemned, orthodox Christians in the West felt indebted to the Roman Church for its unwavering championship of "the faith once delivered to the saints." They were all the more ready, therefore, to defer to it in matters of doctrine and to accept its spiritual authority. 

The popes as leaders. The Roman Church won its commanding position partly because some of the early popes were able leaders in temporal as well as spiritual affairs. Thus, it is said that Pope Leo succeeded in diverting Attila and his Huns from an attack on Rome, and when the Vandals sacked the city he also intervened to prevent its destruction (p. 269). About a century later, another pope, Gregory the 

Great, helped to prevent another tribe of barbarians from overrunning central Italy. We also find Gregory sternly repressing heresies wherever they arose and sending out monks and missionaries as far away as distant Britain. 

When he closed his remarkable career, the papacy had reached a commanding place in western Christendom. During the eighth century the alliance of the popes and the Franks (p. 277) helped further to establish the papacy as an ecclesiastical monarchy, ruling over both the souls and bodies of men.

Power of the papacy. The pope was the supreme lawgiver of the Church. His decrees might not be set aside by any other person. He made new laws in the form of "bulls," ¹ and by his "dispensations" he could in particular cases set aside old laws, such as those forbidding cousins to marry or monks to obtain release from their vows. The pope was also the supreme judge of the Church, for all appeals from the lower
