MEDIEVAL UNIVERSITIES 

attended the lectures given by a master of the cathedral school of Notre Dame. Abélard himself soon set up as a lecturer. Few teachers have ever attracted so large and so devoted a following. His lecture room under the shadow of the great cathedral was filled with a crowd of youths and men drawn from all countries.

Education 359 University of Paris. The fame of Abélard led to an increase of masters and students at Paris, and so helped to pave the way for the establishment of the University of Paris, later in the twelfth century. It became a center of learning, particularly in theology and philosophy, and had over five thousand students. It furnished the model for 

Oxford University in England, as well as for learned institutions in Scotland, Denmark, Sweden, and Germany.

University of Bologna. In southern Europe, universities were modeled more or less upon the University of Bologna, in Italy. This university developed out of a law school where the Code of Justinian (p. 245) was the chief subject of study.

In contrast to the University of Paris, which stressed theology and philosophy, the one at Bologna emphasized the study of law. Bologna was the center from which the Roman legal system made its way into France, Germany, and other continental countries.

Colleges. The members of a university usually lived in a number of colleges. These seem to have been at first little more than lodging houses, where poor students were cared for at the expense of some benefactor. As the colleges increased in wealth, through the gifts made to them, they became centers of instruction under the direction of masters. 

At the universities of Oxford and Cambridge, where the collegiate system has been retained to the present time, each college possesses separate buildings and enjoys the privilege of self-government.

Faculties. The subjects of instruction in a university were grouped under the four faculties of arts, theology, law, and medicine. The first-named faculty taught the "seven liberal arts," that is, grammar, rhetoric, logic, arithmetic, music, geometry, and astronomy. Theology, law, and medicine then, as now, were professional subjects, taken up after the completion of the arts course. Owing to the constant movement of students from one university to another, each institution tended to specialize in one or more fields of learning. Thus, Paris came to be noted for theology;

Medieval Civilization 

Montpellier, Padua, and Salerno for medicine; and Orléans, Bologna, and Salamanca for law. Among the most famous of the professors and scholars was Thomas Aquinas, an Italian monk. He taught at Paris, Cologne, Rome, and Bologna. 

When he died, he left behind him a large work entitled Summa Theologiæ (“Compendium of Theology”). As the name indicates, it contains a complete statement of medieval religious belief. 

Methods of teaching. A university did not need an extensive collection of libraries, laboratories, and museums. 

The only equipment necessary consisted of lecture rooms for the professors. Not even benches or chairs were required, for students often sat on the straw-strewn floors. The high price of manuscripts compelled professors to give all instruction by lectures.

Methods of study. Most medieval universities did little to encourage original research. Law students memorized the Code of Justinian. Medical students learned anatomy and physiology from old Greek books, instead of in the dissecting room. Theologians went to the Bible, the Church 

Fathers, or Aristotle for answers to the questions that perplexed them. They were thus satisfied to appeal to authority, rather than take the trouble of finding out things for themselves. 

97. SCIENCE AND INVENTION 

Science. Many scholars of the Middle Ages looked back to the classical writings, particularly those of Aristotle, as the source of all information. Not all medieval scholars, however, were willing to accept Aristotle as the last word on science and nature. For example, Roger Bacon (12141294), a Franciscan friar and a lecturer at Paris and Oxford, severely criticized in his writings the habit of relying upon Aristotle for all knowledge. He turned away from theology and philosophy to mathematics and science. The twelfth and thirteenth centuries were, in fact, marked by a healthy interest in science. Long encyclopedias, written in Latin,

Science and Invention 361 contained all available information about the world. The study of physics, chemistry, and astronomy made conspicuous progress, partly as a result of the influence of Arabian scholars. Considerable work was also done in arithmetic and algebra, continuing the researches of the Arabs in these subjects. It was from this period that the Arabic numerals, with their symbol for zero, began to displace finger counting and the abacus in western Europe. 

Inventions. Scholars in the Middle Ages were also interested in practical inventions. Thus Roger Bacon foresaw a time when machines for flying would be constructed "wherein," as he said, "a man sits revolving some engine by which artificial wings are made to beat the air like a flying bird." Various practical inventions which were made in the later Middle Ages include spectacles and magnifying glasses, later to be developed into the telescope and microscope; mechanical clocks, en- 

FIRING A CANNON 

From an English book of 1590. abling man to mark the passage of time with fair accuracy; and mirrors of glass, replacing those of burnished metal.

Three other inventions worked out at this period had such important effects on civilization that they deserve more detailed treatment. These inventions were the mariner's compass, gunpowder, and the printing press. 

The mariner's compass. We do not know just who invented the mariner's compass. The Chinese have been credited with the discovery that a needle, when rubbed with a lodestone, has the mysterious power of pointing to the north. The Arabs may have introduced this rude form of the compass among Mediterranean sailors. The instrument, improved by being balanced on a pivot so that it would not be affected by choppy seas, was first used by Europeans in the thirteenth century. It enabled sailors to find their bear-

Medieval Civilization ings even in murky weather and on starless nights. The mariner's compass came to be of great aid in the long voyages of discovery which were undertaken during early modern times.

They regarded it as merely a sort of firework, producing a sudden and brilliant flame, and did not suspect that in a confined space the expansive power of its gases could be used to hurl projectiles. Gunpowder was occasionally manufactured as a propellant during the fourteenth century, but for a long time it made more noise than it did harm. Small brass cannon, throwing stone or iron balls, began at length to displace the medieval siege weapons, and still later muskets took the place of the bow, the crossbow, and the pike. The revolution in the art of warfare introduced by gunpowder had vast importance. It destroyed the usefulness of the castle and enabled the peasant to fight the mailed knight on equal terms. Gunpowder, accordingly, must be included among the forces which brought about the downfall of feudalism. 

The printing press. The Chinese were the first to print books by using movable type, that is, a type for each letter. 

The art was found in Europe by the middle of the fifteenth

Customs and Manners 363 century. Who invented it there is not known with certainty, but a German printer, Johann Gutenberg of Mainz, seems to have been the first to print on a large scale. The oldest large printed book which issued from his press was a Latin 

Bible, probably printed in 1454.

Significance of printing. Printed books could be multiplied far more rapidly than manuscripts could be copied by hand. 

They could also be far more accurate than manuscripts, for, when an entire edition was printed from the same type, mistakes in the different copies were eliminated. Furthermore, the invention of printing destroyed the monopoly of learning possessed by the universities and people of wealth. Books were now the possession of the many, not the luxury of the few. Any one who could read had opened to him the gateway of knowledge; he became a citizen, henceforth, of the republic of letters. Printing, which made possible popular education, public libraries, and, ultimately, cheap newspapers, thus became a force emancipating mankind from bondage to ignorance. 

98. CUSTOMS AND MANNERS 

Popular beliefs. A great many people in our time have a number of superstitions.

People in the Middle Ages had even more. Thus Roger Bacon thought that flying dragons

From a book printed in 1579. 

The phoenix was, supposedly, a bird which, after living for five hundred years, burned itself to death and then rose again full grown from the ashes. existed and that eating their flesh lengthened human life. 

Works on natural history soberly described fabulous creatures that never existed. Various plants and minerals were credited with marvelous powers; for example, the sapphire, when powdered and mixed with milk, was supposed to heal ulcers and cure headaches. Magicians made talismans, or

Medieval Civilization lucky objects for personal use, and various powders which were supposed to inspire hatred or affection in the person taking them. Many days were regarded as unlucky - days 

THE UNICORN 

on which one ought not to buy or sell, to plant a field, or to start on a journey.

Of all the superstitions of the time, the belief in witches was perhaps the most harmful. Witches were supposed to have sold themselves to the Devil, receiving in return the power

Medieval peoples believed that many fabu- to work magic. At night lous creatures lived in the interior of Asia. One of these was the unicorn, with the head and body of a horse, the hind legs of an antelope, the beard of a goat, and a long sharp horn set in the middle of the forehead. The picture above is reproduced from an old-time "Historie of Four-Footed Beastes.' "9 they rode on broomsticks through the air and assembled in some lonely place for feasts, dances, and wild revels. There were various tests for the discovery of witches, the most usual being the ordeal by cold water. Thousands of harmless persons were put to death on the charge of being witches in league with the Devil.

Indoor games. It is pleasant to turn from the superstitions of the Middle Ages to the games, sports, and festivals which helped to make life agreeable alike for rich and poor, for nobles and peasants. Some indoor games are of eastern origin. Chess, for instance, arose in India as a war game. 

On each side a king and his general, with chariots, cavalry, elephants, and infantry, met in battle array. These survive in the rooks, knights, bishops, and pawns of the modern game. Chess formed one of the chief pastimes within the castles of the lords. Playing cards are another Oriental invention. They were introduced into Europe in the fourteenth century, either by the Arabs or the gypsies. Their first use seems to have been for telling fortunes. 

Outdoor sports. Many of our outdoor sports are derived

WATER TEST FOR WITCHCRAFT 

This form of ordeal rested on the old belief that pure water would reject an impure person. Any one accused of witchcraft might therefore be thrown bound into a stream; if he floated he was guilty; if he sank he was innocent and had to be rescued. from those played in medieval times. How one kind of game may become the parent of many others is seen in the case of the ball-play. The ancients tossed and caught balls as children do now. They also had a game in which each side tried to secure the ball and throw it over the adversary's goal line. 

This game lasted on into the Middle Ages, and from it football has descended. The ancients seem never to have used a stick or bat in their ball-play. The Persians, however, began to play ball on horseback, using a long mallet for the purpose, and introduced their new sport throughout Asia. 

Under the Asiatic name of pulu (= polo) it found its way into Europe. In this way polo gave rise to the various games in which balls are hit with bats, including tennis, hockey, golf, baseball, and croquet. A common outdoor sport of the nobles was hunting. Deer, bears, and wild boars were hunted

Medieval Civilization with spears and hounds; for smaller animals trained hawks, or falcons, were employed. Bear baiting and cockfighting were also popular. It was not until the nineteenth century that an English society for the prevention of cruelty to 

BEAR BAITING From the Luttrell Psalter. 

animals succeeded in getting a law passed which forbade these cruel sports. Most civilized countries now have similar laws.

Festivals. Many customs centered around the celebration of festivals, which were in some instances derived from the ceremonies of pagan worship. April Fool's Day was a relic of the festivities which celebrated the approach of spring. 

May Day, another festival of spring, honored the spirits of trees and of all budding vegetation. The persons who acted as May kings and May queens represented these spirits.

The Morris dance was especially associated with May Day and was danced round a Maypole to a lively and capering step. The name Morris is a corruption of the word Moorish, and refers to the origin of this dance in Spain. On Midsummer Eve (June 23), which marked the summer solstice, came the fire festival, when people built bonfires and leaped over them, walked in procession with torches round the fields, and rolled burning wheels down the hillsides. Hallow Eve, so called from being the eve of All Saints' Day (November 1), also seems to have been a survival of a heathen celebration. Witches and fairies were supposed to assemble

Customs and Manners 367 on this night. The festival of Christmas, coming at the winter solstice, kept some heathen features, such as the use of mistletoe with which Celtic priests once decked the altars of their gods. The Christmas tree, however, is not a relic of heathenism. Mumming had a particular association with 

Christmas. Mummers were bands of men and women who disguised themselves in masks and skins of animals and then serenaded people outside their houses. The mummers often performed little plays in which Father Christmas, Old King Cole, and St. George were familiar figures. 

Plays. Many plays of a religious character came into vogue during the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. 

The earliest were the "miracles." They presented in dramatic form scenes from the 

Bible and stories of the

This religious setting did not prevent the introduction of clowns and buffoons. The miracle play after a time passed from the clergy to the guilds (p. 343). Singly or together the guilds of a town presented annual exhibitions. An exhibition might last for several days and have as many as fifty scenes, beginning with creation and ending with Doomsday. The 'moralities" dealt with the struggle between good and evil, rather than with religious history. Characters such as 66

Houses. Medieval Europe was dotted with feudal castles. 

As feudalism declined and private warfare lessened, many of the huge and uncomfortable castles were either torn down or made over into country houses. Though less bare and inconvenient than castles, they were still poorly lighted, illventilated, and in winter scarcely warmed by the open wood fires. It was a great improvement when glass windows came to be substituted for wooden shutters or oiled paper. The introduction of chimneys to keep heat in and let smoke out formed yet another improvement. After the Gothic style came to be used for secular buildings, beautiful and commodious residences were often erected by nobles and merchants in the cities.

Furniture. People in the Middle Ages, even the well-

Customs and Manners 369 to-do, got along with little furniture. The great hall of a country house contained a long dining table, with benches used at meals, and a few stools. The family beds often occupied curtained recesses in the walls, but guests might have to sleep on the floor of the hall. Servants often slept in stables. Few persons could afford rugs to cover the floor; the poor used rushes. Utensils were few, and articles of glass and silver were practically unknown, except in the houses of the rich.

Costume. The pictures in old manuscripts give us a good idea of medieval dress. It naturally varied with time and place, and according to the social position of the wearer. 

Laws were sometimes passed, without much result, to regulate the quality, shape, and cost of the costumes to be worn by different orders of society. The moralists of the age were shocked, then as now, when tightly fitting garments, which showed the outlines of the body, became fashionable. The inconvenience of putting them on led to the use of buttons and buttonholes. Women's headdresses were often of extraordinary height and shape. Not less remarkable were the pointed shoes worn by men. The points finally got so long that they hindered walking, unless tied by a ribbon to the knees. 

Food and drink. Ale and beer formed the drink of the common people, taking the place that tea and coffee now hold. The upper classes regaled themselves on costly wines. 

Medieval cookbooks show that people of means had all sorts of elaborate and expensive dishes. Dinner at a nobleman's house might include ten or twelve courses, mostly meats and game. The lord and his retainers sat down to a gluttonous feast and, as they ate and drank, watched the pranks of a professional jester or "fool," listened to the songs and music of minstrels, and, it may be, heard with wonder the tales of far-off countries brought by some traveler. Knives, forks, and napkins were conveniences unknown in medieval times. 

Food was conveyed to the mouth with the fingers and sometimes with hunting knives or daggers.

Medieval Civilization 99. NATIONAL LANGUAGES AND LITERATURES 

Latin as an international language. Latin continued to be an international language throughout the Middle Ages. 

The Roman Church used it for papal bulls and other documents. Prayers were recited, hymns were sung, and sometimes sermons were preached in Latin. It was also the language of men of culture everywhere in Christendom. 

University professors lectured in Latin, students spoke Latin, lawyers addressed judges in Latin, and the merchants in different countries wrote Latin letters to one another. All learned books were composed in Latin until the close of the sixteenth century.

Two groups of national languages. Besides this international language of Latin, each European country during the later Middle Ages had also its own national tongue. The 

Romance languages (French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, and Rumanian) were derived from the Latin spoken by the Romanized inhabitants of the lands now known as France, Italy, Spain, Portugal, and Rumania. The Germanic or

Teutonic peoples who remained outside what had been the limits of the Roman world continued to use their native tongues during the Middle Ages. Thus arose modern 

German, Dutch, Flemish, and the various Scandinavian languages (Danish, Norwegian, Swedish, and Icelandic).

English. The English language occupies a position midway between the Romance and the Germanic languages. 

The rough, guttural speech of the Anglo-Saxons, in course of time, underwent various changes. Christian missionaries introduced many Latin terms for church offices, services, and observances. The Danes, besides contributing some names of places, gave us that most useful word are and the habit of using to before an infinitive. After the Norman conquest, the Norman-French influence helped to make the language simpler by ridding it of the cumbersome declensions and conjugations which it had in common with all Germanic tongues. Songs of the troubadours. As the new national languages of medieval Europe developed, new national literatures also A pleasant glimpse of gay society is afforded by the compositions of the troubadours. These professional poets flourished in the south of France, but many of them traveled in other countries from court to court. Their verses were sung to the accompaniment of some musical instrument, generally the lute. Love and deeds of chivalry were the two themes which most inspired the songs of the troubadours. 

National epics. Northern France gave birth to long narrative poems (epics) describing the exploits of mythical heroes or historic kings. Such poems enjoyed high esteem in aristocratic circles and penetrated all countries where feudalism prevailed. Many of the French epics dealt with 

Charlemagne and his reign. The oldest and at the same time the finest of them is the Song of Roland. It tells how 

Roland, one of Charlemagne's mighty warriors, fought against the Moors in Spain and how, overcome by numbers, he died gloriously on the field of battle, with his face to the enemy and a prayer on his lips that "sweet France” might never be dishonored. The greatest epic composed in Germany during the Middle Ages was the Nibelungenlied ("Song of the 

Nibelungs"). It centers about the hero Siegfried, a figure of romance and not of history.

Arthurian romances. In the United States many of us learn about medieval chivalry and knighthood from reading the tales about King Arthur and the Knights of the Round Table. Whether Arthur ever lived in fact or not we do not know, but he lives in medieval romances as the model of chivalry. Sir Thomas Malory's Death of Arthur, or, as it is usually called, Morte d'Arthur, was one of the first books

National Languages and Literatures 

373 to be printed in England and contains many tales about Arthur. From these, Tennyson, in his Idylls of the King, and other modern poets have drawn their inspiration. 

Robin Hood ballads. If King Arthur was the ideal knight,

Robin Hood was the ideal yeoman. According to the old 

English ballads this outlaw flourished in the second half of the twelfth century, and led, with his merry men, an adventurous life in Sherwood Forest, engaging in feats of strength and hunting the king's tall deer. Bishops, sheriffs, and gamekeepers are his only enemies. He has the greatest pity for the common people, and robs the rich to give to the poor. Courtesy, generosity, and love of fair play are some of the characteristics which made him a popular hero. The ballads about him were sung by country folk for hundreds of years.

Chaucer and Dante. In the later Middle Ages there lived two great writers, who became famous both for their writings and for the influence of their writings upon the formation of new national languages. One of these was the English author, Geoffrey Chaucer (1340-1400). His poems became so famous that they helped to establish English as a national language with a literature of its own. Chaucer's English is very different from Anglo-Saxon and quite like our English, though the modern reader is sometimes troubled by the old spelling and by certain words not now in use. His best known work is the Canterbury Tales, a collection of stories told by a group of pilgrims of Chaucer's day as they make their way along the country roads to the cathedral town of Canterbury. The other great writer was the Italian poet 

Dante (1265-1321), who lived almost a century earlier than 

Chaucer. Dante's Divine Comedy describes an imaginary visit to hell, purgatory, and paradise. It was the first supremely great literary work in western Europe since the fall of Rome. It established Italian as a national language. 

Even yet, the reading of Dante's poetry is an introduction to the thought of the Middle Ages - its piety, philosophy, poetry, love of nature, and love of knowledge.

Unit VI TRANSITION TO MODERN CIVILIZATION 

How changes in learning, religion, geography, and government opened the door to modern civilization 

(CHAPTERS XII-XIV)

PRESENTATION 

Late in the Middle Ages important changes in medieval civilization began. This transition from medieval to modern civilization was a gradual process. (1) Fundamental changes in scholarship, art, science, and literature resulted from the revival of Greek and Roman culture. This classical revival started a movement which is known as the Renaissance. It was flourishing in Italy by the fourteenth century; it spread from Italy throughout western Europe. (2) During the 

Renaissance geographical knowledge and discovery also increased. 

Columbus, Da Gama, and Magellan found new trade routes and new worlds, and vastly extended European commerce. The Portuguese built an empire in the East Indies, and the Spanish built one in America. (3) Fundamental changes in civilization also resulted from the break-up of religious unity among western Christians. 

In the late Middle Ages leaders like Wycliffe and Huss secured large followings that became heretical movements. The Church was also weakened by the Babylonian Captivity and the Great Schism. Religious disputes reached their climax early in the sixteenth century when Martin Luther headed an open revolt which has become known as the Reformation. It spread over northern 

Europe, assuming various forms, such as Lutheranism, Calvinism, and Anglicanism. The steps which the Catholic Church took to maintain itself are called the Catholic Counter Reformation. The religious quarrels produced an outburst of intolerance and wars which convulsed much of western Europe for more than a hundred years. (Chapter XII) 

This transition period also saw important changes in government. 

Late in the Middle Ages the Tudor kings developed autocracy in England, but in the seventeenth century the Stuart kings failed as autocratic rulers. They were forced by the Puritan and Glorious revolutions to give up many of their powers. On the other hand, autocracy flourished in France, Russia, and Prussia. Under autocracy arose a group of critics, especially in France, who assailed its principles and practices. At the same time, some rulers made it their chief concern to promote the welfare of their subjects by encouraging industry, commerce, and culture. These rulers are called enlightened despots. (Chapter XIII) 

The expansion of Europe overseas went on rapidly during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Great Britain built up a sea power and acquired, at the expense of France, an imperial realm in both India and North America. As an offset to these gains, she lost, through the American Revolution, the Thirteen

Colonies. (Chapter XIV)

CHAPTER XII REMAKING MEDIEVAL CIVILIZATION

- MARCO POLO 

Shifting the center of gravity. Medieval civilization, we have seen, centered in the Mediterranean. Areas as far away as England, Scandinavia, and Russia received their religion from centers like Rome and Constantinople. The customs, manners, literature, and art of these remote areas were deeply colored by the Christian civilization which centered in the Mediterranean. Even their commerce moved from the north and west through the Mediterranean to the east, and back again. The Mediterranean was the center of the world. In this chapter we shall see that center slowly shifting away from the Mediterranean. (1) The papacy, with its home at Rome, will lose something of its dominant position in western Christianity. (2) Geographical discoveries will turn the course of commerce from the Mediterranean into the Atlantic. (3) The revival of classical literature and art will tend to shift the center of intellectual interest away from theology to "the more human" concerns of this life. Three outstanding aspects, then, of medieval civilization underwent a change as Europe moved into modern times. As a well-known historian has said, "the center of gravity of human culture" was changed. 379

100. THE CLASSICAL REVIVAL 

The classics in the Middle Ages. We have already seen (p. 261) that knowledge of Greek and Roman writings (the classics) did not entirely disappear in western Europe after the barbarian invasions. The monastery and cathedral schools of the Middle Ages kept alive the study of ancient books. The Benedictine monks copied the works of pagan as well as Christian authors. The rise of universities made it possible for the student to study Latin literature at more than one center of learning. Reverence for the classics was expressed again and again in the writings of the Italian poet Dante (p. 373). On the other hand, many ancient manuscripts in both Latin and Greek lay in the monasteries and cathedrals neglected and blackened with the dust of ages. 

Renewed interest in Latin. Late in the Middle Ages there began a definite movement to revive the study of the classics. 

Petrarch (1304-1374), a younger contemporary of Dante, and like him a native of Florence, was one of the leaders in this movement. He devoted himself with tireless energy to classical studies, composing many Latin works and traveling widely in Italy and other countries in the search for ancient manuscripts. When he found in one place two lost orations of Cicero and in another place a collection of Cicero's letters, he was transported with delight.

He kept copyists in his house, at times as many as four, busily copying the manuscripts that he had discovered or borrowed. "My tireless spirit pores over the pages," he writes, "until it has exhausted both fingers and eyes, and yet I feel neither hunger nor cold."

Petrarch knew almost no Greek. His copy of Homer, it is said, he often kissed, though he could not read it. 

PETRARCH 

After a miniature in the Laurentian Library, Florence.

The Classical Revival 

381 Renewed interest in Greek. The renewed interest in 

Latin literature, due to Petrarch and others, was soon followed by the revival of Greek literature. Petrarch's friend and disciple, Boccaccio, was the first to bring to Italy manuscripts of the Iliad and the Odyssey. Having learned some 

Greek, he wrote out a translation of these poems. In 1396 a scholar from Constantinople began to lecture on Greek in the University of Florence. He afterwards taught in other 

Italian cities and aided in preparing a Greek grammar the first book of its kind. The fall of Constantinople in 

1453 caused many learned Greeks to go to Italy, where their conversation and lectures greatly stimulated the study of 

Greek. "Greece had not perished, but had emigrated to Italy."

The spread of humanism. The ancient Greek and Latin languages and literatures came to be called the humanities, and the study of them, humanism. In the universities, the humanities displaced the old scholastic philosophy as the chief subject of instruction. From the universities the study of the humanities spread to the lower schools. From educational centers, humanism spread throughout the Italian peninsula. Libraries were established for the safe-keeping of classical manuscripts, professorships of the ancient languages were endowed, and scholars were given opportunities to pursue researches. Even the popes shared in this zeal for humanism. One of them founded the Vatican Library at Rome, which has the most valuable collection of manuscripts in the world. 

The new literature.

We have seen that late in the Middle Ages there began in western Europe the development of the native or vernacular languages and literatures (pp. 370372). The growth of the vernacular was retarded somewhat by the renewed interest in classical languages and literature. 

Scholars who devoted themselves to the classics sometimes looked with contempt upon books written in the vernacular. 

In time, however, western scholars and poets wished to rival the literary achievement of classical antiquity; thus pride

in the development of a native literature was aroused. 

Among the many authors of the Renaissance period whose works are still frequently read may be mentioned: (1) the 

Florentine historian and diplomat, Machiavelli, who wrote The Prince, a guide for rulers; (2) the Spanish writer Cervantes, whose Don Quixote is a burlesque upon romantic tales about medieval chivalry; (3) the French essayist, Montaigne, who wrote essays on a great variety of subjects; (4) the English statesman, Sir Francis Bacon, whose Essays are filled with practical wisdom, and who undertook to found a system of knowledge based upon observation rather than upon the authority of Aristotle; (5) and the poet and dramatist Shakespeare, who is quite generally regarded as the greatest of writers.

The new architecture. Just as the humanists went back to Greek and Latin literature, so the architects of the late Middle Ages began to go back to Greek temples and Roman domed buildings for their models. Long rows of Ionic or 

Corinthian columns, spanned by round arches, became again the prevailing architectural style. Perhaps the most important feature of the revived classical architecture was the use of the dome for the roofs of churches. The majestic cupola of St. Peter's at Rome has become the parent of many domed structures in the Old and in the New World. 

Architects, however, did not limit themselves to planning churches. The magnificent palaces of Florence, as well as some of those in Venice, are monuments of this era. 

Sculpture. The development of architecture naturally stimulated related arts, such as sculpture and painting. The 

Italian sculptors began to copy the ancient bas-reliefs and statues preserved in Rome. The greatest of Italian sculptors was Michelangelo (1475-1564). Though a Florentine by birth, he lived most of his life in Rome. He also won fame in architecture and painting. The dome of St. Peter's was finished after his designs, while the paintings (frescoes) on the ceiling of the Sistine chapel in the Vatican display his genius as a painter.

Painting. The Italian painters had found one of their chief opportunities in the decoration of churches and monasteries. Consequently their art was largely religious in character. Artists chose many subjects from the Bible or the lives of the saints. They did not trouble themselves to secure correctness of costume, but painted ancient Jews, Greeks, and Romans in the garb of Italian gentlemen. 

Many of their pictures were water colors painted on the plaster walls of churches and palaces. Such paintings are called frescoes. Many of them have suffered severely by injuries to the walls and from the effects of moisture, dust, and light. After the process of mixing the colors with oils instead of water was discovered, pictures on wood or canvas became common. Italian painters excelled in the art of painting people-portraiture; they were less successful with landscapes. Michelangelo, Leonardo da Vinci, Raphael, Titian, and Correggio - all of whom lived between 1450 and 1600are often called the Old Masters of Italian painting.

The classical revival extends beyond Italy. Scholars and artists in Germany, France, Holbein the Younger (1497-1543). Proband England continued the in- ably an excellent likeness of Erasmus. tellectual movement that was begun in Italy. The foremost of these scholars was Erasmus (1466-1536), a Hollander. 

His travels and extensive correspondence brought him in touch with many learned men of the day. The most important achievement of Erasmus was an edition of the New

Testament in the original Greek, with a Latin version. This work led to a better understanding of the New Testament

and also facilitated translation of the Scriptures into the modern European languages. Italian architects found a cordial reception in France, Spain, the Netherlands, and other countries, where they introduced the new styles of building and ornamentation. The celebrated palace of the 

Louvre in Paris, which is used today as an art gallery and museum, dates from the sixteenth century. The new type of sculpture also spread beyond Italy and throughout 

Europe. Painters in northern countries at first followed

Italian models, but afterward produced masterpieces of their own.

The Renaissance. The French word renaissance means rebirth or revival. The word is particularly applied to that rebirth or revival of classical learning and art which has just been discussed. The beginnings of the Renaissance go back to the fourteenth century; the movement culminated in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Italy was its original home. There it first appeared, there it found widest acceptance, and there it reached the highest development. From Italy the Renaissance spread beyond the Alps and made the round of western Europe. 

101. THE NEW SCIENCE 

The scientific revival.  were not by any means ignorant of science (p. 360), but its study naturally received a great impetus when the Renaissance brought before educated men all that the Greeks had done in mathematics, astronomy, physics, medicine, and other subjects. The invention of printing also fostered the scientific revival by making it easy to spread knowledge abroad in every land. 

The pioneers of Renaissance science were Italians, but students in France, England, Germany, and other countries soon took up the work of enlightenment. 

The earth and the universe. Throughout the Middle 

Ages most people believed that the earth was the center of the universe. Beginning with the sixteenth century, a suc-

The New Science 

385 cession of astronomers and mathematicians demonstrated that the earth is only one member of the solar system. (1) First place among these men must be given to Copernicus (1473-1543), the founder of modern astronomy. He was a Pole, but he lived many years in Italy. Patient study and calculation led him to the conclusion that the earth turns upon its own axis, and, together with the other planets, revolves around the sun. The Copernican theory met much opposition, not only in the universities, which clung to the time-honored Ptolemaic system, but also among theologians, who thought that it contradicted statements in the Bible. 

Moreover, people could not easily reconcile themselves to the idea that the earth is only one member of the solar system that it is only one of many worlds. 

(2) An Italian scientist, Galileo (1564-1642), made one of the first telescopes. It was about as powerful as an opera glass, but he turned it on the heavenly bodies with wonderful results. He found the sun moving unmistakably on its axis, Venus showing phases according to her position in relation to the sun, Jupiter accompanied by revolving moons, or satellites, and the Milky Way composed of a multitude of separate stars. Galileo rightly believed that these discoveries confirmed the theory of Copernicus. (3) Another man of genius, the German Kepler (15711630), worked out the mathematical laws which govern the movements of the planets. He made it clear that the planets revolve around the sun in elliptical instead of circular paths, or orbits. (4) Sir Isaac Newton (1642-1727), continuing Kepler's work, showed by mathematical calculation that the motion. of the planets about the sun, and of the moon about the earth, can be explained as due to the same force of gravity which makes the apple fall to the ground. This discovery that all the movements of the heavenly bodies obey one simple physical law is a landmark in the history of science. 

Anatomy and physiology. Two other scientists gained fame in a field far removed from astronomy. Vesalius (1514-

1564), a Fleming, who studied in Italian medical schools, gave to the world the first careful description of the human body based on actual dissection. He was thus the founder of modern human anatomy. Harvey (1578-1657), an Englishman, after observing living animals, announced the discovery of the circulation of the blood. He thereby founded human physiology.

The scientific method. Copernicus, Galileo, Kepler, Vesalius, Harvey, and their fellow workers built up the scientific method. Students in the Middle Ages had mostly been satisfied to accept what Aristotle and other philosophers had said, without examining the basis of their statements (p. 360). Kepler, for instance, was the first to disprove the

Aristotelian idea that, as all perfect motion is circular, therefore the heavenly bodies must move in circular orbits. Similarly, the world had to wait many centuries before Harvey showed Aristotle's error in supposing that the blood arose in the liver, went thence to the heart, and by the veins was conducted over the body. The new scientific method rested on observation and experiment. Students learned at length to take nothing for granted, to set aside all authority, and to go straight to nature for their facts. As Sir Francis Bacon (1561-1626), one of Shakespeare's contemporaries and a severe critic of the old scholasticism, declared, "All depends on keeping the eye steadily fixed upon the facts of nature, and so receiving their images as they are, for God forbid that we should give out a dream of our own imagination for a pattern of the world." Modern science, to which we owe so much, is thus, in part, a product of the Renaissance. 

102. GEOGRAPHICAL DISCOVERY 

Geography in the Middle Ages. The Greeks and Romans had become familiar with a large part of Europe and Asia, but much of their learning was forgotten or misunderstood during the Middle Ages. Even the wonderful discoveries of the Northmen in the North Atlantic (p. 283) gradually

Geographical Discovery 

387 faded from memory. The Arabs, whose conquests and commerce spread over so much of the Orient, far surpassed the Christian peoples of Europe in knowledge of the world. 

In the late Middle Ages, however, there was in western Europe a considerable growth of geographical knowledge. 

The Crusades promoted geographical knowledge by fostering pilgrimages and missions in Oriental lands (p. 312). Numerous merchants also visited the East.

Marco Polo's book. The story of the Polos, as written down at Marco's dictation, became one of the most popular works of the Middle Ages. In this book people read of far 

Cathay (China), with its wealth, its huge cities, and swarming population; of mysterious and secluded Tibet; of Burma, Siam, and Cochin-China, with their palaces and pagodas; of the East Indies, famed for spices; of Ceylon, abounding

in pearls; and of India, little known since the days of Alexander the Great. Even Cipango (Japan) Marco described from hearsay as an island whose inhabitants were civilized, and so rich in gold that the royal palace was roofed and paved with that metal. The accounts of these countries naturally made Europeans more eager than ever to reach the East. 

Trade with the East. Europeans wanted to reach the 

East largely for purposes of trade. Many important articles used in medieval Europe came from the East. Eastern spices-cinnamon, pepper, cloves, nutmeg, and gingerwere used freely in medieval times to preserve as well as to season food. Precious stones, drugs, perfumes, gums, dyes, and fragrant woods also came from the East. 

Rivalry for the eastern trade. Eastern goods destined for Europe were brought from various places in Asia to some port at the eastern end of the Mediterranean (p. 347); from there they were transported to Italy and other countries of western Europe. The business of transporting these goods was largely in the hands of Italian and German merchants. 

About 1450 two other European peoples appeared as competitors for this profitable trade with the East. These two peoples were the Portuguese and the Spaniards. The Portuguese were the first in the field. 

The Portuguese have a leader Prince Henry. The

Portuguese preceded the Spaniards in developing the eastern trade partly because the Portuguese had in Prince Henry the Navigator an able leader. The son of a Portuguese king, he gave up a military career and for more than forty years devoted his wealth, learning, and enthusiasm to geographical discovery. Under his direction better maps were made, the compass was placed on vessels, and seamen were instructed in all the nautical knowledge of the time. Prince 

Henry then dispatched expedition after expedition southward to explore the African coast.

In the second place, to this exorbitant expense were now added the exactions of the Turks (p. 348). In the third place, the jealousy of Venice and other cities endangered Portuguese ships that would attempt to sail to the eastern Mediterranean. The problem before the 15

The only way they could do so was by finding a new route to the East, and this would almost certainly have to be by water. They believed that they might reach India by sailing southward from their own country in western Europe, and around the African continent. 

They hoped that they would then be within reach of the Indies and its rich wares. The Portuguese were soon able to prove the correctness of their theory.

The Portuguese reach India.

Columbus's discovery. The Spanish queen, Isabella, aided 

Columbus in outfitting a small fleet with which he could put his theories to a test. When he started out, he firmly believed that a journey of only four thousand miles would bring him to Cipango (Japan) and the realms of the Great Khan of Cathay (China). Actually, after a voyage of several weeks, he reached a group of islands off the southeastern coast of North America, thousands of miles from the Indies

Geographical Discovery 

393 (India, China, and adjacent islands). Believing, however, that he had reached an island in the Indies, Columbus called the natives Indians. The name West Indies, now applied to the islands discovered by Columbus, remains as a testimony to this error.

Significance of Columbus's discovery. When Columbus returned to Spain in 1493 he carried no valuable cargoes of gold, spices, or mahogany wood — just a few naked savages and some worthless beads. Naturally, his countrymen could not immediately appreciate what he had done. Six years later, when Vasco da Gama returned from India, his ships were loaded with gems, spices, and rich goods from the East. 

Naturally, every one could behold and appreciate what Vasco da Gama had done. Nevertheless, the "unprofitable" voyage of Columbus has continued to pay world-wide dividends. 

Columbus's discovery shifted the center of history from the Mediterranean to the Atlantic; it opened the doors of limitless opportunities to Europeans; and it marked for us the beginning of modern history. 

Magellan's fleet sails round the world, 1519-1522. So far no one had yet realized the dream of Columbus to reach the lands of spice and silk by sailing westward. Ferdinand 

Magellan, a Portuguese navigator in the service of Spain, believed that a route to the Indies could be found by sailing around the barrier of land which had stopped Columbus. 

The Spanish ruler, Charles I, grandson of the Isabella who had supported Columbus, looked with favor upon Magellan's ideas, and provided a fleet of five vessels for the undertaking. 

Magellan crossed the Atlantic and sailed southward along the eastern coast of South America. When he reached the southern end of the mainland, he turned westward through the narrow, stormy strait which has been called, in his honor, the Strait of Magellan. After he had passed through the strait, he found himself once more upon the open sea; its waters were so quiet and peaceful, contrasted with those of the Atlantic, that he named it the Pacific Ocean. The American Indians 395 had at last discovered a way to reach the Indies by sailing westward. Magellan continued voyaging across the Pacific for more than a hundred days, and finally reached the Philippine Islands, where he was killed in a fight with the natives. His men, however, managed to reach the goal of the journey -the Spice Islands in the Indies. A single ship carried back to Spain the few sailors who had survived the hardships of a journey lasting nearly three years. 

Significance of Magellan's voyage. In the history of geographical discovery, three events stand out as supremely important. The first of these was Da Gama's discovery of the water route to India; the second was Columbus's discovery of the New World; the third was the voyage of 

Magellan's fleet around the world, the first circumnavigation of the globe. Magellan's voyage proved that America, at least on the south, had no connection with Asia, and that the western sea route to the Indies really existed. Furthermore, it revealed the enormous extent of the Pacific Ocean and led to the discovery of many large islands in the East Indies. Men now knew of a certainty that the earth is round, and in the distance covered by Magellan they had a rough approximation as to its size. Magellan stands beside Ďa 

Gama and Columbus in the company of great explorers. 

103. THE AMERICAN INDIANS 

Physical characteristics of the Indians. The natives of 

America, whom Columbus called Indians, resemble Mongoloid peoples in some physical features, such as the reddish brown complexion, the hair, uniformly coarse and black, the high cheek bones, and the short stature of many tribes. On the other hand, the large aquiline nose, the straight eyes, never oblique, and the tall stature of some tribes are not Mongoloid characteristics. It seems safe to conclude that the Indians, whatever their origin, became thoroughly fused into a composite race during long centuries of isolation from the rest of mankind.

Indian culture. The Indians, because of their isolation, had to work out by themselves many arts, inventions, and discoveries. They spoke over a thousand languages and diasigme boviz -09 315 

A MAYA FIGURINE 

Les lects, and not one has yet been bogensi traced outside of America. 

Their implements consisted of newal polished stone, occasionally ani of unsmelted copper, and in 

Mexico and Peru, of bronze. 

The use of iron was unknown w to them. They cultivated 

Indian corn, or maize, but lacked the other great cereals. 

They domesticated the dog, the llama, and the alpaca, but no other animals. They usually lived in clans and tribes, ruled by headmen or chiefs. Their religion probsably did not involve a belief in a "Great Spirit," as is so often said, but rather recognized in all nature the abode of spiritual powers, mysterious and wonderful, whom man ought to conciliate by prayers and sacrifices. Most of the 

American Indians were not 

Savages, but barbarians fairly well advanced in culture.

The American Indians 397 hundred years ago. The temples, shrines, altars, and statues in these ancient cities show that the Mayas had made much progress in the fine arts. They knew enough astronomy to frame a solar calendar of three hundred and sixty-five days, and enough mathematics to employ numbers exceeding a million. The The Aztecs. The so-called Aztecs were an Indian people who came down from the north and established themselves on the Mexican plateau. Here they formed a confederacy of many tribes ruled over by a sort of king, whose capital was Tenochtitlan, on the site of the present Mexico

City. The Aztecs seem to have borrowed much of their art, science, and knowledge of writing from their Maya neighbors. They built houses and temples of stone or sun-dried brick, constructed aqueducts, roads, and bridges, excelled in the dyeing, weaving, and spinning of cotton, and made beautiful ornaments of silver and gold. 

They worshiped many gods, to which the priests offered prisoners of war as human sacrifices. handle is of light-colored wood carved in the form of a man masked with a bird skin. 

Brilliant mosaic settings of turquoise, malachite, and shell embellish the figure. 

The Incas. The lofty table-lands of the Andes were also the seat of an advanced Indian culture. The greater part of the territory now included in Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, and northern Chile came under the sway of the Incas, the “children of the sun," as they called themselves. The Inca power centered in the Peruvian city of Cuzco, and on the shores

of Lake Titicaca, which lies twelve thousand feet above sea level. In this region of magnificent scenery the traveler views with astonishment the ruins of deserted cities, which were built either by the Incas or by the Indians whom they conquered and displaced. The Incas displayed great skill in the manual arts; they were expert goldsmiths, silversmiths, and potters; while as cultivators and engineers they surpassed their European conquerors. 

104. COLONIAL EMPIRES 

Portuguese ascendancy in the East. The Portuguese, after Da Gama's voyage, made haste to secure the wealth of the Indies. By the middle of the sixteenth century they had built up a colonial empire in southern Asia and the adjacent islands and in the eastern part of South America. 

Their possessions included many trading posts in Africa; 

Ormuz at the entrance to the Persian Gulf; the western coast of India; Ceylon; Malacca at the end of the Malay peninsula; and various stations in the Malay Archipelago. 

They also established commercial intercourse with China and even with Japan.

Portuguese trade monopoly. The Portuguese came to the Far East as the successors of the Arabs, who for centuries had conducted an extensive trade on the Indian Ocean. 

Having dispossessed the Arabs, the Portuguese took care to shut out all European competitors. Only their own merchants were allowed to bring goods from the Indies to Europe by the Cape route. Lisbon, the capital of Portugal, was the chief depot for spices and other eastern commodities. The 

French, English, and Dutch came there to buy them and took the place of Italian merchants in distributing them throughout Europe.

Portugal in America. The colonial empire which the 

Portuguese formed in India and the East Indies collapsed during the seventeenth century before the attacks of the French, the English, and the Dutch. Their colonial empire

Colonial Empires 

399 in Brazil lasted until the nineteenth century, and their influence still endures there, in spite of the breaking of political ties. The language, literature, and customs of Brazil are those of Portugal. It is a marvelous thing that this little parent state, insignificant in area, in natural resources, and in population, should have been transplanted, as it were, to the boundless spaces of the New World. 

Spanish ascendancy in the West. The discoverers of the New World were naturally the pioneers in its exploration. 

The adventures of Ponce de León, who discovered Florida in 1513; of Balboa, who sighted the Pacific in the same year; of Cortés, who overthrew the Aztec power in Mexico; of 

Pizarro, who conquered the Incas of Peru; of De Soto; and of Coronado are familiar to every reader of American history. 

These men laid the foundations of the Spanish colonial empire. It included Florida, New Mexico, California, Mexico, Central America, the West Indies, and all South America except Brazil.

Spanish trade monopoly. Spain governed her colonial dominions in the spirit of monopoly. As far as possible, she excluded French, English, and other foreigners from trading with Spanish America. She also discouraged shipbuilding, manufacturing, and even the cultivation of the vine and the olive, lest the colonists should compete with home industries. The colonies were regarded only as a workshop for the production of the precious metals and raw materials. 

This unwise policy partly accounts for the economic backwardness of Mexico, Peru, and other Spanish-American countries.

Intermarriage of Spaniards and Indians. The Spaniards brought few women with them and hence had to find their wives among the Indians. Intermarriage of the two peoples became common at an early date. The result was the mixed race which one still finds throughout the greater part of Spanish America. The Indian strain predominates, because almost everywhere the natives were far more numerous than the white settlers.

Conversion of the Indians. Many of the Indians were converted to Christianity. Devoted monks penetrated deep into the wilderness, bringing with them, not only the Christian religion, but also European civilization. The natives were usually gathered into permanent villages, or “missions," each one with its church and school. Converts who learned to read and write sometimes became priests or entered the monastic orders. The monks also took much interest in the material welfare of the Indians and taught them how to farm, how to build houses, and how to spin and weave and cook by better methods than their own.

Spanish-American culture. The civilizing work of Spain in the New World is sometimes forgotten. Here were the earliest American hospitals and asylums, for the use of Indians and Negroes as well as of Spaniards. Here were the first American schools and colleges. Twelve institutions of higher learning, all modeled upon the University of Salamanca, arose in Spanish America during the colonial period. 

The fine arts also flourished in the Spanish colonies, and architects of the United States have now begun to copy the beautiful churches and public buildings of Mexico and Peru. 

Spain in America. The colonial empire of Spain on the 

American mainland lasted almost exactly three hundred years. During this time Spain gave her language, religion, law, political institutions, economic system, and intellectual life to half the New World. The Spanish colonial empire affords, therefore, a great historical example of the transmission of culture imperially, somewhat as imperial Rome spread Roman civilization throughout western Europe. The work of Spain, like that of Rome, endures. It has left an abiding impress on the millions of Spanish-speaking people between the Rio Grande and the Strait of Magellan. 

105. AMERICA HELPS TO REMAKE EUROPEAN LIFE 

Shifting of trade routes. In the Middle Ages the Mediterranean and the Baltic had been the principal highways

America Helps to Remake European Life 401 

of commerce. The discovery of America, followed immediately by the opening of the Cape route to the Indies, shifted commercial activity from these inclosed seas to the Atlantic 

Ocean. Venice, Genoa, Hamburg, Lübeck, and Bruges gradually gave way, as trading centers, to Lisbon and Cadiz, Bordeaux and Cherbourg, Antwerp and Amsterdam, London and Liverpool. One may say, therefore, that the year 1492 inaugurated the Atlantic period of European history. CERRODE POTOSI wwwred bloc 

Increased supply of gold and silver.  suffered from the lack of sufficient money with which to do business, owing to an inadequate supply of gold and silver. From the beginning of modern times, the world has been better supplied with these precious metals. This increased supply was a direct consequence of the discovery of Amer- ica. The Spaniards secured large quan- טו 

THE GOLD MINES OF POTOSÍ 

From a woodcut of 1555. tities of gold by plundering the Indians of Mexico and Peru of their stored-up wealth. The output of silver much exceeded that of gold as soon as the Spaniards began to work the wonderfully rich silver mines of Potosí in Bolivia. It is estimated that, by the end of the sixteenth century, the American mines had produced at least three times as much gold and silver as had been current in Europe at the beginning of the century.

Consequences of increased money supply. The Spaniards had few industries themselves, and so were obliged to import goods from other European countries. To pay for these goods, Spain had to send to those countries the gold and

silver which she had received from America. Thus Spain acted as a huge sieve through which the gold and silver of America entered all the countries of Europe. Greater amounts of money were thus put into circulation. As every one who has lived through an economic crisis realizes, the value, or purchasing power, of money constantly shifts with the quantity that is in circulation. When every one has plenty of money in his pocket, he can pay a higher price for what he buys of goods or services, and he is more likely to have money to lend. When Spain passed on the gold and silver which she had received from America, the prices of all commodities rose, wages advanced, and manufacturers and traders found more money in circulation which they could borrow to finance their undertakings. One of the economic problems of the Middle Ages was thus solved. 

Effects of the discoveries on the standard of living. But 

America was much more than a treasury of precious metals. 

Many commodities, hitherto unknown, soon found their way from the New World to the Old. Among these were maize, the potato, which, when cultivated in Europe, became the "bread of the poor," chocolate and cocoa made from the seeds of the cacao tree, Peruvian bark, or quinine, so useful in malarial fevers, cochineal, the dye-woods of Brazil, and the mahogany of the West Indies. America also sent to

Europe large supplies of cane sugar, molasses, fish, whale oil, and furs. These new American products became common articles of consumption and so raised the standard of living in European countries.

Political effects of the discoveries. The Atlantic-facing countries, first Portugal and Spain, then Holland, France, and England, became the great powers of Europe. Their trade rivalries and contests for colonial possessions have been potent causes of European wars for the last four hundred years. The Atlantic Ocean formed henceforth, not only the commercial, but also the political, center of the world. 

Effects of the discoveries upon religion. The New World also played an important part in an event which was about

The Church Drifts toward Disunity 

403 to take place in Europe, namely, the Protestant Reformation. The vacant spaces of America offered plenty of room for all who would worship God in their own way. The region now known as the United States furnished in the seventeenth century an asylum from religious persecution, as is shown by the settlement of the Puritans in New England, the Roman Catholics in Maryland, and the Quakers in Pennsylvania. The New World became a refuge for the persecuted of the Old. 

106. THE CHURCH DRIFTS TOWARD DISUNITY 

Religious upheavals. We have seen how, beginning late in the Middle Ages, the classical revival and geographical discoveries were remaking the civilization of Europe. Alongside these two great movements ushering in modern times must be placed the Reformation. The Reformation affected fundamentally the lives and beliefs of all those persons who brought European civilization to the newly discovered America. The story of the Reformation is thus part of the story of America today. In tracing this story we shall notice, first, the development of disagreements among the Christians of western Europe; second, the formation of the Protestant churches; and third, the Catholic Counter Reformation.

The Catholic Church in the thirteenth century. In the thirteenth century the popes were the greatest sovereigns in Europe. They ruled a large part of Italy, had much influence in the affairs of France, England, Spain, and other countries, and in Germany named and deposed emperors. From their capital at Rome they sent forth legates to every European court and issued laws binding on western Christendom. 

Church versus state. In feudal times, when kings were weak and nobles were strong, the activity of the Church in political affairs proved useful and even necessary. As the kings began to subdue the feudal lords and establish their own authority, however, they tried also to extend their control over the Church. They sought to restrict the privileges

of ecclesiastical courts, to impose taxes on the clergy, and to dictate the appointment of bishops and abbots. This policy naturally led to friction between popes and kings, between Church and state.

The "Babylonian Captivity." One of the most violent of these disputes between Church and state occurred between the pope and the king of France. Upon the death of the pope, the king of France secured the election of a Frenchman as his successor. This French pope moved the papal court away from Rome, to the town of Avignon, on the French frontier. The popes lived in Avignon from 1307-1377. This period of nearly seventy years is usually called the Babylonian Captivity of the Church. The long absence of the popes from Rome lessened their authority. Furthermore, the suspicion that they were the mere vassals of the French king seriously impaired the respect in which they had been held. The pope who was in office in 1377 moved the papal court back to Rome.

The Great Schism. The Babylonian Captivity was the result of a quarrel between the papacy and a king. Soon, however, arose a quarrel within the papacy itself. Shortly after the return of the papal court to Rome, an Italian was elected pope. He was unacceptable to some of the cardinals who belonged to the French faction. They declared his election void, and elected another pope to live at Avignon. 

Western Christendom could not decide which one to obey. 

The spectacle of two rival popes, each holding himself out as the true successor of St. Peter, continued for about forty years, from 1378 to 1417. This division, or schism, within the Church itself is known as the Great Schism. It injured the papacy more than anything else that had happened to it. When the schism was finally healed and the Roman 

Church once more had a recognized single head, it was not easy to revive the former undivided loyalty to the pope.

Increasing worldliness of the Church. A number of the popes took much interest in the Renaissance movement.

The Church Drifts toward Disunity 

405 They kept up splendid courts, collected manuscripts, paintings, and statues, and erected magnificent palaces and churches in Rome. Some European peoples, especially in 

Germany, looked askance at such luxury and begrudged the heavy taxes which were necessary to support it. The worldliness of some of the popes was often reflected in the lives of the lesser clergy. Throughout the thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth centuries the Church received much criticism for its worldliness: some persons said that the clergy should imitate the poverty of the apostles; still others complained bitterly over the sums which they had to pay for the upkeep of the Church and its officers.

Growth of heresy. The Babylonian Captivity, the Great 

Schism, and the increasing worldliness of the Church brought many criticisms upon it. Naturally, from time to time appeared leaders who demanded reforms in belief, worship, and conduct. These leaders attracted followers, who thus became less faithful to the Church. Those who demanded fundamental changes in Catholic belief and worship were called heretics, and their teachings were denounced as heresies.

Heretical movements. Some heretical movements spread over wide areas and involved great numbers of followers. (1) One of the important heretical movements was that of the Albigenses, so called from the town of Albi in southern France, where many of them lived. They set up a rival church, with its priests, bishops, and councils. In the thirteenth century the pope at Rome preached a crusade against them and thus started a series of bloody wars. The Albigensian sect did not entirely disappear for more than a century, and then only after numberless trials and executions for heresy. (2) The followers of Peter Waldo, who are called the 

Waldensians, condemned the luxury of the clergy and urged that Christians should live like the twelve apostles. The 

Waldensians regarded the Bible as a sufficient guide to religious life, and allowed every one to preach without dis-

tinction of age, rank, or sex. The Waldensian sect survived severe persecution and now forms a branch of the Protestant 

Church in Italy. (3) Beliefs similar to those of the Waldensians were held by John Wycliffe, master of an Oxford college and a popular preacher. He, too, appealed from the authority of the 

Church to the authority of the Bible; with the assistance 

JOHN WYCLIFFE

A small woodcut from a book published in 

1548. The oldest known picture of Wycliffe and possibly reproduced from a contemporary sketch of him. He is represented preaching or lecturing from a stone pulpit. of two friends, he produced the first English translation of the Scriptures. 

Wycliffe organized bands of "poor priests" to spread the teachings of the Bible through all England. They went out, staff in hand and clad in long, russet gowns, and preached to the common people in the English language wherever an audience could be found. Wycliffe's followers, known as the Lollards, attacked many beliefs and practices of the Church, and also demanded social reforms. 

For instance, they declared that all wars were sinful and were but plundering and murdering the poor to win glory for kings. Though the Lollards were severely persecuted, they sowed the seeds for the Reformation in England and Scotland. (4) The doctrines of Wycliffe reached Bohemia, where they attracted the attention of John Huss, a distinguished scholar in the University of Prague. Huss attacked the clergy in sermons and pamphlets and opposed the supremacy of the pope. He was excommunicated and burnt as a

Formation of Protestant Churches 407 heretic, but his followers, known as the Hussites, kept alive his teachings until the time of Martin Luther. 

The Catholic Church in the fifteenth century. From the foregoing paragraphs, it is plain that in the thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth centuries there were serious disagreements among the Christians of western Europe. Kings quarreled with popes over the question of sovereignty that is, over the question of whether the king or the pope was the higher ruler. Common people, led often by their king, quarreled with the Church over the collection of Church dues. Many of the clergy quarreled with the papacy over religious belief and worship. In short, by the sixteenth century, the Church had drifted far toward disunity. Heretics were numerous and bold. Western Europe was entering that period of religious upheaval which is known as the Reformation. 

107. FORMATION OF PROTESTANT CHURCHES 

Martin Luther, 1483-1546. The views that Wycliffe and 

Huss had popularized were expressed in Germany during the sixteenth century by the real founder of the Reformation, Martin Luther. Luther was the son of a German peasant whose industry and thrift enabled him to give his son Martin a good education in scholastic philosophy at the University of Erfurt. Luther took the degrees of bachelor and master of arts and then began to study law. Soon, however, his interest in religion caused him to enter a monastery. A few years later he visited Rome, only to be shocked by the general laxity of life in the capital of the papacy. He returned to 

Germany and became a professor of theology in the University of Wittenberg, newly founded by Frederick the Wise, elector of Saxony. Luther's sermons and lectures attracted large audiences; students began to flock to Wittenberg; and the elector grew proud of the rising young teacher who was making his university famous.

Tetzel and indulgences. Before long there came into the

neighborhood of Wittenberg a Dominican friar named Tetzel, who granted indulgences in return for money to be used for the completion of St. Peter's church in Rome. What were these indulgences? An indulgence was a letter of pardon relieving the sinner from some or all of the penances (punishments) which the Church would otherwise impose upon him; the sinner, of course, had to be truly sorry (penitent) for his sin, and he had to do some pious act like going on a pilgrimage, joining a crusade, or contributing money for the erection of a church or convent. Thus the sinner who was penitent and had, for penance, done one of these "good works" might receive a letter of pardon— that is, an indulgence.

Why indulgences aroused protest. Many German princes opposed this method of raising funds for the Church because it took so much money out of their dominions. Huss and 

Erasmus had condemned indulgences on religious grounds. 

Luther attacked the indulgences because they were so likely to be misunderstood and misused. He pointed out that common people could not understand the Latin in which the letters of pardon were written, and that ignorant persons often thought that these indulgences wiped away the penalties of sin, even without true repentance.

Luther posts his theses, 1517. Luther set forth these and other criticisms in ninety-five short statements, or, as they were called, theses. He posted his theses on the door of the church at Wittenberg, where all might see them, and offered to debate them with any opponent. So far, Luther had done nothing that was extremely unusual for a medieval scholar; the theses were even composed in Latin, the language of scholars, and not in German, the language of the common people.

Luther burns a papal bull. Almost immediately, however, Luther's theses were translated into German, printed, and spread broadcast over Germany. Their effect was so great that before long the granting of indulgences in that country almost ceased. Luther, the scholarly critic of indulgences,

Formation of Protestant Churches 409 found himself in the position of publicly arguing for beliefs very much like those of Wycliffe and Huss; further, he wrote a bold pamphlet in which he appealed to the "Christian nobility of the German nation" to rally together against Rome. The pope had at first paid little attention to the controversy about indulgences, declaring it "a mere squabble of monks," but he now issued a decree, or bull, against Luther, ordering him to recant or be excommunicated. 

Luther's answer was dramatic and stirred all Germany. 

WORMS CATHEDRAL 

The old German city of Worms possesses in the Cathedral of SS. Peter and Paul one of the finest Romanesque structures in Europe. The exterior, with its four round towers, two large domes, and a choir at each end, is particularly imposing. The cathedral was mainly built in the twelfth century. 

In the presence of a throng of students and townsfolk, in the market square of Wittenberg, he burnt the papal bull. 

Luther is tried as a heretic. The pope then urged the 

Holy Roman Emperor, Charles V, to declare Luther under "the ban of the empire" - that is, to deny him the protection of the laws. Charles was willing to comply, but the 

German princes insisted that Luther must not be condemned

unheard. Accordingly, Luther was summoned before a great assembly (Diet) of princes and ecclesiastical dignitaries at Worms. Here he refused to retract anything he had written, unless his statements could be shown to contradict the Bible. "It is neither right nor safe to act against conscience," said

Luther. The Diet of Worms accordingly proclaimed Luther a heretic and an outlaw, and the pope excommunicated him. 

Luther leads the German Reformation. The support of powerful friends enabled Luther to defy both pope and emperor as long as he lived. He made a German translation of the Bible, which the printing press soon multiplied in thousands of copies, composed many fine hymns and a catechism, flooded the country with pamphlets against the Roman Church, and wrote innumerable letters to his followers. 

Luther became in this way the leader of the German Reformation. 

The Reformed Religion. The Reformation in Germany made a wide appeal. To patriotic Germans it seemed a revolt against a foreign power the Italian papacy. To men of pious mind it offered the attractions of a simple faith based directly on the Bible. Worldly-minded princes saw in it an opportunity to despoil the Church of lands and revenues. 

Luther's teachings, accordingly, found acceptance among a variety of people for a variety of reasons. Priests married, monks left their monasteries, and the Reformed Religion took the place of Roman Catholicism in most parts of northern and central Germany. South Germany, however, has remained Roman Catholic to the present time. 

Peace of Augsburg, 1555. The Reformed Religion had not gained its place in Germany without a struggle. Civil war raged for a number of years, until both sides agreed to the Peace of Augsburg. It was a compromise. The ruler of each state Germany then contained over three hundred states—was to decide whether his subjects should be Lutherans or Catholics. The peace thus failed to establish religious toleration, since all Germans had to believe as their prince believed. However, it recognized Lutheranism as a

Formation of Protestant Churches 

411 legal religion and ended the attempts to crush the German Reformation.

Lutheranism in Scandinavia. 

spread into Scandinavian lands. The rulers of Denmark, Norway, and Sweden closed the monasteries and compelled the Roman Catholic bishops to surrender ecclesiastical property to the crown. Lutheranism became henceforth the official religion of these three countries. 

The Reformation in Switzerland. Luther's contemporary, Huldreich Zwingli, began the Reformation in Switzerland. 

From his pulpit in the cathedral of Zurich,

Zwingli proclaimed that the Scriptures are the sole guide of faith and denied the supremacy of the pope. 

Many of the Swiss cantons accepted his teaching and broke away from the Roman Church.

John Calvin in Switzerland. The Protestants in 

Switzerland soon found another leader in John Calvin (1509-1564), a Frenchman who settled in Geneva.

He wrote out in an orderly, logical manner the main

Roman Catholicism were many. He did away with the episcopate, or rule of bishops, and kept only two sacraments, baptism and the Eucharist. He provided for a very simple form of worship, consisting of Bible reading, a sermon, extemporaneous prayers, and hymns sung by the congregation. 

These features of Calvinism are found today in the Presbyterian and Congregational churches. During his long residence in Geneva, Calvin governed the people with a rod of

iron. There were no more festivals, no more theaters, no more dancing, music, and masquerades. All the citizens had to attend two sermons on Sunday and to yield at least a lipassent to the reformer's doctrines. Nevertheless, Geneva prospered under Calvin's rule and became a Christian commonwealth, sober and industrious. That city still reveres
