Europe in America 469 

120. EUROPE IN AMERICA 

A familiar story. The story of European settlements in 

America is of enormous importance. The coming of the 

Europeans meant the transplanting of their highly developed civilization to a relatively unpopulated but fertile continent. 

The early explorations and settlements by the Portuguese, Spanish, French, English, Swedish, and Dutch constitute a familiar story. The details of this story are studied in the various grades of American schools. Here, therefore, we shall not dwell on the details. Instead, we shall try to envision the broad outlines. We shall emphasize the significance of the American story as a part of the story of world civilization. 

Spain and Portugal in America. Immediately after Columbus's return to Spain the Spaniards sent out colonists. 

Within a quarter of a century they had established settlements in the West Indies, on the northern coast of South America, on the Isthmus of Panama, in Central America, and in Mexico; a few years later they occupied Peru. By 

1574 Spain had settled more than two hundred towns and sent over about 175,000 people. Spanish emigration decreased during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, but on account of the fusion between Spaniards and Indians, Spanish-speaking people continued to increase in numbers. 

By 1750 they occupied (1) what are now the southeastern and southwestern parts of the United States, (2) Mexico, (3) Central America, and (4) the northern, western, and southern parts of South America. The Portuguese occupied the eastern coast of South America and laid the foundations of Brazil. Both Spain and Portugal have deeply affected the languages, manners, and customs of the New World (p. 400). 

France in America. The French did not found any permanent settlements in America for more than a century after Columbus's voyage. Finally in 1608 they established their first successful colony at Quebec on the lower St. 

Lawrence River. The French soon moved farther up the

Expansion of Europe 

St. Lawrence and made other settlements. They explored the Great Lakes (out of which the St. Lawrence flows), opened the fur trade, and undertook to convert the Indians to Christianity. In 1718 they settled New Orleans at the opposite end of the continent; from there they moved up the Mississippi River. The French thus occupied two of the great river valleys of North America - the St. Lawrence and the Mississippi; and, as a glance at the map (p. 477) will show, it is easy to pass, by portages, from numerous tributaries of the Mississippi to the Great Lakes, and thence down the St. Lawrence to the sea. The connection between these two river systems explains to some extent why the French were able to scatter over such extensive areas in America. By 

1750 there were about 80,000 Frenchmen in the vast area from the mouth of the St. Lawrence to the mouth of the 

Mississippi. The French have left their impress upon a great part of Canada, and in the United States such cities as St. Louis and New Orleans still reflect the civilization of their French founders.

England in America. The English, like the French, were slow to take advantage of the opportunities of the New World. Their first settlement was made at Jamestown in 

1607. During the seventeenth century the English founded many colonies along the Atlantic coast east of the Allegheny Mountains. Settlers continued to come, and by 1750 there were more than two million people in the English colonies. 

In addition to the English in these colonies, there were many Irish, Scotch, and Germans, and some Dutch, Swedes, and French Huguenots. The abiding influence of England upon America is apparent throughout the United States and Canada.

Expansion and conflict in America. The foregoing paragraphs indicate the principal areas occupied by the various European countries. But no country was content with its holdings. Each sought to extend its control by exploring new lands and by seizing the territories claimed by its rivals. 

In this manner arose numerous conflicts among Spain, Eng-

Europe in America 471 land, and France. Since the regions occupied by the French and English bordered each other over a wide front, these two peoples naturally came into conflict with each other repeatedly. 

First period of conflict. The struggle between France and England began, in both the Old World and the New, in 1689, when the Glorious Revolution drove out James II and placed William of Orange on the English throne as 

William III (p. 437). The Dutch and English, who had previously been enemies, now became friends and united in resistance to Louis XIV. England joined a league of the states of Europe against France. The struggle extended beyond Europe, for each of the rivals tried to destroy the commerce and annex the colonies of the other. (See the table on page 472 for the names and dates of the wars in this first period.) 

Peace of Utrecht, 1713. The first period of conflict closed in 1713 with the Peace of Utrecht. England secured Newfoundland, Acadia (rechristened Nova Scotia), and the extensive region drained by the rivers flowing into Hudson Bay. 

France, however, kept the best part of her American territories and retained control of the St. Lawrence and the 

Mississippi. The possession of these two waterways gave her a strong strategic position in the interior of the continent. 

Second period of conflict. The second period of struggle between England and France began in 1740. The two great wars which came in this period were fought both in Europe and in America. The War of the Austrian Succession (p. 451), known in American history as King George's War, did not settle the quarrels over boundaries in America. The French and Indian War, beginning in 1754, was soon merged with the European conflict known as the Seven Years' War. This war definitely settled the issue between England and France in America. France had no resources to cope with those of England in America, and the English command of the sea proved decisive. One French post after another was captured. Wolfe defeated the gallant Montcalm under the

Expansion of Europe walls of Quebec and the fall of that stronghold quickly followed. What remained of the French army at Montreal also surrendered. The British flag was now raised over 

Canada, where it has flown ever since.

Peace of Paris, 1763. The second period of conflict closed in 1763, with the Peace of Paris. France ceded to England all her North American possessions east of the Mississippi, except two small islands kept for fishing purposes off the coast of Newfoundland. Spain, which had also been involved

The Birth of a Nation 

473 in the war, gave up Florida to England, receiving as compensation the French territories west of the Mississippi. New

France was now only a memory. But modern Canada has two millions of Frenchmen, who still hold aloof from the British in language and religion, while Louisiana, though shrunk to the dimensions of an American state, still retains in its laws and in many customs of its people the French tradition. 

121. THE BIRTH OF A NATION 

How the English colonies drifted away from the mother country. English colonists in the New World had long been drawing apart from Englishmen in the Old World. 

The political training received by the colonists in their local meetings and provincial assemblies fitted them for selfgovernment, while the hard conditions of life in America fostered their energy, self-reliance, and impatience of restraint. The important part which they played in the conquest of Canada gave them confidence in their military abilities and showed them the value of coöperation; indeed, the Peace of Paris marked a turning point in the history of the English colonies. Relieved of pressure from without, and free to expand toward the west and south, they now had less need of the mother country. 

Mercantilism applied to the English colonies. We have already seen how European countries regarded colonies. 

Most European statesmen, including those of England, believed in mercantilism (p. 462). According to this theory, colonies were looked upon as estates to be operated for the benefit of the country owning them. They were areas from which to draw raw materials and in which to sell the manufactured products of the home country. Therefore, (1) the 

British government discouraged the manufacture in the colonies of goods that could be made in England, and (2) it tried to prevent the colonies from carrying on trade with any country except England. On the other hand, this legislation was not especially repressive for several reasons. (1) The

Expansion of Europe colonists constantly evaded the trade regulations. (2) Great 

Britain formed a natural market for most colonial products. (3) The home government gave bounties, or sums of money, to encourage the production of food and raw materials needed in Great Britain. (4) Ships built in the colonies enjoyed the same exclusive privileges in the carrying trade as Britishbuilt ships; consequently colonial shipping flourished. In considering the treatment that the colonies received from England, it must also be remembered that England spent large sums in defending the colonies.

England's new policy. After the close of the French and 

Indian War (1763), Parliament took steps to enforce the laws regulating colonial commerce and to raise revenue to help pay the costs of that war. To carry out this policy, Parliament passed several new laws, such as the Stamp Act (1765) and the Townshend Acts (1767). At the same time

George III and his ministers sent troops to America and asked the colonies to help support them upon the grounds that the soldiers would protect the colonists against the 

French and the Indians.

English and colonial views of the new policy. Many colonists feared that the British troops were being sent to suppress them rather than protect them. As to the revenue laws, they argued that taxes could be rightfully voted only by their own representative assemblies. It was a natural attitude for them to take, since Parliament, sitting three thousand miles away, had little insight into American affairs. 

Some British statesmen, such as Edmund Burke and William Pitt, sided with the colonists. In general, however, the 

British view was that Parliament really represented all Englishmen and hence might tax them wherever they lived. 

Declaration of Independence. The colonists were so opposed to the principle of parliamentary taxation that they refused to buy tea from British merchants and in Boston even boarded a tea ship and threw the cargo into the water. 

Parliament replied to the "Boston Tea Party" by closing the harbor of that city to commerce and by depriving Mas-

Printer, philosopher, scientist, statesman, and citizen of the world, Franklin was known throughout the capitals of Europe. In France he was often called le grand Franklin.

The Birth of a Nation 475 sachusetts of self-government. These measures, instead of bringing the stubborn colony to terms, only aroused the fears of her neighbors and led to the meeting of delegates from all the colonies, except Georgia, in the First Continental

Congress. It recommended a policy of non-intercourse with 

Great Britain until the colonists had recovered their "just rights and liberties." The Second Congress, which met after blood had been shed at Lexington and Concord, prepared for war and appointed George Washington to command the colonial forces. On July 4, 1776, after the failure of all plans for conciliation with the mother country, it declared that "these united colonies are, and of right ought to be, free and independent states."

The "Tories." No colony at first contained a large majority in favor of separation, and even after the Declaration of Independence numerous loyalists, or "Tories," continued to favor the British cause. After the conclusion of peace the "Tories" emigrated in great numbers to Canada, where they were the first English settlers. They prospered in their new home, and their descendants, who form a considerable part of the Canadian population, are today among the most devoted members of the British Empire. 

The French alliance, 1778. Even had the colonists been unanimous in resistance to Great Britain, they stood little chance of winning against a wealthy country with a population nearly three times their own, trained armies aided by German mercenaries, and a powerful navy. When, however, the resources of France were thrown into the scale, the issue became less doubtful. France, still smarting from the losses suffered in the Seven Years' War, desired to recover as much as possible of her colonial dominions and secretly aided the Americans with money and supplies for some time before the victory at Saratoga led her to enter into a formal, open alliance with them.

Close of the Revolutionary War. The war now merged into a European conflict, in which France was joined by Spain and Holland. Great Britain needed all her reserve

Expansion of Europe power to prevent rebellion in Ireland, defend Gibraltar, and keep her possessions in the West Indies and India. The struggle in America practically closed in 1781, when Cornwallis, blockaded at Yorktown by a French fleet and closely invested by the combined French and American armies, surrendered the largest British force still in the colonies. 

Nearly two years passed, however, before the contestants made peace.

Treaties of Paris and Versailles, 1783. The Treaty of 

Paris between Great Britain and the United States recognized the independence of the former Thirteen Colonies and fixed their boundaries at Canada and the Great Lakes, the 

Atlantic Ocean, Florida, and the Mississippi River. The

Treaty of Versailles between Great Britain, France, and Spain restored to France a few colonial possessions and gave to Spain the Florida territory. Holland, which concluded a separate peace with Great Britain, was obliged to cede to that country some stations in India and to throw open to British merchants the valuable trade of the East Indies. 

Articles of Confederation. The Continental Congress, which had framed the Declaration of Independence in 1776, continued to govern the United States until the adoption of the Articles of Confederation in 1781. The Articles established a mere league of states. The authority of Congress was practically limited to war, peace, and foreign affairs. 

It could not levy taxes, could not regulate interstate commerce, and had no power to enforce obedience on either a state or an individual. Every attempt to amend the Articles by legislative action failed, and the weak and clumsy government which they had set up threatened to collapse. 

Formation of the Constitution. Such were the distressing circumstances under which the Constitutional Convention met at Philadelphia in 1787. To this body the states sent fifty-five delegates, including Washington, who presided, Franklin, James Madison, and Alexander Hamilton. Instead of merely amending the Articles, they prepared an entirely new constitution, which was ratified within a year

by eleven states. Washington, the first President under the new constitution, was inaugurated in 1789. 

George Washington. The founding of the new govern ment gave George Washington an opportunity to write his name on the roll of great men in world history. In 1932 the people of the United States celebrated with pomp and circumstance, and with every evidence of deep affection, the

Expansion of Europe two hundredth anniversary of the birth of Washington. 

History, it has been well said, hardly presents a stronger case of an indispensable man. How much his military talent, practical wisdom, fortitude under the sternest trials, and ability to hold the confidence of both army and people contributed to the final victory in the Revolution is known to all. 

His place is secure in the select company of those who have been privileged to found new states. After the Revolution his correspondence with the leading men of the country helped greatly to nourish sentiments favorable to "a more perfect union"; he presided over the Federal Convention; he did perhaps more than any one else to secure the ratification of the Constitution; and as President during eight critical years he gave to the new republic authority and respect at home and prestige abroad. To Washington, with far more right than even to the old Roman heroes, are applied the proud words - "Father of his Country."

America teaching by example. The American War of 

Independence reacted almost at once on Europe. The Declaration of Independence, setting forth the "unalienable rights of man" as against feudal privilege and oppression, provided eager leaders in France with a formula of liberty which they were not slow in applying to their own country. 

 of 1789 was the child of the American Revolution. Early in the nineteenth century still another revolutionary movement stripped Spain and Portugal of all their continental possessions in the New World. America was, indeed, teaching by example. 

122. PROGRESS OF GEOGRAPHICAL DISCOVERY 

Early exploration of the Pacific. Great Britain soon found at least partial compensation for the loss of the Thirteen Colonies in the occupation of Australia and the islands of the Pacific. That vast ocean, covering more than one-third of the globe, remained little known to Europeans until the latter part of the eighteenth century. Soon after Magellan's

Progress of Geographical Discovery 

479 voyage the Spaniards established a regular commercial route between Mexico and the Philippines and gradually discovered some of the archipelagoes which stud the intervening seas. Sir Francis Drake's circumnavigation of the world (1577-1580) first drew the attention of Englishmen to the Pacific Ocean, but a long time passed before they began its systematic exploration. 

Tasman's voyages, 1642-1643, 1644. In 1642 the Dutch

East India Company sent Abel Tasman to investigate the real extent of the "Great South Land," which is now known bar 66

Captain Cook's ship in his last voyage. When this drawing was made, the ship was being used as a coaling-vessel at Newcastle; hence the addition of steam funnels. as Australia. Tasman's two voyages-among the most notable on record - led to the discovery of Van Diemen's Land (Tasmania) and New Zealand, and proved conclusively that Australia had no connection with the supposed Antarctic continent. (For Tasman's route see the map on page 

694.) The Dutch, however, manifested little interest in the regions which they had found, and more than one hundred years passed before Tasman's work was continued by Captain James Cook.

Cook's voyages in the Pacific, 1768-1779. This famous navigator, the son of a farm laborer, entered the British navy at an early age and by his unaided efforts rose to high. command. Cook's first voyage in the Pacific resulted in

Expansion of Europe the exploration of the coast of New Zealand and the eastern shore of Australia. The second voyage finally settled the question as to the existence of a southern continent, for Cook sailed three times across the Pacific Ocean without finding it. At the instance of George III, Cook undertook a third voyage to locate, if possible, an opening on the coast of Alaska which would lead into Hudson Bay. He followed the American coast through Bering Strait until an unbroken ice field barred further progress. On the return from the 

Arctic region Cook visited the Hawaiian Islands, where he was murdered by the natives.

Bering's Voyages, 1728-1729, 1741. Captain Cook on his third voyage was the first British navigator to sight Alaska.

Here, however, he had been preceded by the Russians, who reached the Pacific by way of Siberia and the Arctic Ocean. 

It still remained uncertain whether or not Siberia was joined to the northern part of the New World. Peter the Great, who showed a keen interest in geographical discovery, commissioned Vitus Bering, a Dane in the Russian service, to solve the problem. Bering explored the strait and sea named after him and made clear the relation between North America and Asia.

Scientific exploration. The eighteenth century thus added greatly to man's knowledge of the world. Cook's voyages, in particular, left the main outlines of the southern part of the globe substantially as they are known today. Systematic exploration for scientific purposes began to take the place of voyages by private adventurers for the sake of warfare or plunder. Geographical discovery must be included, therefore, among the influences which made the eighteenth century so conspicuously an age of enlightenment.

Unit VII REVOLUTION IN HUMAN SOCIETY 

How political, social, and industrial revolutions made the great difference between civilizations of the past and modern civilization 

(CHAPTERS XV-XVI)

PRESENTATION 

The preceding unit carried the story of our civilization into modern times. In this unit we shall see how revolutions political, social, and industrial - remade some of the principles of society. 

Much that was medieval survived into the eighteenth century. 

These survivals seemed especially objectionable in France, where a spirit of enlightenment prevailed. These ideas made the French people aware of the inequalities existing among themselves. They began a revolution by demanding reforms and ended by abolishing the monarchy and executing their king. Out of the chaotic times that followed emerged Napoleon, who seized control and led the French on a crusade of conquest in which they carried to other countries many of the reforms which the Revolution had accomplished in France. In the end the combined powers of Europe overthrew 

Napoleon and banished him. The diplomats gathered at Vienna and tried to restore the Old Régime. They did not succeed, for the peoples of many lands had become imbued with the ideas of liberty, equality, and fraternity. Revolutions continued to break out in Europe and in America, and democracy began to replace autocracy. (Chapter XV) 

While political revolutions were in progress, another revolution of a very different kind was also going on. From about 1776 onward many inventions were developed. The series of changes that resulted in manufacturing, transportation, communication, and economic organization were nothing less than revolutionary. These changes have transformed practically every aspect of man's material surroundings and have deeply affected many of his ideas. This whole movement is therefore known as the Industrial Revolution. (Chapter XVI)

METTERNICH 123. THE FRENCH REVOLUTION How the French Revolution came about. The Puritan 

Revolution and the Glorious Revolution of the seventeenth century and the American Revolution of the eighteenth century had struck mortal blows at absolutism and the divine right of kings. Still more influential in bringing autocracy to an inglorious end was the French Revolution. 

It was a series of events in France, occurring between 1789 and 1795, by which divine-right monarchy gave way to a republic, and class distinctions and privileges gave way to social equality. This revolution started in France, not because the misery of the people had become more unbearable there than in other parts of the Continent, but because 

France was then the most advanced of Continental countries.

French artisans and peasants were free enough and intelligent enough to be critical of their government. Next to Great 

Britain, France contained the most numerous, prosperous, 485

and influential bourgeoisie (middle class). Members of this class furnished the Revolution with its principal leaders. 

Even the nobility and clergy included many men who realized the abuses of the Old Régime and wished to abolish them. 

In short, the revolutionary impulse stirred all ranks of 

French society. 

Louis XV-king, 1715-1774. To understand the outbreak of the French Revolution it is necessary to go back to the long reign of Louis XV. He succeeded the Grand Monarch, Louis XIV. Under Louis XV the government fell more and more into the hands of courtiers and adventurers, whose main concern was to line their own pockets at the expense of the public treasury. The treasury every year faced a deficit. It could only be met by resort to fresh loans, involving still larger outlays for interest charges. So long as the government refused to take proper measures of economy and continued to exempt the clergy and nobility from their share of taxation, little improvement of the financial situation was possible. France, the richest country in Europe, with a population greater than that of any rival state, was reduced to a second-rate power and became virtually bankrupt.

Tyranny of Louis XV. Louis XV, instead of trying to remedy the causes of dissatisfaction, did his best to stifle complaints. A rigid censorship muzzled the press. Postoffice officials opened letters passing through the mails and revealed their contents to the king. Books and pamphlets obnoxious to the government were burned by the common hangman, and their authors were imprisoned. No man's personal liberty was safe, for the police, if provided with a sealed letter (lettre de cachet) signed by the king, could send any one to jail. Suspected persons sometimes remained prisoners for years without trial. Such measures of oppression only increased the opposition to the monarchy. 

Louis XVI-king, 1774-1792. Louis XV was succeeded by his grandson, who became Louis XVI. The new king was only twenty years old when he mounted the throne.

Virtuous, pious, and well-meaning, he was the sort of ruler who in quiet times might have won the esteem of his people. 

He was, however, weak, slow of thought, and slow of decision. It has been well said that Louis XVI "could love, forgive, suffer, and die," but that he did not know how to reign. At his side, presiding over the gay court of Versailles, stood Queen Marie Antoinette, daughter of Maria Theresa of Austria. Marie Antoinette had many enemies in France because of her foreign birth, because she constantly interfered in public affairs, and because of her lavish expenditures on herself and on her favorites. Her enemies called her Madame Deficit.

Turgot's plans for reform. The youthful king began his reign well by appointing Turgot to the most responsible position in the ministry. Turgot, a friend of Voltaire, was an economist and a successful administrator. He drew up a program of reforms providing for (1) freedom of the press, (2) a national system of education, (3) more political power for the bourgeoisie, (4) recall of the Huguenots from the exile into which they had been driven in 1685 when Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes (p. 412), and (5) economic reforms.

Turgot's plans for economic reform. Turgot laid out an excellent program of reforms which would correct the chief economic wrongs of the time. (1) Pensions to useless courtiers were to be cut off. (2) The taxes bearing most heavily on the Third Estate were to be replaced by a general tax on all landowners. (3) Work without pay on public highways and bridges was to be discontinued. (4) The old guilds, which hampered industry, were to be abolished. (5) The vexatious tolls and duties on the passage of grain from one province to another were to be swept away. Could such reforms have been carried out, they might have given France a bloodless and orderly revolution. They were not carried out. The privileged classes would not surrender their privileges, nor favorites their pensions, nor monopolists their unjust gains, without a struggle.

Financial chaos. After two years of office, Turgot was dismissed, and thus was removed the one man who could have saved absolutism in France. The finances of the government went from bad to worse. Turgot's successors relied mainly on fresh loans to cover the deficits of the treasury. From the standpoint of French interest, Louis XVI committed a fatal error in intervening in the Revolutionary War (p. 475).

America was freed; Great Britain was humbled; but the war forced up the public debt of France by leaps and bounds. 

When at last it became impossible to borrow more money, the king yielded reluctantly to the popular demand for the meeting of the Estates-General. Absolutism had failed. 

The Estates-General. The Estates-General was the old feudal assembly of France. It consisted of representatives of the three classes, or estates—namely, the clergy, the nobles, and the unprivileged class (peasants, artisans, and bourgeoisie). 

On the eve of the French Revolution the Estates-General had not met for one hundred and seventy-five years. Awakened from their long slumber, the representatives of the clergy, the nobles, and the unprivileged Third Estate appeared at

Versailles in 1789 to take counsel with the king. In all, there were over twelve hundred members. About half of these belonged to the two privileged orders - the First and Second Estates. It is important to note that of the delegates representing the Third Estate, a few were liberal nobles, about two-thirds belonged to the legal profession, and less than a dozen were from the lower classes. Indeed, the two leaders of the Third Estate were Count Mirabeau and the 

Abbé Sieyès, both members of the privileged classes. As a whole, therefore, the Estates-General represented the most prosperous and intelligent people of France.

cahiers were written by all kinds of people in all parts of France and breathed forth a spirit of resentment and of demand for reform. The problem before the Estates-General, then, was to reform political, social, and economic abuses. 

The immediate question was how to organize the Estates- General in order to undertake this problem of reform. 

Reorganizing the Estates-General. Formerly the three estates had sat separately and voted as units; that is, each estate had one vote. Thus the nobles and clergy, with their two votes, could easily outvote the Third Estate with its one vote. In 1789, however, the Third Estate insisted that the Estates-General represented, not feudal France or social groups, but a new united nation. They demanded, therefore, that every representative be allowed to vote as an individual. Since the Third Estate had been permitted to send twice as many delegates as either the clergy or the nobility, the proposed reorganization would enable representatives of the Third Estate to outvote representatives of the other two estates.

Establishment of the National Assembly. For several weeks the Estates-General debated the proposition of transforming itself into a single body representing the people of France rather than the three feudal orders. The debate reached a deadlock. Then, on the motion of the Abbé Sieyès, the Third Estate boldly declared itself to be the National Assembly, with the right to act for the nation as a whole. The king opposed this move and permitted troops to be posted before the doors of the hall which had been set apart for the Third Estate. When the commoners found entrance to their meeting place barred, they adjourned to a building near by which had been used as a tennis court. Here they took a solemn oath (called the Tennis Court Oath) never to separate, and to continue to meet until they had drawn up a constitution for France. This action brought to their side the representatives of the lower clergy (curés), who were inclined to the popular cause. The king then summoned the three estates before him and made known the royal will that they

should meet separately. The higher clergy and nobility at once withdrew to their own chambers, but the Third Estate did not stir. "We are assembled by the national will," declared Count Mirabeau; "force alone shall disperse us."

The king dared not use force; so he gave way and requested is or out

THE STORMING OF THE BASTILLE 

A picture by a contemporary artist. Lafayette sent the key of the Bastille to Washington at Mount Vernon, with these words: "It is a tribute which I owe as a son to my adopted father, as an aide-de-camp to my general, as a missionary of liberty to its patriarch." the rest of the clerical and noble representatives to unite with the Third Estate in the National Assembly. A fundamental alteration in the governmental structure had thus been brought about. 

Fall of the Bastille, July 14, 1789. Soon came ominous news: Louis XVI had changed his mind about the National

Assembly and determined to dissolve it. A large number of troops were massed near Paris, obviously for the purpose of intimidating the representatives of the people. It was then that the Parisians made the cause of the National Assembly their own. The population of Paris contained many poor and unemployed artisans, and their ranks were swelled at this time by crowds of peasants whom the bad harvests and severe winter of the preceding year had driven into the city. 

Here were all the elements of a dangerous mob. Rioting broke out among the populace, and for several days anarchy prevailed. Reinforced by deserters from the army, the mob attacked and captured the Bastille, a fortress where political offenders had often been confined through lettres de cachet. 

The Bastille at this time held only seven prisoners, all there for just cause, but it stood for the tyranny of the Old Régime, and its fall created an immense sensation throughout France and in other countries. Louis XVI, on hearing the news, exclaimed, "Why, this is a revolt!" "No, Sire," replied a courtier, "this is a revolution."

The Revolution spreads. The example set by Paris was quickly copied in the country provinces. The peasants sacked and burned those local bastilles, the castles, taking particular pains to destroy the legal documents by which the nobles exercised their feudal rights over the people. Royal officials quitted their posts, courts of justice ceased to act, public works stopped, and people ceased to pay their taxes. 

From end to end of France, the Old Régime broke down amid universal confusion.

The end of feudalism. The revolution in the provinces led directly to one of the most striking scenes of French history. 

On the night of August 4-5 (1789), while the National Assembly had under consideration measures for stilling the unrest in France, one of the nobles - a relative of Lafayette urged that it remove the feudal burdens still resting on the peasantry. Then, amid hysterical enthusiasm, noble after noble and cleric after cleric arose in his place to propose equality of taxation, the repeal of the game laws, the freeing

of such serfs as were still to be found in France, the abolition of tithes, tolls, and pensions, and the extinction of all other long-established privileges. A decree "abolishing the feudal system" was passed by the National Assembly within the next few days and was signed by the king. The reforms which Turgot labored in vain to secure thus became accom-

THE DESTRUCTION OF FEUDALISM 

A contemporary cartoon representing the French people hammering to pieces with their flails all the emblems of the feudal system, including the knight's armor and sword and the bishop's crosier and miter. plished facts. It is well to remember, however, that the Old 

Régime had already fallen in France; the decree of the National Assembly did little more than outlaw it. 

The Revolution reaches the king's palace. Times were hard in Paris. Employment was scarce and food was dear. 

The discontent grew in proportion, especially among the women, who had to stand in line many hours at a time waiting to purchase a few loaves of bread at the bakeries. Rumor accused the court and the aristocrats of deliberately causing famine, nay, of plotting to overturn the Revolution by force. 

A newspaper published the statement quite unfoundedthat during a banquet of army officers at Versailles the new 

---

national flag (the tricolor) had been insulted and trampled under foot. Here was the spark which caused the explosion.

On October 5 a mob of hungry women, armed with every sort of weapon, even scythes and pitchforks, set out for Versailles to demand bread of the king. Early in the morning of 

October 6, some of the women made their way into the palace, killed the sentinels, and entered the apartments of Marie Antoinette, who escaped with difficulty. Only the arrival of Lafayette at the head of the National Guard prevented further rioting and bloodshed. The women were finally quieted by the king's promise to remove to Paris with his wife and children. That afternoon the royal family set out on their sorrowful journey to the capital, accompanied by a mob which yelled, "We are bringing the baker, the baker's wife, and the baker's little boy."

AN ASSIGNAT 

Paris. Its ultimate purpose was to write a constitution, but in the meantime it had to govern France. 

(1) The Assembly reformed local government. France had been built up by the gradual welding together of a number of provinces varying greatly in size, and each with its own privileges, customs, and laws. 

The old provinces were now replaced by eighty-three départements, approximately uniform in size and population. 

A map of France today still shows the departments. (2) The 

Assembly reorganized the Church in France. It appropriated church lands and sold them to the peasants, suppressed monasteries, fixed the salaries of the clergy, and took the appointment of them out of the hands of the king and

the pope. (3) The Assembly assumed control of national finances. It passed a decree authorizing the issue of notes to the value of four hundred million francs on the security of the former church lands. To emphasize this security the title of assignats was given to the notes. If the issue of assignats could have been restricted as Mirabeau desired, they might have been a safe means of raising revenue; but the continued needs of the treasury led to their multiplication in enormous quantities. Then followed the inevitable consequences of the circulation of bad money. Gold and silver disappeared from ordinary use, while prices rose so high that the time came when a basket of assignats was needed to buy a pair of boots. In the end the assignats became practically worthless.

The National Assembly writes a constitution. In 1791 the 

National Assembly completed the new constitution for France. It provided for a Legislative Assembly of a single chamber with wide authority over every branch of the government, severely curtailed the powers of the king, and allowed substantial taxpayers to vote. The details of this constitution are here of minor importance, for it was in effect only a short time. Prefixed to the constitution, however, was a Declaration of the Rights of Man which has had enormous influence upon political thought. 

Declaration of the Rights of Man. This memorable docu ment, which shows Rousseau's influence in nearly every line, formed a statement of the principles underlying the Revolution. All persons, so ran the Declaration, shall be equally eligible to all dignities, public positions, and occupations, according to their abilities. No person shall be arrested or imprisoned except according to law. Any one accused of wrongdoing shall be presumed innocent until he is adjudged guilty. 

Every citizen may freely speak, write, and print his opinions, including his religious views, subject only to responsibility for the abuse of this freedom. No one shall be deprived of his property, except for public purposes, and then only after compensation. These clauses of the Declaration reappeared

in the constitutions framed in France and other Continental countries during the nineteenth century. 

Why the new constitution failed. The first phase of the 

Revolution had ended. The government had been reorganized, and a new constitution had been written. Many believed that France would now enjoy the blessings of peace and prosperity. But the Revolution was not over. It soon entered a second phase, brought about by those opposing the new government. Among these were the king and queen, most of the nobles, most of the clergy, and the radicals. Let us see how each of these groups helped to bring the Revolution into a second and more violent phase. 

Flight of the king and queen. The constitution seemed to 

Louis XVI a violation of his rights as a monarch, and Marie Antoinette felt the degradation of her new position. They resolved to escape by flight. Disguising themselves, Marie 

Antoinette as a Russian lady and Louis as her valet, they drove away in the evening from the palace of the Tuileries, where they had been practically prisoners since the mob had brought them from Versailles to Paris. The royal fugitives made for the eastern frontier. Near the border they were recognized, and excited crowds stopped their flight. They were later brought back to Paris. This ill-starred adventure greatly weakened the loyalty of the French people for their king, while the queen, the "Austrian woman," became more detested than ever.

Emigrant nobles. The new government was also opposed by many of the nobles, especially those who emigrated during the Revolution. They gathered along the northeastern frontier of France and kept up an unceasing intrigue against the new government.

Non-juring clergy. We have already seen that the new government separated the French Church from papal control and confiscated church property. The pope therefore forbade the clergy to take the oath of loyalty to the new constitution. Until this time the parish priests had generally supported the popular cause. They now turned against it,

carrying with them their peasant flocks. The clergy who refused to swear loyalty to the constitution were called the non-juring (non-swearing) clergy.

Radicals. Some people opposed the new constitution because it was not radical enough; that is, they thought that it did not go to the root of the troubles in France. They opposed the monarchy, the property qualifications for voting, and the control of the government by the bourgeoisie. The radicals formed clubs to promote their opposition, and founded newspapers through which to attack government by the well-to-do middle class. The most famous of their clubs was the Jacobin, and the most able of their leaders were Marat, Danton, and Robespierre. The radical movement naturally centered in Paris, where there were large crowds of poverty-stricken workingmen without property or steady employment; but there were radical centers throughout 

France. The course of events was soon to give the radicals their opportunity.

The monarchs of Europe interfere. If absolutism and divine right were overthrown in France, they might before long be overthrown in Austria and Prussia. The rulers of 

Austria and Prussia announced their intention of suppressing the Revolution by force. In the face of this threat, the 

French government declared war. The French troops, poorly organized and disciplined, met severe reverses. 

French opinion was exasperated against the monarchy, and suspicion pointed to Louis and Marie Antoinette as the traitors who were secretly revealing the French plans to the enemies. Suspicion passed into hatred when the commander of the invading army issued a proclamation threatening Paris with destruction if harm befell the royal family.

The radicals take charge of the government. At this juncture the Jacobins under Danton organized a popular uprising at Paris (August, 1792). The mob stormed the 

Tuileries, massacred the Swiss Guard, and compelled the 

Legislative Assembly to suspend the king from office. A new assembly, to be called the National Convention, was

Danton, "by striking terror into the royalists." Suspected royalists were butchered without mercy. More than one thousand persons perished in the "September massacres.'

Shortly afterward the National Convention held its first meeting. By a unanimous vote it decreed the abolition of the monarchy and the establishment of the first French 

Republic. 

Enemies of the Republic. "Louis must die, that the country may live," urged Robespierre. So the National 

Convention, by a small majority vote, sent the king to the guillotine. Danton, railing against the enemies of France, could now declare, “We have thrown them as gage of battle the head of a king." One of the enemies of the Republic was gone. Meanwhile, the French forces not only repelled the armies of their foreign invaders, but took the offensive and overran the Austrian Netherlands. After the execution of Louis XVI, Austria, Prussia, Great Britain, Holland, Spain, Portugal, Sweden, Naples, and Sardinia formed a coalition to overthrow republican France. At the same time some peasants in southern France broke out in open revolt against the republic. A tremor of revolt also ran through the cities of Lyons, Marseilles, and Bordeaux, whose bourgeoisie resented the radicalism of the Parisian mobs. 

Thus within and without the new republic was threatened by enemies. 

Committee of Public Safety. This crisis showed the need of a strong central government. The National Convention. met this need by selecting twelve of its members to serve as a Committee of Public Safety, in which at first Danton, and later Robespierre, was the leading figure. The committee received almost unlimited authority over the life and property of every one in France. It proceeded to enforce a general levy, or conscription, which placed all males of military age at the service of the armies. This earliest of draft laws ran as follows: "The young men shall go to fight; married men

shall forge weapons and transport supplies; the women shall make tents and uniforms or serve in the hospitals; the children shall make lint; the old men shall be carried to the public squares to excite the courage of soldiers, hatred of kings, and enthusiasm for the unity of the republic." This new national army, drilled and disciplined, went forth to 

ROUGET DE L'ISLE SINGING THE MARSEILLAISE 

After the painting by Isidore Pils, Louvre, Paris battle singing a new patriotic song, the famous Marseillaise.

The coalition of the European powers broke down under their attack, and France enlarged her limits by annexing parts of the Netherlands and part of Germany lying west of the Rhine.

The Reign of Terror. In order to deal with domestic insurrection the Committee of Public Safety started a policy of terrorism. A law was passed which declared "suspect every noble, every officeholder before the Revolution, every 99

person who had had any dealings with an emigrant noble, and every person who could not produce a certificate of citizenship. This policy started a Reign of Terror which lasted for over a year. People from all classes of society were suspected, convicted, and guillotined. Among the victims of the Terror were Marie Antoinette and, strangely enough, Danton and Robespierre. The execution of Robespierre, who had been the relentless leader in this policy, ended the Reign of Terror. It has been estimated that seventeen thousand persons had been executed under form of law, while many more were massacred without the pretense of a trial.

The Constitution of 1795. It must not be forgotten that the National Convention had been summoned in 1792 to write a new constitution for the Republic. After the end of the Reign of Terror the Convention again took up its task and produced the Constitution of 1795. This new constitution provided for a legislature of two houses, and placed the executive power in the hands of a Directory of five members. While the Convention was still writing the constitution, an event occurred which brought to the front a young artillery officer who was destined to undo the work of this Convention and to remake the map of Europe. A mob attacked the Tuileries, where the Convention was in session. The rioters met a cannonade of grapeshot that sent them flying in confusion, leaving many of their numbers dead in the streets. The officer behind the guns was 

Napoleon Bonaparte. Before turning to his career, let us summarize some of the principles of revolutionary France. 

Revolutionary principles. The French Revolution differed sharply from previous revolutionary movements. The Puritan Revolution and the Glorious Revolution in England were carried out by men of the upper and middle classes, who wished to limit the royal power and establish the supremacy of Parliament. Even the American Revolution was guided by conservative statesmen who were at least as solicitous for the rights of property as for the rights of

man.  also began as mainly a middleclass movement. However, it soon reached the poorer classes and was thus given a different spirit. This new spirit found expression in the famous motto, "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity.”

Liberty, Equality, and Fraternity. "Liberty" meant that the government was to be conducted in accordance with the will of the people, and that they had certain “natural rights" - freedom of thought, speech, publication, worship, and ownership of property. "Equality" meant the abolition of class privileges. All citizens were to be equal in the eyes of the law. "Fraternity" meant a realization of the fact that all individuals belong to a human brotherhood. 

France teaching by example. The principles of 1789 were not confined to France. The revolutionary soldiers passed from land to land, bringing in their train the overthrow of the Old Régime. The effect was profound in the Netherlands, in western Germany, and in northern Italy, countries where the masses of the people had grievances and aspirations like those of the French. During the nineteenth century the revolutionary spirit spread to other European countries, resulting everywhere in a demand for the abolition of the established privileges of wealth, birth, and social position. 

Such has been the service of France as a liberator. 

124. THE ERA OF NAPOLEON 

Early life of Napoleon. Napoleon Bonaparte was born at 

Ajaccio, Corsica, in 1769, only a year after that island became a French possession. He was the second son of an Italian lawyer of noble birth but decayed fortunes. Napoleon attended a preparatory school in France and went through the course of study with credit; he did well in mathematics and devoted much of his leisure to reading history. After a brief military training in Paris, he entered an artillery regiment, thus realizing his boyish desire to be a soldier. He was poor, friendless, and without family influence.

Rise of Napoleon. Napoleon took a keen interest in the reform movement then stirring France. A devoted admirer of Rousseau's philosophy, he hated all privileges, all aristocracy, and for a time, at least, he became a Jacobin. The 

Revolution gave him his first opportunities. He was an artillery officer under the Republic and helped suppress an insurrection in southern France; two years later he defended the National Convention against the Parisian mob. 

Shortly afterward the 

Directory entrusted him with the command of the

French army in Italy. 

Napoleon in Italy.

France was still at war with Austria. It was decided to attack the Austrian possessions in Italy.

Napoleon's army, small and shabbily equipped, seemed a weak instrument for such an attack. 

But to the "Little Corporal," as his men nicknamed him, nothing was impossible. "Soldiers," he cried, "I desire to lead you into

NAPOLEON'S BIRTHPLACE, AJACCIO 

The house is well preserved, and the room in which Napoleon first saw the light of day is still shown to visitors. the most fertile plains in the world. Rich provinces and great cities will be in your power; you will find there honor, glory, and wealth. Soldiers of Italy, will you be wanting in courage and constancy?" Napoleon did not find them wanting in anything. Within less than two years, Napoleon and his army had overcome the Sardinians and the Austrians, and forced them to purchase peace by ceding territories to France.

Napoleon in Egypt. Napoleon next sailed for the East with a large expedition. In Egypt he defeated the Turks,

but in Syria he met reverses. Napoleon left his army to its fate and escaped to France. Here his highly colored reports of victory caused him to be greeted as the conqueror of the 

Near East. 

Napoleon's coup d'état. During Napoleon's absence, affairs had gone badly for France. Great Britain, Austria, and Russia had formed a second coalition against the Republic, put large armies in the field, and driven the French from Italy. Most Frenchmen now looked to Napoleon as the one man who could guarantee victory abroad and order at home. In 1799 Napoleon, with the Abbé Sieyes and other politicians, induced three of the Directors to resign; the other two were placed under military guard. The bayonets of Napoleon's soldiers forced the two legislative houses to dissolve. Thus the Directory of 1795 was overthrown. Such seizure of the government is called a coup d'état, that is, a sudden, decisive exercise of power in overthrowing a government. Napoleon was now master of France. "I found the crown of France lying on the ground," he once remarked, "and I picked it up with a sword."

Constitution of 1799. After the coup d'état, Napoleon proceeded to frame a constitution. It placed the executive power in the hands of three consuls, appointed for ten years. 

The First Consul was supreme, and this office was taken by 

Napoleon himself. To him belonged the command of the army and navy, the right of naming and dismissing all the chief officials, and the proposal of all new laws. Napoleon then submitted the constitution to the people for ratification. 

The popular vote, known as a plebiscite, showed an overwhelming majority in favor of the new government, which is appropriately called the Consulate.

Napoleon's reforms. Napoleon soon showed himself as great in statecraft as in war. (1) He put the local governments of all France directly under his control. He placed a prefect over every department and named the mayors of the towns and cities. This centralizing of authority enabled 

Napoleon to make his will felt promptly throughout France.

(2) The same desire for unity and precision led him to complete the codification of French law. Before the Revolution, nearly three hundred different local codes had existed in France. The National Convention began the work of replacing these various laws - Frankish, Roman, feudal, royal, and revolutionary by a single uniform code. Napoleon and the commission of legal experts over whose deliberations he presided finished the task after about four years' labor. 

The Code Napoléon contained many democratic principles, such as social equality, religious toleration, and jury trial, and carried these principles into the foreign lands conquered by the French. It prevails today, not only in France, but also (with some modification) in Belgium, Holland, Italy, and western Germany. (3) Napoleon felt the necessity of conciliating the Catholics who formed so large a part of the population of France. Accordingly, an agreement, called a 

Concordat, was drawn up, providing for the restoration of Catholicism as the official religion. Napoleon retained the right of nominating bishops and archbishops, and the pope gave up all claims to the confiscated church property. (4) Nor did Napoleon forget the emigrant nobles, or émigrés. 

A law was soon passed extending amnesty to those members of the aristocracy who had fled from France to escape the revolutionists. More than forty thousand families now returned to their native land. up Napoleon's other measures. A long list might be drawn of the other measures which exhibit Napoleon's qualities as a statesman. He founded the Bank of France, still one of the leading financial institutions of the world. He established a system of higher education to take the place of the colleges and universities which had been abolished by a decree of the National Convention. He planned and partly carried out a vast network of canals and inland waterways, thus improving the means of communication and trade throughout France. Like the Romans, he constructed a system of military highways radiating from the capital city to the remotest districts, in addition to two wonderful Alpine

roads connecting France with Italy. Like the Romans, also, he had a taste for building, and many of the monuments which today embellish Paris belong to the Napoleonic era. 

It also seemed to the people of the time that Napoleon had brought France peace at last. In 1800 he defeated the Austrians at Marengo in Italy, and two years later he signed with England the Peace of Amiens. For the first time since 

1793 France was at peace with the world. 

Napoleon becomes emperor, 1804. Napoleon enjoyed the support of all Frenchmen except the radicals, who would not admit that the Revolution had ended, and the royalists, who wished to restore the Bourbon monarchy. When the people were asked to vote on the question, “Shall Napoleon 

Bonaparte be consul for life?" the answering "ayes" numbered over three and a half millions, the "noes" only a few thousands. Another plebiscite decided, by an equally large majority, that the First Consul should become emperor. 

Before the high altar of Notre Dame Cathedral at Paris and in the presence of the pope, the modern Charlemagne placed a golden laurel wreath upon his own head and assumed the title of Napoleon I, Emperor of the French. 

Imperial glory and despotism. The new emperor set up again the etiquette and ceremonial of the Old Régime. Already he had established the Legion of Honor to reward those who most industriously served him. Now he created a nobility. His relatives and ministers became kings, princes, dukes, and counts; his ablest generals became marshals of 

France. "My titles," Napoleon declared, "are a sort of civic crown; one can win them through one's own efforts.”

France, intoxicated with the imperial glory, forgot that she had come under the rule of one man. What hostile criticism 

Frenchmen might have leveled against Napoleon was stifled by the secret police, who arrested and imprisoned hundreds of persons opposed to the emperor. Even the schools and churches were made pillars of the new government. 

Napoleon at war with Europe. The Peace of Amiens did not last long. Napoleon failed to make a commercial

England was victorious. Off Cape Trafalgar Lord Nelson won a great victory over the French fleet in 1805, and put an end to any plan which Napoleon might have had for invading England. On the other hand, Napoleon marched swiftly into Germany and defeated the Austrians at Ulm, and at Austerlitz he won a victory over the combined forces of Russia and Austria. At Jena he shattered the Prussian army and entered Berlin in triumph. At Friedland he met and defeated the Russians. Thus by 1807 Napoleon had again demonstrated his ability as a conqueror. The various nations, except England, sued for peace. 

Napoleon remakes the map of Europe. "Roll up the map of Europe; it will not be wanted these ten years,” exclaimed the English minister, William Pitt the Younger, when he heard the news of Napoleon's victory at Austerlitz. In connection with the wars which have just been described, Napoleon did, in fact, remake the map of Europe. (1) In the first place, he enlarged France by the annexation of neighboring areas. He added Holland, parts of Germany, the States of the Church (including Rome), and parts of Italy. Thus France proper was extended to the Baltic on the north and the Adriatic on the south. (2) Beyond this enlarged France was a belt of dependencies, governed by Napoleon or his appointees. These dependencies included northern Italy, the kingdom of Naples, Switzerland, and the Grand Duchy of Warsaw (formerly part of Poland). 

(3) Many other European states not actually dependent on Napoleon were allied with him. These included Spain, Denmark, Norway, Prussia, and Austria.

Confederation of the Rhine, 1806. We have just observed that Napoleon controlled a belt of dependencies across central Europe. He exercised this control through the Confederation of the Rhine. This organization included in its final

form all the German states except Austria and Prussia. As sovereign of the Confederation, under the title of Protector, Napoleon disposed of its military forces and had charge of its foreign relations. The formation of the Confederation of the Rhine gave the deathblow to the Holy Roman Empire. When Napoleon declared that he would recognize 50 French 10

THE NAPOLEONIC EMPIRE 

30 it no longer, the Hapsburg ruler laid down his ancient crown and contented himself with the title of Austrian Emperor.

Napoleon versus England. Napoleon had conquered the 

Continent. Its countries bowed to his will. But across the 

Channel was an implacable opponent whom Napoleon could not reach - England, mistress of the seas. She had defeated 

Napoleon's navy at Trafalgar and he could not reach her with his army. Napoleon therefore resorted to a kind of trade warfare. At Berlin and Milan (1806-1807) he issued. decrees excluding English goods from continental markets

and ordering French vessels to seize neutral ships which traded with England. This policy of destroying the trade between the Continent and England is called the Continental System. It was ineffective for two reasons. In the first place, England controlled the seas. Napoleon, therefore, could not blockade her ports nor prevent her ships from carrying on trade. In the second place, the continental countries, including France, suffered as much as England because they needed the manufactured goods from England. 

Napoleon clad his own armies in British cloth, and his soldiers marched in British shoes. The continental allies and dependencies of France murmured against the hardships that they suffered under Napoleon's Continental System, and England was not brought to her knees. 

Growing resentment against Napoleon. Napoleon hitherto had been fighting kings, not nations; and he had been uniformly victorious. A change in Napoleon's fortunes was soon to take place. His extortions from the conquered countries, his despotic government, and the hardships imposed by the Continental System all tended to produce hatred of the French emperor. One after another the nations of Europe rose against their common oppressor. France in arms made Napoleon; Europe in arms overthrew him. 

Napoleon at war again. From 1808 to 1814 Napoleon was engaged in almost continual warfare. He conquered 

Spain and Portugal, but the people rose in revolt and called in the English. Under the future Duke of Wellington, the 

English drove the French from Portugal, and Spain was eventually freed from French control. Austria, next to England the most persistent enemy of Napoleon, again (1809) declared war, only to be defeated at Wagram. In 1812 

Russia renounced the Continental System and Napoleon declared war. On his ill-fated invasion of Russia he captured 

Moscow, only to see it kindled in flames, perhaps by the Russians, and he left thousands of his devoted soldiers dead in the snows of a Russian winter. Returning to Germany,

Napoleon was confronted at Leipzig by the greatest allied

army which he had ever faced. This "Battle of the Nations" engaged every European people except the Turks. Napoleon was defeated and withdrew into France. But the Allies pursued their advantage and in 1814 they captured Paris. 

Napoleon was banished to the little island of Elba in the Mediterranean, and the allied diplomats gathered at Vienna in 1814 to try to undo the work of Napoleon. 

Waterloo. While the diplomats were busy at Vienna they were startled to hear that Napoleon had reappeared in France. They refused to allow his restoration to the throne and declared him an international outlaw. Napoleon quickly gathered another army and hurried to meet the allied forces which were gathering in 

Belgium. At Waterloo, near Brussels, the opposing forces met on Sunday, June 18, 1815. Caught between the English forces under Wellington and the Germans under Blücher, Napoleon's army was crushed. 

It became a mob of fugitives. Napoleon himself escaped with difficulty to Paris, where he again abdicated his claims to the throne of France. In order to avoid the 

Prussians, who had orders to take him dead or alive, Napoleon hastened to surrender himself to the English because, as he said, they were "the most generous' of his enemies. The fallen emperor was exiled to the lonely little island of St. Helena in the south Atlantic. 

There he lived the remaining six years of his life, without wife or child, but surrounded by a few intimate friends to whom he dictated his memoirs. 

NAPOLEON AT ST. 

HELENA 

After a drawing by an English officer who attended the emperor.

The Napoleonic legend. After Napoleon's death, at the early age of fifty-two, France forgot the sufferings he had caused her and remembered only the glory. Poets, painters, and singers created out of the "Little Corporal" a legendary figure. The world-despot appeared as a crusader for liberty

and a foe of tyrants; and in this guise he found his way irresistibly to the hearts of the French people. 

Napoleon's achievements. The Napoleonic legend was not without foundation. Despot though he was, Napoleon certainly enjoyed the support of the great majority of Frenchmen, and by his plebiscites he paid at least lip homage to the idea of popular sovereignty. Furthermore, under him citizens of all ranks might freely and equally compete for offices, honors, wealth, and other distinctions. Again, the tremendous campaigns which carried the Napoleonic armies through Europe united the French by a common bond of patriotic and national sentiments. Thus Napoleon's achievements to some extent embodied the threefold revolutionary ideal of liberty, equality, and fraternity. Napoleon was an agent of the Revolution in still other ways, not only in France but also in other lands. Wherever the Code 

Napoléon went, the forms of feudalism and serfdom, class privileges, and social inequalities vanished. The trained officials sent out by the emperor reformed finances, made roads, built bridges, improved harbors, encouraged trade, and fostered education. The inhabitants of the Netherlands, most of the German states, Switzerland, Italy, and Spain discovered, for the first time, what it meant to have an efficient government. Could Napoleon's activity have ended here, he would have earned the unmixed gratitude of mankind. 

125. THE DIPLOMATS TRY TO UNDO THE REVOLUTION Congress of Vienna, 1814-1815. The great international congress at Vienna now took up the task of rebuilding the European state-system and remaking the European map. 

The powers represented were Great Britain, Austria, Prussia, Russia, Sweden, Portugal, Spain, and France. The Congress formed a brilliant assemblage of emperors, kings, princes of every rank, and titled diplomats. When the wheels of diplomacy had been well oiled by banquets, balls, and other

NAPOLEON ON BOARD THE "BELLEROPHON" After the painting by Sir W. Q. Orchardson (1880). Tate Gallery, London.

THE CONGRESS OF VIENNA, 1814-1815 

The ten figures in the foreground are, in order: Wellington, Hardenberg (seated), Löwenhjelm, Noailles, Metternich, Nesselrode, Palmella (seated), Castlereagh (seated), Talleyrand (seated), and Stackelberg (seated).

The Diplomats Try to Undo the Revolution 513 festivities, the monarchs and their advisers undertook the reconstruction of Europe. 

The Congress and democracy. The allied powers were opposed, naturally enough, to all the democratic or liberal sentiments which had been awakened in Europe since 1789. 

 appeared to them as merely a revolt which had overturned the social order, destroyed property, sacrificed countless human lives, and introduced confusion everywhere. Blind to the true significance of the demand for liberty and equality, they sought to bring back the Old Régime of absolutism, privilege, and divine right. Their ideal was Europe before 1789. 

Restoration of the dynasties. The first business before the allied powers was the restoration of old dynasties. 

Spokesmen for the allies asserted the right of European monarchs to govern their former subjects, irrespective of the latter's wishes or of the claims of the rulers whom Napoleon had set up. Accordingly, a brother of Louis XVI became king of France as Louis XVIII.¹ Another Bourbon king,

Ferdinand VII, went back to Spain. Still other “legitimate princes recovered their thrones in Italy. Some of them governed without constitutions or parliaments, using their absolute power to get rid of every trace of the revolutionary era. The restoration of the dynasties spelled reaction. 

The Congress and nationalism. As we have already learned, the fraternal or patriotic feelings so deeply stirred during the revolutionary and Napoleonic era put renewed emphasis on the rights of nationalities. Patriots in one country after another boldly declared that no nation, however small or weak, should be governed by foreigners. Every nation, on the contrary, ought to be free to choose its own form of government and manage its own affairs. To such "submerged nationalities" as the Belgians, Bohemians,

Poles, and Magyars this principle held out the hope of independence; to the Italians and the Germans it held out the 

1 The young son of Louis XVI ("Louis XVII") is supposed to have died in a revolutionary prison in 1795.

hope of unification. In spite of this sentiment, the rulers and diplomats at Vienna disregarded all national aspirations. 

They treated the European peoples as so many pawns in the game of diplomacy.

Territorial readjustments. In general, the territorial readjustments made at this time were intended to compensate the great powers for their exertions against Napoleon. Both 

Austria and Prussia increased their possessions, the one in Italy and the other in Germany. Russia also widened her boundaries by annexations on her western frontier. Great 

Britain, who did not desire continental territories, received additional colonies as a reward for her part in the overthrow of the French emperor.

Work of the Congress of Vienna. The rulers and diplomats failed to satisfy either the democratic or the national aspirations of European peoples. They thus left unsolved the troublesome problems of democracy and nationalism, and these became extremely urgent in the nineteenth century. Nevertheless, the rulers and diplomats deserve credit for some real accomplishments. They reconciled the claims and desires of the chief states. There were now five great 

European powers: Great Britain and France in the West;

Austria and Prussia in the center; and Russia in the East. 

No one of them was strong enough to dominate the others.

Reactionary Austria. Austria, after the Congress of 

Vienna, consisted of more than a score of territories inhabited by Germans, Magyars, Slavs, Rumanians, and Italians. 

To keep them united under a single scepter, the Hapsburgs deliberately repressed all agitation for independence or selfgovernment. The Hapsburgs felt it equally necessary to discourage every popular movement, which, starting in Italy or Germany, might spread like an infection to their own dominions. "My realm," confessed an Austrian emperor, “is like a worm-eaten house; if a part of it is removed, one cannot tell how much will fall." Force of circumstances placed Austria at the forefront of the reaction against democracy and nationalism.
