The Metternich system. The spirit of reactionary Austria seemed embodied in Prince Metternich. An aristocrat to his finger-tips, polished, courtly, tactful, clever, this man became the real head of the Austrian government and the most influential diplomat in Europe. To the rule of Napoleon succeeded the rule of Metternich. He regarded absolutism and 

METTERNICH 

After a portrait by Sir Thomas Lawrence. divine right as the pillars of stable government. All demands for constitutions, parliaments, and representative institutions must consequently be opposed to the uttermost, spies and secret police must be multiplied, press and pulpit must be kept under gag-laws, and all agitators must be exiled, imprisoned, or executed. Such measures of repression seemed quite feasible at a time when the majority of European peoples were ignorant peasants, far removed from public

More Revolutions in Europe 517 life. Democratic ideas could only find followers among the workingmen of the cities and the educated bourgeoisie, both very weak when confronted by the powerful forces at the disposal of governments. Metternich, in fact, found little difficulty in establishing his system in Austria. By organizing the German Confederation he extended his system to many of the independent states. 

Trying to prevent change. The states whose coalitions overthrew Napoleon became in 1815 the arbiters of Europe. 

Great Britain, Austria, Prussia, and Russia renewed their alliance in order to preserve the dynastic and territorial arrangements made by the Congress of Vienna. France under Louis XVIII was soon admitted into the circle of allied powers. One of the clauses of the treaty between them provided that they should hold congresses from time to time for the consideration of the measures "most salutary for the repose and prosperity of nations and for the peace of Europe." Four such congresses were summoned by Metternich. 

He persuaded the sovereigns of Austria, Prussia, and Russia to sign a declaration by which they agreed to use their combined forces to put down any future outbreaks of the peoples against the monarchs. This meant the organization of a sort of international police body to keep order in Europe. 

126. MORE REVOLUTIONS IN EUROPE 

Revolutions of 1820-1823. The sovereigns of Austria, Prussia, and Russia soon had an occasion to apply their policy of suppressing democratic revolutions. In 1820-1823 revolutions occurred in Naples, Sardinia, Spain, Portugal and Greece. An Austrian army quickly occupied Naples and restored "order" and absolutism; liberal leaders were hurried to the dungeon and the scaffold. Almost at the same time a revolt in Piedmont (part of the Sardinian kingdom) collapsed under the pressure of eighty thousand Austrian bayonets. French troops, acting for Metternich's coalition, entered Spain and put Ferdinand once more on his throne.

Ferdinand then indulged in a reign of terror -- exiling, imprisoning, and executing liberals by the thousands. The 

Greek revolutionists, however, were supported by Russia in their revolt against their Turkish masters. A congress of the powers was summoned to meet at St. Petersburg, but it never met because they could not agree upon the policy to pursue toward the revolutionists. In the end Greece became independent of Turkey (1829). 

Revolution in France July, 1830. The first revolution ary movements in Italy and Spain were failures, but in France another revolution soon dealt an effective blow for freedom. It was provoked by the reactionary rule of 

Charles X, who succeeded his brother, Louis XVIII, on the throne. The revolution broke out at Paris in July, 1830. 

Workingmen and students raised barricades in the narrow streets and defied the government. After several days of fighting, the revolutionists gained control of the capital. 

Charles X fled to England, and the old republican flag, the tricolor, was once more raised in France. Those who carried through the uprising wanted a republic, but they found little support among the liberal bourgeoisie. Men of this class feared that a republican France would soon be at war with monarchical Europe. Largely influenced by the aged Lafayette, the Republicans agreed to accept another king, in the person of Louis Philippe, who belonged to the younger branch of the Bourbon family (p. 444). He took the crown now offered to him, at the same time promising to respect the constitution and the liberties of Frenchmen. 

Effect of the July Revolution. The events in France created a sensation throughout Europe. The reactionaries were horrified at the sudden outburst of a revolutionary spirit which for fifteen years they had endeavored to suppress; the liberals were encouraged to renewed agitation for self-government and national rights. Widespread disturbances in the Netherlands, Poland, Italy, and Germany compelled Metternich to abandon all thought of intervening to restore Charles X in France.

More Revolutions in Europe 

519 Revolution in Belgium. The Congress of Vienna, so disregardful of national feeling, had united the Belgians and Dutch into one state under a Dutch king. This arbitrary union of the two peoples led to acute friction between them. Encouraged by the success of the July Revolution in 

France, Belgian patriots raised an insurrection in Brussels.

It soon spread to the provinces and led to a demand for complete separation from Holland. The French government under Louis Philippe naturally favored this course, and Great Britain, a champion of small nationalities, also gave it her approval. The three eastern powers would gladly have stepped in to prevent such a breach of the Vienna settlements, but Austria and Russia had disorders of their own to quell, and Prussia did not dare, single-handed, to take action which might bring her into collision with France. 

Consequently the revolution succeeded, and Belgium became an independent kingdom with a liberal constitution (1831), though the king of Holland did not recognize its independence until eight years later. 

Failure of other revolutionary movements. The attempts of other “submerged nationalities" to secure freedom at this time were not successful. The Poles, whose territory had been partitioned in the eighteenth century between their greedy neighbors, attempted a revolt, but it was put down by Russian troops. Metternich's Austrian soldiers quickly repressed the insurrectionary movement which started again in Italy. Autocracy thus remained in the saddle throughout the greater part of Europe, in spite of the setbacks which it had met in France and Belgium.

Preparation for further revolution. The next eighteen years of European history (1830-1848) witnessed no conspicuous triumphs for either democracy or nationalism on the Continent. Italy and Germany remained as disunited as ever. Bohemia and Hungary continued to be subject to the Hapsburgs, and Poland to the Romanovs. Metternich, though growing old and weary, still kept his power at Vienna. The new rulers who came to the throne at this

time were no less autocratic than their predecessors. But beneath the surface discontent and unrest intensified, becoming all the stronger because so sternly repressed by the governments. Journalists, lawyers, professors, and other liberal-minded men, who might have been mere reformers, adopted radical and even revolutionary views and sought to impress them upon the working classes of the cities, the hungry proletariat. From time to time mutterings of the coming storm were heard; it burst in France. 

The February Revolution in France. Louis Philippe posed as a thorough democrat. He liked to be called the "Citizen 

King," walked the streets of Paris unattended, sent his sons to the public schools, and opened the royal palace to all who 0008

CARICATURE OF LOUIS PHILIPPE 

wished to come and shake hands with the head of the state. 

It soon became clear, however, that under an exterior of republican simplicity Louis Philippe had all the Bourbon itching for personal power. Few Frenchmen, in consequence, supported their sovereign. Both the Legitimists, as the adherents of the exiled Charles X were called, and the Bonapartists, who wished to restore the Napoleonic dynasty, cordially hated him. The Republicans, who had brought about the July Revolution and felt themselves cheated by its outcome, held him in even greater detestation. The growing discontent against the monarchy produced a number of plots and insurrections, which Louis Philippe met with the time-honored policy of repression. All societies were required to submit their proceedings to the government for approval. Editors of outspoken newspapers were jailed,

More Revolutions in Europe 521 fined, or banished. Criticism or caricature of the king in any form was forbidden. On Washington's birthday in the year 

1848 riots broke out in Paris. Workingmen armed themselves, threw up barricades, and raised the ominous cry, "Long live the republic!" Louis Philippe, losing heart and fearing to lose head as well, soon abdicated the throne and as plain "Mr. 

Smith" sought an asylum in England.

Second French Republic. His ab dication and flight did not save the monarchy. The revolutionists in

Paris proclaimed a republic, and the French people outside the capital city supported them in this action. The constitution of the second French Republic formed a thoroughly liberal AYA

This extension of the suffrage to include the masses marks an epoch in the history of democracy. The revolutions of 1789 and 1830 destroyed absolute monarchy and privileged aristocracy in France; the revolution of 1848 overthrew middle-class government and established political equality.

Louis Napoleon president of France. The voters elected to the presidency Louis Napoleon, a nephew of the great Bonaparte and the eldest representative of his family. During the reactionary rule of the Bourbons and the dull, bourgeois monarchy of Louis Philippe, the legend of a Napoleon who was at once a democrat, a soldier, and a revolutionary hero, had grown apace (p. 511). The stories of every peasant's fireside, the pictures on every cottage wall, kept his

memory green. To the mass of the French people the name 

Napoleon stood for prosperity at home and glory abroad; and their votes now swept his nephew into office. 

Effect of the February Revolution. France had once more lighted the revolutionary torch, and this time eager hands took it up and carried it throughout the Continent. 

Within a few months half of the monarchs of Europe were either deposed or forced to grant liberal reforms. No less LIBE

A cartoon of 1848. than fifteen separate revolts marked the year 1848. Those in the Austrian Empire, Italy, and the German states had most importance.

Fall of Metternich. Vienna, the citadel of reaction, was one of the first scenes of a popular uprising. Mobs, which the civic guard refused to suppress, fired Metternich's palace and compelled the white-haired old minister to resign office.

Quitting the capital in disguise and with a price set upon his head, he made his way to England, there to compare experiences with that other exile, Louis Philippe. Thus disappeared from view the man who for nearly forty years had

523 guided the destinies of Austria, one whose name has been handed down as a synonym for illiberal and oppressive government. After Metternich's downfall Vienna was ruled for a time by a revolutionary committee of students and citizens. 

The Hapsburg emperor had to grant a constitution; he also promised many other reforms, which he soon forgot.

The Magyars also revolted and established an independent Hungarian republic. Its first and only president was the patriot Kossuth, whose eloquence and energy gave him a prominent place in the revolutionary movement. "From the charnel-house of the 

Cabinet of Vienna," said Kossuth, "a pestilent wind sweeps over us, benumbing our senses and paralyzing our national spirit." The revolts in Bohemia and Hungary were crushed, however, by the armies of the Austrian monarch and his ally, the Russian tsar. Kossuth escaped to Turkey, but other leaders of the revolution perished on the gallows or before a firing squad.

Revolts in Italy. The revolutionary flood also spread over the Italian peninsula. Charles Albert, king of Sardinia, assumed leadership and declared war on the hated Austria. 

But the dream of a free, united Italy faded before the realities of war. Charles Albert's allies fell away, and after losing the battle of Novara (1849), Albert abdicated and went into exile. His son and successor, Victor Emmanuel II, then made peace with Austria. As we shall later see, the day of 

Victor Emmanuel and Sardinia was yet to come (p. 594). 

Meanwhile, French troops occupied Rome and destroyed the republic which had been set up there by the revolutionary leader, Mazzini. But Mazzini's day was also yet to come. 

Revolution in Germany. Almost all the German states had revolutionary disturbances in 1848. The cry rose everywhere for constitutions, parliaments, responsible ministries, a free press, and trial by jury. A national assembly, chosen by popular vote, met at Frankfort-on-Main to frame a constitution for a united Germany. The majority of the assembly favored a federal empire with a hereditary sovereign. 

The imperial title was offered to Frederick William IV, king of Prussia, but he refused it. He did not wish to exchange his hereditary right to the throne for a sovereignty resting on the votes of the people. Moreover, he knew that the 

House of Hapsburg would not consent to the assumption of the imperial dignity by a Hohenzollern. Nothing remained now except to restore the weak German Confederation under Austrian influence. Some of the more radical Germans tried to set up republics by force of arms. In this desperate venture for freedom, some of the noblest men in Germany took part. Among them were Carl Schurz and Franz Sigel, who afterward emigrated to America and fought in the Civil War. Their efforts in Germany had been in vain. 

Prussian troops suppressed the uprising and sealed the doom of this attempt to establish a German republic. Germany was thus fated to continue for more than twenty years as a collection of disunited states.

Revolutions in South America 525 

127. REVOLUTIONS IN SOUTH AMERICA 

The yoke of Spain. Spain governed her colonies in the 

New World for her own benefit. She crippled their trade by requiring the inhabitants to buy only Spanish goods and to sell only to Spaniards. She prohibited such colonial manufactures as might compete with those at home. She filled the offices in Church and state with Spaniards born in the mother country, to the exclusion of those born in the colonies (Creoles). She imposed a censorship of books and the press and rigidly limited education. All this restrictive system became more burdensome as time went on. By the end of the eighteenth century most Spanish Americans wanted self-government, and some of them wanted complete independence.

Example of the United States. The stirring story of the 

American Revolution and the foundation of a great republic based on democratic principles spread through the Spanish colonies. French translations of the Declaration of Independence and Spanish translations of the Constitution of the United States soon found their way southward. One of the revolutionary leaders exalted Washington as a hero "worthy of the admiration of our age and of the generations to come,' and another leader, the famous Bolívar, described himself as the Washington of South America. The example of the 

United States also led to the adoption of the federative system of government in the first republican constitutions of Mexico, Central America, and several South American countries. 

Influence of France. Even before 1789 some Spanish 

Americans of the intellectual class had become acquainted with the writings of Montesquieu, Voltaire, Rousseau, and the other French radical thinkers (p. 454). A Spanish version of Rousseau's Social Contract enjoyed a wide circulation, thus making known the new gospel of popular sovereignty and the rights of man. The colonists not only read French books, but also watched with growing interest the progress

of the Revolution in France. After their own struggle for independence began, they made "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity" their watchwords, took the liberty cap for their emblem, and out of their Masonic lodges formed secret revolutionary societies after French models. France, as well as the United States, gave them lessons in liberty. 

Revolt against Spain. Latin-American independence was closely bound up with events in Europe. Napoleon Bonaparte, in his efforts to extend French sway over the Continent, overthrew the Bourbon monarchy in Spain and seated his own brother Joseph on the Spanish throne. The colonists refused to recognize this "intruder king," as they called Joseph, and set up what were virtually independent states in all Spanish America. Ferdinand VII, who returned to 

Spain after the downfall of Napoleon (p. 515), tried by force of arms to subdue the revolting colonists, but they had now tasted the sweets of liberty and would not again accept the yoke of Spain. The wars for independence continued in one part or another of Spanish America for more than a decade. 

The United States followed the struggle with sympathetic eyes and sent commissioners to establish commercial relations with the revolting colonies. Great Britain also took an interest in them and helped them with money, ships, and munitions of war. 

The Monroe Doctrine, 1823. Both Great Britain and the United States felt thoroughly alarmed when it appeared that Metternich's coalition (p. 514) might help Spain put down her revolting colonies in America. George Canning, the British foreign minister, made it clear to the governments of France, Austria, Prussia, and Russia that so long as Great Britain controlled the seas no country other than Spain should acquire the colonies either by cession or by conquest. 

Canning's policy received the emphatic support of President Monroe in his message to Congress (1823), in which he said: "In the wars of the European powers in matters relating to themselves we have never taken any part, nor does it comport with our policy so to do. The South American republics. South 

America, at the close of the wars for independence, contained six Spanish-speaking states, namely, "Great 

Colombia," Peru, Bolivia, Chile, Argentina, and Paraguay. These were soon increased to nine by the secession of Uruguay from Argentina and Brazil and the break-up of "Great Colombia" into Colombia, Ecuador, and Venezuela. The nine states thus formed have continued in existence to the present day. 

All of them promptly became republics, with liberal constitutions that had much to say about liberty, justice, and the rights of man. Brazil, however, did not become a republic until 1889.

SIMÓN BOLÍVAR 

A medallion by David d'Angers, 1832.

Simón Bolívar. One of the heroes of Latin-American independence is Bolívar. Member of a wealthy Creole family of Venezuela, educated in Madrid, a student of the French

Revolutions in South America 

529 philosophers, witness in Paris of some of the last scenes of the Revolution, a traveler in the United States, where he had an opportunity of observing free institutions in operation, Bolívar devoted his life and fortune and splendid talents to the cause of independence. He was both warrior and statesman, able to organize legions, direct great campaigns, draft laws, and lay the foundations of republican rule in all the northern part of South America. Besides winning freedom for Venezuela, Bolívar assured it for what are now Colombia and Ecuador, and contributed powerfully to the freedom of 

Bolivia and Peru. Five nations, which he snatched from the rule of Spain, hold him in grateful remembrance as the Liberator.

Revolt against Portugal. Brazil also took part in the revolutionary movement. The Brazilian people felt that the time had come for their enormous country to sever the political ties binding her to weak little Portugal. They set up an independent empire in 1822, with Pedro, the oldest son of the Portuguese king, as its first ruler. He abdicated nine years later in favor of his infant son. Brazil prospered under the benevolent sway of the second Pedro, who was the last monarch to occupy an American throne. lettre de cachet

SAMUEL BUTLER 128. THE COMING OF THE INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION 

Today's marvels and the Industrial Revolution. Two days before Christmas, in the year 1933, the children of the various foreign diplomats stationed at Washington stood before the microphone and sent forth upon the air Christmas greetings from the young people of their countries to the young people of other lands. Their voices reached countless children who were sitting by their radios in their own homes thousands of miles from Washington. This marvel of international communication is only one of the outcomes of a series of great inventions which began more than a century and a half ago. This series of inventions brought about the Industrial Revolution.

Beginning of the Industrial Revolution. The year 1776, the year of the Declaration of Independence, also marks, approximately, the commencement of the Industrial Revolution. No other word except "revolution" so well describes those wholesale changes in industry which, within a hundred and fifty years, have made over and are still making over modern life. This revolution began in Great Britain, spread 532

The Coming of the Industrial Revolution 

533 after 1815 to the Continent and the United States, and now extends throughout the civilized world. 

Inventions before the Industrial Revolution. A list of prehistoric inventions would include levers, rollers, and wedges; bows and arrows, slings, and lassos; oars, sails, and rudders; fishing nets, lines, and hooks; the plow and the wheeled cart;

129. IMPROVEMENTS IN MANUFACTURING 

The flying shuttle. The revolution in manufacturing began with the textile industry. In the eighteenth century, weaving was still done on the hand loom, the operation of which involved the laborious process of pushing the shuttle containing the crosswise thread to the far end of the loom and then pulling it back. In 1733 the Englishman John Kay invented the flying nicating motion to the spindle shuttle, which enabled the operator to send the shuttle back and forth through the wharve. carefully and evenly by merely pulling a cord. 

Three revolutionary inventions. Kay's device doubled the speed of weaving, so that the spinners, who still used the spinning wheel, could not keep up with the weavers. Prizes were offered for a better spinning machine. In 1764 James

Hargreaves, a poor workman of Lancashire, invented the spinning jenny-named in compliment to his industrious wife, Jenny. This machine carried a number of spindles turned by cords or belts from the same wheel, and operated by hand, but it spun several threads at one time and thus speeded up the process of spinning. In 1769 Richard Arkwright invented a machine by which both the quality and the quantity of spun thread could be improved. Arkwright's

Improvements in Manufacturing

In 1779 Samuel 

Crompton combined the essential features of the Hargreaves and Arkwright machines into what became known as the "mule," because of its hybrid origin.

Cartwright's power loom, 1785. These three inventions again upset the balance in the textile industry, for now the spinners could produce more thread and yarn than the weavers could convert into cloth. The invention which revolutionized weaving

Industrial Revolution was made by Edmund Cartwright, an English clergyman, who had never even seen a weaver at work. He constructed a loom with an automatic shuttle operated by water power. 

Improvements in this machine enabled a single operator to produce more cloth than two hundred men could weave on the old-fashioned hand loom. 

Whitney's cotton gin, 1794. Both spinners and weavers required for the new machinery an abundant supply of raw material. They found it in cotton, which previously had been much less used than either wool or flax. The supply of raw cotton would have been quickly exhausted had not the cotton gin, invented by Eli Whitney of Connecticut, made it possible to separate the seeds from the cotton fibers much more rapidly than slaves could do it by hand. 

The steam engine. The expansive force of steam, though known in antiquity, was first put to practical service at the close of the seventeenth century, when steam pumps were invented for ridding mines of water. The earliest steam engine was a crude affair. After the steam entered the cylinder and pushed the piston upward, cold water had to be sprayed into the cylinder in order to condense the steam. This alternate heating and chilling used too much coal and took too much time. James Watt, a Scotchman of mechanical genius, patented an improved steam pump in 1769, a year also memorable for Arkwright's first patent. The inventor himself was a poor man, but he entered into partnership with a wealthy manufacturer of Birmingham, who took an intelligent interest in the new machine and supplied the necessary funds for making it a commercial success. By providing a separate condenser into which the steam was led after it moved the piston and by enclosing the cylinder in an airtight jacket to maintain its heat, Watt overcame the two greatest defects of the steam pump. These and other improvements opened up new fields of usefulness for steam power. In 1785, the year of Cartwright's invention, the 

Watt engine began to be set up in factories for the operation of spinning machines and looms. Steam power only slowly

Improvements in Manufacturing 

537 displaced water power, owing to the fact that manufacturers had already invested much money in water-driven cotton mills. Watt's invention led to "the age of steam,” for the steamboat and the locomotive are children of the steam engine.

The age of iron and steel. The growing use of machinery called for an increased production of iron. Northern and north-central England contained vast deposits of iron ore, but until the latter part of the eighteenth century they had been little worked. Improved methods of smelting with coal and coke, by means of the blast furnace, were then adopted. Steel, a product of iron, began to be made on a large scale only after the middle of the nineteenth century. 

In 1856 the Englishman, Henry Bessemer, invented the process called after him, by which cast iron was decarbonized by forcing a blast of air through the molten metal. The 

Bessemer process reduced the cost of a ton of steel to less than a seventh of what it had been. Other improvements in steel-making now enable the poorest iron to be converted into excellent steel, thus opening up extensive fields of lowgrade ore in France, Germany, and other countries. Used in every form, from building girders to watch springs, steel is the mainstay of modern industry.

The age of coal. The use of iron and steel and the operation of the new machinery required an abundant, inexpensive fuel. Coal had long been burned in small quantities for domestic purposes; applied to the steam engine and the blast furnace it was to become an almost boundless source of power and heat. Various improvements in mining cheapened its production, one of the most notable being Sir Humphry Davy's use of wire gauze to protect miners' lamps from the explosion of the gas called fire-damp. His first safety lamp was invented in 1816. This simple device enabled the most dangerous mines to be worked with comparative safety. 

The age of oil. Mineral oil, or petroleum, has become an industrial rival of coal since the first oil well was sunk in Pennsylvania in 1859. There are now several hundred prod-

Industrial Revolution ucts of petroleum, the most important being kerosene for illumination, gasoline (petrol) for gas engines, and fuel oil for oil-burning ships and locomotives. The United States is still the chief producer of oil, but large quantities are also furnished by Mexico, Venezuela, Russia, Rumania, Irak, and other countries.

The age of rubber. One may say, finally, that ours is an age of rubber. It has become of increasing economic importance ever since an American, Charles Goodyear, discovered in 1839 the process of "vulcanization," by which greater hardness and durability are imparted to it. Rubber trees flourish in various tropical lands. The demands of the automobile industry have led to the systematic growing of the trees, so that plantation rubber from Ceylon, southern India, and the East Indies now supplies the market. Artificial or synthetic rubber is also being made, but not as yet on an extensive scale.

Those on the Continent were built chiefly during the nineteenth century and before the era of railroads. The widespread use of the automobile has now produced another good-roads movement on a tremendous scale. The result is already seen in the many thousands of miles of smooth concrete highways linking city with city, state with state, and nation with nation.

Canals. The expense of transportation by road led people in antiquity and the Middle Ages to send their goods by river routes, whenever possible. Canal-building in Europe began

Committee, 1907. toward the close of the medieval period, especially after the invention of locks for controlling the flow and level of the water. The great era of the canal was between 1775 and 1850, not only in Great Britain and on the Continent, but also in the United States. Canals relieved the highways of a large part of the growing traffic, but the usefulness of both declined after the introduction of railroads. Ship canals have begun to be constructed within recent years, as a result of the general adoption of steam navigation on the ocean.

The steamboat. The earliest successful steamboat seems to have been a tug built in Scotland for towing canal boats. 

Robert Fulton, an American engineer who had lived in Eng-

Industrial Revolution land and France, adapted the steamboat to river navigation. 

His side-wheeler, the Clermont, equipped with a Watt engine, began in 1807 to make regular trips on the Hudson between New York and Albany. Twelve years later an American vessel, the Savannah, provided with both sails and a steam engine, crossed the Atlantic in twenty-nine days. The first ship to cross without using sails or recoaling on the way was the Great Western, in 1838. The trip took her fifteen days. 

Steam navigation. Various improvements after the middle of the nineteenth century added greatly to the efficiency of 

THE "GREAT WESTERN" 

ocean steamers. Iron, and later steel, replaced wood in their construction, with a resulting gain in strength and buoyancy. 

Screw propellers were substituted for clumsy paddle wheels, and turbine engines, which apply the energy of a jet of steam to secure the rotation of a shaft, were introduced. The size of steamers, also, has so increased that the Great Western, a boat of 1378 tons and 212 feet in length, would appear a pygmy by the side of the seventy-thousand ton "leviathans" which now cross the Atlantic in five days or less. The recent and rapid improvement of the oil-burning "internal combustion" engine (invented by a German, Rudolf Diesel) has already made the motor ship a formidable rival of the steamship and may, in the future, displace it, as the steamship displaced the sailing vessel.

Railroad transportation. Many technical improvements the increased size of locomotives and cars, air brakes, and the use of steel rails in place of iron rails, which supported only light loads and wore out rapidly - have extended the usefulness of the railroad far beyond the dreams of its earlier promoters. Electric traction. Modern electric traction dates from the early eighties of the last century, when the overhead trolley began to take the place of horse cars and cable cars in cities.

The automobile. The earliest application of steam power to transportation was neither the railway nor the steamboat but the road engine. As far back as 1801 an English inventor constructed a steam carriage for passengers. Development of the airplane. Swift was the development of the airplane. Eleven years after that first flight over the

Carolina sand dunes, aviators were fighting in the air over France, and soon after the return of peace they were spanning every ocean and circumnavigating the globe. Every one knows of the spectacular achievement of Charles A. Lindbergh, who, in 1927, made a solo flight from New York to 

Paris (3160 miles) in thirty-three and a half hours. Miss 

Amelia Earhart in 1932 flew from Newfoundland to Ireland in little more than thirteen hours. She is the first woman to accomplish this perilous journey. The development of the airplane has been followed in both Europe and the United States by the establishment of regular air lines for carrying mail and passengers between the principal cities. 

The airship. Two Frenchmen, the Montgolfier brothers, invented the balloon in the latter part of the eighteenth century. Experiments in balloon navigation continued throughout the nineteenth century, and finally Count Zeppelin, an officer in the German army, produced an airship which consisted, not of one balloon, but of a row of bags enclosed in an enormous shell of aluminum trellis work. It carried two cars, each provided with a gas motor. The trial of this 

Zeppelin in 1900 showed how nearly the problem of a dirigible balloon had been solved. Other successful airships were soon constructed in France and England.  stimulated their development, as was the case with the airplane. 

A British dirigible was the first to cross the Atlantic (July, 1919). It carried a crew and passengers from Scotland to 

Long Island, a distance of thirty-two hundred miles, in a trifle more than 108 hours. The return trip took only three days.

The submarine. As far back as the Revolutionary War, an American inventor constructed a tiny submarine and tried, without success, to sink a British warship. Robert Fulton,

Improvements in Communication 

545 encouraged by Napoleon, made several submarines. In one of them he descended to a depth of twenty-five feet, remained below for four hours, and succeeded in blowing up a small vessel with a torpedo. Under-water boats, propelled by steam power, were used by the Confederates in the Civil War. From about this time inventors in several countries worked on the problem of the submarine. One of the most successful was an Irish-American, J. P. Holland, who sold the boat named after him to the United States in 1898. The improvement of the submarine from this time is a familiar story. Thus, in the course of about a century, man has completed the conquest of land and air and sea. 

131. IMPROVEMENTS IN COMMUNICATION 

The telegraph. Scientists of the eighteenth century, who knew about the Leyden jar, often discussed the idea of using electricity to communicate at a distance, but a practicable apparatus for converting the electric current into intelligible signs did not appear until the nineteenth century. Samuel 

F. B. Morse, an 

American, deserves perhaps the greatest credit for the invention of the telegraph. It found an immediate application on the railroads and in the transmission of government messages. Later, it made its way into

Submarine cables. Hardly any one at first believed that a telegraph line could be carried across the ocean. Experiments soon showed, however, that wire cords, protected by wrappers of gutta-percha, would conduct the electric current under water. A cable was laid from Dover to Calais in 1851. 

A group of American promoters, including Cyrus W. Field, then took up the project of an Atlantic cable which should "moor the new world alongside the old." Discouraging failures marked the enterprise. The first cables were broken by the ocean, and the line which was finally laid soon became useless, owing to the failure of its electrical insulation. After the 

Civil War, Field renewed his efforts, and in 1866 a cable two thousand miles long was successfully laid and communication perfected. There are now several thousand submarine telegraph lines in operation, bridging electrically all the oceans.

The telephone. Experimentation with rude forms of the telephone began in the same decade which produced the telegraph. Little progress took place until 1876, when Alexander 

Graham Bell, a native of Edinburgh but later a resident of Boston, first successfully transmitted human speech electrically. Many improvements have since been made in the telephone by Bell himself, Thomas A. Edison, and others.

Long-distance messages are now transmitted, not only by land, but also by means of special cables under the sea. 

Wireless telegraphy and the radio. The invention of wireless telegraphy may be said to date from 1896, when an Italian, Guglielmo Marconi, took out his first patent. Three years later wireless messages were sent between France and England across the Channel. A trans-Atlantic service by

Newspapers. Weekly and daily newspapers also began to appear in the seventeenth century, but they were luxuries reserved for subscribers of the middle and upper classes. The cheap newspaper for the masses developed much later. The

Industrial Revolution London Times installed the first steam printing press in 1814. 

A paper-making machine, which produced wide sheets of unlimited length, came into use soon after. To these inventions must be added the linotype machine, which, in newspaper offices, where rapid composition is necessary, has superseded handwork in setting type. European governments for a long time tried to keep newspapers from reaching the common people, first by stamp duties and then by taxes on paper and advertisements. The new communication. 

Many inventions in communication the instantaneous camera, the motion picture, the phonograph, the radio, television - are so recent that we have scarcely as yet begun to realize their possibilities. Properly directed, they will furnish the common people in civilized countries with an education in art, music, and the drama which in former days could be secured only by persons of wealth and leisure. Their great service promises to be that of democratizing culture, as cheap newspapers and books have democratized knowledge.

Industrial Revolution of the craft guilds, toward the close of the medieval period (p. 428), prevented many apprentices and journeymen from ever becoming masters. Consequently, workers often left the cities and settled in the country or in villages where there were no guild restrictions. The movement gave rise to the domestic system, as found, for example, in the British cotton industry. A middleman, with some ready money, would purchase a supply of raw cotton and distribute it to the spinners and weavers. They, in turn, converted the raw cotton into thread or cloth, on their own spinning wheels and hand looms, in their own homes. They usually eked out their small wages by cultivating a garden plot. Something like the domestic system still survives in the sweatshops of modern cities where clothing is made "on commission.' 99 Factory system. It is clear that under the domestic system the middleman provided the raw materials, took all the risks, and received all the profits. The workers, on the other hand, had to accept such wages and labor upon such conditions as he was willing to offer. The separation of laborers and employers, which thus began under the domestic system, became complete under the factory system. Arkwright's, Crompton's, and Cartwright's machines were too expensive for a single family to own; too large and heavy for use in private houses; and they needed water power or steam power to operate them. The consequence was that the domestic laborer abandoned his household industry and went with hundreds of others to work in a mill or factory. The employer now not only provided the raw materials and sold the finished product, but he also owned the machinery and the workshop. The word "manufacturer" (Latin manu, facere, to make by hand) no longer applied to the handworker, but to the person who employed others to work for him.

Division of labor. Machinery and the factory system introduced a minute division of labor into industry. There are forty operations involved in the manufacture of readymade clothing; nearly one hundred in the manufacture of

Development of Modern Capitalism 

551 shoes; and over a thousand in the construction of a fine watch. Many men, working together, may turn out in a few minutes an article which one man in former times required weeks or months to produce. The division of labor, besides saving time, also increases output. 

Large-scale production. Machinery, the factory system, and the division of labor made it possible to manufacture on a large scale and in enormous quantities for world-wide markets. Within a century and a half, 1760-1910, the value of British cotton goods rose from one million dollars to six hundred times that amount. Similar increases were made in other textile manufactures of Great Britain. It is said that all the women and children in the world, working by hand with the old-fashioned spinning wheel, could not produce as much thread as is now made by a comparatively few working with machines. 

Capitalism. Machinery, the factory system, division of labor, and large-scale production account, finally, for modern capitalism. The word "capital” may be briefly defined as wealth used in producing more wealth. The capitalist is the man who puts what money he has and what money he can borrow into industrial enterprises from which he expects to make a profit. If his expectations are realized, he makes more money and perhaps becomes a "captain of industry" and a millionaire, as did Arkwright, the “father of the factory system." He may conduct the business alone or as a partner with others; in either case he gives it his personal attention. Should the business continue to expand and require more capital for buildings, machinery, and raw materials, the capitalist may get together with other capitalists, who, in order to operate the business, organize a corporation which sells its shares to the general public. In that case, the owners of the business do not all give it their personal attention. This tends to be more and more the situation today, when the ownership of factories, mines, railroads, steamship lines, public utilities, and other enterprises is so widely distributed among investors. For instance, the American Tele-

Industrial Revolution phone and Telegraph Company had in 1932 over 700,000 stockholders, every one of them a capitalist to the extent of his interest in the corporation. The capitalist investor intrusts the management of the business to a board of directors and takes his profits when there are profits - in the shape of dividends. 

"Big business." 

The corporation sometimes forms only a unit in a larger organization of many related companies. 

The United States Steel Corporation affords an instance of a gigantic consolidation owning over a hundred "plants" in various parts of the country and employing a quarter of a million men. The Ford Motor Company, which manufactures not only automobiles but also trucks, tractors, and airplanes, is another familiar example of a "big business." 

Capital and labor. Capitalism is no new thing. The contrast between the rich man who can hire others to work for him and the poor man who has only his labor to sell — that contrast can be traced back to the beginnings of civilization. 

Every form of society has been capitalistic in the sense that there has always been private ownership of some kinds of capital. Modern capitalism, however, is responsible for the appearance of a distinct, well-marked "working class," a class of landless, toolless "hands" employed in industrial enterprises. Between them and their employer there is seldom any intimate personal relationship; indeed, their employer is often a corporation. Though free politically, as slaves and serfs in former days were not, they are economically dependent. They must keep their jobs. When depressions come, they lose their jobs and join the mournful ranks of the unemployed. Even when regularly employed, they are in danger of being overworked and underpaid. 

Modern capitalism thus makes possible the "exploitation" of the working class. What steps has society taken, in the years since the coming of the Industrial Revolution, to protect its members from such exploitation? This question will be treated in the following section in much more detail.

Controlling an Industrialized Society 

553 

133. CONTROLLING AN INDUSTRIALIZED SOCIETY 

New conditions bring new ideas. The Industrial Revolution, as we have seen, altered men's ways of making a living. Thus arose new problems as to the relationship of one man and his activities to other men and their activities. 

These problems were met by (1) formation of trade unions, (2) enactment of labor legislation, and (3) public ownership of some industries.

Rise of trade (labor) unions. As we have seen, a wageearning class began to develop with the coming of the Industrial Revolution. Trade unions are combinations of wage earners to maintain or improve the conditions under which they labor. These associations began to appear in Great 

Britain during the eighteenth century when the domestic system gave way to the factory system. Under the new conditions of industry, an employer could not know many of his employees personally; their relations, henceforth, tended to become impersonal. At the same time, the workers in any one establishment or trade, being thrown more closely together, came to realize their common interests and to appreciate the need for organization. 

Trade unions prohibited. The unions immediately encountered opposition. The common law treated them as conspiracies in restraint of trade and hence as illegal. Moreover, the employers used their influence in Parliament to secure the passage of a long series of measures designed to prevent what were called "unlawful combinations of workmen." The last of these measures, passed in 1800, even provided the penalty of imprisonment at hard labor for persons who combined with others to raise wages, shorten hours, or in any way control the conditions of industry. 

Trade unions legalized. Agitation by trade-union leaders induced Parliament in 1824 to repeal all the laws against combinations of wage earners and to replace them, a year later, by a new and more liberal statute. Laborers might now lawfully meet together for the purpose of agreeing on

Industrial Revolution the rate of wages or the number of hours which they would work, so long as the agreement concerned only those who were present at the meeting. This qualification was removed a number of years later. Finally, laws passed by Parliament between 1871 and 1876 declared that nothing done by a group of laborers should be considered illegal unless it was also illegal when done by a single person. This legislation thus gave the working classes the full right of combination for which they had long been striving. 

Trade unionism in the United States. The organization of American trade unions began early in the nineteenth century, but their great and rapid growth has taken place since the Civil War. Probably about ten per cent of the male wage earners belong to them. While this may seem a small proportion, it must be remembered that their membership consists chiefly of skilled laborers. Most of the trade unions are affiliated with the American Federation of Labor, which was founded in 1886. 

Evils of the factory system. Improvement in the lot of the working classes has taken place not only through the activities of trade unions and other voluntary associations; laws have also been passed to regulate industry. As the 

Industrial Revolution spread, the need for government regulation became apparent. The crowded factories were unsanitary. Hours of labor were too long. Wages were on the starvation level. Furthermore, the use of machinery led to the employment of women and children, for whose labor there had been previously little demand outside the home. 

Their excessive toil amid unhealthful surroundings often caused disease and deformity or brought premature death.

Much excuse existed for the passionate words of one reformer that the slave trade was "mercy compared to the factory system."

The "let-alone" policy. These evils were naturally most prominent in Great Britain, where the Industrial Revolution began. Little effort was made at first to remedy them. The working classes exercised no political influence;

Controlling an Industrialized Society 

555 indeed, by the laws against combinations they had been prohibited from forming trade unions for their protection. 

Statesmen, instead of meeting the situation by remedial legislation, adopted the laissez-faire, or "let-alone," policy. The government, they declared, should keep its hands off industry. The greatest good to the greatest number could only be secured when "economic laws" of supply and demand were allowed to determine the wages and conditions of employment, just as they determined the prices, quantity, and quality of commodities produced. 

Labor legislation. "Let alone" naturally became the watchword of selfish employers, to whose avarice and cruelty it gave full rein. Yet there were also humane employers who felt that the state ought to protect those who could not protect themselves. After some agitation the first Factory 

Act was passed in 1802. It limited the hours of labor of pauper children bound out as apprentices in cotton mills. 

A second Factory Act (1819) gave some protection to children who were not pauper apprentices. A third Act was passed in 1833, applying to all textile factories and not merely to cotton mills. It prohibited the employment of children under nine years of age; limited the number of working hours of those between nine and eighteen; and forbade night work. Skilled inspectors were also provided to enforce the law. In 1842 Parliament passed a law forbidding the employment in mines of women, of girls, and of boys under ten. 

Five years later Parliament took the still more radical step of passing the Ten-Hour Act, which restricted the labor of women and children in textile factories to ten hours a day. 

This measure became a law only after the fiercest opposition on the part of manufacturers, but it proved so beneficial that henceforth the desirability of labor legislation was generally admitted.

Labor legislation today. Government regulation of industry before long became a reality. At the present time governments restrict the employment of children so that they may not be deprived of an education. They limit the

Industrial Revolution hours of labor, not only of children and women in most industries, but also of men in mines and factories. They require employers to install safety appliances in their plants and to take all other precautions necessary for the preservation of the lives, limbs, and health of their employees. 

Government control of the conditions of labor has been carried farthest in those countries which since the World War have established dictatorships - as, for example, Italy, Germany, Russia, and Turkey. But even parliamentary governments have found it necessary to enact much labor legislation. Thus Great Britain has unemployment insurance (the so-called dole); health insurance for protection against sickness and disease; and pensions for widows, orphan children, and elderly persons without independent means of support. In the United States, the National Industrial Recovery Act of 1933 (the NRA), by its provision for the adoption of industrial codes represents an attempt to employ the prestige and power of the federal government to regulate some of the conditions of industry and labor. 

Extension of state enterprise. The modern state, in all civilized countries, does many things which people did for themselves during the Middle Ages. The state maintains an army and navy, administers justice, provides a police system, and furnishes public education. No one now questions either the need or the desirability of such activities. 

As we have just learned, the state also subjects private industry to ever-increasing regulation for the benefit of the less fortunate members of society. Furthermore, it engages in a variety of industrial undertakings. 

Examples of state enterprise. Governments sometimes monopolize different branches of business for financial reasons to raise a revenue. A good example is the monopoly of the sale of tobacco and matches in France and Italy. 

Moral considerations may combine with financial reasons, as illustrated by the public monopoly of the manufacture and sale of alcoholic liquors in various countries. The post office is always in government hands, not so much for revenue

Socialism 

557 as to secure cheap communication between different parts of the country. In Great Britain and on the Continent telegraphs and telephones are managed by the government in connection with the post office, and the government parcel post does all the business which in the United States is partly absorbed by private express companies. Coinage is everywhere a public function, as well as banking in most European countries. Some countries have also public forests, mines, and canals. On the Continent railroads are mostly stateowned and state-managed. Nearly all the French lines are privately owned, but they will belong to the government upon the expiration of their franchises. Both British and 

Continental cities generally own and operate such public utilities as street railways, gas and electric lighting plants, and waterworks. In the United States, municipal ownership has been common in the case of waterworks, but less common in other cases.

End of laissez-faire. Thus, as we have seen, "Let alone" is no longer the watchword of society with regard to industry. 

Wage earners have won the right to organize for the purpose of promoting their own interests, the state passes laws to protect the worker in industry, and industry itself is sometimes owned and operated by the government. Complete belief in the doctrine of laissez-faire finds few followers at the present time. 

134. SOCIALISM 

What is socialism? Nowadays, socialism is generally contrasted with capitalism. Socialism is the name given to a new economic order which its advocates propose to set up in the place of the capitalistic system. Present-day socialists unite in making the following demands. First, the state shall own and operate the instruments of production, that is, land and capital. Under this arrangement rent, interest, and profits, as sources of personal income, would disappear, private property would consist simply of one's own clothing,

Industrial Revolution household goods, money, and perhaps a house and a garden plot. Second, the leisure class shall be eliminated by requiring everybody to perform useful labor, either physical or mental. Third, the income of the state shall be distributed as wages and salaries among the workers, according to some fairer principle than obtains at present. It is important to note that labor legislation is not properly described as socialistic, since it does not abolish private property, the factory system, and rent, interest, and profits.

Socialism and the Industrial 

Revolution. The socialist movement is, in large part, an outcome of the Industrial Revolution, which widened the gulf between the capitalists and the landless, toolless, wage-earning proletariat. Vastly more wealth was now produced, but it was unequally distributed. The few had too much; the many had too little. Radical reformers, distressed by these inequalities and dissatisfied with the slow progress of the labor movement and government regulation of industry, began to proclaim the necessity of a wholesale reconstruction of society. 

ROBERT OWEN 

After a plaster medallion by 

Miss Beech.

Robert Owen and coöperation. In Great Britain the most prominent of these early radicals was Robert Owen, a rich manufacturer and philanthropist, who did much to improve the conditions of life for his employees. He also did pioneer work as an advocate of trade unionism and labor legislation, at a time when neither had many influential friends. Among his innovations were coöperative shops, where workmen could buy goods cheaply and divide the profits among themselves. This principle of coöperative distribution met great success in England, and Owen deserves

Socialism 

559 credit as its originator. He also advocated coöperation in production. His special remedy for social ills was the establishment of small coöperative communities, each one living by itself on a tract of land and producing in common everything needed for its support. Owen's experiments in cooperative production all failed, including the one which he established at New Harmony, Indiana, in 1825. Owen thus belongs in the class of "Utopian” socialists, men who dreamed of ideal social systems which were never realized. 

Louis Blanc and "social workshops." In France a journalist and author, named Louis Blanc, did much to popularize socialistic ideas among workingmen. Blanc believed that every man had a right to remunerative employment. 

To provide it, he proposed that the state should furnish the funds for what he called "social workshops." These were to be managed by the operatives themselves, who would divide the profits and get rid of capitalists altogether. 

The provisional government which was established by the revolutionists in France in 1848 set up workshops on Blanc's plan and promised two francs a day to every registered workingman. Crowds came from all parts of France to take advantage of the offer, and before long there were over one hundred thousand additional laborers in Paris, with nothing to do but plant "trees of liberty" in rows. The drain upon the treasury and the demoralization of the people by this state charity soon led to the collapse of the whole scheme. It should be said in justice to Blanc that the government seems to have purposely mismanaged the workshops in order to discredit the socialist movement. This result occurred, and for a time socialism became almost extinct in France.

Karl Marx, 1818-1883. Meanwhile, a new socialism, more systematic and practical than the old, began to be developed by German thinkers. Its chief representative was Karl

Marx. He studied at several German universities and received the degree of Doctor of Philosophy. Becoming interested in economic subjects, he founded a socialist newspaper

Industrial Revolution to advocate the cause of the working classes. After the failure of the revolutionary movement of 1848-1849, the 

KARL MARX 

oh Yo God government suppressed Marx's newspaper and expelled him from Germany.

He went to London and lived there in exile for the rest of his days, finding time, in the midst of a hard struggle for existence, to write his famous work, Das 

Kapital (Capital). The first volume appeared in 1867.

This massive work, covering the whole field of economics, has been translated into many modern languages.

It has profoundly influenced human thought and action. 

Marxism. Marx felt little sympathy with ideal schemes, like those of the Utopian socialists, to make over society. 

He described such schemes sarcastically as "pocket editions of the New Jerusalem." In contrast to Owen, Blanc, and other earlier socialists, he sought to build up a system of socialism based on economic principles. Put in its simplest form, Marxism asserts that, while labor is the source of all value, laborers receive, in fact, only a fraction of what they produce. All the rest goes to the capitalistic bourgeoisie, or middle class, who are said to produce nothing. Capitalism, however, is the inevitable result of the Industrial Revolution. 

Marx believed that, like feudalism, it forms a stage-a necessary stage - in the development of mankind. He also predicted that it would disappear with the progress of democracy, which, by giving the proletariat the vote, will enable them to displace the bourgeoisie, take production into their own hands, and peacefully introduce the socialist state.

The Communist Manifesto, 1848. The socialistic ideas of 

Marx are more briefly and popularly set forth in the Com-

Progress and Poverty 561 munist Manifesto, which he and his associate, Friedrich Engels, put forth in the revolutionary year of 1848. It demanded, among other things, abolition of property in land and application of all rents of land to public purposes; a heavy, graduated income tax; abolition of the right of inheritance; centralization of credit in the hands of the state by means of a national bank with an exclusive monopoly; state ownership of the means of communication and transport; state ownership of factories and other instruments of production; national cultivation of the soil; and compulsory labor for all. The conclusion of the Communist Manifesto is frequently quoted by socialists: "The proletarians have nothing to lose except their chains. They have a world to gain. Proletarians of all lands, unite!"

Socialism and politics. During the seventies of the last century the coworkers of Marx in Germany founded the Social Democratic Party. It provided a model for similar organizations of Marxian socialists in Great Britain, France, Italy, Austria, Russia, Australia, Japan, and the United States. In 1914 the socialists throughout the world polled about eleven million votes and elected over seven hundred representatives to the various parliaments. All these parties had a Right, or moderate, group, and a Left, or more radical, group. 

135. PROGRESS AND POVERTY 

Economic progress. Few would wish to retrace their steps to an age when there were no factories, no railroads, and no great mechanical inventions. Machinery now does much of the roughest and hardest work and, by saving human labor, makes it possible to shorten hours of toil. Already the normal working day has been decreased to eight hours from the ten and twelve hours which were usual not so many years ago, and the six-hour day and the five-day week seem likely to be generally adopted in the near future. The world's workers thus have opportunities for recreation and education previ-

Industrial Revolution ously denied them. Modern industrialism has made it possible to introduce the necessaries and comforts, and even many of the luxuries, of life among all peoples in all lands. 

Poverty. Despite the wonderful inventions and scientific discoveries which have so increased the productive powers of man, there are still millions of human beings in the Christian world who lead lives of grinding toil and are without an income sufficient for their barest needs. The reasons for this poverty are as complex as modern life. Some poverty is brought about by faults of personal character or by physical and mental defects; other poverty is the consequence of lack of education, bad surroundings, corrupt or inefficient government, unemployment, high cost of living, and monopolies. 

Prevention of poverty. In the last century and a half many means for preventing poverty have been suggested and tried. Among these have been the activity of trade unions, labor legislation (old-age pensions, state insurance against sickness, disability, and unemployment, the minimum wage, and workmen's compensation laws), education of the unskilled, improved housing, and social welfare work. 

These are some of the ways whereby men have sought to bring about a more equal and equitable distribution of wealth among those who produce it.

Unit VIII MODERN CIVILIZATION 

How modern life and thought were enriched, only to be endangered by a world war 

(CHAPTERS XVII-XX)

PRESENTATION 

Between the revolutions of 1848 and the outbreak of the World War in 1914, the political institutions of modern man were being transformed by democracy and nationalism. In Great Britain, the people slowly made the parliamentary system responsive to their will. In France, Napoleon III established a despotism, but he was overthrown in 1870 and a third republic established. In Italy, Sardinia led native rulers in throwing off the yoke of Austria and in forming the Kingdom of Italy, in 1870. In Germany, the states under the leadership of Prussia edged Austria out of their affairs and formed the German Empire in 1871. In Austria-Hungary, the United States, Russia, and the Balkans national movements led to territorial increases and strong national governments. Along with nationalism generally went democracy; but there were exceptions - notably in Russia. (Chapter XVII) 

Meanwhile, man's economic and social activities, as well as his feelings and ideas, were undergoing radical changes. Population, wealth, industry, and commerce increased tremendously, giving rise to new problems of commercial organization, of the distribution of wealth, and of social justice. Marvelous discoveries in science altered man's knowledge and ideas of the universe and increased his ability to use the powers of nature. All these changes were mirrored in literature, the arts, philosophy, and the social studies. (Chapter XVIII) In the nineteenth century Europe renewed its interest in colonial expansion, especially in order to acquire trade areas. Africa was partitioned among European powers. In Asia, Great Britain extended her control in India and won trading centers in China, while Russia expanded southward, and eastward across northern Asia to the Pacific. Other powers pushed into China, which was saved from dismemberment only by the Open Door policy. Meanwhile 

Japan took on western ways, became a world power, and acquired various areas on the mainland of Asia. Imperialism was also extended to most of the islands of the Pacific. In America the Monroe 

Doctrine protected the growing Latin republics from European imperialism but left them distrustful of the United States. promote peace and harmony in the Americas, the Pan-American 

Union was organized. (Chapter XIX) 

Το Rivalry between the modern nations led to entangling alliances, struggles for military and naval supremacy, and clashes over territorial expansion. One crisis led to another until Europe was involved in war in 1914. Germany, Austria-Hungary, Turkey, and 

Bulgaria were opposed by nearly all the other countries. The 

United States was drawn into the conflict in 1917, throwing its men and wealth to the side of the Allies. In 1918 the Central 

Powers were exhausted, and surrendered. The destruction of modern civilization was thus halted. (Chapter XX)
