CHURCH OF THE RESURRECTION OF CHRIST, LENINGRAD 

Built on the spot where Alexander II was assassinated. came to the throne in 1855. It seemed that he might prove a more enlightened and benevolent ruler than his immediate predecessors had been. He pardoned political offenders, relaxed the censorship of the press, and issued a new code of laws based on those of western Europe. He improved the courts of justice, long notorious for their incompetence and corruption. More important still, he intrusted the administration of roads, schools, churches, and other local concerns

to provincial and district assemblies (zemstvos), freely elected by all classes of the people. His most memorable achievement was the abolition of serfdom, which had lasted longer in Russia than in any other European country. Before long, however, Alexander II fell back upon the oppressive methods of rule that had marked his predecessors. 

Nihilism. The intense disappointment of the educated classes (the intelligentsia) at Alexander's relapse into the traditional ways of Russian monarchs gave rise to nihilism. 

The young people who embraced this doctrine had lost all faith in the existing order of things; they believed in nothing (Latin nihil). Russia, they urged, must make a clean sweep of autocracy, of the Orthodox Church, and of every other institution that had come down from an unreasoning, unscientific past. When the ground had been thus cleared, it would be possible to reconstruct a new and better society. 

The nihilists before long began to seek converts among the masses, most of whom were peasants. The government soon got wind of the movement and imprisoned or exiled those who took part in it. 

Political terrorism. The nihilists decided that since the government ruled by terror, it was to be fought with terror. 

A secret committee of nihilists at St. Petersburg condemned to death a number of prominent officials, spies, and members of the hated secret police, and in some cases succeeded in assassinating them. On the very day that Tsar Alexander had agreed to some sort of constitution and parliament for Russia, he was killed by a bomb. His son succeeded him as Alexander III. The revolutionists offered to abandon their campaign of terrorism if a representative assembly, elected by manhood suffrage, was summoned, and if freedom of press, of speech, and of assembly was granted. Alexander III, undeterred by his father's fate, determined to crush the revolutionists. His director of police ferreted out and punished the leading terrorists so remorselessly that revolutionary nihilism almost disappeared. The handful of terrorists could not overthrow an autocracy which commanded the

Russia Struggles for Popular Government 

617 support of the official classes, of the Orthodox Church with its tens of thousands of priests, and of the stolid, conservative peasants, who formed the bulk of Russia's millions. 

Beginning of industrialism in Russia. It was at this time that the country, for centuries almost wholly agricultural, began to be industrialized. The emancipation of the serfs allowed many of them to flock to the cities, where they furnished an abundant supply of cheap labor. The government also started railroad building on an extensive scale and induced foreign capitalists to invest in Russian coal mines, iron mines, oil fields, and other natural resources. Factories sprang up like mushrooms, and millions of Russians, especially in the western portion of the empire, became factory workers. Such economic changes could not fail to affect the life of the people in many ways. Old cities grew rapidly and new cities developed. A middle class appeared, together with an industrial proletariat more intelligent and far less conservative than the peasantry. The workingmen organized trade unions, conducted strikes, and, as in Germany, lent a receptive ear to socialistic agitators against autocracy. 

These middle and lower classes were fertile soil for the seeds of revolution.

How the Revolution of 1905 began. The opposition to autocracy, which had apparently been suppressed during the reign of Alexander III, revived during that of his successor, Nicholas II (reigned 1894-1917). Not only the intelligentsia, but also the middle and lower classes, now took up the liberal cause. Enlightened members of the nobility, as in France before the Revolution, added their voices to the rising volume of criticism. Then came the Russo-Japanese 

War (1904-1905), revealing in pitiless fashion the government's incapacity and corruption. On Sunday, January 22, 1905, an event occurred which stirred public feeling to its depths. A radical priest organized a procession of working people, men and women, to march through the streets of the capital and lay their grievances before the Little Father in person. When they reached the royal palace, they were re-

ceived, not by the tsar, but by Cossacks, who greeted them with volleys of musketry. This was the massacre of "Red Sunday.' 99 The Revolution of 1905. The months which followed witnessed an epidemic of strikes throughout Russia. Every strike had a twofold purpose - the improvement of economic conditions and the securing of a constitution. In October, 1905, a general strike began in St. Petersburg and other large cities, together with a stoppage of railway transportation all over the empire. The strike fever extended to the middle class; teachers dismissed school and judges court; merchants closed their stores and doctors their offices; even the ballet dancers refused to dance. With life in Russia virtually at a standstill, no alternative remained to the government but submission. The tsar promised the Russians freedom of conscience, speech, meeting, and association; he further promised that a representative assembly (Duma) should be elected on a wide franchise, and that henceforth no law should be valid without the Duma's consent.

The tsar and the Duma. The first Russian parliament, or 

Duma, met the following year (1906). It spent most of its time struggling with the tsar, who at last dissolved it. Three other Dumas met between 1907 and 1914. The tsar so modified suffrage qualifications that the membership of the Duma was confined mainly to large landowners, wealthy manufacturers, and other representatives of the propertied, conservative classes. Even these he often distrusted. They accomplished some useful legislation, but did not succeed in winning liberty for the people nor in reforming fundamentally the processes of government. Consequently, when Russia was caught in the maelstrom of the World War, its political organization and its economic system were inadequate to meet the strains put upon them. Before the war was over, the tsar had been driven from the throne and the country was in chaos. The Russian people then entered on a series of social, economic, and political experiments (p. 672).

The Rise of Nationalism in the Balkans 

621 land did several things to preserve the health of the "sick man." This problem of what to do with the "sick man's" property (often called the Eastern Question) caused many diplomats to forget the fact that the Balkans were already occupied by Slavs, Greeks, Bulgarians, and Rumanians who had ideas of their own as to what to do with the 

Balkans. Thus the recovery of the Balkans is a complicated story of (1) subject nationalities trying to win their freedom and (2) international intrigue in which each of the 

Great Powers was trying to win some advantage for itself. 

Emerging nationalities in the Balkans. In the nineteenth century the peoples of the Balkans were stirred by the same enthusiasm for nationality which had so profoundly moved the Italians and Germans. By 1829 

Montenegro, Serbia, and 

Greece had achieved their independence. Then international rivalries entered the struggle.

FLORENCE NIGHTINGALE 

2000 bas 

Miss Florence Nightingale did remarkable work during the Crimean War for the relief of sick and wounded British soldiers. 

To her self-sacrificing labors are also due many improvements in hospital management, sanitation, and the training of nurses. 

The Crimean War. In 1853 

Tsar Nicholas I, impatient because the "sick man" had not died, provoked a war with the Turkish sultan. England, alarmed lest Russia become too powerful in the eastern 

Mediterranean, sided with Turkey. France and Sardinia also joined England, and the Crimean War followed. Russia suffered defeat, and the Turks secured a new lease on life

in Europe. The peace conference assembled at Paris in 

1856. In their anxiety to keep Russia out of Constantinople, England and France abandoned the tradition, which had come down from the Crusades, that the Turks were a barbarous people and the enemies of civilization. Henceforth Turkey was to be treated as a recognized member of the European family of nations.

The Balkans in turmoil. The Peace of Paris had provided for a protectorate, under Russian supervision, over some of the Balkan lands. Out of this arrangement emerged, in 

1862, the new country of Rumania. In 1877, Russia again declared war on Turkey, and the terms of the treaty of peace provided for the creation of Bulgaria in the Balkans. In 

1912 four Balkan powers - Greece, Montenegro, Serbia, and 

Bulgaria — united to expel Turkey from Europe. They succeeded in reducing her area in Europe to a small region about 

Constantinople. Then the Balkan allies fell to quarreling, and then to fighting among themselves over the area which they had conquered. Thus nationalism had promoted the uprising of peoples which led to the cutting down of the Turkish domain. But the intense nationalism of these new states prevented the peaceable division of what had been won from Turkey. The Balkans continued to be a serious problem to the peace of Europe. As we shall see, they provided the scene for the act which started the World War.

CHAPTER XVIII MODERN LIFE AND THOUGHT 

All the great sources of human suffering are in a great degree, many of them entirely, conquerable by human care and effort. 

JOHN STUART MILL

What this chapter is about. In the previous chapter we saw how modern civilization was marked by struggles over democracy and nationalism. In this chapter we shall see how modern civilization manifested itself in men's thoughts and daily life. We shall try to realize that the discovery of a new chemical element, the creation of a new school system, or the advancement of a new theory of the universe may affect man's civilization as profoundly as a new constitution or the overthrow of a despotic ruler. In other words, modern civilization is complex and varied, and all kinds of activities combine to give it richness and fullness. 

147. MODERN POPULATION 

Increase in population. One of the most important features of modern times is the enormous growth in population. 

During the nineteenth century the number of people in 

Europe more than doubled (from 175,000,000 to 400,000,000).

The number of people in the United States mounted from about 4,000,000 in 1790 (when the first census was taken) to nearly 123,000,000 in 1930.

Migrations. Another aspect of population in modern times is the migration of people from one country to another. 

There has been an enormous emigration of Europeans during the past hundred years to lands beyond the seas. 

United States received about thirty-nine million immigrants The 625

between 1820 and 1930, nearly all coming from Europe. 

Millions more went to the British colonies and to South America. The migration movement became most marked after the middle of the nineteenth century, when the improvements in steam navigation so greatly multiplied and cheapened facilities for travel on the ocean. The present tendency of new countries is to limit the number of immigrants they will receive in any one year and by various tests, both physical and mental, to select only the desired class of settlers. 

The new Immigration Act of the United States, which came into force in 1929, very greatly reduced immigration into this country. During the fiscal year 1931–1932 the number of aliens permanently departing exceeded, for the first time in our history, the number of new immigrants admitted. 

The United States no longer freely opens her gates to all the world.

Growth of cities. The increased population of the leading industrial countries has been largely concentrated in cities. 

This growth in cities was made possible by the rise of the factory system and the improvement of facilities for travel and transportation. At the opening of the nineteenth century, western Europe was still mainly rural, as eastern Europe is today. In 1800 Europe had fourteen cities of more than one hundred thousand inhabitants; in 1900 it had one hundred and forty such cities. Now there are many more.

London in 1800 contained under a million inhabitants; today it has seven millions within its borders. Paris contains five times as many people as it had shortly before the French Revolution. Berlin has twenty times as many people as it had during the reign of Frederick the Great. În 1800 the 

United States had only six cities of over eight thousand inhabitants, whereas by 1930 it had over six hundred cities of more than ten thousand population. 

The Industrial Revolution and modern population. The 

Industrial Revolution had a large part in the three aspects of modern population that have just been noted - increase in population, migrations, and growth of cities. The number

of people who can be supported in a given region now depends less on the amount of food which they raise than on their production of raw materials and manufactured goods to exchange for food. Industrialized Belgium and Great 

Britain, with only a limited agriculture, support more inhabitants to the square mile than any other countries; while the population of such industrial states as New York, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Massachusetts far exceeds that of many of the agricultural commonwealths of the Middle West. There are, of course, certain agricultural countries (Egypt, the Ganges valley and delta in India, part of China) where the rich soil, coupled with a very low standard of living on the part of the inhabitants, has also made possible an enormous growth of population within the last century. The map on page 627 gives some idea of the density of population in different parts of the world. 

Distribution of wealth. The Industrial Revolution made it possible for the civilized world, for the first time in history, to produce cheaply and rapidly everything needed for the economic well-being of a large population. The cornucopia of the practical scientist and the engineer has been shaken over the whole earth, scattering everywhere those material things the possession of which should make life healthier and happier for every one. Yet the goal thus reached has not brought universal prosperity. Man invents the machinery for mass production; he increases output; and he reduces the costs of manufacture until the markets are glutted with commodities that cannot be sold. They cannot be sold because the power to purchase them is lacking. We have not yet discovered how to distribute properly the quantity of commodities so as to bring the comforts and luxuries of modern life within the reach of all. "Technological unemployment." The introduction of machinery at first threw many people out of employment. 

Then it was discovered that the machines called for more labor than they displaced and that the workers who had lost their jobs were usually reabsorbed in industry. Consider

Agriculture and Land Tenure 

629 how such recent inventions as the automobile and the radio have increased the need for human hands to make, distribute, and maintain them. Today, however, we face a different situation. New scientific processes and practical inventions multiply with such rapidity as to throw the whole organization of labor out of gear. So many labor-saving devices and so many wonderfully efficient machines are being introduced that employment now drops sharply and always tends to decrease further. The result is "technological unemployment" on a great scale. The consequent loss of wages means lessened purchasing power and therefore a lessened demand for the goods which mass production has created. 

The goods are available, but unemployment makes it impossible for people to secure and enjoy them. This situation has been growing for many years in both Europe and the United States, and it was brought home vividly to multitudes in the United States during the depression which began in 1929. 

Remedies of unemployment. Our economic difficulties are man-made; the solution of them must also be man-made. If we have achieved a miracle in reducing the costs of manufacture by machinery, we should achieve another miracle in so stabilizing wages and salaries that it will be possible for us to buy all that we can produce. We must realize that uninterrupted mass consumption is just as essential as is mass production. To attain this result many efforts have been made. These include reduction of the hours of labor and the development of insurance systems to provide for unemployment, sickness, disability, and old age. The purpose of these and similar measures is to keep the purchasing power of our vast population equal to the production power of our industrialized civilization. 

148. AGRICULTURE AND LAND TENURE 

Agriculture in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. 

The agricultural system of the Middle Ages (p. 332), with its wasteful "open field" and fallow lands, its backward methods,

and its scanty yield, began to be revolutionized in modern times. The Dutch were the first scientific farmers, and from them English farmers learned many secrets of tillage. Deeper plowing, more thorough pulverization of the ground, more diligent manuring, the shifting or rotation of crops from field to field, so that the soil would not have to lie fallow every third year, and the introduction of new crops, including turnips, clover, and rye, were some of the improvements which doubled the yield of agricultural land. The weight of cattle and sheep was also much increased through careful selection in breeding. It is significant of the revived interest in agriculture that George III contributed articles to a farm journal and that Washington, in his quiet retreat at Mount Vernon, invented a plow and a rotary seed drill. 

Agriculture since 1800. The improvements in agriculture have now extended to every progressive country. Machinery de colbe wah teba. royd 

MCCORMICK REAPER 

The reaper with a vibrating cutter, as first patented by Cyrus H. McCormick in 1834. 

The inventor afterward established large works in Chicago for manufacturing the reaper and other agricultural machines. replaces the ancient scythe, sickle, flail, and other implements. One machine, of American invention, not only reaps the grain, but threshes it, winnows it, and delivers it into sacks at a single operation. The introduction of cheap artificial fertilizers makes profitable the cultivation of poor lands formerly allowed to lie idle. The advance of engineering science leads to the reclamation of marshes and arid wastes. 

Finally, steam navigation allows a country to draw supplies

Agriculture and Land Tenure 

631 of wheat, meat, and other foodstuffs from the most distant regions, with the result that the specter of famine, so common in the Middle Ages, has well-nigh disappeared from the modern world. 

Inclosures. The "open-field" system of cultivation, whereby the same person tilled many small strips in different parts of the manor, was so wasteful of time and labor that medieval farmers began to exchange their scattered strips for compact holdings which could be inclosed with hedges or fences and cultivated independently. This inclosure movement continued in western Europe all through the modern period, until at length the old "open fields" had been practically abandoned in favor of separate farms and individual tillage. 

British landlordism. Inclosures meant better farming everywhere, but in Great Britain they also helped to create the large estates so characteristic of that country. The lord of the manor, not satisfied with inclosing his demesne lands, often managed to inclose those of the peasants as well, and even the meadows and forests, which had been formerly used by them in common. At the present time ten thousand persons own two-thirds of all England and Wales; seventeen thousand persons own nine-tenths of Scotland. The rural population of Great Britain consists of a few landlords, numerous tenant farmers who rent their farms from the lords, and a still larger number of laborers who work for daily wages and have little interest in the soil they till. 

Land tenure on the Continent. In France a considerable part of the agricultural land belonged to the peasants even before the Revolution. Their possessions increased in the revolutionary era, as the result of legislation confiscating the estates of the Crown, the Church, and the nobles. France today is emphatically a country of small but prosperous and contented farmers. The agrarian reforms of the French Revolution spread to Belgium, Switzerland, western Germany, and northern Italy, where peasant proprietorships have long been common. Many other parts of Europe, however, re-

mained under the medieval manorial system throughout the nineteenth century. The land was owned by a few noble families and was worked by peasants, either as tenants or as day laborers.

Land tenure in Russia. After the abolition of serfdom in 

Russia (1858-1861), the nobles were required to sell a portion of their estates to the peasants. About half of the agricultural area of European Russia thus changed hands. Henceforth the farming land was intrusted to the entire village (mir) for redistribution at intervals among the inhabitants. 

All that the peasant really possessed in his own right was a house and a garden plot. The peasants were dissatisfied. 

One of the first acts of the revolutionists in 1917 was to confiscate the huge imperial domains and many estates of the nobility. This land was then partitioned among the peasants. 

The Soviet government now owns many farms and operates them with the aid of American tractors, harvesters, and threshers. It also provides machinery and equipment for the numerous collective farms that are worked in common by the peasants. Whether these state and collective farms will spell the doom of private ownership of land remains to be The outcome will be watched with interest, for in Russia about seven-eighths of the people live wholly or mainly by agriculture. seen. 

149. DEVELOPMENT OF COMMERCE 

Commercial expansion. A tremendous expansion of commerce followed the improvements which the Industrial Revolution brought in manufacturing, transportation, and communication. It is estimated that the commerce of the world increased over twelve hundred per cent in the nineteenth century. This expansion continued into the twentieth century.

British commerce. Great Britain profited most from this commercial expansion. (1) The Industrial Revolution be gan in Great Britain, and for many years she alone had large

Development of Commerce 

633 quantities of manufactured goods to export. (2) Great

Britain's success as a colonial power fostered her commerce, for the bulk of the trade of British colonies and dependencies is with the mother country. German commerce. The threefold increase of Germany's foreign trade between 1871 and 1914 was part of the remarkable industrial development which followed her unification. Germany, on the eve of the World War, ranked next to Great Britain among commercial nations. German imports were mostly foodstuffs to supply the rapidly growing population and raw materials for the expanding factories of the empire. The exports were mainly manufactures, coal, and beet sugar.

French commerce. France in 1914 stood third among 

European countries in volume of foreign trade. The French people excel in the creation of such artistic luxuries as millinery, laces, gloves, perfumes, and fine china, and these, together with silks and wines, comprise the bulk of their exports. The low, flat coast and few harbors of France have not encouraged the growth of a merchant marine. The 

French are obliged to depend largely upon the British, Norwegians, and other neighbors for shipping. 

Commerce of the United States. The foreign trade of the 

United States during the nineteenth century remained small in proportion to the increasing wealth and population of the country. Our resources are so great and so varied that we can obtain by internal trade nearly everything we need. 

Were our commerce interrupted we should lack such commodities as coffee, tea, tropical fruits, and rubber; on the other hand we should lack neither the necessaries of life nor most of the raw materials for our industries. The United 

States is more nearly independent, industrially, than any other leading country. Nevertheless the growth of American commerce has been exceptionally rapid within recent decades, especially the increase in the exports of manufactures. 

Commercial organization. The organization of commerce shows wonderful changes since the Middle Ages. There is now so steady a flow of commodities from producers through wholesalers and retailers to consumers that the old system of weekly markets and annual fairs is all but obsolete. Distinctively modern are produce exchanges for trade in the great staples (wheat, cotton, wool, sugar, etc.) and stock exchanges for buying and selling the stocks and bonds of corporations. 

In modern commerce it is possible to get insurance against almost every possible misfortune. The farmer insures his crop against hail or windstorm; the merchant, his stock against theft or fire; and the shipowner, his vessel against loss at sea. Marine insurance arose in medieval Italy, but for centuries it has centered at Lloyd's in London. The first fire insurance policies were written in London after a great

Development of Commerce 

635 fire there during the reign of Charles II. Other forms of business insurance originated much more recently. The growth of life insurance companies during recent years has been extraordinary. The Industrial Revolution, which so increased the wealth of the civilized world, naturally made banking more than ever an indispensable agency of monetary transactions on a large scale. There arose a class of private or "investment" bankers, controlling millions and even billions of dollars deposited with them by insurance companies, big business men, and other investors. 

Commercial freedom. Many obstacles impeding the exchange of goods in the Middle Ages disappeared in modern times. State police finally suppressed highway robbery. 

Piracy, once so common, became obsolete in the era of modern steam navigation. The burdensome tolls imposed by feudal lords on transportation and travel were no longer exacted, now that feudalism itself had died out. A movement also began to reduce the high duties levied by every European nation on imports and exports. 

Free trade in Great Britain. One nation went still further in the nineteenth century and adopted free trade. In 1815 

Great Britain enjoyed a virtual monopoly in most lines of industry. Having no reason to fear the competition of foreign manufacturers, it was to her advantage to lower or abolish the duties on imports, especially those on raw materials. William Pitt the Younger began the work of tariff reform; Sir Robert Peel continued it in the 'forties; and 

Gladstone completed it. Great Britain continued to be a free-trade nation until 1931, when a new revenue act went into effect imposing high duties on a long list of imported manufactured articles. However, these duties are lowered or else entirely remitted on products of the British colonies and Dominions.

Repeal of the Corn Laws. For many years Corn Laws restricted or prohibited the importation of wheat or other grains, so that there would be a larger profit for British farmers. Manufacturers and factory workers objected to

the high prices which resulted, and after much agitation the obnoxious laws were repealed in 1846. Great Britain since then has secured the bulk of her food abroad, from the fertile wheat areas of the United States and the British colonies, TARIFES TARIFFS "THE MAN WHO DARED TO PUT UP 

HIS UMBRELLA TOO"

Protective tariffs. In the nineteenth century, France, Germany, the 

United States, and other countries adopted the policy of protective tariffs. They sought in this way to build up their own "infant industries" in order to supply the home market and even to compete with Great Britain in the markets of the world. The growth of protection thus formed a sequel to the national movement which had developed in Europe. The movement for protection by means of high tariffs gained force after the World War.

Ship canals. International trade has been promoted by the construction of many ship canals to shorten the voyage between two seas. The Suez Canal, an open cutting through the desert sands, and the Panama Canal, provided with locks, rank as the greatest of these engineering works. The Corinth 

Canal, through the isthmus of that name, enables ships to avoid the long and stormy voyage around southern Greece.

The Kiel Canal, completed shortly before the World War,

Development of Commerce 

637 connects the North Sea with the Baltic. It is owned by 

Germany, but the peace treaty with that country specified that it shall be open without restriction to the mercantile marine of every country. The Welland Canal, which enables ships to go around Niagara Falls, has been recently enlarged to permit the passage of the largest Great Lakes vessels. An ambitious scheme for a waterway, twenty-seven feet deep, between the St. Lawrence River at Montreal and Lake Ontario, is under consideration by the governments of the United States and Canada. Should this scheme be realized, places as far west as Detroit, Chicago, Milwaukee, and Duluth will become deep-sea ports, open to the ocean commerce of the world.

Crises and depressions. Commercial progress has been frequently interrupted during the past century by economic crises and depressions. They are a product of the Industrial 

Revolution. Arising in one country, perhaps as a result of bad banking, overissue of paper money, excessive speculation, unwise investments, or failure of crops, they tend to spread widely until all civilized countries are involved. 

What happens during a crisis is familiar to every one. Capitalists refuse to invest in new railroads, factories, and other undertakings; bankers will not lend money; merchants, unable to borrow, go into bankruptcy; and manufacturers, receiving fewer orders, either reduce their output or shut down their plants. Then follows a period of depression, or "hard times," with low prices, low wages, much unemployment, and widespread destitution. These conditions mean that the purchasing power of the masses is sharply curtailed, and therefore the depression is prolonged. Before “good times" return, many persons have lost their place in the economic order, social discontent has grown, and governments are endangered. Such occurrences marked the early nineteen-thirties throughout much of the world. The conditions thus brought about led, in many countries, to an increase in governmental control and management of business.

150. HUMANITARIAN MOVEMENTS 

Social reform. The "brotherhood of man" was taught by 

Hebrew prophets, by certain Greek philosophers, and by the early Christians, and the medieval Church always preached the natural equality of all men, if not on earth, at any rate in heaven. Our own age is characterized by a great growth of humanitarian sentiment. Social betterment in past ages has been undertaken by religious bodies, by guilds, trade unions, and similar associations, by governments, by private corporations, and by prophets, philosophers, and preachers, working alone or with only small groups of their followers. 

There has usually been little coöperation among social workers. Our own age, however, is notable for the creation of numberless organizations, some local, some national, and some international in character, and all having as their object the improvement of human relations. 

Abolition of slavery. Slavery had all but died out in Christian lands by the close of the Middle Ages. It revived, on a much larger scale, after the era of geographical discovery, which opened up Africa as a source of slaves and America as a field for their profitable employment. Anti-slavery agitation began in the seventeenth century with the Quakers, who excluded slave-owners from membership in their religious society. Denmark was the first country to declare the trade in African slaves unlawful. Great Britain and the United

States took similar steps in 1807-1808. The French revolutionists abolished slavery in the colonies of France, but Napoleon restored it. Great Britain in 1833 passed a law to free the slaves in the British West Indies, paying one hundred million dollars to their former masters as compensation. This measure is a monument to the labors of a great and good man, William Wilberforce, who devoted his wealth, his energies, and his powerful oratory to the cause of the oppressed Negroes. Slavery afterward peacefully disappeared in the colonial possessions of France, Portugal, and Holland, but in the United States only at the cost of civil war. Brazil abol-

639 ished slavery as recently as 1888. It has not yet entirely disappeared from Africa and Asia, where at least five million. human beings are still held in bondage. The final extinction of slavery throughout the world is a task which has recently been undertaken by the League of Nations.

Crime and punishment. The penal code of eighteenthcentury Europe must be described as barbarous. Torture of an accused person, in order to obtain a confession, usually preceded his trial. Only a few countries, Great Britain among them, forbade its use. the jury system did not prevail, trials were usually held in private and without cross-examination of witnesses before an impartial judge. Prisons were private property, and the inmates, whether innocent or guilty, had to pay their keeper for food and other necessaries.

Branding, flogging, and exposure in the pillory formed common punishments for minor offenses. Death was the punishment for murder, arson, burglary, theft, forgery, counterfeiting, and many other crimes. The British code included as many as one hundred and sixty offenses for which the penalty was death. Transportation to America or to Australia was often substituted, however, for the death penalty. Executions took place in public, on the mistaken theory that to see them would deter others from crime.

Reform of the penal code. These appalling conditions aroused much criticism from reformers. An Italian nobleman, Beccaria, had so many constructive ideas for the sci-

entific treatment of crime and criminals that he ranks as the founder of modern penology. His work, On Crimes and 

Punishments, which appeared in 1764, bore early fruit in the general abolition of torture and of such ferocious punishments as burning alive, breaking on the wheel, and drawing and quartering. Penal reform in France was hastened by the Revolution. Great Britain began in the early nineteenth century to reduce the number of capital offenses, until only high treason, piracy, and murder remained. Capital punishment has now been abolished by a number of European countries, including Spain, Portugal, Holland, Norway, ELIZABETH FRY

Much has been done within the past century to improve sanitary conditions in prisons, to abolish striped clothing, the lock step, and other humiliating practices in the treatment of prisoners, and, by means of juvenile courts and reformatories, to separate first offenders from hardened criminals. The idea is now to make confinement less a punishment than a means of developing the convict's self-respect and manhood, so that he may return to free life a useful member of society.

Mentally defective persons are no longer regarded with amusement or contempt, but are rather considered as pitiful victims of heredity or of circumstances for which they are not responsible. Control of intoxicating liquor. The crusade against alcoholism further illustrates humanitarian progress. During the 

World War a number of European countries restricted the manufacture and consumption of alcoholic liquors, and since the war public regulation has continued in one form or another. Sweden and Norway put the liquor traffic (excluding that in beer and light wines) under the control of companies which are themselves controlled by the government. Total abolition of the liquor traffic was long agitated in the United States by the a wall. 

Prohibition Party, by private organizations such as the 

Woman's Christian Temperance Union (under the presidency of Miss Frances E. Willard), and by the Anti-Saloon

League. Maine was the first state to adopt legal prohibition, and many states in the Middle West and the South afterward took the same action. Prohibition sentiment at length led to the adoption, in 1919, of a constitutional amendment (the Eighteenth) forbidding the manufacture, sale, or transportation of intoxicating liquors throughout the country and their importation into it. It was hoped that under prohibition the new generation then growing up would be un-

accustomed to alcoholic liquors and that the habit of using them would die out. Opposition to prohibition, the mixing of political corruption with its enforcement, and the desire to secure additional revenue for the government in the hard years 1929-1933, led to the repeal of the Eighteenth Amendment in 1933. The United States is now experimenting with various methods of State control of the sale of alcoholic beverages.

Philanthropic agencies. Efforts to relieve poverty and suffering have given rise to charity societies, associations for improving the condition of the poor, "community chests," dispensaries, free clinics, free hospital wards, anti-tuberculosis leagues, fresh-air funds, and numerous other philanthropic agencies in both Europe and America. The Salvation Army was started in Great Britain by William Booth, a Methodist

United States and other coun tries. The Young Men's

The Red Cross. The Red 

Cross owes its inspiration to a young Swiss, Henri Dunant, who had witnessed one of the bloody battles of the Austro- Sardinian War (p. 597), and whose experience prompted him to urge the formation of relief societies for the care of sick and wounded soldiers. The result was an international gathering at Geneva in 1864 and the framing of an agreement to lessen the horrors of modern warfare. The ten states

Foundations. Princely and more than princely benefactions for charitable and educational purposes have been made during recent years by men of wealth, particularly in the United States. Andrew Carnegie devoted to public purposes over $350,000,000. His largest and most notable endowment was for the Carnegie Corporation. Its income is to be used for promoting civilization in whatever way seems best to the trustees. The gifts of John D. Rockefeller, Sr., exceed $500,000,000. The Rockefeller Foundation, which was established "to promote the well-being of mankind throughout the world," is his most extensive endowment. The Rhodes Scholarships at Oxford, endowed by Cecil Rhodes, and the Nobel Prizes are also typical of the great international benefactions of our time. 

151. EMANCIPATION OF WOMEN 

Disabilities of women. Woman's position in Europe a century ago was what it had been in the Middle Ages position of dependence on man. She received little or no education, seldom engaged in anything but housework, and for support relied on husband, father, or brother. After marriage she became subject to her husband. In Great 

Britain she could neither make a will nor enter into a contract without his consent. All her possessions belonged to him.

Any money that she earned or inherited was his and might be taken to pay his debts. The law even deprived her of control over her own children. Similar disabilities rested upon Continental women.

Woman's rights. The humanitarian sentiment evoked by the French Revolution began by freeing slave and serf, but presently demanded the emancipation of women also. 

The demand received a powerful impetus when modern industrialism opened new employments to woman outside the home and thus lessened her economic dependence on

man. The agitation for woman's rights has so far succeeded that most civilized countries now permit her to own property, engage in business, and enter the professions on her own account. Her educational opportunities have also steadily widened. Wesleyan College in Georgia and Mount Holyoke 

Female Seminary in Massachusetts were the pioneer colleges for women in America. Both were incorporated in 

1836. Oberlin College (1833) was the first private institu-

This age limit has since been lowered to twenty-one years, to accord with that for male electors. Australia, New Zealand, and Canada have woman suffrage, as well as Mexico, Brazil, and China.

152. DEMOCRATIC EDUCATION 

Elementary education in the United States. The schools of the Middle Ages were neither secular nor public nor free. 

Clergymen taught them, the Church generally controlled them, and the few pupils who attended them paid fees for their tuition. One result of the Reformation was the introduction into some of the German states, Holland, Scotland, and the Puritan colonies of New England of elementary schools supported by general taxation, so that every one might be able to read and interpret the Scriptures intelligently. This free public-school system, which it is the glory of the reformers to have established, gradually spread

throughout the United States during the nineteenth century and became entirely secular in character. No one did more to advance it in this country than Horace Mann. As secretary of the Massachusetts state board of education, he established the first normal school for the training of teachers, and in his annual reports he argued persuasively that common schools are the pillars of democracy. 

Secondary education in the United States. The first 

American high school opened in Boston in 1821. It was for boys exclusively. The Massachusetts legislature, six years later, passed the first law requiring the establishment لال

Outside of this state great difficulties were met in setting up a highschool system. 

Secondary education was expensive and in the opinion of many persons needless. Why should taxes be menius's Orbis Pictus (Illustrated World). In spite of all obstacles, however, the high-school movement has spread everywhere in the United States, until there are now many thousands of such schools offering a four-year course and freely open to both boys and girls. The present tendency to establish junior colleges practically extends the high-school course to six years by adding to it various subjects of collegiate grade.

Public schools in Great Britain. British statesmen for a long time looked with disfavor upon projects for public

Democratic Education 647 schools. Education, they thought, unfits the people for manual labor and nourishes revolutionary ideas. "If a horse knew as much as a man, I should not like to be its rider," declared a peer in Parliament when voting against an appropriation for educational purposes. After the extension of the suffrage to the working classes (p. 580), the government set up for the first time a national system of instruction. "We must educate our masters," it was said. Elementary education in Great Brit- ain is now free, compulsory, and secular. Many parents, however, prefer to send their children to private institutions under the control of the Anglican Church. The public and private schools together have well-nigh abolished illiteracy in 

Great Britain. 

Public schools in 

France. The French revolutionists believed that "next to bread, education is the first need of the people." They prepared 1 

FIRST HIGH SCHOOL, BOSTON, MASSACHUSETTS 

After an old print. an elaborate scheme for public schools, but never carried it into effect. Napoleon also aimed to set up a state system of education through primary and grammar grades to the lycées, or high schools. Lack of funds and of experienced lay teachers handicapped the emperor's efforts, and at the close of the Napoleonic era the majority of French children still attended private schools conducted by the Church. 

France waited until the 'eighties of the last century before securing a truly national system of education. The French government now appropriates large sums for educational purposes, and illiteracy is today practically non-existent.

Public schools elsewhere on the Continent. Prussia began to reorganize elementary education along modern lines as early as the reign of Frederick the Great and carried the work further after her crushing defeat by Napoleon. The public-school movement has made much progress in other Continental countries during recent years. The percentage of illiteracy is still high in Italy and higher still in Spain, Portugal, and the Balkan states, while in Russia (until recently) most of the peasants were too ignorant to sign their names. The Soviet government is now engaged in the colossal task of reducing illiteracy and extending school facilities to its many millions of subjects. Thus Europe comes more and more to agree with the United States that at least the rudiments of an education should be the birthright of every child.

Higher learning in the United States. The American state university, with its wide curriculum of both liberal and practical subjects, is a nineteenth-century innovation. Previous to its establishment private denominational institutions prepared men for the ministry and a few other learned professions. Several southern states (notably Virginia in 

1817) were the first to found universities, but as a movement it really began with the chartering of the University of Michigan in 1837, the year of the admission of that state into the Union. State universities, co-educational in character, are now found in nearly all the commonwealths. Their work is supplemented not only by numerous private colleges and universities, but also by grants from interested persons of wealth and influence. The rapid growth in student enrollment and the enormous increase in endowments are features of recent educational progress in the United States. 

Higher learning abroad. England until the nineteenth century had only two universities (Oxford and Cambridge), Scotland had four, Ireland one, and Wales none. The democratic movement has led to a demand for a wider diffusion of knowledge and greater opportunities to acquire it, so that now there are twenty universities in the British Isles.

New institutions of learning have been founded on the Continent and in South Africa, India, China, Japan, and Latin America, many of them since the World War. They form

153. RELIGION IN MODERN SOCIETY 

Development of religious toleration. The union of Church and state seemed to make conformity to the established religion a requirement of good citizenship. Until about 

1700, non-conformity to the established religion was considered a crime. The government stood ready to punish

it by fines, imprisonment, or even death. A noteworthy step toward religious toleration was taken near the close of the sixteenth century when French Protestants (Huguenots) were granted freedom of private worship everywhere and freedom of public worship in many villages and towns (pp. 412413). In 1689 the British Parliament passed the Toleration Act, granting religious freedom to all Christians except 

Catholics and Unitarians. ists in the Declaration of the Rights of Man announced that no one should be disturbed on account of his religious opinions, provided he did not thereby trouble public order. Frederick the Great established toleration in Prussia. It was secured in the rest of Germany and in Austria-Hungary and Italy only during the nineteenth century. Men of different beliefs have found that they can live peaceably side by side in the same country.

Separation of Church and state. The spread of toleration was accompanied by the separation of Church and state. To 

Roger Williams and William Penn in the seventeenth century belongs the honor of having founded in Rhode Island and in Pennsylvania, respectively, the first political communities where religious matters were taken entirely out of the hands of the civil government. The idea of separating Church and state found expression in the First Amendment to the 

Constitution of the United States. Congress is forbidden to make any law "respecting an establishment of religion." 

This restriction does not bind the several states, but most of their constitutions repeat the federal prohibition. Church and state are absolutely separate in Canada, Mexico, Brazil, and some of the smaller Latin-American countries. In Ireland, the Church and state were separated by the Liberal party under Gladstone. A similar separation now prevails in Australia, South Africa, and other parts of the British Empire; in England, however, the Anglican Church continues as the official religion. In France, both Roman Catholic and Protestant bodies now depend upon voluntary contributions for support. The Russian Communists disestablished

Religion in Modern Society 

651 the Orthodox Church as being an ally of the old tsarist régime. The constitutions of Czechoslovakia, Poland, and republican Spain also provide for the separation of Church and state. Italy continues to recognize Roman Catholicism as the state religion, but grants religious toleration to 

Protestants and other non-Catholics.

New Protestant sects. The multiplication of sects, which began with the Reformation (p. 418), has gone on rapidly in modern times. The Unitarians, who rejected the doctrine of the Trinity, gained followers in Poland and Hungary and later in the British Isles and the 

United States. Seventeenthcentury England produced the Baptists, whose name was derived from their insistence on immersion of adults as the only proper form of baptism. The 

Society of Friends, or Quakers, as they are commonly called, also arose in England at this time. Their founder was George 

Fox, a weaver's son. The 

Quakers rejected all religious ceremonial, had no paid ministers, and observed neither bap- in the possession of W. R. Cassels, tism nor the Lord's Supper. 

JOHN WESLEY 

After a painting by George Romney London.

War and Negro slavery were condemned as unchristian by the Quakers. The Methodists (so called from their methodical ways) of the eighteenth century continued the Puritan tradition in England. Their founder was an Anglican clergyman, John Wesley. He and his associates worked. among the common people and won a large following by the fervor of their preaching and the piety of their lives. The 

Methodists finally separated from the Anglican Church and became an independent denomination. Other sects, including the Adventists, Universalists, and Disciples of Christ, and

even new religions, such as Mormonism, Spiritualism, and Christian Science, have originated in the United States and spread thence to European lands. 

Missions. The conversion of the non-Christian world is the stupendous task to which Christian peoples have addressed themselves since the Middle Ages. The work of 

Roman Catholic missionaries in Christianizing most of the Filipinos and the Indians of Latin America and Canada was largely accomplished in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Several Protestant denominations founded missionary societies in the eighteenth century, and by the middle of the nineteenth century almost every branch of Protestantism, in both Europe and America, had representatives throughout the non-Christian world. Missionaries establish schools and colleges, build hospitals, introduce scientific medicine and sanitation, familiarize the natives with inventions and discoveries, and often succeed in stamping out cruel superstitions, together with such practices as cannibalism and human sacrifice. Native converts become, in turn, the means of extending modern civilization among their countrymen.

The world religions. Perhaps a third of the earth's peoples are Christians. The adherents of Roman Catholicism number possibly 325,000,000; those of the Protestant denominations, possibly 200,000,000; and those of the Greek Church, possibly 150,000,000. Soviet Russia has disestablished the 

Orthodox Church and discourages religious observances; so it is difficult to estimate the number of Greek Christians. 

The Jews are estimated at 15,000,000. For the other world religions the following figures must be considered merely rough approximations: Moslems, 250,000,000; Brahmanists (in India), 225,000,000; Buddhists (China, Japan, Tibet, Mongolia, Indo-China), 525,000,000. The total of all these religious groups does not correspond exactly with the best estimate of the world's population (p. 22). The discrepancy can be explained by the fact that many religions are not included in those listed here.

154. MODERN SCIENCE 

Natural science. The word science is sometimes used to mean learning in general, or organized knowledge. The word is here used, however, in a more restricted sense, as a shortened term for natural science. To us, then, science is systematic, classified, organized knowledge of the world of nature. 

Science thus defined is almost as old as humanity. Modern science, however, really arose during the Renaissance. Investigators then began to hark back to the methods of observation and experimentation which the Greeks had begun. 

Scientific research was promoted also by the invention of printing, which spread knowledge abroad in every land. Observation and experimentation have also been helped by the numerous mechanical inventions which characterize modern civilization. Science now depends on the use of precise instruments of research as much as industry depends on machinery.

Astronomy. Many pages would be needed to enumerate the achievements of modern astronomers. Eighteenthcentury astronomers found a new planet, Uranus; computed the distance between the earth and the moon; and showed that our solar system as a whole is moving toward a point in the constellation Hercules. Nineteenth-century astronomers found another planet, Neptune; measured the distances of some of the fixed stars; and began the colossal task of photographing and mapping the heavens. Twentieth-century astronomers have found still another planet, Pluto. They have also learned much about the temperature of the stars as indicated by their different colors-red, orange, yellow, and bluish-white; about the sizes of the stars; about the incredible number of the stars, and about their equally incredible remoteness. They are so far away that astronomers use for a celestial yardstick the "light year," that being the distance which light, traveling at a speed of about 186,300 miles a second, covers in a year.

Modern physics. Modern scientists have tried to explain

the nature of electrical activity. Benjamin Franklin identified lightning with electricity. Volta succeeded in storing up electrical energy in a cell- the voltaic cell. The German, Röntgen, discovered in 1895 that an electric discharge through gases generates radiations which penetrate many substances opaque to light. Not knowing their character, he called them X-rays. Three years later the Frenchman, Curie, assisted by his Polish wife, obtained from the mineral, pitchblende, the marvelous radium. It is a more intense producer of the X-rays than any other substance, yet wastes 

9th roimh away with incredible slowness. oel Physicists have now found oelab 

Cordes many other radioactive subsve stances and have proved that fewer radioactivity is due to the ans breaking up of atoms, which, instead of being indivisible, as once thought, are themselves composed of particles of electricity. An atom is believed to contain a nucleus, with a positive electric charge, and a number of electrons, negatively

MADAME CURIE 

charged, which revolve with tremendous speed around the nucleus. This amounts to saying that matter is electricity and that electricity is matter. 

Madame Curie and her husband shared with another scientist the Nobel prize for their wonderful discovery, and after her husband's death Madame Curie herself received the prize in 1911 for her distinguished service. After many years of university lectures and continued research in the laboratory, she died in July, 1934, the greatest woman scientist in history. 

Applied physics. During the past one hundred years applied physics has created the Age of Electricity. No one ever did more to make the use of electricity practical than the English scientist, Michael Faraday. By his wellplanned experiments he demonstrated in 1831 the true re-

Modern Science 

655 lation between electricity and magnetism when he produced an electric current by rotating a copper disk between the poles of a magnet. The result was the invention of the electric dynamo; reversed in action this became the electric motor. Then followed the amazing developments which have made it possible to transmit electric power for many miles to light our cities, draw our trains, and run our factories. 

The telegraph, the submarine cable, and the telephone are other results of Faraday's epochal experimentation. More recently, wireless telegraphy and the radio have developed from the discovery in 1887 by the German, Hertz, of the electric-magnetic vibrations known after him as "Hertzian waves." Wireless telephony, telephotography, and television mark still more recent advances in long-distance communication.

Modern chemistry. Greek philosophers had taught that earth, air, water, and fire compose the original "elements" out of which everything else is made. Chemists in the eighteenth century disproved this idea by their work on the gases. 

The discovery of oxygen by the Englishman, Priestley, in 1774, became the corner stone of modern chemistry. About the same time, hydrogen was discovered and water was shown to be a mixture of this gas with oxygen. The Englishman, John Dalton, early in the nineteenth century, advanced the atomic theory of matter by showing that all forms of it acted as if composed of atoms and that these united to form molecules. Thus, the union of two atoms of hydrogen with one atom of oxygen produces invariably a molecule of water (H2O). More recent chemists have demonstrated that all matter exists in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state according to the degree of heat to which it is subjected, and that it is composed of one or more of ninety-odd atoms (called "elements"), which combine with one another in fixed proportions.

Applied chemistry. Applied chemistry has given us illuminating gas, friction matches, powerful explosives such as dynamite and nitroglycerine, Portland cement for concrete

roads and buildings, artificial fertilizers, rayon (artificial silk), aluminum, stainless steel, wood-pulp paper, and beet sugar. Perhaps the most remarkable products of applied chemistry are the derivatives of coal-tar, a by-product of coal when the gas is removed from it. This black, sticky substance, when touched by the chemist's fairy wand, becomes the source of many useful products, including aniline dyes, perfumes, flavoring extracts, drugs, carbolic acid, naphtha, and saccharine. The chemist now creates in his laboratory innumerable substances which had never existed before or else had been produced only by plants or in the bodies of animals.

Modern geology. In the eighteenth century the Scotchman, James Hutton, showed how the rocks had been formed and were still being formed by natural processes. His work was continued in the nineteenth century by the Englishman, Sir Charles Lyell. Lyell sought to explain the changes which have produced mountains, valleys, plains, lakes, seacoasts, and other geologic features. These were formerly explained as the result of sudden violent movements (cataclysms). 

Lyell explained them as the result of the contraction of the globe, erosion by water, glaciers, frost, wind, and other forces working gradually over immense periods of time. The acceptance of this explanation, coupled with the discovery of fossils in the stratified rocks, made it necessary to estimate the age of the earth and of life on the earth by untold millions, instead of a few thousands, of years. 

Biology. Eighteenth-century explorers brought back to

Europe from America and the Pacific many new kinds of plants and animals, thus greatly encouraging their study. 

The careful classification of plants by the Swede, Linnæus, helped to give to botany a more scientific character. His contemporary, the Frenchman, Buffon, performed much the same service for zoölogy by publishing an encyclopedic work on "natural history," which enjoyed wide popularity. 

Modern biological work rests on the discovery (made in the nineteenth century) that all living things, both plants and

Modern Science 

657 animals, are composed of cells containing the transparent jelly, or protoplasm, which is the basis of life. The cell is as fundamental in biology as the atom is in physics and chemistry.

The Darwinian theory. Even before the English naturalist, Charles Darwin, published the Origin of Species (1859), biologists argued that existing plants and animals, instead of being separately created, had evolved or developed from a few ancestral forms. Darwin was the first to show how evolution might have occurred by means of "natural selection." He pointed out that many more individuals of each species are born than can possibly live to rear their offspring; that, in consequence, there is a constant "struggle for existence"; and that the fittest, which survive, are the strongest, the swiftest, the most cunning, the most adaptable. Such characteristics, handed down by heredity, tend to become more and more marked in succeeding generations, until at length entirely new species arise. Investigators since Darwin have made important additions to the evolutionary theory, but we still have much to learn about the origin and progress of life on the earth. 

CHARLES DARWIN 

After a photograph taken in 1868. 

Applied biology. Both botany and zoology have their practical applications. Insect pests are combated and the diseases of plants and animals are counteracted by the researches of trained scientists. There has also been a steady improvement of the domestic plants and animals as the result of careful selection in breeding. The work of Luther Burbank in this field is known to every one. The success of the biologists

with the lower creation has led to proposals for the improvement of man himself by encouraging the union of persons of sound stock and by discouraging or prohibiting the union of those who are unfit in either mind or body. This is the movement known as eugenics, the science of being "well born." 

Our limited knowledge of some of the factors involved in the case of human beings has prevented the extensive application of eugenics.

Modern medicine. The advance of biological science is also responsible for the germ theory of disease. Some time 

LOUIS PASTEUR 

after the middle of the seventeenth century a Dutchman, Leeuwenhoek, who knew how to make better microscopes than any one else of his time, gazed through one of his own lenses at a drop of water and saw it teeming with creatures which wriggled about and devoured food and gave every evidence of being alive. During the nineteenth century the researches of the Frenchman, Pasteur, upon vegetable microorganisms (bacteria) and upon the correspondingly minute animals called protozoa proved that harmful germs are responsible for many diseases.

Pasteur has probably saved more human lives than all the world conquerors have ever sacrificed merely by his advocacy of "pasteurization" of heating liquids until the germs within them are destroyed. Pasteur's beneficent work was soon continued by Koch, a Prussian, who isolated the germs producing tuberculosis and cholera; and in recent years those producing diphtheria, typhoid fever, influenza, pneumonia, lockjaw, bubonic plague, and other A distinguished biologist whose researches laid the foundation for present knowledge of the causes of transmissible disease and of modern methods of prevention. His discovery of a successful treatment for hydrophobia has been the means of saving thousands of lives.

Modern Science 

659 

In some cases counter dread scourges have been identified. poisons called antitoxins are now administered to counteract the bacterial toxins or poisons. Another step in medicine is the discovery that certain diseases are spread in some one particular way. The bite of one species of mosquito causes malaria and that of another yellow fever; lice transmit typhus; the tsetse fly carries the sleeping sickness; and fleas on rats convey the bubonic plague to man. 

No bacteria or protozoa have yet been found for a considerable group of diseases. Some of these are insect-borne, like typhus, and others, like smallpox and infantile paralysis, are called virus diseases. Much study is being given to these diseases in many laboratories. New knowledge is being gained, and we may look forward with confidence to a time when contagious and infectious diseases may be first controlled, and then eliminated from civilized countries. Quarantine regulations are very important in gaining this control. 

Modern surgery. Meanwhile, surgery has been revolutionized by the use of anæsthetics, such as nitrous oxide (laughing gas), ether, and chloroform. Their use in England and the United States goes back to the 'forties of the last century. Not only did they relieve pain, but by producing unconsciousness they made it possible for the surgeon to perform long and difficult operations. These were still attended with great risk of infection until Lister, an English surgeon, discovered that carbolic acid is a powerful germicide, which, applied to wounds, would prevent them from festering. The result of his discovery was the general adoption of antisepsis. Surgeons now pay a great deal of attention to asepsis as well; that is, to methods of keeping their instruments and dressings free from germs or other harmful organisms. Another advance in surgery has resulted from the use of the X-ray, which reveals the presence of foreign substances in the body and the condition of the bones and internal organs. A purely scientific discovery thus comes to have an immediate application to the health and happiness of mankind.

155. MODERN GEOGRAPHICAL DISCOVERY 

Unmapped regions, 1800. Half the globe was still unmapped in 1800. Canada, Alaska, and the Louisiana territory were so little known that a geography published at that time omits any reference to the Rocky Mountains. South 

America, though long settled by white men, continued to be largely unexplored. Slight information existed about the 

Pacific islands and Australia. Much of Asia remained sealed

ROBERT E. PEARY 

to Europeans. Accurate knowledge of Africa did not reach beyond the edges of that continent. The larger part of the 

Arctic realm had not yet been sofic discovered, and the Antarctic realm had barely been touched.

Filling in the map. Discoveries and explorations in the nineteenth century carried forward the geographical conquest of the world. The great 

African rivers were traced to their sources in the heart of what had once been the "Dark 

Continent." In Asia, the headwaters of the Indus and the Ganges were reached; the 

Himalayas were measured and shown to be the loftiest of mountains; Tibet, the mysterious, was penetrated; and the veil of darkness shrouding China, Korea, Indo-China, and other Asiatic countries was lifted. Travelers penetrated the deserts of inner Australia and finally crossed the entire continent from south to north. The journeys of Alexander von 

Humboldt in the Amazon and Orinoco valleys (1799-1804) inaugurated the systematic exploration of South America, while those of Lewis and Clark (1804-1806) opened up the Louisiana territory. Still later, Alaska, the Northwest Territories of Canada, and Labrador began to emerge from

Modern Geographical Discovery 

661 their obscurity. Even Greenland was crossed by Nansen, a Norwegian, and its coast was charted by Danish geographers and the American Peary. 

Arctic exploration. Voyages in search of the Northwest 

Passage had already revealed the labyrinth of islands, peninsulas, and ice-bound channels north of the American continent. Many heroic but fruitless attempts had also been made to reach the North Pole. About 1895 Nansen came within two hundred and seventy-two miles of the pole. An 

Italian expedition, a few years later, got still farther north.

The honor of actually reaching the pole was carried off by des 

Peary in 1909. He bevie traveled the last stagesald of the journey by t sledge over the ice and reached his goal in company with a colored servant and several Eskimos. Nansen's and Peary's journeys showed that no land exists in the all north polar basin.

They have traced the course of the great ice barrier, discovered extensive mountain ranges, and even found volcanoes belching forth lava amidst the snows. In 1907-1909 a British expedition under Sir Ernest Shackleton attained 88° 23' S., or

156. PHILOSOPHY AND THE SOCIAL STUDIES

Greeks. Modern philosophy may be said to begin with

Adam Smith and economics. A Scotch professor of philosophy, Adam Smith, helped to establish modern economics. 

His famous work, the Wealth of Nations, appeared in 1776, the year of American independence. It formed a new declaration of independence for industry and commerce. 

According to Smith, the state should limit itself to only three duties: "first, the duty of protecting the society from the violence and invasion of other independent societies; sec-uri b ondly, the duty of protecting, as far as possible, every member of the society from the injustice or oppression of every Scottish National Portrait Gallery, Edinother member of it, or the medi 

ADAM SMITH 

iods A medallion by James Tassie in the burgh. duty of establishing an exact administration of justice; and thirdly, the duty of erecting and maintaining certain public works and certain public institutions, which it can never be for the advantage of any individual or small number of individuals to erect and maintain." These three duties having been discharged, the state should not interfere any further with that system of natural liberty which leaves every man "perfectly free to pursue his own interest in his own way, and to bring both his industry and capital into competition with those of any other man or order of men."

This is the famous doctrine of laissez-faire (let alone), and it made a profound impression upon business men and statesmen. We have already seen (p. 557) how the doctrine of laissez-faire has been slowly modified in a changing economic world. Adam Smith, however, is still referred to as the classic economist and his famous book is frequently read. 

Sociology. The name sociology for the general study of human society was introduced in the nineteenth century by the French philosopher, Auguste Comte. It was popularized by Herbert Spencer and later writers. Sociologists try to show how languages, laws, moral codes, religions, and customs arise and develop by group action and how the individual is affected at all points by the group or groups to which he belongs. The various social studies, including economics, politics, jurisprudence, ethics, and comparative religion, are usually treated as departments or subdivisions of sociology. 

The new history. The study of history has been much influenced by the sociologists and the economists. It is no longer confined to a narrative in chronological order of political and military events; it is rather an account of the entire culture of a people. Some historical students do not limit their inquiries to civilized man, but also investigate the culture of savage and barbarous peoples, as found today or once found in remote ages. History, so considered, is closely related to anthropology (the study of man), one of the most fascinating of the newer branches of learning. 

157. LITERATURE AND THE ARTS 

Literature in modern civilization. Literature has held an important place in modern life. On the one hand, lyrics, dramas, narrative poems, and novels have reflected the changing interests and problems of modern people; on the other hand, modern civilization has to some extent been shaped by literature. During the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries began the Romantic movement. Its followers shifted the center of their interest from classi-

Literature and the Arts 665 cal standards to the observation of natural scenery and the more romantic feelings of the human heart. Among the 

Romantic writers in Germany may be mentioned Heine and

Goethe (author of Faust), and in England Burns, Byron, Shelley, and Keats. Walter Scott, another writer of this school, used the novel to give a romantic picture of the Middle Ages and chivalry; Victor Hugo used it for the colorful portrayal of the revolutionary movement in France. 

Dickens and George Eliot in England, and Tolstoy in Russia wrote many works picturing the injustices of contemporary life, thus arousing sentiment for reform. The latter half of the nineteenth century produced many famous writers, such as Tennyson, Browning, Carlyle, Lowell, Longfellow, and a host of others. Modern civilization also witnessed the development of realism in literature — an attempt to represent man and his society without idealizing either. The English 

Hardy, the French Zola, and the Spanish Blasco Ibáñez are among the better known writers of the realistic school. 

An age of reading. Common schools, free libraries, cheap printing, and improved illumination (especially the electric light) have made the pleasures of reading, once confined to the cultured few, available for everybody. The almost complete abolition of the censorship of books and newspapers also helped to make the modern period an age of reading. 

Modern music.  knew the pipe-organ, harp, flute, drum, trumpet, and many other instruments.

These were often played together, but with no other purpose than to increase the volume of sound. There was not the slightest idea of orchestration. After the Renaissance new instruments began to appear, including the violin, viols of all sizes, the slide trombone, and the clarinet. Percussion action, applied to the old-fashioned spinet and harpsichord, produced in the eighteenth century the piano. Meanwhile, the symphony, a tone poem combining all musical sound into a harmonious whole, began to take its present form. The great symphonists - Haydn, Mozart, Beethoven, and their successors - thus created a new art to enrich the life of mankind.

mb Another master of music, Richard Wagner, created the musical drama, which unites music, poetry, and acting. Wagner believed that the singer should also be an actor and should adapt both adapt both song and gesture to the orchestra. He vi also gave much attention to the scenery and stage setting in order to heighten the dramatic effect. Painting. Many eminent painters worked during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. As time went on, artists devoted themselves more and more to portraits, landscapes, and other non-religious subjects. They realized that beauty is to be found everywhere, and so they turned to life and nature as a whole for inspiration. The nineteenth-century painters excelled in portraiture, and some of them produced landscape paintings which unquestionably surpass the best work of the "Old Masters" of the Renaissance. Painting flourishes especially in France, where the leading artists receive their training and exhibit their pictures at an annual exposition, the Salon at Paris. The increasing number of art schools, municipal art galleries, and local exhibitions open to the public spreads the enjoyment of painting and sculpture among the masses.

Universal expositions. In modern times men believe firmly in the idea of progress in all fields, particularly in industry. 

Exhibitions of progress in commerce, industry, art, science, and government are held from time to time. The idea of a universal exposition, to which all countries should send the products of their industry and commerce, first took shape in the Crystal Palace Exhibition (London, 1851). Since then

European expositions have been numerous, each one larger than its predecessor. The United States began with the 

Philadelphia Centennial of 1876. This was followed by many other world's fairs. Notable among them were those held at Chicago in 1893, at Buffalo in 1901, at St. Louis in 

1904, at San Francisco in 1914, and again at Philadelphia in 1926. In 1933, in the midst of a world depression, Americans
