158. IMPERIALISM AND WORLD POLITICS 

Expansion of Europe. Colonial expansion, begun by 

Spaniards and Portuguese in the sixteenth century and continued in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries by French, English, Dutch, and Russians, reached its greatest extent during the past hundred-odd years. It is principally this movement which gives such world-wide significance to European history. The languages, literatures, religions, laws, and customs of Europe have reached almost all mankind. 

Colonial expansion and modern industrialism. This wonderful expansion of European peoples and European civilization was largely an outcome of the great industrial changes in modern times. Improvements in means of transportation (railroads, canals, steam navigation) permitted an extensive emigration from Europe into other continents. Improved communication (the telegraph and the telephone) made easier the occupation and government of remote dependencies. The growth of manufacturing in Europe also gave increased importance to colonies as sources of supply for raw materials and foodstuffs, as markets for finished goods, and as places of investment for the surplus wealth accumulated by the capitalists whom modern industrialism created. 

Imperialism. The word "imperialism" conveniently describes all this activity of the different nations in reaching out 671

Imperialism for colonial dependencies. Sometimes imperialism leads to the declaration of a protectorate over a region, or to the marking off a sphere of influence where other powers agree not to interfere. Sometimes it goes no farther than the securing of concessions in undeveloped countries such as Mexico, Brazil, or China. Very frequently, however, imperialism results in the complete annexation of a distant territory, with or without the consent of the inhabitants. 

Imperialism and nationalism. Imperialism is closely related to nationalism in two ways. In the first place, a strong sense of nationalism leads a country to undertake to secure overseas territories. In the second place, the imperialistic ambitions of the great powers more than once led them to disregard the rights of weaker nations in Africa, Asia, and other parts of the world. Great Britain subdued the two 

Boer republics in South Africa. Italy attempted to conquer the independent nation of Abyssinia, and Great Britain, France, Germany, and Russia at one time threatened to divide up China.

Imperialism and democracy. It has been impossible for even the most democratic of modern nations to grant selfgovernment to their rude and backward subjects. Where the level of civilization is higher, as in Egypt and India, the prevailing illiteracy of the inhabitants forms a great obstacle in the way of democracy. Great Britain, however, has raised round herself a circle of self-governing daughters in Canada, Australia, and South Africa, and France permits some of her colonies to send representatives to the French legislature. 

Other instances of the bestowal of free institutions upon native peoples will be referred to as we proceed with the story of European expansion in the Old World.

Imperialism numerous obstacles to exploration: mountain ranges approached close to the sea; rapids and falls hindered river navigation; dense forests and extensive deserts blocked the explorer, and the unhealthfulness of the climate in many regions threatened him with death.

Peoples of Africa. Northern Africa is inhabited by various branches of the white race. The rest of the continent has been held by the black race since prehistoric times. Besides the true Negroes, there are the Bantus, Pygmies, Hottentots, and Bushmen. 

Africa before 1800. Little more than the Mediterranean shore of Africa was known in antiquity. Here were Egypt, the first home of civilization, and Carthage, Rome's most formidable rival for supremacy. 

During the earlier Middle Ages all North Africa fell under

Arab domination. Arab missionaries, warriors, and slavehunters also spread along the eastern coast and established trading posts as far south as the mouth of the Zambesi River.

The vast extent of the continent was first revealed to Europeans by the Portuguese discoveries in the second half of the fifteenth century (p. 390).

The Portuguese imitated the Arabs in founding stations upon 'both the eastern and western coasts, where they did a profitable business in ivory, gold, gum, rubber, and especially in black men, who were seized and exported by thousands annually to be sold as slaves. The merchants of Spain, Holland, France, and Great Britain also shared in this traffic. Europeans did not try to settle in Africa, except at the Cape of Good Hope, where the Dutch had a colony after the middle of the seventeenth century (p. 464).

DAVID LIVINGSTONE

The Opening Up and Partition of Africa 

675 

Opening up the Dark Continent. The penetration of 

Africa has been mainly accomplished by following the course of its four great rivers the Niger, the Nile, the Zambesi, and the Congo. In the last decade of the eighteenth century, the British African Association, then recently founded, sent Mungo Park to explore the Niger River. He and his successors explored the basin of that river and revealed the existence of the mysterious city of Timbuktu, an Arab capital never previously visited by Europeans. Shortly after the middle of the nineteenth century, the sources of the Nile 

River were determined.

About the same time, an intrepid Scotch missionary and explorer, David Livingstone, traced the course of the Zambesi. Starting from the Cape of Good Hope, he worked his way northward and discovered the wonderful Victoria Falls. On one of his journeys, Livingstone disappeared for years; the 

New York Herald sent the reporter, Henry M. Stanley, 01 to find him. In 1871, he found Livingstone in the heart of Africa, greeting him RA Late holis hoffap 

Our vide

SHT Tanottam wog 

HENRY M. STANLEY 

After a photograph taken in 1886. with the historic words, "Dr. Livingstone, I presume?' 

Stanley's second exploring trip in Africa was epoch-making, for he followed the mighty Congo all the way to its mouth. 

The Spanish and Portuguese in Africa. The division of 

Africa among European powers followed promptly upon its exploration. Spain, Portugal, Belgium, Germany, Italy,

France, and Great Britain all took part in the scramble for African territory, particularly during the 'eighties and the 'nineties of the last century. The Spanish possessions are small compared with those of the other powers. Except for

Imperialism the northern coast of Morocco, they are not of great importance. Portugal controls the two valuable regions of Angola and Portuguese East Africa (Mozambique). 

The Belgians in Africa. The possessions of Belgium grew directly out of Stanley's discoveries. He realized what sources of wealth might be tapped in the rubber, ivory, and palm oil of the vast Congo basin and persuaded Leopold II, king of the Belgians, to supply the funds for the establishment of trading stations in that part of Africa. The Congo 

Free State, which thus came into being, formed practically Leopold's private property. The forced labor demanded of the natives and the cruel punishments inflicted upon them stirred up so much criticism in Europe and America that Leopold finally converted his African holdings into a colony called the Belgian Congo. Its area has now been considerably increased by the addition of former German territories. 

The Germans in Africa. Soon after Germany attained national unity, she made her appearance among colonial powers. Treaties with the native chiefs and annexations resulted in the acquisition of extensive regions in Southwest 

Africa, East Africa, the Cameroons, and Togo. They were all conquered by the Allies during the World War. 

The Italians in Africa. Italy was another late comer on the African scene. She secured Eritrea on the Red Sea and 

Italian Somaliland. An Italian attempt to annex Abyssinia ended disastrously, and that ancient Christian “empire” still keeps its independence. Italy's most important African colony is Libya, conquered from Turkey in 1911-1912. The country in Turkish hands was misgoverned and undeveloped, but its fertile coast is well adapted to agriculture, and even the barren interior may become valuable through irrigation. 

The French in Africa. The beginnings of French dominion in Africa reach back to the seventeenth century, when Louis XIV began to acquire trading posts along the western coast and in Madagascar. It was not until the nineteenth century, however, that the French entered seriously upon the work of colonization. France now holds Algeria, Tunis, most of

677 Morocco, the valleys of the Senegal and Upper Niger, part of the Guinea coast, French Somaliland, and the island of Madagascar. The map shows that the African possessions of France exceed in area those of any other power, but they include the Sahara Desert.

Cape Colony. Great Britain has secured, if not the lion's share, at any rate the most valuable share of Africa. Besides extensive possessions on the Guinea coast, she holds a solid block of territory all the way from the Cape of Good Hope to the borders of Egypt. Cape

Colony was captured from the Dutch during the Napoleonic wars. Though small in extent, it had great importance as a half-way station on the route to both India and Australia and also as a convenient basis for expansion northward into the African continent. 

CECIL RHODES 

Natal, Orange Free State, and the Transvaal. The Dutch farmers, or Boers, did not take readily to British rule. Many of them, with their families and flocks, moved from Cape

Colony into the unknown country beyond. This wholesale emigration -the "Great Trek" - resulted in the formation of the Boer republics of Natal, Orange Free State, and the Transvaal. Natal was soon annexed by Great Britain, but the other two republics remained independent. The discovery of the world's richest gold mines in the Transvaal led to a large influx of Englishmen, who, since they paid taxes, demanded a share in the government. The champion of 

British interests was Cecil Rhodes, an Oxford student, who had found wealth in the Kimberley diamond fields. The 

Dutch settlers, under the lead of President Paul Kruger of the Transvaal, were just as determined to keep the govern-

Imperialism ment in their own hands. Disputes between the two peoples resulted in the South African War (1899-1902). The Boers put up a brave struggle for independence, but they were overcome by sheer weight of numbers. 

Union of South Africa, 1909-1910. The war had a happy outcome. Great Britain showed a wise liberality toward her former foes and granted them self-government. Cape 

Colony, Natal, Orange Free State, and the Transvaal soon came together in the Union of South Africa. The Union has a governor-general appointed by the British Crown, a common parliament, and a responsible ministry. Cape Town and Pretoria are the two capitals, and both English and Dutch are official languages. 

British occupation of Egypt. The Egyptians have been subject to foreigners for over twenty-four hundred years. 

The Persians came to Egypt in the sixth century B.C.; then the 

Macedonians under Alexander the 

Great; then the Romans under 

Julius Cæsar; and afterward the

Arabs and the Ottoman Turks. 

Turkish sultans controlled Egypt until the early part of the nineteenth century, when the very able pasha, Mehemet Ali, made himself almost an independent soverast eign. His successors took the title ⚫gn of khedive, or ruler. Their misgovernment gave Great Britain and France an excuse for setting up a Dual Control over Egypt, in the interest of European bankers who had purchased the securities of that country. Financial intervention soon passed into military occupation, as the result of a revolt against the khedive. It was suppressed by Great Britain alone in 1882, France having refused her coöperation. The British now had a free hand in Egypt. In 1914, upon the outbreak of the war

Cape-to-Cairo Railway. Great Britain controls the foreign affairs of Egypt and also keeps soldiers there for the protection of the Cape-to-Cairo Railway and the Suez Canal. 

The strategic importance of Egypt as the doorway to Africa will be much increased by the completion of the Cape-to-Cairo 

Railway. This transcontinental line starts from 

Cape Town, then crosses 

Bechuanaland, Rhodesia, and the Belgian Congo, and will ultimately link up with the railway already in operation between Khartum, Cairo, and Alexandria on the Mediterranean. principal unfinished section is in the Anglo- 

Egyptian Sudan. When completed the line will be nearly six thousand miles in length, of which about two thousand miles will be by steamer on lakes

Suez Canal. The completion of the Suez Canal has likewise put Egypt on the main oceanic highway to the Far East. 

The canal is a monument to the great French engineer, Ferdinand de Lesseps. It was opened to traffic in 1869. The

European control of Africa. A comparison of the map of 

Africa today with a map showing Africa in 1871 reveals how completely the continent has come under the control of European powers during the last sixty-odd years. Not quite seven per cent is occupied by native states (Egypt, Abyssinia, and Liberia). The white population of Africa numbers only about 4,000,000 out of a total population of about 150,000,000. Expansion in this part of the world thus represents conquest by whites, rather than their permanent settlement and home-building. 

160. THE GREAT POWERS IN ASIA 

The European advance in Asia. The Europeanization of 

Asia was not far advanced at the beginning of the nineteenth century. Europe knew only Siberia, which Russia had appropriated, and those parts of India which had been annexed by Great Britain. All western Asia, including Asia Minor,

Syria, Mesopotamia, and Arabia, belonged to the Ottoman Empire and remained unaffected by European influence. 

On the eastern side of the continent lay China and Japan, old and civilized but stagnant countries, whose backs were turned upon the rest of the world. Within the past hundred years, however, European traders, missionaries, and soldiers have broken through the barriers raised by Oriental peoples, and now the largest part of Asia is either politically or economically dependent upon Europe.

British conquest of India. We have already seen how the 

British gained a foothold in India in the eighteenth century (pp. 465-468). Following the Seven Years' War (17561763), the British gradually extended their control over all India. Once the British had settled there, its conquest was almost inevitable. Sometimes the Indian princes attacked the British settlements and were repulsed and conquered;

Imperialism sometimes the lawless condition in the native states led to British intervention; sometimes, again, the British desire to find defensible frontiers resulted in annexations. The entire peninsula, covering an area half as large as the United States, is now under British control. 

British government of India. The East India Company continued to govern India until after the middle of the nineteenth century. In 1857 came the Sepoy Mutiny, a sudden uprising of the native soldiers (sepoys) in the northern part 

"THE LION'S VENGEANCE ON THE BENGAL TIGER" 

A cartoon by Sir John Tenniel which appeared in the English journal Punch for August 22, 1857. of the country. Bloodily conducted, it was as bloodily suppressed. The mutiny disclosed the weakness of company rule and resulted in the transfer of all governmental functions to the Crown. Queen Victoria afterward assumed the title 

Empress of India. A viceroy and the officials of the Indian 

Civil Service administer the affairs of about two-thirds of the country. The remainder is ruled by native princes under British control.

Indian nationalism. Great Britain enforces peace throughout the peninsula, builds railways and canals linking every part of it together, stamps out the famines and plagues which used to sweep away the inhabitants, and has begun

their education in schools of many grades. All this work tends to foster a sense of nationality, something hitherto lacking in India. Educated Hindus, familiar with the national and democratic movements of the last century in Europe, have begun to voice their aspirations for a united Indian nation. This may come in time, together with more and more privileges in self-government. Most of the Indian people are illiterate; old religious hatreds divide them; the caste system (p. 56) stands in the way of establishing a basis of common understanding among them. We can therefore see that the steps by which India could obtain democracy and nationalism upon European or American models would have to be slow. Furthermore, the economic value of India to Great Britain seems to make it unlikely that she will ever voluntarily concede Indian independence. 

Russia in Asia. (1) Russia in northern Asia. The Russians were established in Siberia before the close of the seventeenth century. Their advance over this enormous but thinly peopled region was facilitated by its magnificent rivers, which furnished highways for explorers and fur traders. 

Northern Siberia is a waste of swamp and tundra, where the terrible climate blocks the mouths of the streams with ice and even in summer keeps the ground frozen beneath the surface. Farther south comes a great belt of forest, the finest timbered area still intact on the face of the earth, and still farther south extend treeless steppes, adapted in part to agriculture and in part to herding. The country also contains much mineral wealth. In order to secure an outlet for 

Siberian products, Russia compelled China to cede the lower Amur valley with the adjoining seacoast. On this eastern seacoast, the Russians founded the town of Vladivostok as a naval base. In 1900 Russia completed the Trans-Siberian 

Railway between Leningrad and Vladivostok. There are now important branch lines in Manchuria, thus affording Russia outlets to ice-free harbors on the Pacific, particularly at Port Arthur. (2) Russia in central Asia. Russia also widened her boundaries in central Asia by absorbing Turke-

Aral Sea.

Great Britain and France in southeastern Asia. Indo- 

China, except for the nominally independent state of Siam, is under British and French control. Great Britain holds 

Burma and the Straits Settlements. France holds Tonkin, Anam, Laos, Cambodia, and Cochin-China. All these possessions have been acquired at the expense of China, which formerly exercised a vague sovereignty over southeastern Asia.

Chinese isolation. The rugged mountains and trackless deserts which bound three sides of China long shut it off from much intercourse with the Western world. The proud disposition of its people, to whom foreigners were only barbarians ("foreign devils"), likewise tended to keep China isolated.

Before the nineteenth century the only Europeans who gained an entrance into the "Celestial Empire" were a few missionaries and traders. The merchants of Portugal established themselves at Macao, and those of Holland and Great Britain at Canton. There was also some traffic overland between Russia and China. Foreign trade, however, had no attraction for the Chinese.

Foreign powers push into China. The difficulties experienced by merchants in China led at length to hostilities between that country and Great Britain. The war that resulted is called the Opium War because the question of foreign traffic in opium was involved. The British, with their modern fleet and army, had an easy victory and in 1842 compelled the Chinese government to open additional ports and cede the island of Hongkong. Other nations now hastened to secure commercial concessions in China. Many more ports were opened to foreign merchants; Europeans were granted the right to travel in China; and Christian missionaries were to be protected in their work among the inhabitants.

Foreign powers annex Chinese territory. Foreign aggression was soon followed by annexations of outlying portions

of Chinese territory. Great Britain acquired Burma; France took Indo-China; and Russia secured the Amur district. 

Meanwhile, Japan, just beginning her national expansion, looked enviously across the sea to Korea, a tributary king dom of China. The Chino-Japanese War (1894-1895) fol lowed. Completely defeated, the Chinese had not only to renounce all claims to Korea, but also to surrender to Japan the island of Formosa and the Liaotung peninsula in Manchuria. Japan's gains aroused the jealousy of Russia, who saw the road to an ice-free harbor on the Pacific blocked by the Japanese occupation of the 

Liaotung peninsula. Russia took her grievance to 

France and Germany, and together the three powers induced the Japanese to accept a money indemnity 

THE "BREAK-UP" OF CHINA 

After a cartoon in Punch. from China in lieu of territory on the mainland. The coalition then seized several Chinese harbors and divided much of the country into spheres of influence. The long-expected partition of China seemed at hand. 

The "Open Door" in China. European capitalists, with the backing of their respective governments, entered immediately upon a keen contest for railroad concessions and other public improvements in China. The American government, which at this time had just come into possession of the Philippines (p. 692), felt that all foreigners ought to enjoy equal opportunities for trade and investment of capital in China. 

Accordingly, President McKinley, through his secretary of state, John Hay, proclaimed in 1899 an "Open-Door" policy for China. Great Britain endorsed this policy, and the other

Imperialism powers followed her example. It thus became an accepted principle that no foreign country should enjoy exclusive commercial privileges in any part of the Chinese territories. 

The Boxer uprising, 1900. The foreign powers were not, however, to have their own way in China. A Chinese secret society, popularly called the Boxers because boxing was part of their athletic program, began an anti-foreign movement. 

It spread like wildfire throughout the country. They destroyed European churches, business houses, and residences, and murdered missionaries and native Christians. The foreigners in Peking took refuge within the legations (official residences of foreign diplomats), where after a desperate defense they were finally relieved by an international army composed of European, Japanese, and American troops. The powers then made peace with China and promised henceforth to respect her territory. 

They insisted, however, on the payment of a large indemnity for the damages done during the Boxer uprising. Part of the American share of the indemcended the throne in 1908, nity was later returned to the Chinese, who used it to provide scholarships for

The Chinese Revolution, 1911-1912. Events now moved rapidly. Educated Chinese, many of whom had studied abroad, saw clearly that their country must adopt Western ideas and methods if it was to remain a great power. The demand for thorough reforms in the government soon became a revolutionary propaganda, directed against the unprogressive Manchu (or Manchurian) dynasty, which had ruled China for nearly three hundred years. The leader of the movement was Sun Yat Sen, a doctor of medicine and a Christian in religion. A revolution broke out late in 1911; it spread with great rapidity throughout the provinces, and

in 1912 led to the abdication of the child-emperor. China then became a republic. 

The Chinese republic. The Chinese of the northern provinces differ from those of the southern in physique, speech, and customs. These differences have always kept the two sections apart, and since the revolution have prevented any real unification of the country. Constant struggles between ambitious military governors, together with much brigandage in the interior districts, have also helped to pro-X duce unsettled conditions throughout most of China.

SUN YAT SEN 

Patriotic Chinese honor his memory as the great inspirer of the revolution. They still look forward, as he did, to the creation of a united and democratic nation, able to rule itself and also strong enough to preserve its rights and territories against the encroachments of foreign powers.

The Japanese islands. In the Pacific Ocean, not far east of China, stretches a crescent-like group of islands. There are six large ones and three thousand smaller ones. They constitute Japan. Its inhabitants call it Nippon ("Rising 

Sun"). Little more than one-eighth of the area of Japan can be cultivated, because of its generally mountainous character. Rice and tea form the principal crops, but fruit trees

Imperialism of every kind known to temperate climates flourish and flowers bloom luxuriantly. The deep inlets of the coast provide convenient harbors, and the numerous rivers, though neither large nor long, supply abundant water power. Below the surface lie considerable deposits of coal and metals. 

The Japanese and their civilization. The Japanese are descended mainly from Koreans and Chinese, who displaced the original inhabitants of the islands. The immigrants seem to have reached Japan in the early centuries of the Christian era. Except for their shorter stature, the Japanese resemble the Chinese in physique and personal appearance. 

Chinese and Korean immigrants brought with them their arts and crafts. Embassies from Japan also visited China, in order to learn at first hand the language, customs, and religions of that country. The moral system of Confucius found ready acceptance in Japan, where it strengthened the reverence for parents and the worship of ancestors. Chinese 

Buddhism, introduced into Japan by way of Korea, brought new ideas of the spiritual life and of salvation by prayer and self-renunciation. Writing, literature, philosophy, the fine arts, the calendar, medicine, education, law, official costumes, court ceremonialism, and even the popular superstitions of Japan reflected the abiding influence of China. From the older country the younger country received a cultural legacy comparable to that which the modern nations of Europe have inherited from ancient Greece and Rome. 66 The mikado and the shogun. Like the Chinese, the Japanese had an emperor, or mikado (mi, "sublime," and kado, 'gate"). He reigned, but from the end of the twelfth century onward he did not rule. Another official, the shogun (sho, “general,” and gun, "army"), usurped the chief functions of government. The mikado thus became only a puppet ruler, having the shadow of authority but not its substance. No attempt was made to depose him, however, because of his acknowledged sanctity.

Japanese feudalism. The period of the shogunate also formed the feudal period in Japan. Two-thirds of the arable

land was parceled out among less than three hundred nobles (daimios), who held their estates from the shogun in return for military service when called upon. The daimios lived in fortified castles upon their vast estates and enjoyed all the rights of petty sovereigns. They levied taxes, coined money, administered a rude justice, kept up armies, and indulged in constant warfare with one another. Their knights, or retainers, were called samurai. Far beneath this warrior class came the commoners, grouped as husbandmen, artisans, and traders, the last standing lowest in the social scale. The commoners, though much more numerous than the samurai, really counted for nothing, except to pay the taxes and labor all their days for the comfort and luxury of their superiors. This feudal system presents a close parallel to that which existed in western Europe during the 

Middle Ages. mono

Japanese patriotism. The military ideals of feudalism prevailed in Japanese society. A samurai, the "man that handled the bow and arrow," as he styled himself, was exclusively a fighter. He despised money, regarded all breadwinning pursuits with contempt, and lived only to serve his lord. Fealty to the daimio required him, if necessary, to sacrifice wife, children, liberty, and even life itself. Extreme sensitiveness on points of honor also characterized a samurai; his sword must instantly leap from its scabbard to avenge a personal affront or one to his lord.

This moral code, with its insistence upon courage, loyalty, and personal honor, resembles the code of chivalry which prevailed in feudal Europe. This feudal loyalty did not disappear when feudalism began to disappear in Japan, about seum, London.

Imperialism 

1871. Transformed into loyalty to the nation, as personified in the mikado, it has become the source of that ardent patriotism so characteristic of the modern Japanese. 

Opening the door to Japan. The first European visitors to Japan were Portuguese merchants and Jesuit missionaries, who came in the sixteenth century. The Japanese government welcomed them at first, but finally expelled all foreigners from the country. Except for a few Dutch traders, Europeans were warned not to approach the shores of Japan upon pain of death. Japan continued to lead a hermit life until the middle of the nineteenth century. Foreign intercourse began in 1853-1854, with the arrival of an American squadron of steam warships under Commodore M. C. Perry.

He induced the shogun to sign a treaty which opened two Japanese ports to American ships. The diplomatic ice being thus broken, various European nations soon negotiated commercial treaties with Japan. 

The Japanese revolution. Thoughtful Japanese, in spite of their disapproval of foreigners, could not fail to recognize the superiority of the Western nations in the arts of war and peace. A group of reformers, including many prominent daimios, now carried through an almost bloodless revolution. 

As the first step, they compelled the shogun to resign his office, thus leaving the way open to the mikado, Mutsuhito, to be the actual instead of merely the puppet ruler. Most of the daimios then voluntarily surrendered their feudal privileges (1871). This patriotic act made possible the abolition of serfdom and the formation of a national army on the basis of compulsory military service. Japan later secured a written constitution, with a legislature of two chambers and a cabinet responsible to the mikado. He is guided in important matters by a group of nobles, called the "Elder Statesmen," who form the real power behind the throne. 

Japan adopts Western ideas. The revolutionary movement affected almost every aspect of Japanese society. 

Codes of civil, commercial, and criminal law were drawn up to accord with those of western Europe. Universities

and public schools were established upon Western models. 

European costumes came into use among the official and educated classes. Buildings in the cities began to follow 

Western architectural styles. Railroads and steamship lines were multiplied. The abundant water power and cheap labor of Japan made possible the introduction of European methods of manufacturing. Factories sprang up, and machine-made goods began to displace the products of handwork. Japan thus became a modern industrial nation and a competitor of Europe for Asiatic trade.

Japan becomes a world power. Japan then entered upon a career of territorial expansion in eastern Asia. Her merchants and capitalists wanted opportunities for money-making abroad; her rapidly increasing population required new regions suitable for colonization beyond the limited area of their own islands. As we have learned, the Chino-Japanese War (1894-1895) brought Korea under Japanese influence and added Formosa to the empire. Just ten years later Japan and Russia clashed over Manchuria and the Liaotung peninsula. The inequality of the Japanese in numbers and resources was more than made up by their preparedness for the conflict, their bravery, and the ability of their generals. After much bloody fighting by land and sea, both sides accepted the suggestion of President Theodore 

Roosevelt to arrange terms of peace. The Russo-Japanese 

War (1904-1905) was closed by a treaty signed at Portsmouth, New Hampshire. It recognized the claims of Japan in 

Korea, gave to Japan a lease of the Liaotung peninsula, and provided for the evacuation of Manchuria by both contestants. Russia also ceded to Japan the southern half of the island of Sakhalin. Japan was now a great power. Great 

Britain first recognized this fact and hastened to conclude an offensive and defensive alliance with the "Island Empire." 

Both France and Russia also entered into an understanding with Japan for the preservation of peace in the Far East. 

As the twentieth century dawned, European and Asiatic affairs were inextricably intertwined.

Imperialism 161. WESTERN CIVILIZATION IN THE PACIFIC The islands of the Pacific. Modern Western civilization was carried not only to the mainlands of Africa and Asia, but also to the islands of the Pacific. The principal islands near the mainland of Asia are the Japanese, the Philippines, and the Malay islands (Sumatra, Java, and Borneo). The principal islands unconnected with the Asiatic mainland are Celebes, New Guinea, Australia, Tasmania, and New Zealand.

There are also a vast number of islands and islets, either volcanic or coralline in origin, scattered throughout the Pacific. 

The United States in the Philippines. Magellan discovered the Philippine Islands on his voyage around the world in 1521 (p. 393). For the next three hundred and fifty years the islands belonged to Spain. Upon the outbreak of war between the United States and Spain in 1898, the Philippines were seized by the United States. The Filipinos, who were already in revolt against Spanish rule, also opposed rule by Americans. Over two years of continuous fighting were required to break down the native resistance and to capture their leader, Aguinaldo. The policy of the United States in the Philippines was soon disclosed. Under the direction of Judge W. H. 

Taft, the first governor-general, an amnesty was extended to all rebels who would take the oath of allegiance to the United States. A police force made up of native soldiers and officered by white men was organized to maintain order. The agricultural lands belonging to the friars were purchased for the benefit of the people. Hundreds of American school-teachers were introduced to train Filipino teachers in English and modern methods of instruction. Large appropriations were made for roads, harbors, and other improvements. The 

United States also set up a Filipino legislature, which at the present time is entirely elected by the natives. 

Philippine independence. Agitation by Filipinos for independence continued under American control. Opposition to Philippine independence comes from (1) those who believe that the Filipinos are not ready for self-government, (2) those

Western Civilization in the Pacific 

693 who believe that the United States should keep the islands as military and naval bases, and (3) those whose manufacturing and commercial interests might suffer by American withdrawal. Philippine independence is favored by (1) those who believe in independence on principle, and (2) those whose industries in the United States are adversely affected by the tariff-free goods from the Philippines. American opinion in general seems to favor withdrawal from the islands as soon as the inhabitants have clearly shown themselves capable of maintaining a stable government. The United States, by act of Congress, has afforded the Filipinos an opportunity to secure independence after a probationary period, provided certain conditions are fulfilled. Final action has not yet been taken.

Holland in the Malay Archipelago. The Malay Archipelago forms the largest group of islands in the world. The equator passes through the middle of the group, giving them a tropical climate. The British own part of Borneo and New 

Guinea. By far the larger part of the Malay islands, however, is owned by the Dutch, who seized them from the Portuguese in the seventeenth century. They were transferred in 

1798 from the Dutch East India Company to the royal government. The Dutch have met the usual difficulties of 

Europeans in ruling subject peoples, but their authority seems now to be thoroughly established throughout the archipelago. The government is fairly enlightened, and much progress has been made (particularly in Java) in educating the natives and in bettering their economic condition. Holland freely opens her possessions to traders of other nations. 

Dutch merchants continue, however, to dominate the commerce of the islands.

The Australian Commonwealth. The development of 

Australia, from a small military station and penal colony to a self-governing Dominion of over six million people, ranks among the great achievements of the past century. Australia is the most isolated of all the inhabited continents. 

Captain Cook, on the first of his celebrated voyages (p. 479),

Imperialism raised the British flag over the island continent, the area of which is three-fourths that of Europe and exceeds that of the United States. Australia served for many years as a penal station, to which the British transported convicts. After the introduction of sheep-farming and the discovery of gold in the nineteenth century, more substantial colonists followed.

where the climate is cool and there is plenty of water and pasture land (central and western Australia are desert lands). 

Flocks and herds now form the chief element of Australia's wealth. Wool, beef, and mutton are exported. The value of Australia's agricultural products is now more than twice that of her gold mines, to which her original prosperity was due. Forests and fisheries are important national assets. 

Manufacturing and commerce have increased rapidly in recent years. The five states into which Australia is divided, together with the neighboring island of Tasmania, have

Pan-Americanism 695 united into the Australian Commonwealth. This federation follows American models in its written constitution, its senate and house of representatives, and its high (or supreme) court. A governor-general, sent from England, represents the British Crown.

The Dominion of New Zealand. Twelve hundred miles southeast of Australia are the two islands which form New Zealand. Their temperate climate, abundant rainfall, and luxuriant vegetation attracted British settlers, who now number more than a million. The country was raised in 1907 from the rank of a colony to that of a Dominion, thus taking a place beside Australia among the self-governing divisions of the British Empire. It cannot fail to become a rich, populous, and prosperous country with the opening up of the Pacific Ocean to the civilizing influences which so long centered in the Mediterranean and the Atlantic. 

162. PAN-AMERICANISM 

Expansion of the United States. We have already seen how the United States expanded across the continent to the Pacific (p. 608). In 1867 the United States purchased Alaska from Russia and thus acquired its first non-contiguous area. 

In the last decade of the nineteenth century the United States began to secure possessions overseas. The Hawaiian 

Islands, lying about two thousand miles off the coast of California, were annexed in 1898. The same year saw the acquisition of the Philippines, Guam, and Porto Rico as the result of the war with Spain. The Samoan island of Tutuila and the Danish West Indies (renamed the Virgin Islands) have also come into American hands.

Enforcement of the Monroe Doctrine. We have seen (p. 587) how Napoleon III tried to create a Mexican empire for France, but this breach of the Monroe Doctrine was soon repaired. President Cleveland enforced the doctrine in 1895, when he intervened in a dispute between Great Britain and Venezuela, in order to prevent an alleged en-

Imperialism croachment by the former country upon the Venezuelan boundary of British Guiana. The Monroe Doctrine, though not a part of international law, is now generally recognized by the leading powers. Due to its existence, no new European colony has been established in the New World since 1823. It has preserved the American continents from being overrun and exploited during the last hundred years - a contrast to the fate of so much of Asia, Oceania, and Africa during the same period. The construction of the Panama 

Canal has further involved the United States in the affairs of Latin America. 

Pan-Americanism. The United States is sometimes represented by Latin Americans as a giant nation destined to absorb Mexico, Central America, and the West Indies. This is the so-called "Yankee Peril." It is the purpose of the 

Pan-American movement to establish more cordial relations between the United States and Latin America. Pan-Americanism rests on the fact that the northern republic and her southern neighbors, however unlike in many respects, are one in their independence of Europe and detachment from European concerns, in their governmental system, and in their political ideals. They form a distinct family of nations and ought to coöperate for the promotion of their common interests. If the Monroe Doctrine remains the national policy of the United States, Pan-Americanism, it is urged, should become the international policy of the two Americas. 

Pan-American congresses. The Pan-American ideal may be said to date back to 1826, when Bolívar invited the United States to participate in an international gathering at Panama. 

Congress made the necessary appropriations to send delegates to Panama, but they did not arrive until after the meeting had adjourned. The United States took no part in any subsequent gathering with the Latin-American countries until 1889. In that year James G. Blaine, secretary of state under President Harrison and long an advocate of Pan- 

Americanism, presided at Washington over the first "International Conference of American States," popularly called

Pan-Americanism 

697 the Pan-American Conference. Later conferences were held at Mexico City, Rio de Janeiro, Buenos Aires, Santiago de Chile, and Havana. The Seventh Pan-American Conference met at Montevideo, the capital of Uruguay, in December, 1933. Delegates of twenty-one independent nations of the western hemisphere attended this Conference. The delegates passed a unanimous resolution approving the policy of nonintervention in the internal affairs of one another. 

Pan-American Union. One result of the First Pan-American Conference was the foundation of the Pan-American Union, an international organization maintained in Washington by the twenty-one American republics. It is controlled by a governing board made up of the secretary of state of the United States and the diplomatic representatives of Latin America in Washington. The Pan-American Union has for its aim the “development of commerce, friendly intercourse, good understanding, and the preservation of peace” among all American countries.

CHAPTER XX THE WORLD WAR 

But that old, old, sickeningly monotonous, and heart-rendingly antiquated, oft-repeated experiment of militarism and war, that was tried again in 1914-1918, how the historian of civilization hates to record it. . . . 

- LYNN THORNDIKE 

Our army is in the field, our navy is ready for battle behind them stands the entire German nation - the entire German nation united to the last man.

GERMAN CHANCELLOR TO THE REICHSTAG 

The Past and the Present are in deadly grapple, and the peoples of the world are being done to death between them. 

WOODROW WILSON 

The approaching crisis. We have traced the growth of nationalism and the accompanying development of patriotism in the nineteenth century. We have also traced the remarkable development of science, industry, and commerce in modern times. Finally, we have seen how modern nations reached out across the seas for dependencies on which they could build empires. We shall now see how, out of these developments, arose rivalries, fears, envies, and hatreds that culminated in a world conflict. And we shall see the modern nations almost destroy the civilization they had done so much to create. 

163. THE STRUGGLE FOR ALLIES 

Germany's position among the nations. The German Empire, from the hour of its birth, took the first place on the Continent. In order to create the empire, Bismarck had engaged in victorious wars with Denmark, Austria, and 700

The Struggle for Allies 

701 France. Now that it existed, Bismarck's problem was to win for it friends and allies in the family of nations. 

Germany wins an ally. The "Iron Chancellor" turned first to Austria-Hungary. He had prepared the way for good relations with that country by his moderation in arranging terms of peace at the close of the Austro-Prussian War in 1866. After that war, Austria had begun to seek in the Balkans compensation for the territory which she had lost in Germany and Italy. Bismarck soon had an opportunity to win the good will of Austria by supporting her Balkan policy. 

In 1878, at the Congress of Berlin, which had been called to decide the control of territory in the Balkans, Bismarck supported the Austrian occupation of the Balkan provinces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and successfully opposed the extension of Russian influence in the Balkans. In 1879 Germany and Austria-Hungary made a secret alliance. A significant feature of it was the agreement to aid each other if either should be attacked by Russia or by another power which had the help of Russia. 

The Triple Alliance. Bismarck scored a further triumph in 

1882, when he persuaded Italy to throw in her lot with Germany and Austria-Hungary, thus forming the Triple Alliance. 

Italy, like Germany, was a newly unified country needing friends and allies. Further, Italy was filled with resentment against France, which had just established a protectorate over Tunis. This Turkish province, the region of ancient 

Carthage, contained a large Italian population, and Italy herself had hoped to snatch it from the sultan's feeble hands. 

The Triple Alliance continued unbroken until after the opening of the World War. It was secretly joined in 1883 by the new Balkan country of Rumania. Henceforth, the Triple 

Alliance was in effect, though not in name, a quadruple alliance. Thus within a few years, four important countries were allied together - Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy, and Rumania.

The beginning of another alliance. The creation of the 

Triple Alliance was a challenge to France and Russia. Bis-

marck had avoided throwing France and Russia together by making a treaty with Russia by which she and Germany bound themselves to benevolent neutrality in case either should be attacked. After Bismarck's retirement in 

1890, however, Kaiser William II did not continue the compact with Russia. Thus the way was open for an alliance between autocratic Russia and republican France. Russia, which assumed the rôle of "big brother" to the Slavs in the Balkans, feared Austria-Hungary's aggression in that quarter. 

France was smarting over the humiliation of her defeat by Germany in 1870–1871, and was alarmed at the growing power of that country in European affairs. Thus the time was clearly ripe for a Franco-Russian understanding. Close relations between the two countries were promoted when the tsar's government, in order to build the Trans-Siberian Railway and develop Russian industries, sold large blocks of securities to French investors. A secret military convention or agreement between the two countries was drafted in 1892 and ratified two years later. They agreed that in case either country was attacked by its neighbor, the other country would come to its assistance. France no longer stood alone, and Germany on her eastern flank had a possible enemy. It was the "nightmare coalition" so feared by Bismarck.

The diplomatic position of Great Britain. Great Britain was not yet involved in these Continental entanglements.

She was not a friend of either France or Russia, for the colonial aims of France in Africa and of Russia in Asia clashed with her own. On the other hand, the British attitude toward Germany and the other members of the Triple Alliance was most friendly throughout the period of Bismarck's chancellorship. To avoid giving offense to Great Britain, Bismarck carefully observed Belgian neutrality during the war of 1870-1871, and for the same reason he long opposed the acquisition of colonies by Germany. As the 'nineties advanced, however, Great Britain and Germany began to draw apart. One reason was the amazing industrial development of Germany, which by this time had made her a serious

The Struggle for Allies 

703 competitor of Great Britain in foreign markets. Another reason was the aggressive colonial policy of Germany under 

William II. The most important reason, however, was

Germany's declared purpose to build up a great navy as well as a great army. To the average Britisher the new German navy seemed a dagger pointed at his country's heart. The sympathetic attitude of the kaiser and his associates toward the Boers, both before and during the South African War (p. 678), further disturbed the serenity of Anglo-German relations. Great Britain reaches an understanding with France. The early years of the twentieth century therefore saw Great

Britain seeking new friendships on the Continent. The first step was reconciliation with 

France. Official visits of King 

Edward to Paris and of President Loubet to London were followed in 1904 by a definite treaty between the two countries, adjusting their colonial 66 ENTENTE CORDIALE APRIL 1904 APRIL 1914. 

'AFTER TEN YEARS" 

claims. France recognized the A cartoon by Bernard Partridge, which paramount position of Great appeared in Punch for April 22, 1914.

Britain in Egypt; Great Britain gave to France a free hand in Morocco. Agreements were also made relating to other regions. These agreements were not a formal alliance. They did not provide for military measures, either for offense or defense. Nor did they have special reference to Germany or any other power. They were merely an entente cordiale ("cordial understanding"). Their significance lay in the fact that they healed the ancient feuds between the two nations and prepared the way for closer coöperation in the future. 

The Triple Entente, 1907. Three years later Great Britain and Russia, who for half a century had jealously watched

each other's expansion in Asia, composed their differences. 

The Anglo-Russian agreement in 1907 settled the troublesome questions relating to Persia, Afghanistan, and Tibet in a manner satisfactory to both Russia and Great Britain. 

Thus, by 1907, Russia had an agreement with Great Britain, Great Britain had an understanding with France, and France had an alliance with Russia. This triple relationship constituted the Triple Entente, and was in existence when the 

World War broke out.

The new balance of power. Thus by 1907 the chief European powers were lined up in two great diplomatic camps. 

On the one hand there was the Triple Alliance, composed of Germany, Austria-Hungary, and Italy, with Rumania as a secret ally. On the other hand was the Triple Entente, composed of France, Russia, and Great Britain, with Japan as a definite ally of Great Britain. 

164. THE STRUGGLE FOR COLONIAL EMPIRE 

The new imperialism. European expansion went on rapidly after 1871. One country after another tried to form an empire overseas. This new imperialism was especially fostered by the revival of national sentiment in Europe. 

Both Italy and Germany wished to obtain colonial dependencies where their people could settle and keep the language, customs, and traditions of the homeland. France sought compensation for her “Lost Provinces" by acquiring African possessions. Russia, Japan, and the United States acquired additional territories. Great Britain, the leading colonial power in the world for more than a century, took renewed pride in her dominions and prepared to extend them as occasion offered. European peoples could not compete for markets, trading-posts, spheres of influence, protectorates, and colonies in every part of the world without becoming as bitter rivals abroad as they were at home. Imperialism, as well as nationalism, thus sowed the seeds of future conflict between them.

The Struggle for Colonial Empire

Berlin to Bagdad. A glance at the accompanying map shows that Germany and her ally, Austria-Hungary, together

constituted in Middle Europe a solid block of territory which stretched southeastward toward the Balkans. Beyond the Balkans lay the Ottoman Empire (Turkey), which extended far into Asia. Only the Balkan states lay across the road from Berlin, through Constantinople, to Bagdad in Asiatic Turkey. In his ambition to find Germany a place in the sun, William II turned his attention toward Asiatic Turkey. There, in the fertile regions of Asia Minor and Mesopotamia, he saw many opportunities for German capitalists, merchants, and colonists. The realization of these opportunities was dependent upon easy and quick communication. 

Consequently, the Germans undertook to build a railroad from Constantinople to Bagdad, near the head of the Persian Gulf. Germany would thus have direct connection between 

Berlin and Bagdad. Much of the line had been completed by the opening of the World War. German capitalists also began to construct branch lines in western Asia. These plans naturally aroused the suspicion and jealousy of England, who felt that her control of the Suez Canal and the route to India was endangered. In addition, the kaiser had announced himself as the protector of all Mohammedans, many of whom now lived in colonies or protectorates of England, France, and Russia.

Austria-Hungary annexes two Balkan provinces. Germany's "peaceful penetration" of Asiatic Turkey formed only a part of the kaiser's policy. European Turkey, the 

Balkan states, and Austria-Hungary were to unite with Germany in a huge combination for purposes of offense and defense. The success of this scheme for a "Middle Europe" seemed to be furthered by the annexation of two Balkan provinces. Taking advantage of a revolution in Turkey, Austria- 

Hungary in 1908 annexed Bosnia and Herzegovina. These two provinces had been freed from the Turks by Serbia and Russia, but the Congress of Berlin had handed them over to Austria-Hungary to occupy and administer. Their annexation raised a storm of protest in Serbia. The inhabitants of 

Bosnia and Herzegovina are Slavs, and Serbia expected some

The Struggle for Colonial Empire 

707 day to unite them and the Montenegrins into a Jugoslavic (South Slavic) state to stretch from the Danube to the Adriatic. Russia also seethed with indignation at what she considered an affront to Slavic peoples by a Germanic power:

Russian troops now began to move toward the Austrian border. Germany ranged herself on the side of Austria- 

Hungary. Both France and Great Britain refused to join 

Russia in a general European war, and that country, not yet recovered from the struggle with Japan, thereupon gave way, withdrew her support from Serbia, and looked on in deep humiliation while the Central Powers (Germany and Austria-Hungary) proceeded to reap the fruits of their diplomatic triumph.

The Central Powers gain another triumph in the Balkans. 

The First Balkan War (1912-1913) produced another international crisis. Early in the course of the struggle the 

Serbians seized a port in the Turkish province of 

Albania, in order to gain access to the Adriatic. The 

Montenegrins also captured an important Albanian town. Austria- 

Hungary would not consent to these annexations, which barred her

A general European war again seemed near, until Serbia and Montenegro yielded to the pressure put upon them by the great powers and gave up their conquests. The result was the formation of a new Albanian state under Ger-

The Balkan situation in 1913. The Second Balkan War 

(1913), however, had one outcome disappointing to the Central Powers. The Treaty of Bukharest, closing the war, left 

Germany's vassal, Turkey, with only a footing in Europe; it humiliated Bulgaria, the friend of Austria-Hungary; and it planted a hostile Serbia squarely in Macedonia, where she blocked the "Middle Europe" scheme. Even before the treaty had been signed, Austria-Hungary made ready to attack Serbia, but held her hand when Italy refused to coöperate, on the ground that the terms of the Triple Alliance required its members to aid each other only in the case of a defensive war. Germany also seems to have dissuaded Austria-Hungary from undertaking her perilous adventure in 1913. But the hour for a general European conflict was just about to strike. 

165. THE STRUGGLE FOR MILITARY AND NAVAL SUPREMACY 

Armed peace. Between 1871 and 1914 there were wars in the Balkans, in Asia, and in Africa. The nations of western 

Europe, however, did not draw the sword against one another. Yet at no other period had there been such enormous expenditures for armaments, huge standing armies, and colossal navies. Western Europe enjoyed peace, but it was an "armed peace" based upon fear.

New means of destruction. The improvements in weapons after 1871 made warfare a branch of applied science requiring expert technical knowledge both on the battlefield and in the munitions factory. The new or perfected means of destruction included the breech-loading rifle, machine gun, and smokeless powder, together with the continuous enlargement of cannon and the use of long-range, high-explosive projectiles. In death-dealing efficiency these new means of destruc-

The Struggle for Military and Naval Supremacy 709 

tion threw all previous inventions into the shade. Having done so much to create modern civilization, science seemed ready to destroy it. 

Europe becomes an armed camp. The wars of early modern times were fought by comparatively small armies After Partridge London Punch 

"THE BLESSINGS OF PEACE" 

Hans and Jacques (together): "And I hear there's more to come!" 

A cartoon that appeared in Punch, February 26, 1913. made up of volunteers and hired soldiers. Gradually, however, the idea arose of the "nation in arms" throwing its entire man-power into a struggle with other nations. The 

French revolutionists introduced a general levy, or conscription (p. 499), and Napoleon continued this method of filling

the depleted ranks of his soldiers. Prussia, after her defeat by Napoleon, adopted universal military service in time of peace as well as in time of war. All able-bodied men were to receive several years' training in the army and were then to pass into the reserve, whence they could be called to the colors upon the outbreak of hostilities. During the nine- 

"VISITING GRANDMAMMA" 

Queen Victoria: "Now, Willie dear, you've plenty of Soldiers at home; look at these pretty Ships 1

European nations, except Great Britain, adopted this system.

Europe thus became an "armed camp," with five million men constantly under arms and with more millions immediately ready for the call to arms. 

Rivalry on the sea. 

Great Britain found sufficient protection in her fleet. It had long been the British policy to maintain it at a strength at least equal to that of any two other powers. Germany, however, would not acquiesce in British maritime supremacy. Under the inspiration of the kaiser 

Germany started to build a mighty navy. Helgoland, off the mouth of the Elbe, was converted into a naval base, a second Gibraltar. The Kiel Canal, originally completed in 1896, was enlarged in 1914 to allow the passage of the largest warships between the Baltic and the North Sea. Great Britain watched these preparations with unconcealed dismay. Her answer was the complete reorganization of the British fleet, the scrapping of nearly two hundred vessels as obsolete, and

The Struggle for Military and Naval Supremacy 711 

the laying-down of dreadnoughts and super-dreadnoughts.

The naval rivalry threatened to become so enormously expensive that British statesmen twice proposed a “naval holiday," that is, an agreement to keep down the rate of increase. Germany refused to enter into an arrangement which would have left Great Britain still mistress of the seas. 

Peace proposal of Nicholas II, 1898. The crushing burden of standing armies and navies produced a popular agitation in many countries to abolish warfare. The movement took practical shape as the result of a proposal by Tsar Nicholas II for an international conference, which should arrange a general disarmament. On August 24, 1898, the diplomatic representatives attending the weekly reception at the court of St. Petersburg were handed a circular in which the tsar and his minister for foreign affairs described with remarkable clarity and insight the exact state of affairs then existing between the nations of Europe. The tsar's circular read in part as follows: "The preservation of peace has been put forward as the object of international policy. In its name the great states have concluded between themselves powerful alliances; the better to guarantee peace, they have developed their military forces in proportions hitherto unprecedented, and still continue to increase them without shrinking from any sacrifice. All these efforts, nevertheless, have not yet been able to bring about the beneficent results of the desired pacification. . . . It appears evident, then, that if this state of things continues, it will inevitably lead to the very cataclysm which it is desired to avert, and the horrors of which make every thinking being shudder in anticipation."

Peace conferences at The Hague. As the result of the tsar's proposal, delegates from twenty-six sovereign states met in 1899 at The Hague, Holland, in the first International 

Peace Conference. A second International Peace Conference of forty-four sovereign states assembled in 1907. Attempts were made at these gatherings to lessen the horrors of future wars by prohibiting, for instance, the use of asphyxiating gases and the dropping of projectiles from balloons.

Neither conference could agree, however, to limit armaments or military expenditures, much less to provide for general disarmament. 

166. HOW THE WORLD WAR BEGAN 

The Sarajevo assassination. On June 28, 1914, the heir to the Austrian throne and his wife were assassinated at Sarajevo, the capital of Bosnia. The heir was the archduke 

Francis Ferdinand, nephew of Francis Joseph I, the Hapsburg emperor of Austria-Hungary. The murderers, who were 

Bosnians and therefore Austrian subjects, had been supplied with weapons from a Serbian arsenal and by a Serbian officer belonging to a secret society called the Black Hand. 

It is now known (though not at the time) that some members of the government of Serbia were aware of the plot and failed to prevent the impending tragedy. The Sarajevo assassination was therefore a political crime, the natural outcome of the propaganda among the Jugoslavs (South Slavs) for the expulsion of Austria from the Balkans as she had been expelled from Italy and Germany.

Austria's ultimatum to Serbia. Nearly a month passed. 

Then on July 23 Austria-Hungary sent a note to Serbia, harsh, peremptory, and, except in name, an ultimatum. It demanded that Serbia suppress anti-Austrian publications and societies; dismiss from the army or the civil service all those having anything to do with the anti-Austrian propaganda; get rid of anti-Austrian teachers and textbooks from the public schools; and allow representatives of the Austro- 

Hungarian government to take part in the Serbian investigation of the Sarajevo crime. Forty-eight hours only were granted for the unconditional acceptance or rejection of the ultimatum.

Serbia's reply. Serbia replied within this time limit and agreed to all the Austrian demands except those which required the presence on Serbian soil of representatives of the Dual Monarchy. Such an arrangement, Serbia pointed out,

would violate her rights as a sovereign state- would make her, in fact, an Austrian vassal. She also expressed willingness to submit the entire dispute to arbitration by the Hague Tribunal (p. 758) or to the mediation of the great powers. 

Austria-Hungary rejected the Serbian reply as unsatisfactory; on July 28 declared war upon her little neighbor; and on 

July 29 bombarded Belgrade, thus firing the first shots of what was to be the World War.

How other European countries were brought into the quarrel. So far, the conflict was between Austria-Hungary and the small Slav state of Serbia. But Russia, the “big brother" of the Slavs in the Balkans, could not allow the conquest of Serbia. Yet if Russia attacked Austria-Hungary, Germany must come to the aid of her ally, Austria-Hungary; and France, bound to Russia in firm alliance, would then be obliged to attack Germany. The alliances of the great powers, instead of preserving peace, thus threatened to involve most of Europe in war. Efforts to prevent such a catastrophe began at once. European peace could be kept only if Austria-Hungary and Russia were prevented from clashing.

Attitude of Austria-Hungary and Germany. The Triple 

Entente first asked Austria-Hungary to extend the time limit for the answer from Serbia. Austria-Hungary refused the request. Great Britain and France then urged Serbia to make her answer to the ultimatum as conciliatory as possible. 

After the Serbian reply had been delivered, Great Britain, through Sir Edward Grey, minister for foreign affairs, suggested that the four great powers not directly involved should hold a conference in London to adjust Austro-Serbian relations. France, Italy, and Russia accepted the suggestion. 

Germany would not do so, on the ground that the whole dispute concerned only Austria-Hungary and Serbia. 

Attitude of Russia and France. Russia had yielded to the Central Powers in the Balkan crises of 1908 and 19121913 (p. 706). This time, however, her foreign minister did not back down. This time he could count unreservedly

How the World War Began 

715 upon French support, which had been lacking in previous crises. Raymond Poincaré, the very influential president of France, and his colleagues in the government, had made it perfectly clear to the tsar's advisers that, in case hostilities broke out, France would "fulfill her obligations under the alliance." When, therefore, news came of the bombardment of Belgrade, Russia started a partial mobilization of her armies along the Austrian frontier. This was soon extended into a general mobilization upon the entire western border of the Russian Empire. Russia thus served notice on the Central Powers that she would fight rather than merely look on while they deprived Serbia of independence and destroyed Russian influence in southeastern Europe. bo sub tol yd 971 don 

Germany declares war on Russia and France. Russian general mobilization compelled Germany herself to mobilize and at once. She could not afford to wait until her slower-moving antagonist had brought enormous forces into the field. The kaiser's government, accordingly, sent an ultimatum to Russia ordering that country to start demobilization within twelve hours or accept the consequences (July 31). Russia did not reply. The kaiser then signed the document declaring that a state of hostilities existed between Germany and Russia (August 1). 

War with Russia meant also war with France, the ally of Russia. Asked by Germany what was to be her attitude in the coming struggle, France replied that she "would do that which her interests dictated," and began to mobilize. Germany then declared war on France (August 3). 

WILLIAM II

Great Britain declares war on Germany. The German plan of campaign involved a swift, crushing blow at the French before Russian mobilization could be completed. 

This rapid movement against France would have to proceed through the small neutral state of Belgium, for a comparatively level plain, well provided with roads and railways, stretches from Germany through Belgium and France to the environs of Paris; furthermore, France had not so strongly fortified her frontier on the side of Belgium. But the neutrality of Belgium had been guaranteed by the European powers, including France and Prussia, in both 1831 and 1839; furthermore, Great Britain had for centuries regarded it as essential to her own well-being that no strong military power should occupy the Belgian coast and thus threaten British control of the Channel. Germany, in her moment of necessity, decided to disregard these two obstacles to crossing through Belgium. The German government addressed a note to Belgium, demanding permission to move troops across that country into France. Belgium refused permission, and the German army then entered Belgium by force (August 4). When news came that German troops were entering Belgium, the British government sent an ultimatum to Germany, requiring assurances by midnight that 

Belgian neutrality would be respected. Germany would not give them. About midnight, August 4, Great Britain declared war on Germany.

The opposing forces at the outbreak of the war. (1) The 

Allies at the outbreak of hostilities quickly converted the 

Triple Entente into a triple alliance. Great Britain, France, and Russia engaged not to make peace separately and to accept a general peace only on terms agreeable to all of them. 

Great Britain, with her fleet, her money, and eventually her army, formed the keystone of the coalition. (2) The 

Central Powers, though less populous and wealthy than their antagonists, possessed in the German army the finest war machine in the world. They also had unity of command. for the German general staff largely directed military oper-

ations. Above all, they were prepared. Austria-Hungary had already massed part of her army against Serbia, while Germany, by means of her strategic railroads, could move and concentrate troops on her eastern and western frontiers with greater speed than either Russia or France. Should it prove to be a short war, the Central Powers seemed likely to win an overwhelming victory. 

167. EVENTS OF THE WAR 

Our interest in the war. The details of the World War are of great significance to military engineers and students of military history. Even the average citizen of the world in 1914-1918 was interested in the details of a half-mile advance on a remote sector of the battle-front. Often he followed his daily newspaper closely for such details. With the lapse of time, however, the average citizen loses his interest in the details of dates, numbers of soldiers engaged, and areas conquered or lost. Today it is sufficient for most of us if we can grasp the general course of the war; if we can appreciate the vast numbers who took part, the enormous costs, the countries engaged, and the general movement of events. Therefore let us try to take a bird's-eye view of the World War.

The Allies save Paris. Hostilities between the two opposing sides began on the western front. The German army moved through the tiny duchy of Luxemburg, and then into Belgium. Belgian resistance delayed by at least twelve days the arrival of the Germans on the frontiers of France. 

The French thus gained time to complete mobilization and the British to send an expeditionary force of a hundred thousand men. The Anglo-French army retired before the 

German invaders, who crossed the Marne River and came within fifteen miles of Paris. The battle of the Marne lasted an entire week (September 6-12, 1914); it was a series of conflicts in which 2,500,000 men participated along a front of more than a hundred miles. The Germans were

finally forced back with heavy losses of men and materials on both sides. German plans for a speedy triumph had been upset and Paris had been saved.

Deadlock on the western front. Both sides now bent every effort to extend their lines northward to the sea. The 

Allied forces (British and French) reached the sea first, and in the first battle of Ypres (October-November, 1914) maintained their lines against a determined attack by the Germans. Fighting now became general along a six-hundred mile front extending from the Vosges Mountains on the 

Swiss border to the North Sea. Along this crooked front, both sides dug deep trenches, from which small groups issued from time to time, crossed a deadly “no man's land,” and hurled shells and explosives into the opposing trenches.

Large and concerted efforts along the whole front were made by both sides. Outstanding among these far-flung engagements were (1) the second battle of Ypres (April- 

May, 1915); (2) the five months' siege of Verdun by the

Germans (February-July, 1916); and (3) the battle of the 

Somme (July-November, 1916). In the spring of 1917 

the German army, under General Hindenburg, retired to a shorter and more defensible line nearer the German frontier. 

From April to December, 1917, the Allies moved into the territory evacuated by the Germans and conducted a steady offensive against the apparently unbreakable Hindenburg line. The approach of winter put an end to active operations, and the deadlock on the western front continued into another year.

Russia's part in the war, 1914-1917. There was no deadlock on the eastern front. As soon as the war started, the 

Russians began to put large forces in the field. They planned a simultaneous advance against (1) the Germans in East Prussia and (2) the Austrians in Galicia (a province on the eastern frontier of Austria-Hungary). In East Prussia the 

Russians met misfortunes. In the first month of the war (August, 1914), Russian armies which entered East Prussia were surprised and almost annihilated by Hindenburg at

the battle of Tannenberg. The following January (1915), the Russians again entered this part of Germany, but were again overwhelmingly defeated. In Galicia the Russians had better luck. They overran all this Austrian province and by the spring of 1915 began to penetrate the Carpathian passes into Hungary. German troops were then brought over from the western front, Hindenburg took command of the eastern armies of the Central Powers, and they started a terrific "drive" in Poland and Galicia. The Russians were hampered by lack of guns and ammunition; the Germans made full use of poison gas and a smothering fire of high-explosive shells. By the end of 1915, the Central 

Powers had extended their conquests in the east until that front stretched from the Gulf of Riga to the Rumanian frontier (see map on the next page). The following year (1916), the Russians made a successful counter attack. By the opening of 1917, however, Russia's part in the World War had been played. The inefficient government of the tsar was collapsing, and the Russian Revolution of 1917 was at hand. The group of revolutionists who finally gained control in Russia did not approve of the war and made peace with the Central Powers. The story of this revolution and its results will be told in the next chapter. 

Turkey in the war. Turkey was largely controlled by 

Germany, and, fearful of Russia's designs on Constantinople, she entered the war on the side of the Central Powers soon after the outbreak of hostilities. The Allies tried to strike a blow against Turkey by capturing Constantinople itself. An

Anglo-French fleet in 1915 tried vainly to reach that city by forcing their way through the Turkish defenses of the Dardanelles Straits. The Anzacs (so called after the initials of the words "Australian and New Zealand Army Corps") made heroic efforts to secure a footing on the peninsula of Gallipoli, and the troops were finally withdrawn from this graveyard of Allied hopes. 

The war in the Balkans. Turkey was cut off from her associates in central Europe by the belt of Balkan states
