stretching across southeastern Europe. These included Serbia, Montenegro, Bulgaria, Rumania, Albania, and Greece.

As soon as the war broke out, Montenegro joined Serbia against the Central Powers. Three of the states, however 

Bulgaria, Rumania, and Greece - at first remained neutral.

Bulgaria had both geographic and racial reasons to fear Austria-Hungary, but she remembered that Serbia had been her most successful foe in the Second Balkan War (p. 708).

After long hesitation, Bulgaria threw in her lot with the 

Central Powers (October, 1916). The situation in the Bal kans thus changed over night. Little Serbia, which earlier in the war had twice expelled the Austrians, quickly collapsed under the double attack of Austro-Germans from the north and Bulgarians from the east. Serbia's ally, Montenegro, was likewise overrun, together with northern Albania. 

These successes of the Central Powers opened railway communications between Berlin and Constantinople. Rumania, however, decided (August, 1916) to join the Allies. Her armies promptly invaded Austria-Hungary. A counterstroke by Germans, Austrians, and Bulgarians drove them out and led to the conquest of two-thirds of Rumania. The 

Rumanian collapse brought enormous advantages to the Central Powers. They now had access to the grain fields and oil wells of Rumania, their battle-front was shortened by five hundred miles, and their communication with Bulgaria and Turkey was made easier. In Greece, King Constantine managed to preserve neutrality until the middle of 1917. 

Then the Allies, having lost nearly all the Balkans and fearing that Greece would join the Central Powers, entered Greece and deposed King Constantine. At the same time, Venizelos, a vigorous champion of the Allies, became prime minister of Greece. Thus by 1917, in southeastern Europe, the Allies held control of but one country, Greece. 

Italy in the war. Italy, it will be remembered, before 1914 was allied with Austria-Hungary and Germany. She did not, however, enter the war in 1914, claiming that she was not bound to assist the Central Powers in a war in which she

regarded them as the aggressors. The Allies accordingly sought Italy's help. They offered Italy an opportunity to secure (1) Italia Irredenta, namely, those regions around

Trent and Trieste still "unredeemed" from the grasp of Austria-Hungary (p. 599), and (2) a share of Turkish territory. Italy accordingly entered the war in May, 1915, on the side of the Allies. The entrance of Italy added another front and almost completed the encirclement of the Central Powers. After some of the most daring fighting of the whole war, the Italians began to make their way toward Trieste, during the summer of 1916. But the break-up of Russia after the Revolution freed large forces of the Central Powers for service against Italy. Late in 1917, an Austro-German attack forced the Italians back as far as the Piave River. 

There, with the help of French and British troops, the Italians made a firm stand.

The Allies and the Central Powers, 1917. The military situation in Europe at the end of 1917 clearly favored the 

Central Powers. On the western front they held Luxemburg, nearly all of Belgium, and a broad strip of northern France containing valuable coal and iron mines. On the eastern front they held the richest industrial districts of the Russian 

Empire. They had overrun Serbia, Montenegro, northern

Albania, and a large part of Rumania. They had taken most of Venetia from the Italians. Their own territorial losses to the Allies were insignificant in area and population. A different picture, however, was presented outside of Europe and on the sea. 

The Allies capture the German colonies. The sea-power of the Allies enabled them to capture Germany's colonial possessions. In Africa, the German colonies were taken over by the British and French, aided by Boers and Belgians. In the 

Pacific, German possessions south of the equator were conquered by the Australians and New Zealanders, and those north of the equator (including Kiauchau in China) were captured by the Japanese.

The Allies free Turkish subjects. Turkey also lost her

outlying possessions. (1) Great Britain proclaimed a protectorate over Egypt and set up a new ruler, who was to be independent of the sultan at Constantinople. (2) The British encouraged a revolt of the Arabs against the Turks. Arab troops secured Mecca and Medina, the sacred places of Arabia, and established the kingdom of Hejaz, which extends along the eastern coast of the Red Sea. (3) An expeditionary force under the British invaded Mesopotamia by way of the Tigris River and entered Bagdad in triumph. (4) Another British army, starting from Egypt, invaded Palestine and took possession of Jerusalem. The Holy City, after nearly seven centuries, was again in 

Christian hands. 

THE VICTORIA CROSS 

Established in 

1856 for acts of bravery in battle. It is a bronze Maltese cross with the royal (lion and crest crown) in the center and below it a scroll

Allied control of the sea. The fleets of the Allies quickly swept the merchantmen of the Central Powers from the ocean, and compelled their warships to keep the shelter of home ports. Once only did the German our." fleet slip out of Kiel harbor, to be met by the British battle 1291 891 inscribed "For Valcruisers off the coast of Jutland (May 31, 1916). Both sides suffered heavy losses in the engagement which followed. With the approach of darkness, however, the German ships returned to their safe anchorage and did not emerge again during the remainder of the war. Allied control of the sea led to an immediate blockade of Germany and Austria-Hungary. Three results followed. The Allies were able freely to import food and raw materials from their colonies and neutral states. They kept the ocean lanes safe for the transportation of troops from Africa, India, Australia, and Canada. They also destroyed the commerce of the Central 1914 

THE IRON CROSS

Powers, who were henceforth hard pressed to find the necessary sinews of war for their armies and food for their civilian population.

The blockade. The Allied blockade of the Central Powers became more and more stringent. At first, it prevented the importation into Germany only of munitions and other materials used for military purposes. In 1915 Great Britain also declared foodstuffs contraband, and as such liable to seizure if carried from neutral countries in neutral ships to Germany. 

The Central Powers relied on submarines (U-boats) to break the blockade. During the first months of the war the submarines attacked only enemy warships, but before long they began to destroy without warning enemy merchantmen. 

After the British made food contraband, Germany declared the waters around the British Isles a "war zone," where all enemy merchantmen would be sunk, whether or not passengers and crews could be rescued. Neutral vessels were warned against trespassing within the zone. The attempt to enforce such a blockade brought about the entrance of the 

United States into the World War.

How the United States was brought into the war. When the war broke out, President Wilson declared the neutrality of the United States. But neutrality proved impossible. In the first place, American citizens could not avoid being interested in the war and taking one or the other side. In the second place, the American government could not avoid being drawn into diplomatic controversies with both sides. President Wilson made repeated and vigorous protests to Great Britain regarding the infringements by that country of our neutral rights at sea, especially the keeping of American ships in British ports to determine whether or not the ships carried contraband goods. Germany's proclamation of a "war zone" raised a more serious issue. President Wilson protested at once, declaring that the United States would hold the German government to a “strict accountability” for American ships destroyed or American citizens killed. Germany disclaimed all responsibility for "accidents" which

might occur. U-boats proceeded to torpedo the great 

British liner Lusitania, with the loss of 1195 persons, including over one hundred American men, women, and children (May 7, 1915). American ships and those of other neutral nations were also sunk. A "war of notes" between the 

United States and Germany resulted in a German pledge not 50 30 60-20 10

However, in January, 1917, Germany withdrew her pledge and notified the American government of her purpose to sink at sight all ships, both enemy and neutral, found within areas near the British Isles and France, and in the greater part of the Mediterranean. Only narrow "safety lanes" to one British port and to Greek waters were left open for a limited amount of neutral traffic inside the barred zone. President Wilson then

broke off diplomatic relations with the German government. 

Upon his advice, Congress declared war against Germany on April 6, 1917. Similar action was taken as to Austria- 

Hungary in December of the same year. Diplomatic relations with Turkey and Bulgaria were severed, but war was not declared against these two countries. 

A world "safe for democracy." The people of the United 

States, the President said, had no quarrel with the people of the Central Powers, who were led blindly into the war by their autocratic governments. Our quarrel was with these governments alone. The United States, in consequence, asked nothing for herself— neither annexations nor indemnities. She fought to uphold the freedom of the seas, to defend the rights of small nations and oppressed nationalities, to put down divine-right monarchy, secret diplomacy, and militarism, to promote among mankind that ordered liberty under law which she had long enjoyed, and to make the world "safe for democracy." 

The United States 

Part of the navy 

War preparations of the United States. prepared on a colossal scale for the war. was immediately sent to Europe, including a number of torpedo boats and destroyers to fight the German submarines. 

Our naval forces, with some assistance from those of Great Britain, also planted more than seventy thousand mines in the North Sea for a distance of two hundred and forty miles from the Orkney Islands to the coast of Norway. This deadly marine barrage shut out German submarines from ingress into the Atlantic, for the narrow Strait of Dover had already been closed by mines and nets. The government adopted conscription as the most rapid and democratic method of raising an army, and two months after the declaration of war over ten million young men were registered for service. Officers' training camps were established, and thirtytwo cantonments - virtual cities, each housing forty thousand men were set up within ninety days to accommodate the soldiers under training. Congress made huge appropriations for the construction of airplanes, for building cargo

ships to replace those sunk by the enemy, for loans to the Allies, and for the purchase of immense quantities of food, clothing, and munitions. The money was raised partly by increased taxation, partly by borrowing (the Liberty Loans). Other features of the American war program in- 

Icluded fuel control, food control, under the direction of Herbert Hoover, and government operation of railroads, express companies, and telegraph and telephone lines. American engineers in France also constructed docks, storage depots, barracks, and even entire railways for the reception of troops. 

Military situation at the beginning of 1918. The year 1918 saw the end of fighting in the World War. 

Let us therefore, before going into the events of that year, try to get a general view of the military situation in Europe in the spring of 1918. (1) On the eastern front, the Russians were out of the war, the new revolutionary government having signed a treaty of peace with the 

Central Powers at Brest- REMEMBER BELGIUM ENLIST TO DAY BRITISH RECRUITING POSTER 

Litovsk, March 3, 1918. In southeastern Europe, the Central 

Powers were also in a strong position. Turkey was in the war on their side, and most of the Balkans were under their sway. Only in Greece did the Allies have a foothold. On the Austro-Italian front, the Austrians and Germans had checked the Italians late in 1917. Thus the Central Powers were now free to turn their attention to the western front. (2) Great Britain, France, and Italy recognized this fact and prepared to remain on the defensive until the United States

The Allies, now under the vigorous leadership of Lloyd George in Great Britain, Clemenceau in France, and Orlando in Italy, could afford to wait. (3) The Central Powers, however, could not afford to wait. The blockade still shut off supplies, the United States was lending great sums of money to the Allies, and streams of transports were carrying fresh American troops in ever larger numbers to France. Germany realized that her supreme effort to gain a victory must be made in 1918, or never. 

Germany's last drives. Having gathered every available man and gun, Field Marshal Hindenburg and his associate, General Ludendorff, in March, 1918, started a drive against the Allies on the western front from Arras to La Fère. The battle which followed surpassed in intensity every previous engagement on the western front. 

By terrific massed attacks, the

Germans regained in a few days all the ground so slowly and painfully won by the Allied offensives in 1916 and 1917.

In April the Germans launched another drive to the north, between Arras and Ypres, against the British guarding the road to the Channel ports. 

The enemy again drove a deep wedge into the British line. 

French reinforcements arrived 

MARSHAL FOCH 

on the scene in time to check the German advance. A third drive at the end of May, between Soissons and Reims, brought the Germans back once more to the Marne at Château-Thierry, only forty-three miles from Paris, but French and American troops halted the advance. Renewed German efforts in June and July to pierce the Allied line and reach 

Paris were fruitless. And now the tide turned.

The turn of the tide. The critical condition of affairs had led the Allies to establish unity of military action by putting all their forces under one commander, the French general Foch. He now possessed the reinforcements sent by both 

Great Britain and Italy to help hold the long line from the sea to Switzerland, together with more than a million American soldiers under General Pershing. The Americans had already seen actual service in engagements at Cantigny, in the Belleau Woods, and at Château-Thierry. July 18, 1918,

GENERAL PERSHING 

is a memorable date, for on that og day the Allies began the series of dns rapid counterstrokes, perfectly e 8 coördinated, which four months later brought the war on the western front to a victorious conclusion. How the French and 

Americans pinched the Germans out of the Marne salient; how the Americans, in their first independent operation, swept the enemy from the Saint-Mihiel salient, south of Verdun, thus getting within range of the great fortress of Metz, and started an advance east of the Argonne

Forest which carried them to Sedan; how the British, with 

French and American assistance, broke the "Hindenburg 

Line"; how the Belgians, British, and French liberated

Flanders- these are only the outstanding events of a period perhaps unsurpassed in interest and importance since the dawn of history. 

Collapse of Germany's allies. With disaster impending on the western front, Germany could no longer support her associates in the other theaters of the war. In the Balkans, a vigorous offensive by British, Greek, Serbian, French, and

Italian troops led to Bulgaria's unconditional surrender, September 29, 1918. Turkey, now isolated from Germany

and Austria-Hungary, was the second to collapse. She signed an armistice on October 30. The collapse of Austria- 

Hungary was not far off. The Italians, under General Diaz, drove the Austrians out of northern Italy, occupied Trent and Trieste, and captured six hundred thousand prisoners and seven thousand guns. Austria-Hungary then signed an armistice, November 3. As in the cases of Bulgaria and 

Turkey, it amounted to an unconditional surrender. The 

Austrian emperor abdicated, and the Dual Monarchy began to break up.

The end of the war. As Germany during that fateful summer and autumn of 1918 began to taste the bitterness of defeat, the popular demand for peace and democratic government threatened the throne of the kaiser. He made one concession after another. But the red flag was hoisted over the 

German fleet at Kiel, and Berlin and other cities fell into the hands of revolutionists. Then William II abdicated, both as emperor and as king of Prussia, and fled to Holland. Germany soon became a socialist republic. On November 11, 1918 — a memorable day in the history of the world — the new German government signed an armistice with the Allies and the United States. (The United States had insisted that it was not one of the Allies, but only an associate of theirs in the war.) 

Terms of the armistice. Germany agreed to return all prisoners of war; to surrender her submarines, the best part of her fleet, and immense numbers of cannon, machine guns, and airplanes; to evacuate Belgium, Luxemburg, France, and Alsace-Lorraine; and to allow the joint occupation by 

Allied and American troops of the Rhinelands, together with the principal crossings of the Rhine (Mainz, Coblenz, and Cologne). The German government agreed to the armistice on the understanding that the peace settlement would accord with President Wilson's "Fourteen Points," which had been accepted by the Allies as a summary of their war aims. 

The "Fourteen Points." During the war, spokesmen for both sides had tried to formulate statements of the objectives

for which they were fighting. The most famous statement of war aims was delivered by President Wilson in an address to 

Congress on January 8, 1918. He set forth what he considered a program for a just and lasting settlement. While the President spoke only for the United States, his “Fourteen 

WOODROW WILSON 

Points" met general acceptance in Great 

Britain, France, and 

Italy as embodying the war aims of the Allies. 

The "Fourteen Points" included: abolition of secret diplomacy; freedom of the seas; removal of economic barriers between the nations; reduction of armaments; impartial adjustment of colonial claims; evacuation by 

Germany of all conquered territory and the restoration of Belgium and Alsace-Lorraine; readjustment of

Italian frontiers along the lines of nationality; an independent Poland; self-government for the different peoples of 

Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman Empire; and, finally, the formation of a general association of nations.

The end of an era. Most students of history feel that the close of the World War marked also the close of an era in the history of civilization. The war left a legacy of problems. 

Treaties of peace had to be made; public finances had to be rearranged; huge war debts had to be paid; devastated areas needed reconstructing; toppling governments were to be reëstablished; millions of veterans, many of them crippled, needed to be reabsorbed into civilian life; numerous

national animosities had to be lived down; industry had to be readjusted; vexatious territorial adjustments had to be made; and international relations had to be rebuilt. The attempts to grapple with these problems have engaged the attention of mankind since the close of the World War. 

How civilization has fared while confronted with these problems constitutes the story of the next unit - The World Today.

Unit IX THE WORLD TODAY 

How the peoples of the world are trying to reconstruct society 

(CHAPTERS XXI-XXII)

PRESENTATION The Peace Conference following the World War found great difficulty in adjusting reparations and in redrawing the map of Europe in accordance with the principle of national self-determination. The war itself left the world a legacy of debts, maimed soldiers, and weakened racial stocks; on the other hand, it left also a longing for peace and a realization of the interdependence of nations. 

Belief in the necessity of peace has found expression in a League of Nations, a World Court, disarmament conferences, and peace pacts. 

(Chapter XXI) 

Following the war a great many new republics were set up, but many of them have become dictatorships. The disordered and changing civilization of mankind has appeared in the new governments. In Russia, the revolutions of 1917 led to a proletarian dictatorship and earnest attempts to establish communism. Russia inaugurated planned control of the production and distribution of goods. In Italy the Fascists under Mussolini set up a dictatorship which has gained autocratic control. Through the Corporate State 

Mussolini plans to direct all industry as well as political activity. 

In Germany, a republic was set up and gave promise of achieving stability. The necessity of paying reparations, the dissatisfaction over other aspects of the Treaty of Versailles, and the economic depression resulted in 1933 in the rise of a dictator Adolf Hitler, leader of the Nazis. In Turkey, the Nationalists rose to power, expelled the sultan, and set up a republic; the first president, Mustafa Kemal, has become practically a dictator in order to westernize, secularize, and industrialize the new Turkish nation. In 

India, China, and Japan national sentiment is arising, and Japan is establishing herself as a great imperial power. The British Empire emerged from the war with increased possessions and enhanced prestige but confronted by perplexing problems of imperial organization. There is hope that the increased communication and intermingling of peoples will promote a better understanding among the nations of the world. (Chapter XXII)

· COVENANT OF THE LEAGUE 168. MAKING PEACE 

The Peace Conference. The war left a legacy of problems. 

In order to deal with them a peace conference was necessary. 

Accordingly, on January 18, 1919, there assembled at Paris seventy official delegates representing most of the countries that had opposed the Central Powers in the war. Representatives from neutral states were admitted to the conference when matters affecting their countries came up for discussion. Representatives from the Central Powers and their associates were altogether excluded. 

The seventy official delegates were aided by over a thousand experts on geography, history, race conditions, international law, commerce, and other technical matters, and by numerous clerks. 

Premier Clemenceau of France was unanimously chosen chairman of the conference. The two ranking delegates of each of the five great powers - the United States, Great Britain, France, Italy, and Japan — constituted a Supreme Council to discuss and formulate the business of the conference. This council of ten members was soon reduced to one of five. Even- 739

International Problems tually both Japan and Italy dropped from the inner circle, and there were left the "Big Three" - Clemenceau, Lloyd 

George, and President Wilson. The Big Three decided among themselves many of the most important questions. 

Very few of their decisions were made public. This apparent relapse into the ways of the old and discredited secret diplomacy aroused criticism at the time, especially from those who did not realize the mag- Tamponitude of the task before the 

GEORGES CLEMENCEAU 

as conference and the need of sar haste in restoring peace.

The Peace of Paris. 

Within six months the most important treaty, that with 

Germany, was completed.

The German delegates pro tested that its harsh terms violated Wilson's Fourteen 

Points (p. 731), but they secured only minor modifications and were obliged to sign. The ceremony of signing occurred on June 28, 1919, in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles. This treaty is called the Treaty of Versailles. In the same year, treaties were signed by Austria and Bulgaria, and in the following year by Hungary and Turkey. The Turkish government, however, never ratified the signature of its delegates. These five treaties, together with other arrangements and agreements among the Allies themselves, are called the Peace of Paris, 1919-1920. 

The United States and the Peace of Paris. The United 

States never ratified the treaties made at Paris. Her delegates signed them, but the Senate refused to give the two-thirds vote necessary for ratification. The chief stumbling block to approval by the Senate was Article X of the Covenant of the League of Nations, which reads as follows: "The

741 members of the League undertake to respect and preserve as against external aggression the territorial integrity and existing political independence of all members of the League. In case of any aggression, or in case of any threat or danger of such aggression, the council shall advise upon the means by which this obligation shall be fulfilled." Many senators said that this Article would put the military and naval forces of the United States at the disposal of the League and thus impair the constitutional right of Congress to declare war. tive of the precise obligations which the United States was willing to accept under it. On both occasions when the amended treaty came to a vote in the Senate, it failed to pass by the necessary two-thirds majority. The treaties were not yet ratified by the time of the presidential campaign of 1920. Consequently, in that campaign the League of Nations became an issue, the Republicans opposing it and the Democrats upholding it. 

The Republican victory, resulting in the election of Senator Harding, was followed in the summer of 1921 by the passage of a congressional resolution which declared the war of the United States with Germany at an end. This resolution was promptly signed by the President. Treaties of peace negotiated by the administration, not only with Germany, but also with Austria and Hungary, were later ratified by the Senate.

The terms of peace. The peace treaties written at Paris were lengthy documents. That with Germany alone would fill a book. To consider them in detail is therefore impossible, but we can get a general idea of their contents. (1) The

International Problems

Peace Conference changed many boundaries and brought new states into existence. These changes will be treated in detail in the section of remaking the map of Europe (pp. 743748). (2) The Peace Conference, especially at the insistence of Wilson, drew up a plan for a league of nations, and made it an integral part of the various treaties. The organization and activities of this league will be treated in the section on organizing for peace (pp. 759-767). (3) All of Germany's overseas colonies were taken from her. Most of them were assigned to one or the other of the victorious Allies. (4) Germany was disarmed, being compelled to abandon compulsory military training, to destroy her fortifications on the Rhine and the Baltic, to stop the making of munitions, and to surrender her navy and most of her merchant vessels. (5) Germany was also required to make good in money, materials, or labor some of the injuries which her armies, cruisers, and submarines had caused, and to pay the cost of Allied occupation of part of Germany. This requirement was called reparation.

The problem of reparations. The amount of reparations to be collected in money and commodities was not fixed at first. 

The Allies set up a Reparations Commission, with power to inquire into Germany's resources and to fix the time and manner of her contributions. In 1921 the German government agreed to pay, over a series of years, the equivalent of about thirty-three billion dollars. The failure of Germany to make regular payments led in 1923 to the seizure by French and Belgian troops of a rich industrial district in Germany called the Ruhr. The Germans declared themselves practically bankrupt; the French and Belgians declared they would continue to occupy German territory until payments were made. This deadlock was broken in 1924 when a committee headed by Charles G. Dawes, a former director of the budget of the United States, drew up the Dawes Plan for balancing the German budget and stabilizing Germany's currency. Germany made reparations payments under this arrangement until 1929. It was then replaced by the Young

Remaking the Map of Europe 

743 Plan, named after Owen D. Young, who served as chairman of a new committee. This plan provided for a considerable reduction in the total reparations which Germany was expected to pay. In the very year that the Young Plan went into effect, however, the world depression began. The apparent danger of a complete financial collapse of Germany induced President Hoover in 1931 to propose a delay (moratorium) for one year on all reparations and debt payments between nations.

The Lausanne agreement. When the moratorium expired in 1932, there was still little prospect of further payments by Germany. Finally, debtors and creditors met in conference at Lausanne, Switzerland, and reached an agreement reducing Germany's reparations to a lump sum-less than a billion dollars to be paid over a period of years. These payments were to be made through the Bank of International Settlements often called the World Bank - which had been established in 1930 at Basel, Switzerland, in accordance with the Young Plan. 

169. REMAKING THE MAP OF EUROPE 

Why was the map of Europe remade? Before the World

War, Germany, Austria-Hungary, and Russia all contained within their respective boundaries "submerged nationalities" - groups of people who, because of common descent, language, and ideals regarded themselves as one nation which was oppressed by the government ruling them. When the 

Central Powers lost the war, and when revolutions broke out in Germany, Austria-Hungary, and Russia, an opportunity was at hand for these submerged nationalities to unite and form independent states. Furthermore, Italy wanted to complete her national unification by gaining from Austria the "unredeemed provinces" of Trent and Trieste, and France wanted back the "lost provinces" of Alsace and Lorraine (p. 589). When the Central Powers lost the war, naturally Italy and France had an opportunity to see that

International Problems these boundary changes were made. In short, the defeat of the Central Powers, the revolutions in Europe, and the Peace Conference each had something to do with remaking the map of Europe. Remaking the Map of Europe 

745 ward but bending to the east, we reach the boundary between Denmark and northern Germany. Here between the 

North and Baltic seas stretches a small strip of land joining Germany and Denmark. On this strip are the provinces of 

Schleswig and Holstein which Germany annexed in 1864. 

The treaty at the close of the World War provided that northern Schleswig should be returned to Denmark in case a majority of the inhabitants voted for the change. In accordance with the results of two popular votes (plebiscites) of 1920, a large part of northern Schleswig became a part of 

Denmark. (4) Moving eastward across the Baltic Sea we arrive in western Russia. Here along the shores of the Baltic were the provinces that formerly belonged to Russia. Out of these provinces arose the four small republics of Finland, Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania. (5) On the southern shore of the Baltic, at the mouth of the Vistula River, stands the old and important commercial city of Danzig. Before the war Danzig and the surrounding territory were a part of Germany. The story of what happened to Danzig cannot be understood until we have seen how the Poles after the World War reëstablished their kingdom lying between 

Germany and Russia.

How the Polish Question arose. When the World War broke out Europe was troubled by the so-called Polish Question. Their own country having been destroyed, the Poles were divided among various countries, some being in Russia, others in Austria, and still others in Prussia. In 1772 Catherine II of Russia, Maria Theresa of Austria, and Frederick the Great of Prussia joined in the first partition of Poland, by which that country lost about one-third of its territory. 

In 1793 the second partition of Poland occurred, but only Russia and Prussia shared in it, for Austria was busily at war with the French revolutionists. Two years later, 1795, came the final (third) partition of Poland among its three neighbors. The brave but futile resistance of Polish patriots led by Kosciusko, who had fought under Washington in the Revolutionary War, threw a gleam of glory upon the last days

International Problems of the expiring kingdom of Poland. The Polish patriots resented foreign control and longed to reëstablish their own country. Their restlessness under foreign rule, from the eighteenth century until the outbreak of the World War, constituted the Polish Question in Europe. Hard indeed was the fate of the Poles during the World War. For example, the Russian Poles had to fight against their brothers in the armies of Austria and Germany. At the close of the war, when revolutions swept over Germany, Austria, and Russia, the Poles reunited to establish the independent Polish republic, and the Peace Conference at Paris helped to define its boundaries.

The new Polish republic. The new Poland is about the size of our state of Montana. In Europe, this must be regarded as a relatively large country. It was formed out of parts of Russia, Austria, and Germany - the countries which had partitioned Poland in the eighteenth century. 

The new Poland had one possible outlet to the sea — the Vistula River, which flowed northward through German territory to the city of Danzig on the Baltic Sea. Danzig, however, and its surrounding territory were inhabited almost entirely by Germans. If this city, with its neighboring area, remained in German hands, Poland would have no access to the sea.

Therefore the Peace Conference at Paris made Danzig a free city under the protection of the League of Nations, and assigned to Poland a considerable strip of territory connecting Danzig and Poland. This strip of land is known as the Polish Corridor. It cuts through eastern Germany, completely separating East Prussia from the rest of Germany, thus giving Poland an outlet to the sea. 

Remaking the map of central Europe. (1) Southwest of 

Poland, in central Europe, is the new republic of Czechoslovakia. During the war the Czechs and Slovaks, like the Poles, had to fight for a country which they did not regard as their own, namely, Austria-Hungary. When the Dual Monarchy fell to pieces after the war, the Czechs and Slovaks established their own country. It includes the former subdivisions

Remaking the Map of Europe 

747 Its of Bohemia, Moravia, Austrian Silesia, and Slovakia. capital was established in the famous old city of Prague in Bohemia. The young republic of Czechoslovakia was guided skillfully through a very trying period by its first president, Professor Thomas G. Masaryk. (2) The old Dual Monarchy of Austria-Hungary dis- appeared when its subject nationalities were formed into new states. There remained, however, the states of Austria and Hungary. Austria is a republic. It came into being immediately after the downfall of the Hapsburg monarchy, at the close of the war. The new Austria is a small, inland state, German in culture and chiefly German in population. Its union (Anschluss) with Germany is forbidden by the Versailles

Remaking the map of southeastern Europe. (1) East of 

Hungary lies Rumania. It was awarded the large Russian province of Bessarabia, lost in a previous war, and also Bukowina and the Hungarian province of Transylvania, to which its claims were rather slight; the area of Rumania was thus nearly doubled. (2) South of Hungary, along the eastern coast of the Adriatic Sea, dwelt the Jugo (South) Slavs.

They were composed of several peoples: Serbs and Croats in the independent states of Serbia and Montenegro and in several provinces in Austria-Hungary, and Slovenes in an-

International Problems other Austrian province. All these provinces united to form the "kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes," commonly called Jugoslavia. In order to establish it, both Serbia and 

Montenegro gave up their separate governments and united with the former Jugoslav provinces of Austria-Hungary. (3) South of Jugoslavia, the former little principality of

Albania was formed into a republic after the war, but its president became more and more a dictator and, at length, a full-fledged king. A defensive alliance concluded in 1917 with Italy made Albania practically an Italian protectorate. (4) Italy extended its boundaries to the northeast by annexing the Austrian Tyrol and Trent, as well as the Adriatic coastal region that includes Trieste and Fiume. (5) In the far southeast important changes in boundaries affected Bulgaria and Greece. Bulgaria gave up part of Thrace to Greece and thus lost its outlet on the Ægean Sea. 

The remade map of Europe. We have now surveyed the principal boundary changes which were brought about by the war, the revolutions, and the Peace of Paris. Germany and Russia, shorn of their alien elements, became essentially national states. Austria and Hungary arose as national states, each with a homogeneous population. New national states appeared in Jugoslavia, Albania, Czechoslovakia, Poland, Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, and Finland. Other countries completed their national unification: France, by the acquisition of Alsace-Lorraine; Italy, by securing Italia 

Irredenta; and Rumania, by the incorporation of adjoining territory. Whether or not all these territorial changes prove to be permanent, they certainly recognized, as never before, the principle of national self-determination.

-PORTUGAL 

The cost in human lives. The Allies mobilized about forty million men and the Central Powers about twenty million men, making a grand total of sixty million combatants from beginning to end of the struggle. It is impossible to give an exact statement of the casualties. Probably ten million soldiers lost their lives in battle or as a result of wounds, accidents, and disease. Probably twenty million soldiers were wounded, perhaps a quarter of them being permanently disabled in body or in health. The death loss among non-

International Problems combatants, as the result of pestilence, famine, and massacres, has been estimated at twenty millions. The total mortality directly traceable to the World War would thus amount to thirty millions. These appalling figures must be greatly increased if account is taken of the loss of population due to the decline of the normal birth rate and the increase of the normal death rate among European peoples. Not more than five million lives had been lost in battle in all the wars from the time of the French Revolution to 1914. 

The war and the race. The ten million soldiers who fell in the war were mostly picked men. They had passed tests for physical and mental fitness; they were in the prime of life and health and strength; they should have been the virile fathers of the next generation. France, who lost altogether 1,750,000 soldiers, had sixty per cent of her young men killed in battle or as the result of battle. The mortality in the German, British, and other European armies reached a high figure. This is necessarily the outcome of a system in which the fittest go to the slaughter. The war, therefore, injured the race fiber of the principal European nations. Its evil effects in this direction must make themselves felt over a long stretch of years. 

Money cost. A conservative estimate of the direct money cost of the war to the belligerent nations is $186,000,000,000. 

This sum, colossal as it is, does not take into account the indirect cost, including the destruction of property on land and sea, the depreciation of capital, the interruption of trade, the loss of production due to the employment of the world's workers in military activities, the payments for war relief, and the expenditures of neutral nations. Such items would amount to many more billions. The cost of the war is a sum so great as almost to defy the imagination. It is a thousand dollars for every mile of the distance from the earth to the sun and back again.

Financing the war. The war was financed to some extent by increased taxation, especially in Great Britain and the United States, but chiefly by borrowing. The nations, in the

BRITISH EMPIRE 

first place, issued vast quantities of paper money. Such forced loans are easily made on the Continent, where the governments control all the banks and possess a monopoly of note issue. In the second place, the nations sold their bonds, or promises to pay, to all who would buy them. The amounts raised were far greater than had been supposed to be 39

Public finances after the war. The end of the war left the whole financial world in chaos. All the belligerents had to impose heavy additional taxes, in order to meet the interest on their huge debts and repair the destruction caused by the struggle. Many of them found it difficult to avoid bank-

International Problems ruptcy. Great Britain and the United States were the only important belligerents which from the start balanced their budgets and did not show a large gap between income and expenditure. Some of the countries, particularly Germany and Russia, indulged for a time in an orgy of paper-money inflation, with the result that both the mark and the ruble became practically worthless. Even the French franc and the Italian lira depreciated to a fraction of their pre-war value.

National debts. The financial burden which our own and future generations must carry is shown by the gigantic national debts. These now total nearly ten times what they were before the war. The debt of Great Britain, at the peak in 1920, was $40,000,000,000; that of the United States, at the peak in 1919, was $26,596,000,000. Such sums have been well described as "astronomical," recalling the prodigious figures in which astronomers reckon distances. We cannot really grasp them. The Russian debt, both internal and external, which had reached a high figure at the time of the Revolution, was repudiated by the Soviet government. The Turkish 

Nationalists likewise repudiated the indebtedness which the old Ottoman Empire had contracted abroad. 

Debts of the Allies to the United States. The Allies borrowed heavily from the United States during the war. The capital sums owed by them now exceed $11,000,000,000, and if interest payments spread over the next sixty-odd years were to be computed, the total would be almost twice as much. Great Britain and France are our principal debtors. 

The problem of meeting the interest charges and paying off the principal has been complicated by the failure of the Allies to collect additional reparations from Germany. The problem is further complicated by the economic difficulty of transferring large sums of money from one country to another. Many economists and students of public affairs urge, therefore, that the war debts be canceled by the United States or else be settled for a much smaller lump sum, in order to restore sound financial conditions throughout the

world, including the United States itself. The serious economic situation in the leading countries caused President 

Hoover, on July 1, 1931, to propose the postponement for one year of all payments on all intergovernmental debts and reparations. Since then most of the governments have postponed or defaulted in the payment of these debts. Only 

Finland has met all its payments. 

Lessons of the World War. We have just seen that the war bequeathed mankind a legacy of (1) killed and maimed people, (2) weakened racial stocks, and (3) unbalanced finances. These are only some of the unfortunate aftermaths of the war. Not all of the legacy of the war, however, was evil. The war impressed upon men everywhere certain valuable lessons. Among these were (1) an increased awareness as to the real causes of modern wars, (2) an increased awareness that the interests of one nation are tied up with those of other nations, and (3) an increased awareness of the danger of war to modern civilization. These valuable lessons were also part of the legacy of the war. 

The real causes of modern wars. Long before 1914 mighty forces making for war had been present in Europe. What these were we have already learned. First, there was extreme nationalism, a sentiment which had gained ground all through the nineteenth century. It bred ill will between European peoples. It made difficult any real sympathy or understanding between them. Each people developed an exaggerated sense of "national honor" and stood ready to fight over the slightest insult to the government or even to a single citizen. 

Second, there was economic imperialism, producing European expansion, annexations of foreign territory, and the struggle for markets, concessions, investments, and spheres of influence in new and undeveloped regions. Such advantages were often gained by sheer force or by diplomatic pressure backed by armies and navies. Third, there was secret diplomacy and, connected therewith, the whole system of entangling alliances. 

Enormous power was thus placed in the hands of ambassadors and foreign-office ministers. They often made the most

International Problems serious and binding agreements without the knowledge of the people at large or even the knowledge of parliaments. Fourth, there was militarism, including the fear-producing competition in armaments. Thus nationalism, imperialism, secret diplomacy, and militarism constituted four fundamental causes of war. Still other forces made for international hostility. The presence in Europe of so many submerged nationalities, longing for independence and self-government, formed a grave danger. The numerous territorial and boundary disputes, resulting from previous wars and ill-made peace treaties, also contributed to the general insecurity. 

Modern wars are world-wide.  impressed a second lesson upon the minds of many statesmen and students of public affairs. This lesson was that the nations of all the world now belong to a family of nations who cannot remain unaffected by the acts of one another. Thus the World 

War involved Europe, the largest part of North America and South America, much of Africa, two-thirds of Asia, and most of Oceania. Improved methods of transportation and communication have brought all civilized peoples so close together that a shot fired in the Balkans soon provoked an international crisis and at length produced a world-wide conflict. The nations, while remaining politically independent, are now economically and socially interdependent. 

Their isolation is forever ended. The fate of one becomes the fate of all. It was impossible to localize the last war; it will be equally impossible to localize the next war. 

Modern warfare is dangerous to civilization. Before the 

World War, many persons could be found to argue that warfare is only an aspect of the universal struggle for existence, in which the weak are destroyed, the strong survive, and civilization is accordingly promoted. But the World War showed men that modern warfare is so destructive that civilization itself is endangered by it. Let us pass in review primitive warfare, warfare in historic times, and modern warfare, in order to observe by comparison the greater destructiveness of modern warfare.

(1) Primitive warfare. Clans fought with clans and tribes with tribes long before nations warred with nations. Primitive man fought his fellows with the club, spear, and sword that he had first used against wild animals. Primitive wars were doubtless on a small scale. They were raids for food, for booty, and for slaves, or they arose out of disputes between rival communities over a hunting ground or pastures and wells. Such wars may sometimes have contributed to human progress by binding people together in a common enterprise and by accustoming them to discipline and selfsacrifice. (2) Warfare in historic times. When man passed from savagery and barbarism to civilization, wars increased in scope and number. Much history, as commonly written, is a record of fighting. During ancient times Egypt, Babylonia, Assyria, and Persia built up great conquering states. In classical antiquity the Romans spread their sway over three continents. The triumph of Rome gave peace to Europe for several centuries, but after the break-up of the empire came the Middle Ages, when Europe for a thousand years was overrun by barbarian invaders and feudal knights. (3) Modern warfare. Modern nations depend for an army only in part upon professional soldiers. In times of crises every able-bodied citizen is expected to bear arms in his country's defense. Thus modern warfare involves the entire nation. Present-day warfare also uses all the agencies of modern science and invention. Everything indicates that the next war, if on the scale of the last one, will be still more destructive of life and property. Airplanes, submarines, battleships, and armament are being rapidly improved. "Tanks" are evolving into land battleships, equipped with field guns as well as machine guns. Poison gases, powerful enough to disable or kill thousands of people at one time, have been discovered and perfected. Disease germs, capable of polluting the water supply of whole areas, blight to destroy crops, anthrax to slay horses and cattle, and plague to sweep away entire populations are being prepared in the chemical

International Problems laboratories of more than one great country. Modern warfare thus threatens to become a sort of collective suicide of the nations.

Abolition of war. The catastrophe of 1914-1918 therefore gave new strength to the peace movement. Thoughtful men were impressed as never before by the horrors of armed conflict. They were fearful of fresh horrors to come. They were aware that no limits, except the habitable globe itself, could be set to the possible scope of another war. They realized that the roots of war sink deep into the soil of the past, and that all countries are responsible in greater or less degree for its existence. They asked, therefore, if the time had not come to end forever armed conflict between nations. Cannot war be abolished, as cannibalism, human sacrifice, blood revenge, witchcraft persecution, slavery, and other anti-social practices have been abolished, by the common sense and common wisdom of mankind? If this is to be done, we now perceive that it can be done only by setting up international agencies to prevent the outbreak of war. Attempts to arouse sentiment against war and to organize international agencies to prevent war constitute the peace movement. This movement has been developing for centuries. 

171. THE PEACE MOVEMENT 

Early Christianity and warfare. The Christian Church formed the first peace society and launched the first peace movement. Christianity introduced into Europe an exalted conception of the sacredness of human life. It condemned homicide of any kind and therefore regarded war as unlawful. 

After Christianity became the official religion of the Roman Empire, however, it became impossible to preserve a pacifist attitude. That empire had been built up by successful warfare, and only by warfare could it be defended against its barbarian foes. The use of the cross on the standards of the imperial army testified to the change that had come over the spirit of Christianity.

The Peace Movement 

757 The medieval Church and warfare. The Church in the 

Middle Ages, while by no means a pacifist organization, in general cast its influence on the side of peace. It deserves credit for many efforts to stamp out private warfare between feudal nobles. The Church, however, encouraged public warfare against heretics and infidels. The institution of chivalry and the military orders of monks, such as Templars and Hospitalers (p. 313), illustrate the union between Christianity and militancy.

Protestantism and warfare. The rise of Protestantism did not produce a change in the attitude of official Christianity toward war. Most of the Protestant churches were state churches, and their ministers, considering themselves in the public service, usually supported whatever war their governments undertook. Nevertheless, Christian sects arose which opposed all war. The English Lollards in the fourteenth century taught that homicide in war is forbidden by the New Testament. The sixteenth-century Anabaptists, who had many followers in Germany and other countries, believed that Christians should not bear arms or offer forcible resistance to wrongdoers or wield the sword. The Society of 

Friends (commonly called Quakers) likewise took an attitude of uncompromising pacifism. 

Promoting sentiment for peace. Strong protests against war were voiced at various times by isolated reformers, for instance, by Erasmus and Voltaire. The nineteenth century saw the rise of peace societies, numbering several hundreds, throughout the world. Their first international congress took place as early as 1843. These societies held regular meetings and maintained a permanent bureau at Bern, Switzerland. They helped to arouse public sentiment in favor of arbitration of disputes between nations, reduction of armaments, and gradual removal of the causes of war. 

The Pan-American Union (p. 697) had for its purpose the furtherance of good relations among all the twenty-one republics of the New World. The peace movement was also promoted by private benefactors. Alfred Nobel, the Swedish

International Problems inventor of dynamite and other explosives, who left his fortune for the establishment of international prizes, directed that one of these should be annually awarded to the person or society rendering the greatest service to the cause of human brotherhood. This has become known as the Nobel 

Peace Prize. Andrew Carnegie gave ten million dollars as an endowment to hasten the abolition of war, "the foulest blot on our civilization." The endowment was particularly intended to encourage studies in economics, history, and international law, so that the world's peoples might know one another better and so avoid many sources of friction. 

International arbitration. The nations began to resort increasingly to arbitration as a means of adjusting differences between them. Over two hundred awards were made by arbitral courts during the nineteenth century, and every one was carried out. After 1900 many leading countries concluded treaties with one another, pledging themselves to submit to arbitration all controversies except those affecting national honor or vital interests (such as independence). 

Argentina and Chile went still further and in 1902 bound themselves to arbitrate every dispute which might arise between them. The United States, while W. J. Bryan was secretary of state in President Wilson's administration (19131915), made no less than thirty treaties with foreign countries, requiring the submission of disputes to impartial inquiry by an international body and a delay of a full year before going to war. Nearly all of these “Bryan treaties” are still in effect. They show the desire of the nations for peace. 

The "Hague Tribunal." International arbitration received a great impetus at the two Hague conferences of 1899 and 1907. The assembled powers could not agree to limit armaments, but besides revising the laws of war they set up at The Hague, Holland, a Permanent Court of Arbitration to which the nations might resort. This "Hague- 

Tribunal" settled a number of controversies which in earlier days might have led to war. It thus marked a distinct advance toward international peace.

An international league. Then came the World War, in which the Allies held themselves out as the defenders of international law and as the champions of nationality and democracy. Their enormous sacrifices during the struggle promised, to be in vain, unless some means could be found to prevent future wars. Obviously, it would be necessary to organize for peace. An international league therefore began to seem, not a utopian scheme, but rather a practical necessity. Such thoughts as these were repeatedly expressed by responsible statesmen among the Allies, especially by Lloyd George and 

President Wilson. 

172. ORGANIZING FOR PEACE 

Formation of a league of nations. As soon as the Peace 

Conference opened at Paris, a committee representing the allied and associated governments began work on the various proposals which had been put forward from time to time for an international league. This committee presented to the conference a constitution for the League of Nations. The constitution, called a Covenant, was a short, simple, and dignified document, written in large part by President Wilson. After various modifications, the Covenant was accepted and inserted in the peace treaty with Germany. The signing of that treaty, and its subsequent ratification, put the League of Nations into active operation. 

Membership in the League. Over fifty nations belong to the League. At one time or another, every important country in the world except the United States and Russia has been a member. Any self-governing state, dominion, or colony may be enrolled by a two-thirds vote of the members. Any member may, after two years' notice, withdraw from the League, if at the time of withdrawal it has fulfilled all its international obligations. 

Organization of the League. The League consists of an assembly, a council, and a secretariat. (1) The assembly

International Problems consists of representatives of all the nations belonging to the League. Each member-nation has one vote in the assembly. It meets once a year in Geneva, Switzerland, for the purpose of discussing matters of international interest. (2) The council consists of representatives of five leading nations plus representatives from nine lesser powers. It meets three times a year to decide on actions to be taken in the name of the League. All important decisions of the council require a unanimous vote. (3) The secretariat consists of a Secretary-General, with an office at Geneva, and a staff of assistants. The secretariat functions as the administrative office through which the world-wide activities of the League are handled. Several hundred persons are employed by the secretariat.

Functions of the League. The great purpose of the League is to organize the world for peace. The achievement of this purpose involves the following four functions: (1) the administration of internationalized areas, such as Danzig and the Saar Basin; (2) the supervision of mandates; (3) the promotion of social betterment by means of international coöperation; (4) the prevention of war.

The League and mandates. A mandate is an order given by the League of Nations to an advanced country to assume control of some backward area; the word mandate is also used to designate the area so controlled. The former colonies of Germany and the countries in the Near East liberated from Turkey became mandates. The mandatory system represents a praiseworthy departure from the usual method of disposing of enemy territories conquered in war. These territories, instead of being annexed, will be governed by the conquerors as trustees for the League. The nations in charge of mandates submit annual reports to the League, which has final authority to pass judgment on the manner in which they have discharged their trusteeship. The mandatory system rests on the principle that backward and undeveloped countries, unable yet to achieve or preserve independence, ought to be treated as international responsi-

bilities, not as opportunities for national profit and aggrandizement. If these good intentions are realized, a step will have been taken in getting rid of some of the evils of imperialism.

The League and social betterment. The League serves as a convenient agency for dealing with certain matters that concern all its members. Among these are (1) the prevention and control of disease, (2) the regulation of the traffic in dangerous drugs, (3) the relief of suffering throughout the world, (4) the betterment of industrial conditions in the various countries, and (5) the solution of international financial problems. The International Labor Office, under the League of Nations, recommends to the different governments needed labor legislation and sponsors annual international labor conferences.

The League and world peace. The League has also provided means for the abolition of secret diplomacy and “international anarchy." Any treaty or international agreement concluded by League members must be registered with the secretariat and published. Unless so registered it shall not be binding. This regulation, if faithfully observed, should do away with the old secret diplomacy. As long as the various nations regard themselves as having the right to fight when and how and whom they please, war cannot be avoided. The League has begun to deal with this "international anarchy."

Accomplishments of the League. The League has already headed off or snuffed out a number of wars between European countries. These would have been minor wars at the start, but no one can tell how great they might have become before they ended. The League settled a serious dispute between 

Sweden and Finland as to the ownership of the Åland Islands; it gave the islands to Finland, and Sweden acquiesced in the decision. The very troublesome question of the division of southern Silesia between Germany and Poland was referred to the League for solution; its award, drawing a new frontier line, was accepted by both countries. The League has aided

International Problems in the upbuilding of Austria and Hungary by means of international loans to these almost bankrupt countries and by the supervision of their finances. The humanitarian activities of the League are numerous. It has returned to their homes about three hundred thousand prisoners of war in Russia and other countries. It has checked an epidemic of typhus and bubonic plague in eastern Europe that might easily have spread over the entire continent. It is engaged in efforts to stamp out the traffic in opium, a drug which has become such a curse in Oriental countries. The treaties signed by various nations of central Europe, to remove discrimination against racial and linguistic minorities within their borders, form still another accomplishment of the League. (For recent difficulties of the League with Japan and Germany see pages 792, 786.) While the League is by no means perfect and has sometimes failed in its attempts, these accomplishments demonstrate that it is an active force for world peace. 

A World Court. The Covenant of the League provided for the establishment of a Permanent Court of International Justice. The purpose of this "World Court" was to make easier the peaceful settlement of disputes between nations. 

It was set up at The Hague in 1922. It consists of fifteen judges chosen by the council and the assembly of the League and representing different races, languages, nationalities, and legal codes. All of the major countries except Russia and the 

United States, and most of the minor countries, joined this supreme court of the nations. The World Court is a body of permanent judges holding regular sessions in a definite place and at definite times. It may hear and determine any question relating to the interpretation of a treaty or to a matter of international law which is submitted to it by the parties concerned. The court also acts as a legal adviser to the League of Nations, being empowered to give an advisory opinion upon any dispute or question referred to it by the council or by the assembly. 

Work of the court.

The World Court holds its regular annual sessions in the beautiful Peace Palace provided by

Andrew Carnegie at The Hague. It has already heard, considered, and passed judgment on a number of contested international cases, besides giving many advisory opinions in matters of international concern. The judgments and opinions rendered were accepted as final by the contestants, thus AA 4 

THE PEACE PALACE AT THE HAGUE 

A gift of Andrew Carnegie for the use of the "Hague Tribunal" and for international conferences. It is also the seat of the new "World Court." settling in a reasonable and legal way many disputes which otherwise might have been left to force and the arbitrament of the sword.

Progress toward disarmament. The League of Nations and the World Court are not sufficient by themselves to abolish wars. Disarmament also is needed. One nation alone, however, cannot afford to disarm. Disarmament can therefore be accomplished only by international action. The 

United States and Great Britain, as far back as 1818, agreed to dismantle forts and eliminate naval armaments on the waterways separating American from Canadian territory. 

The principle of disarmament was applied to the countries defeated in the World War. Under the peace treaties Ger-

International Problems many, Austria, Hungary, and Bulgaria were obliged to accept an immense reduction of the armed forces which they had respectively maintained. It was a one-sided arrangement, of course, but the Treaty of Versailles held out the prospect of a future limitation of the military forces of all countries.

Financial burden of armaments. The financial burden which armaments now entail has made the nations more willing to favor disarmament. This burden is best appreciated in the light of the annual expenditures of the great powers. 

In submitting the federal budget for 1930-1931, President 

Hoover declared that seventy-two cents out of every dollar of the estimated expenditures of the government for that year would be devoted to payments of principal and interest on the national debt, the maintenance of the army and navy, pensions, and veterans' compensation and hospitalization. 

The annual budgets of Great Britain and France would reveal much the same situation. It may be said that all the great nations of the world spend the larger part of their income in paying for past wars and in preparing for future wars. Relief for the taxpayer can come only with the reduction of armaments, either by each nation on its own initiative or by concerted international action. 

Disarmament conferences. The United States, though keeping aloof from the League of Nations, has joined the movement for disarmament. In response to President Harding's invitation, a Conference on the Limitation of Armament met at Washington in 1921-1922. Nine nations (the United 

States, Great Britain, France, Italy, Belgium, Holland, Portugal, Japan, and China) took part in it. The five principal naval powers represented undertook to scrap or convert to peaceful uses a large number of their capital ships (battleships and heavy cruisers), and so to limit construction of such ships that after a ten-year building "holiday" the United States and Great Britain should have an equal tonnage, Japan sixty per cent of the tonnage of either of these countries, and France and Italy a still smaller amount. The

five powers also signed a treaty by which they agreed not to use submarines as commerce destroyers, as had been done by 

Germany in the World War. Further naval disarmament conferences were held at Geneva in 1927 and in London in 1930. A general conference met at Geneva in 1932, and reassembled in 1933, but was mainly unsuccessful. Germany's announced intention of withdrawing from the League, and her actual withdrawal from the conference temporarily proved a serious obstacle. Some encouragement is felt, however, because of the fact that nations are keenly aware of the necessity of disarming. The conference which assembled at Geneva in 1934 considered the problem of the limitation of air as well as land armaments and endeavored to secure an international agreement for the control of the manufacture and sale of munitions. Infinite patience and years of ceaseless toil by statesmen and publicists will be required before the nations agree to live henceforth on a peace footing and not on a war footing. 

The Locarno pacts. Thus far we have seen that the attempts of the nations "to organize peace" have included a league of nations, a world court, and disarmament conferences. A fourth step toward organizing peace consists of various treaties, or pacts, by which the nations agree to refrain from war. One of the most important of these pacts was that signed at the Swiss town of Locarno in 1925 by representatives of Great Britain, France, Germany, Italy, and other countries. The Locarno pacts, if maintained, should remove the Rhineland area (Alsace-Lorraine) out of the realm of international controversy, protect Belgium from aggression, and secure a peaceful settlement of future disputes between Germany and her eastern neighbors. They ought to make for peace on the war-torn Continent. 

The Pact of Paris. In 1927 Aristide Briand, the French minister for foreign affairs, proposed to Frank B. Kellogg, the American secretary of state, the conclusion of a pact between France and the United States renouncing war as “an instrument of policy." To this proposal Secretary Kellogg

International Problems replied that such an agreement ought not to be confined to two countries, and should be multilateral (many-sided) in character, and open to all countries. Diplomatic correspondence on the subject of such a treaty resulted in the formulation by the government of the United States of a General Pact for the Renunciation of War. It was signed at Paris in 1928 by Gn duly accredited representatives in behalf of fifteen of the leading nations (Australia, Belgium, Canada, Czechoslovakia, France, int Germany, Great Britain, India, at the Irish Free State, Italy, Japan, New Zealand, Poland, South 

Africa, and the United States).

It is a brief document, containing only three Articles, of which the first and the second are here quoted: 

ARISTIDE BRIAND 

1. The High Contracting Parties solemnly declare in the names of their respective peoples, that they condemn recourse to war for the solution of international controversies, and renounce it as an instrument of national policy in their relations with one another. 

2. The High Contracting Parties agree that the settlement or solution of all disputes or conflicts of whatever nature or of whatever origin they may be, which may arise among them, shall never be sought except by pacific means.

Adherences to the Pact of Paris. The third and concluding 

Article of this document provided for ratification by the fifteen signatory powers. After these ratifications the pact was proclaimed in operation by President Hoover in 1929. 

The pact was to remain open as long as necessary for acceptance by other powers, and a considerable number of them have willingly signed it. In this way, and through the influence of the League of Nations, nearly all civilized peoples have been brought or are being brought within the scope of

the pact — a degree of universality without a parallel in the history of the peace movement. 

Significance of the Pact of Paris. The Pact of Paris contains no "sanctions" or guarantees such as were provided at Locarno. There is no force, save moral force, behind it. It does not entirely get rid of resort to war, for military action under the Covenant of the League of Nations or under the Locarno pacts is not prohibited. Furthermore, the right to conduct a war of self-defense is not taken away, and since "self-defense" is an extremely flexible term, a loophole is left for evasion of the obligations imposed by the pact. A nation anxious to fight can always declare that it is acting in selfdefense. There are those, therefore, who consider the pact an empty mockery. It would seem, rather, that the Pact of 

Paris should be regarded as an extraordinary manifestation of the desire for peace on the part of civilized men and as an expression of their growing unwillingness to resort to armed conflict in any form, at any time, and for any reason. 

The regulation of munitions. Still another problem which has a bearing upon the maintenance of peace is that of traffic in war materials. In 1934 a number of articles calling attention to the evils connected with the manufacture and sale of munitions appeared in various magazines. The public was shocked to learn that, even during the World War, the makers of munitions sold their products to the enemy as well as to their own countries. The Senate appointed a committee to investigate the whole problem and to “inquire into the desirability of creating a government monopoly" to manufacture the implements of war, thus removing the dangers inherent in their manufacture by private companies. It was feared that the manufacturers of munitions were instrumental in prolonging the war between Paraguay and Bolivia. Consequently, President Roosevelt, by authority of Congress, declared an embargo on war materials destined for those countries. Concerted action in regard to munitions by the countries of the world would seem to be a necessary preliminary to an assured peace.
