CHAPTER XXII CIVILIZATION IN TRANSITION 

They say I am a dictator. I say, No. There are ten thousand dictators in the party. 

- ADOLF HITLER 

The laboring masses are drawn to knowledge because it is indispensable to their victory. Nine-tenths of them realize fully that knowledge is a necessary tool in their struggle for freedom, that their failures are explained by their lack of education, and that they must now make enlightenment actually accessible to all. 

173. POST-WAR EUROPE 

- N. LENIN

The passing of a political system. The victory of the Allies and the revolutions which swept over Europe upon the defeat of the Central Powers resulted in the toppling of many thrones. Two emperors, those of Germany and Austria; two tsars, those of Russia and Bulgaria; six kings, those of 

Prussia, Saxony, Bavaria, Württemberg, Hungary, and

Greece; one sultan, and a crowd of princes, dukes, and grand dukes renounced their hereditary rights and sought refuge either in obscurity or in exile. More than a score of sovereigns dethroned represent part of the balance sheet of the war.

The states of Europe after the war.  and the peace treaties following it have left thirty sovereign states in Europe. Seventeen of these were republics. Germany, Austria, Czechoslovakia, Poland, Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, Finland, Greece, Spain, Irish Free State, Soviet Russia, and Turkey (as far as it is a European power) were added to the republican column, which before the war included only France, Switzerland, Portugal, and tiny San 770

Post-War Europe 

771 Marino. The other thirteen countries were monarchies, the new ones being Hungary, Jugoslavia, Albania, and Iceland.

They were, however, constitutional monarchies, similar to those found in other parts of Europe.

Democracy at high tide. During the war much was heard of making the world safe for democracy. After the war there was an impressive growth of constitutions and democratic institutions, especially in central Europe. These constitutions established manhood suffrage and often woman suffrage as well. They separated church and state, where the two had previously been united. They also provided for a system of common schools, so that the people might understand and appreciate democratic institutions. Another noteworthy feature of the constitutions was the adoption of the cabinet system of government, after the English model (pp. 582-584). The presidents of the new republics enjoy far less authority and influence than the sovereigns whom they displaced. Their position rather resembles that of the head of the French republic (p. 592).

The rising tide of dictatorships. In spite of this temporary trend toward constitutional democracy, there has been an extensive growth of dictatorships. Many European countries are now governed by dictators: Italy by Mussolini and the Fascists; Germany by Hitler and the Nazis; Russia by the Communists; Poland by Pilsudski; Hungary by 

Admiral Horthy; Jugoslavia by King Alexander; Portugal by General Carmona; and Albania by King Zog. Even

Spain, which in 1931 expelled the Bourbon dynasty and became a republic, had for a while a virtual dictator in the premier and war minister, Azaña. To this list might be added the dictatorship of Mustafa Kemal in Turkey, for a small part of that country is still included in Europe. 

Some of these countries still maintain the forms of constitutional democracy, while they are in fact dictatorships. 

Meaning of dictatorship. A dictatorship means governing without responsibilty to a parliament, continuance in office without recall by a popular vote, and suppression of

free speech and a free press. Such elements of dictatorship occur in all the instances mentioned, though the degree of personal rule varies from country to country. In general, it represents a breakdown of democratic institutions in countries where democracy has not become deeply rooted. 

The idea of dictatorship is itself not new. Julius Cæsar and Augustus in ancient times, and Napoleon I and Napoleon III in modern times are familiar instances of strong men who, by force or guile, won their way to supreme power. 

Some present-day dictatorships, however, are new in organization and purposes.

Types of dictatorship. The European dictatorships are either of the Fascist type found in Italy or of the Bolshevist (communist) type found in Russia. Their principles are sharply opposed. The one aims to preserve private enterprise in business and the capitalistic system; the other would abolish capitalism. The one is essentially a dictatorship of the middle classes, while the other is a dictatorship of the workingmen and peasants. Both recognize, however, a common foe in democracy, as that has been worked out in western Europe and America during the past century and more. 

Both repudiate many democratic institutions. To Fascism and Bolshevism alike these are feeble, ineffective, and unable to cope with the many problems of our modern industrialized society. Fascism and Bolshevism agree that political democracy must be replaced by a new and planned order based upon economic activities and groups. The efforts to create such an order in Italy and Russia are discussed below. 

174. SOVIET RUSSIA 

The downfall of the Romanovs. The inefficient and corrupt government of the tsar was, as we have seen (p. 618), unable to survive the strain of the World War. A severe shortage of food in the capital city, Petrograd (St. Petersburg) brought matters to a crisis. Rioting broke out, and the troops were ordered to suppress it with bullet and bay-

Soviet Russia 

773 onet in the usual pitiless fashion. But the old army, so long the prop of autocracy, had perished in battle or languished in German prison camps. The new army, mostly recruited from peasants and workingmen since the war, refused to fire on the people. The government found itself helpless. The Duma (national legislature) then induced the tsar to sign the penciled memorandum which, on March 15, 1917, ended the Romanov dynasty after three hundred years of absolute power.

The provisional government, March-November, 1917. 

The Russians who controlled the revolution of March, 1917, belonged to the party of Constitutional Democrats, representing the middle class, or bourgeoisie. They set up a provisional government and announced many liberal reforms: liberty of speech and of the press; the right of suffrage for both men and women; a general amnesty for all political offenders and Siberian exiles; and a popular assembly to draw up a constitution for Russia. The United 

States and the western Allies promptly recognized the provisional government. The socialists, however, were not satisfied with these measures. They planned to give the revolution an economic rather than merely a political character. 

The socialist leader was a young lawyer named Alexander Kerensky. By July, 1917, he had become the most powerful member of the provisional cabinet and almost a dictator. 

Kerensky turned out to be neither a Cromwell nor a Napoleon, at a time when Russia required a combination of both. 

Being a socialist, he did not please the Constitutional Democrats, and being only a moderate socialist, he did not please the radical socialists. 

Rise of the Bolshevists. Throughout the summer of 1917, the most radical group of socialists (the Bolshevists) were gaining control of the most important revolutionary organizations, namely, the soviets. These were councils representing workingmen and soldiers. The chief of these soviets was the Petrograd Council of Workingmen's and Soldiers'

Delegates. The socialistic propaganda for a general peace

on the basis of "no annexations and no indemnities" also made rapid headway with the army at the front. The troops began to elect their own officers, to fraternize with the enemy, and to desert in large numbers. The Petrograd soviet won the support of the army. The Bolshevists, under the leadership of N. Lenin and Leon Trotsky, won control of the Petrograd soviet, and gradually extended their control to other soviets throughout Russia. Lenin and the Bolshevists promised (1) to conclude an immediate peace with the Central Powers, (2) to place industry under control of the workers, (3) to divide the land among the peasants, (4) to ration food in the starving cities. These plans appealed to the factory workers and the soldiers. In November, 1917, the Petrograd soviet led a second revolution which overthrew the provisional government under Kerensky and brought the Bolshevists, under Lenin and Trotsky, to power. 

Lenin and Trotsky. Lenin was born of Russian parents and was brought up in the Orthodox faith. He received an education in economics and law at the University of Petrograd. His socialistic activities soon resulted in a three years' exile to Siberia. After his release he went abroad and became prominent in the revolutionary circles of many European capitals. Trotsky, a Russian Jew, also suffered exile to Siberia as an undesirable agitator, the first time for four years, the second time for life. Having managed to escape, Trotsky went to western Europe and later to the United States. After the Russian Revolution of March, 1917, both men returned to their native country and engaged in socialistic propaganda, with the results that have been seen. Lenin became premier and Trotsky foreign minister (later minister of war) in the new Bolshevist government set up in November, 1917.

Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, March 3, 1918. The Bolshevists made peace with the Central Powers. The breakdown of the 

Russian army enabled the Germans to force hard terms upon the Bolshevists. They had to agree to recognize the independence, under German auspices, of both Finland and the

Soviet Russia 775 Ukraine. They also agreed to give up all claims to Poland and other western provinces of the Russian Empire previously overrun by the German armies. This humiliating treaty deprived Russia of about a fourth of her population and a fourth of her arable land, including the richest agricultural regions, the chief industrial districts, most of the iron mines and coal mines, and many of the principal railways of the former empire. Had the Brest-Litovsk Treaty lasted, Germany would have been the winner of the World War, whatever might have been the outcome of the conflict elsewhere in Europe. 

From Russian Empire to U.S.S.R. The Treaty of Brest- 

Litovsk did not last very long. The victorious Allies compelled Germany to repudiate it, thus making possible the creation of the republics of Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, and Poland (pp. 745–746). The Bolshevists recognized the independence of these countries in accordance with the principle of self-determination of nationalities. Russia thus lost most of her subject and alien peoples in Europe, and became a national state, inhabited almost entirely by Russians. 

The capital was moved from Petrograd (which the Bolshevists had renamed Leningrad) to Moscow. The Bolshevists reorganized the territories under their control. They created a great federation of seven states, known as the Union of 

Soviet Socialist Republics (U.S.S.R.). The largest and most important state is Soviet Russia, or, as it is officially called, the Russian Socialist Federated Soviet Republic. Other members are White Russia, Ukrainia, and Transcaucasia. 

There are also three republics in central Asia. Soviet 

Russia grants to the federated states some degree of independence in local concerns, but requires them to maintain a Soviet government and controls their foreign relations. 

The Soviet constitution. Russia possesses a constitution. 

It grants the franchise to men and women over eighteen years of age, if they are "productive" laborers. This means, in practice, that all employers of labor for profit (except peasants who hire other peasants on their farms) cannot vote or hold any public office, or serve in the army. Most mem-

bers of the middle class are thus excluded from political rights. The same exclusion applies to clergymen and monks and, of course, to the former nobles. The supreme organ of authority is the All-Union Congress of Soviets, which meets at least once in two years. During the intervals between its sessions the govern- 

NIKOLAI LENIN 

sqipement is conducted by levo a Central Executive phoWad Committee.

The Communist 

Dictatorship. Back of the Soviets stands the 

Ji ate Communist Party, the by only legalized political party in Russia. 

Since Lenin and Trotsky were the leaders of this party, they were the dictators of 

Russia. They repudiated the foreign and domestic debts of the old tsarist government. They abolished private property in land, took over the great estates without compensation to the former owners, divided them up, and leased them to the peasants. They "nationalized" railways, shipping, banks, forests, and mines. 

They seized the factories, which were to be operated henceforth by the workingmen and for the workingmen. These things were done by a small party of communists, whose numbers, at the time, reached scarcely half a million. In short, the Bolshevist régime was and still is not a dictatorship by all the proletariat, but rather a dictatorship by a part of the proletariat claiming to rule in the interest of all the proletariat. In order to establish this dictatorship the

Soviet Russia 

777 party employed terrorism- - exiling, imprisoning, or executing their enemies.

Economic transformation. What has really been happening in Russia? Closed factories, disorganized railroads, and starving cities made it impossible for the Bolshevists to establish a completely communistic society at once. Under these circumstances the Bolshevists began to compromise between communism and capitalism so far as to allow private trade and private enterprise in the smaller industries. 

Foreign capitalists, by means of contracts and concessions, were also invited to invest in Russia. This was the New 

Economic Policy (NEP) introduced in 1921. Economic re covery had become so marked by 1928 that the Bolshevists, now under Stalin's resolute leadership, decided to resume the interrupted march toward complete communism. Their decision found expression in the Five-Year Plan (19281933). It involved, during these years, a great enlargement of government-owned industries, a great extension of government-owned railroads and other means of transportation, and an enormous expenditure for machinery, electrification, and other improvements in both European and Asiatic Russia. An example of the Five-Year Plan in operation was the completion in 1932, by American engineers, of a huge power plant on the Dnieper River, making that river navigable for thirteen hundred miles and supplying electric energy for an industrial territory larger than New England. 

Applied to agriculture the Five-Year Plan called for a large increase in the number of both government-managed farms and coöperative farms, the latter being those worked in common by the poorer peasants. Stalin's program of "collectivized agriculture" seemed to have met success by the end of 1933. The harvests of that year were larger than for many previous years, and there was less resistance by the peasants to the collection of grain by the government. On the other hand, the villagers were short of manufactured goods, partly because of inadequate distribution.

Social transformation. To control the economic life of

Russia is not enough for the Bolshevists. They would also make over Russian society. The people are to be educated in the doctrines of communism by a system of free and compulsory public schools, ranging from the kindergarten to the university, with special emphasis on science and technology. 

The Bolshevists have deprived the Orthodox Church — the prop of tsarism and aristocracy - of all government support, have confiscated its immense wealth, and have closed its schools. Many cathedrals and larger churches are now used as museums and workers' clubs. For the Bolshevists "religion is the opiate of the people" (as Marx declared), directing to a visionary world the thoughts and energies that ought to be devoted to this world. The communist ideal of equality comes near to realization in Russia, where there are no class distinctions in the way of dress or bearing; where the women, both unmarried and married, are all at work with the men; and where both marriage and divorce are simply arranged by signing papers at a registry office. Thus, the Bolshevists seek to change the culture of one hundred and sixty million people. If they succeed, it will be perhaps the greatest social transformation ever known. STALIN 

The future of Bolshevism. 

Lenin's death in 1924 and the downfall and exile of Trotsky three years later have left Joseph

Stalin, the general-secretary of the Communist Party, as the most powerful figure in the Soviet government. Bolshevism, with all that it implies in the way of revolutionary politics, economics, and sociology, seems to be seated more firmly in the saddle than at any time since 1917; at any rate, the Bolshevists are more numerous, better disciplined, and more determined than ever to impose their system throughout the length and breadth of Russia.

Fascist Italy 779 

175. FASCIST ITALY 

Breakdown of the old order in Italy. Italy after the war was a land of unrest, with many idle men, endless strikes, seizure of factories by the workers, and serious disorders fomented by the communists, who wanted to bring about a proletarian revolution after the Russian model. The government proved to be unable to cope with the situation; law and order had seemingly broken down; revolution impended.

Then Mussolini and his Fascists appeared on the scene. 

MUSSOLINI 

Mussolini and the Fascists. Benito Mussolini was born in 

1883, the son of an illiterate blacksmith of radical tendencies and active in the socialist movement of his community. The youthful Mussolini also became a socialist, but of such advanced opinions that for a time he had to take refuge in Switzerland. 

After returning to Italy, he edited socialist newspapers and quickly gained a reputation for brilliancy and audacity as a critic of the government. The outbreak of the World War found him an ardent supporter of the Allies, and when Italy entered the struggle he volunteered for service as a private in the trenches and fought with distinction until incapacitated by a serious wound. His war experiences made him less and less an internationalist and more and more a nationalist and patriot. Finally, he broke away from his socialist connections and became the head of a new party. This was the Fascist Party (Fascisti), which found an emblem in the old Roman fasces, a bundle of rods wrapped about an ax and carried before the highest magistrates as a symbol of authority. The Fascists were mostly young men, the virile soldiers of the war. Mussolini organized them, trained them as a military force, and filled them with his own enthusiasm for reviving the greatness of Italy.

The March on Rome. When revolution impended in Rome, Mussolini and his black-shirted Fascists, mobilized from all parts of the peninsula, marched on Rome in four columns and peacefully occupied the capital. The king, Victor 

Emmanuel III, sided with them, and the weak-kneed parliament voted dictatorial authority to Mussolini. A new government, headed by Mussolini as premier and minister for foreign affairs, thus came into existence. This was in 1922. 

In 1932 he celebrated what is unusual with most dictators ten years of power. How has he kept his power so long and what has he done with it?

The Fascist dictatorship. For about ten years Mussolini exercised his dictatorship through the constitutional forms that already existed in Italy. Victor Emmanuel III sat undisturbed on his throne, and the Italian parliament still met and enacted laws. Neither king nor parliament, however, enjoyed real authority. All candidates for parliamentary office had first to be passed upon by the Grand Council of the Fascist Party, which in turn was appointed by Mussolini himself. The list of acceptable candidates was then submitted to the voters for approval. Balloting was not secret, and those who voted against men approved by Mussolini soon felt the weight of his displeasure. Parliament thus consisted of Mussolini's followers. Its powers, furthermore, were strictly limited. Only the premier (Mussolini) could initiate measures, issue regulations having the force of laws, and appoint and discharge government employees. Mussolini also appointed and held responsible to himself the principal officials of the towns and cities. Without going into further details, it may be said that personal freedom and democratic institutions disappeared under the Fascist dictatorship.

The Fascist régime. Nevertheless, Mussolini and his "Black Shirts" can point to much material progress under the Fascist régime. The national resources of Italy in minerals and water power have been developed. Waste lands and malarial regions have been reclaimed for farms. Peasant

Fascist Italy 781 proprietorship has been encouraged by the breaking up of large estates. The railways have been reorganized and the currency has been stabilized. In short, Fascist Italy is now in process of rapid industrialization and modernization - a belated effort to catch up, economically, with the other great powers. Italian foreign policy is also marked by a new aggressiveness. The Fascists are determined that henceforth Italy shall play a more prominent rôle throughout the Mediterranean, thus reviving, in some measure, the ancient overlordship of Rome. The combination of a military dictatorship with imperialism is a dangerous one, which has often involved the Continent in strife. Whether it will do so under Mussolini, time alone can tell. 

The Corporate State. Mussolini has not rested with the establishment of himself as the dictator of Italy and the Italians. Believing that democracy, capitalism, and socialism have all failed, he has tried to build a state for the future on different principles. The result is the Corporate State. Except for Soviet Russia, it is the most ambitious national planning organization in the world today. The purpose of the Corporate State is to coördinate economic and political life, and to plan and control the productive life (agriculture and industry) in the interest of the state. The Corporate 

State is founded upon national confederations of employers and national syndicates of labor. In 1930, Mussolini organized the Council of Corporations consisting of representatives from these various corporations and other groups. Late in 1933 he announced that the parliamentary Chamber of Deputies must be replaced by the National Council of Corporations. Thus Mussolini's corporative state seems to embody features of private capitalism, socialism, and the medieval guilds. In this state the principle of private initiative will be subordinated to that of responsibility to the state, and the state will be organized along economic lines. 

The future of Fascism. Fascism sets up a state whose selfappointed leaders shall work together, unselfishly and harmoniously, to realize the ideal of an efficient, powerful, and

prosperous Italy. The Fascist state thus seems to be the old "enlightened" despotism under another name. We are told that Mussolini, by disciplining the Italians and making them more competent, "has changed the spirit of a whole nation." If that be true, his work will endure. The problem remains, however, what will happen to Fascism when il Duce ("the Leader") meets his end. It is the problem inherent in every despotism. 

176. THE RISE OF DICTATORSHIP IN GERMANY 

The socialistic upheaval. Socialists took the leadership of the revolutionary and republican movements in many European countries after the World War.

There are two types of socialism, however. Moderate socialists rely on the ballot to abolish capitalism and introduce state ownership of the means of production: they are democrats in their political thinking and accept the democratic principle of majority rule. Radical or extreme socialists advocate a violent revolution to overthrow the capitalistic middle class, the hated bourgeoisie, and bring in a dictatorship of the urban proletariat. These socialists, therefore, preach "class conflict"; they as the would employ "direct action" only effective method of reconstructing society. The contrast between the two socialistic parties was well marked in Germany, where the principles of Karl Marx and his followers first became popular among workingmen. 

HINDENBURG 

A bust by Ernesto di Fiori.

The German republic. The moderate socialists (Social 

Democrats) before the war were the chief opponents of militarism and autocracy in Germany, and even in 1914 a bold minority of them resisted the war fever then sweeping over

The Rise of Dictatorship in Germany 

783 the country. The events of 1918 strengthened their hands; both the army and the navy became saturated with the revolutionary spirit; and a few days before the signing of the armistice a mutiny broke out among the sailors in the fleet at Kiel. It spread swiftly to the great ports of Bremen, Lübeck, and Hamburg, and next to Potsdam and Berlin. 

The government could not prevent an uprising, for the soldiers in the capital refused to obey orders and some of them went over to the revolutionists. The kaiser then fled and the imperial chancellor resigned office. A socialist leader,

Friedrich Ebert, became head of a provisional government. 

The German republic was born (p. 731). Ebert and his associates summoned a national assembly which met at Weimar in 1919 and drafted a constitution. Under this constitution 

Germany became a genuinely democratic state, with universal suffrage and freedom of press and of assembly. 

President von Hindenburg. When the first president,

Friedrich Ebert, died in 1925, he was succeeded by the national hero, Field-Marshal von Hindenburg, who after the war had been living in retirement on his estate in East Prussia. Many people in Germany and outside of Germany feared that his election, by putting into the presidency a Prussian noble and army man, meant an early restoration of the Hohenzollerns. But Hindenburg was as faithful in his devotion to the new republic as he had been to the old empire. The affection of the German people for him was shown by his reëlection in 1932, although he was then in his eighty-fifth year. He died August 2, 1934.

Economic problems of post-war Germany. Many economic problems confronted the new republic. One of these was the inflation of the currency after the war. Paper money, issued by the government in enormous amounts, rapidly depreciated in value, until at length over four trillions of paper marks were required to buy what a dollar (based on gold) would purchase. It was the same disastrous experience that the French revolutionists had with their assignats (p. 495). This worthless currency was finally withdrawn

from circulation, being replaced by an issue of "gold marks." 

Reparations to the Allied powers also delayed the financial recovery of Germany. At last in 1932 the Lausanne agreement (p. 743) put an end to what had become an intolerable burden. Germany continued to suffer, however, from the world-wide depression which resulted in unemployment, industrial disorganization, and strangled commerce. 

Political problems of post-war Germany. These economic problems were coupled with many political problems. 

Under an able foreign minister, Gustav Stresemann, Germany pursued a policy of conciliation with her former foes, the results of which were seen in her entrance into the League of Nations and the World Court and in her signatures to the Locarno pacts and the Pact of Paris. Stresemann's death in 1929 was a severe blow to this policy. Since then there has been a revival of ultra-patriotic agitation, marked by much display of steel helmets, big parades of war heroes, and the demonstrations of the Nazis, or National Socialists.

The rise of Hitler and the Nazis. The leader of the Nazis was Adolf Hitler, an Austrian by birth, who served in the German army during the war. He organized the "Brown 

Shirts," in imitation of Mussolini's "Black Shirts," and as the latter led his followers to Rome and seized the government (p. 780), so Hitler planned to march on Berlin and make himself a Fascist dictator. Restoration of Germany's lost colonies and territories in Europe, disavowal of the Versailles Treaty, revival of German military power, and general wellbeing were some of the prospects which the Nazis held out to the populace. By 1932 they had become the largest single party in Germany. No party, however, had enough seats in the Reichstag to support a cabinet formed from its own members; attempts to form coalition cabinets failed. Twice during 1932 President von Hindenburg offered Hitler a place in a coalition cabinet. Each time, however, he refused, insisting that he would be content with nothing less than the supreme position in the cabinet-that of chancellor. At

The Rise of Dictatorship in Germany 

785 last, in January, 1933, he was made chancellor. He insisted upon holding new elections promptly, in order to mobilize behind himself and his party the will of the people. During the campaign the Nazis reminded the people of their defeat in 1918 and the miseries they had since suffered, blaming these upon the Social Democrats and communists. Now, said the 

Nazis, was the chance to make Germany once more a self-respecting state. This appeal, coupled with pressures of one kind and another, resulted in a victory at the polls for Hitler and the Nazis. He at once began taking over practically every political subdivision of the Reich dhonnloveY SISW

HITLER 

and started a reign of terrorism against pacifists, Jews, and opposing political parties, especially the Social Democrats and the communists. When the new Reichstag met on 

March 21, 1933, Hitler presented to it an Enabling Act by which he would be given almost unlimited power for four years, without having to receive the sanction of the Reichstag or the signature of the president for any of his acts. 

The Reichstag acquiesced. The Enabling Act of 1933 may therefore be said to mark the close of the democratic republic (the Second Reich) which had been established by the constitution of Weimar in 1919. Germany thus entered the 

Third Reich, a period of dictatorship by Hitler and the Nazis.

On the death of Hindenburg in 1934 Hitler at once assumed the power of the President, but not the title.

Hitlerism. Hitlerism in many ways resembles Fascism. 

It (1) glorifies the national state and its history, (2) disapproves of parliaments and democracy, (3) prevents the formation of other political parties besides the National Socialists, and (4) aims at an extensive reorganization of the state, especially along economic lines. In foreign policy Hitlerism also resembles Fascism, for both adopt an aggressive policy in dealing with other nations. Hitler's announced intention of withdrawing from the League and his actual withdrawal from the disarmament conference late in 1933 increased the distrust of other nations. Hitler's foreign policy embraces (1) the right of Germany to rearm on a basis of equality with other nations, (2) reannexation of Danzig and the

Polish Corridor, (3) settlement of the dispute with France over the Saar Basin, and (4) union (Anschluss) with Austria. 

Nazi uprisings in Austria in the summer of 1934 failed. 

177. PROBLEMS OF THE NEAR EAST 

Rise of nationalism in Turkey. Six years before the World

War, a revolution broke out in the Turkish sultan's dominions. This was the work of the Young Turks, a group of patriotic reformers who aimed to revive and modernize the Ottoman Empire. They won over the army and carried through a sudden, almost bloodless, coup d'état. The terrified sultan (Abdul Hamid II) had to issue a decree restoring the constitution granted by him at his accession but afterward annulled. His despotism vanished, and the Ottoman 

Empire, with an elective parliament, a responsible ministry, and a free press, took a place among democratic states. It soon became evident, however, that the Young Turks were nationalists as well as democrats. They intended to weld together all the peoples of the Ottoman Empire into a single nation, with Turkish as the favored language and Islam the only privileged faith.

Efforts of the Nationalists to save Turkish territories. 

During the World War, the victorious campaigns of the Allies

Problems of the Near East 

787 (p. 723) compelled the Turks to surrender Syria, Palestine, Mesopotamia, and Arabia - all countries chiefly Arabic in population and language. The Peace Conference at Paris drew up a treaty which, besides depriving Turkey of the territories overrun by the Allies in the war, also gave Greece a further slice of Turkey in 

Europe (eastern Thrace) and the city of Smyrna and its environs in Asia Minor. A new and vigorous Turkish government, however, under the Nationalists, had been set up at 

Angora in Asia Minor. This government would not ratify the treaty. The Nationalists found an able leader in Mustafa 

Kemal, a Turkish officer who had won distinction in the 

Gallipoli campaign. He organized a strong army, drove the Greeks out of Smyrna, and took possession of Constantinople and eastern Thrace. 

TURKISH PARISAMENT "THE ADOPTED FATHER" 

Abdul Hamid: "Well, if any one had told me a year ago that I should have come to this!" A Punch cartoon.

Treaty of Lausanne, 1923. The Allies, confronted with this situation, which their disagreements and bickerings with one another did so much to bring about, had to consent to a new treaty far more favorable to Turkey than the one originally framed. The Treaty of Lausanne was signed in 1923. 

It allowed the Turks to keep both eastern Thrace and Smyrna and also recognized Turkish sovereignty over the waterways leading from the Mediterranean to the Black Sea. treaty further provided for the compulsory exchange of Greeks living in Asia Minor for Turks living in Greece, so that each country might henceforth be freed from the alien element in its population. The Countries freed from Turkey. The Turks did not recover, however, their Arabic possessions. The French now hold

Syria under a mandate from the League of Nations. The 

British have the mandate for Palestine. They are pledged freely to open the Holy Land to the Jews - a people without a country for eighteen hundred years. A good many “Zionists," or Jewish nationalists, have recently moved into Palestine, but Jews do not form as yet more than one-sixth of the total population. Mesopotamia has become the independent kingdom of Irak (Arabic Iraq). Arabia contains several independent states, one of which is Hejaz. Both 

France and Great Britain are doing much useful work in the Near East. Good roads, modern schools, scientific agriculture and irrigation, and orderly government should redeem it from the long blight to which it has been subjected by 

Turkish misrule.

Republic of Turkey. The expulsion of the Greeks from 

Asia Minor and the peace settlement at Lausanne were the direct result of Mustafa Kemal's leadership of the Turkish

Nationalists. They bestowed upon him the title of Ghazi ("the Victorious"), and looked to him for further leadership.

The Nationalists deposed the sultan and did away with the caliphate, or spiritual authority which the Ottoman rulers had asserted over the Moslem world. A national assembly, meeting in 1923, proclaimed Turkey a republic and unanimously elected Mustafa Kemal to be its president. The capital is Angora in Asia Minor, but Constantinople (henceforth known by its Turkish name Istanbul) remains the cultural center of the republic. The new national state was indeed much smaller than the old empire. On the other hand, Turkey had gained in compactness and racial unity by the loss of Syria, Mesopotamia, Palestine, and Arabia and the expulsion of alien Greeks from its territory. It was this new 

Turkey which Mustafa Kemal, in 1923, set about creating into a secular, industrialized national state on the model of 

Western countries. 

Westernization of Turkey. Mustafa Kemal, as president, exercises a practical dictatorship. His task is one of Westernization, of bringing Turkey into step with the twentieth cen-

Problems of the Far East 789 tury. Some of his reforms suggest those of Peter the Great in Russia (p. 446); for instance, the prohibition of wearing the fez (the national headgear for men), and the optional discontinuance of the veil for women. It has been said of the 

Turks that as soon as they took off their fezzes they began to use their minds. At any rate, there have been striking changes in the educational system. The study of the English language is now compulsory for schools. The cumbrous 

Oriental characters of the Turkish language have been replaced by those of the Latin alphabet, and Oriental numeral signs by those used in western Europe. The solar calendar has been substituted for the lunar calendar used in Moslem lands. Islam itself has been disestablished. No longer the official religion, it is henceforth merely a recognized faith like Christianity and Judaism. Other radical changes include the abolition of both slavery and polygamy, the freeing of women from the seclusion of the harem, and the adoption of a modern system of law based on Western models. Economically, also, the new republic makes progress, with the construction of highways and railroads and by the transformation of Angora from a dingy Oriental town into a worthy capital city. Mustafa Kemal's rule over a people who have never known democracy has much to commend it. 

178. PROBLEMS OF THE FAR EAST 

Gandhi. The agitation for nationalism in India increases, rather than lessens, with the years. Great movements often crystallize around great personalities, and so it is with Indian nationalism, which has found a leader in Gandhi. A 

Hindu of good family, he received a legal education in London and for many years practiced his profession in South Africa. 

Here he became prominent as a champion of the downtrodden Indians and other Asiatics who had settled in Cape Colony. 

Returning to India, Gandhi threw himself unreservedly into the agitation for Indian independence. His earnestness and sincerity, his ascetic life, and his eloquence soon made a deep

impression on the unlettered people who listened to him: they thought of him as a saint and gave him the title of Mahatma, or Great Soul. Gandhi has especially relied on a campaign of "non-violent non-coöperation" to bring the British government to terms. This takes the form of avoiding army service, of surrendering all public offices, of withdrawing children from the schools, of refusing to pay rent. or taxes, and of boycotting British goods. The ordinary methods of repression are useless under such conditions. Of what avail are machine guns and bayonets against millions who sit passively and refuse to obey the law? The result of non-coöperation has been much unrest in India ever since the 

World War. 

The situation in India. British India, which includes twothirds of the area of the country and three-fourths of the population, is ruled directly from London through a cabinet officer called the secretary of state for India. The actual administration rests in the hands of an appointive viceroy, assisted by two councils and the officials of the Indian Civil Service. The remainder of India consists of native or feudatory states, about seven hundred in number. These continue to be ruled by their own princes, under the protection of Great Britain. A round table conference on Indian affairs, which Gandhi attended, was held in London in 1931, and plans were there formulated for a new federal government, leading toward a Dominion status for India. A new capital was dedicated with great pomp at New Delhi in 1931. Much progress has been made in organizing under the new constitution but the problem is difficult and final adjustments of conflicting interests will necessarily require time. 

The situation in China. More than two decades have now passed since the Chinese Revolution overthrew the decrepit Manchu dynasty and set up a republican government with a constitution and a presidency on Western lines. The new republic entered the family of nations with bright prospects, but these were soon blasted. The first fruits of the revolution have been greater disorder than China has known for

Problems of the Far East 791 centuries. Ever since 1912 China has been rent by civil conflicts, due to the greed for power and plunder on the part of military leaders and governors, by the activities of the communists, and by brigandage in the unprotected provinces. 

Warfare, disease, and famine have taken, and still take, a heavy toll of human lives in the unhappy country. To all these troubles there was added, in 1932, the Japanese invasion of Chinese territory below the Great Wall. Japan even sent a fleet to Shanghai, landed a large force of marines, and fought bloody battles with the city's defenders, in order to prevent a boycott of Japanese goods by the Chinese Nationalists. This boycott had arisen as a protest against the 

Japanese policies in Manchuria.

Manchuria. The Chinese outer territory of Manchuria, rich in coal and minerals, well forested, with one of the most fertile soils in the world, and as yet thinly populated, lies at the front door of Japan. Her purpose to take it from 

China's nerveless hands, whenever an opportune occasion arose, to colonize it and to develop it, has been manifest ever since the Russo-Japanese War. Economically, Japan needs Manchuria because of its rich resources; it is her "life-line." Japanese imperialists argue that she also needs it politically, as a barrier against Soviet Russia; for them it is her "first line of defense" against the Russian colossus. 

Manchukuo. In September, 1931, a section of track of the South Manchurian Railway, which belongs to Japan, was blown up near Mukden. This act of aggression was attributed by the Japanese authorities to Chinese troops, aided and abetted by the Chinese government. The next day the Japanese army stationed in Manchuria began an advance, steady and remorseless, which never ceased until most of this former province of China had come under the control of the "island empire." Manchuria has not been formally annexed to the empire, as was Korea. It has been erected into the puppet state of Manchukuo, whose ruler is the ex-emperor of China, now known as P'u-Yi. The Japanese wrote its constitution; their "advisers" control its

government; and their troops occupy its territory from the 

Siberian frontier on the north to the Great Wall on the south. Manchukuo in fact, if not in name, is a protectorate of Japan.

The League of Nations and Japan. A commission of the 

League of Nations, under the chairmanship of the earl of Lytton, has made an inquiry, on the spot, into the whole troubled situation in the Far East. The report of the commission to the League does not justify Japan's conduct, which is declared to be inconsistent with her treaty obligations. 

As a way out, the proposal is made that Manchuria become an autonomous (self-governing) state, which would have the assistance of foreign advisers but would not be controlled by either China or Japan. A solution along these lines, Lord 

Lytton believes, is essential to the preservation of peace and justice for the world's peoples. The old issue between international anarchy and international coöperation has thus been raised again, this time in distant Manchuria. 

179. THE BRITISH EMPIRE 

The world's largest empire. , resulting in the capture or destruction of most of the German fleet, confirmed Great Britain's position as mistress of the seas. 

Her naval bases are located at convenient intervals on nearly all the great trade routes. The United Kingdom (England, Scotland, Wales,, and Northern Ireland) is the cradle and center of an empire that includes approximately one-fourth of the habitable area of the globe and one-fourth of the world's population. No such wide dominion was ever built up before, either in ancient or in medieval times. All the races of man, all stages of culture from savagery to civilization, all the principal religions, and nearly all the principal languages of mankind are represented in the British Empire.

Ireland. One member of the British Empire, however, has only recently accommodated itself to such membership.

The British Empire 

793 For centuries Ireland was dissatisfied under English rule and carried on a continual agitation against the Anglican church, against British landlords, and for home rule. During the 

World War the Irish under the leadership of the Sinn Fein (Irish for "ourselves alone") Party proclaimed a republic, but it was suppressed by British troops. After the close of the war agitation for independence was renewed, and in 1922 the Irish Free State was set up. Great Britain granted to it the same measure of independence that is enjoyed by Canada and the other self-governing Dominions of the British Empire. Ulster (the northern province of Ireland) insisted, however, upon exclusion from the Free State and maintains its own "Government of Northern Ireland," with representation in the British Parliament. The Irish people have thus secured the right to rule themselves, but Great Britain still keeps some control over them in military and international matters.

Subdivisions of the British Empire. The British Empire is a complex and apparently inharmonious organization of many types of governments. It consists of (1) the United 

Kingdom, which now includes Northern Ireland but not the Irish Free State, (2) the Irish Free State, (3) India, (4) various protectorates and spheres of influence, (5) the Crown colonies, and (6) the self-governing Dominions. The government of Great Britain and the United Kingdom has already been treated (pp. 582-584). As respects government, both the Irish Free State and India stand by themselves and somewhat distinct from the rest of Great Britain's empire. The status of the rest of the subdivisions of the empire will be reviewed.

Protectorates, spheres of influence, and mandates. Great 

Britain has also several protectorates in Africa, including the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan and tropical districts valuable for their productions but generally unfit for European settlement. She likewise possesses certain spheres of influence in 

Africa and other parts of the world, where foreign countries agree not to acquire territory or control, either by treaty or

annexation. Various mandates were also accepted at the close of the World War by Great Britain and her Dominions. 

Crown colonies. The most numerous group of British possessions is composed of the Crown colonies. They are all under governors appointed by the Crown. In a few Crown colonies the governor exercises entire authority, both legislative and executive; in the others he is assisted by councils which are sometimes nominated by the Crown and sometimes selected by the colonists. This system of government resembles that of the royal colonies in North America before the Revolution. The Crown colonies lie chiefly within the tropics and contain relatively few English-speaking inhabitants. Examples are the British West Indies, British Guiana, Sierra Leone, Nigeria, Ceylon, and the Straits Settlements. 

Newfoundland, after unsatisfactory experiences with selfgovernment, has recently become a Crown colony. 

The Dominions. The group of self-governing colonies, or 

Dominions, includes Canada, Australia, New Zealand, and

South Africa. Their government closely parallels that of the 

United Kingdom. In each colony there is a governor-general, an upper chamber, and a popularly elected assembly. Each one has also a prime minister and the cabinet system. Without interference from Great Britain, they tax themselves, impose tariff duties, even on British goods, control immigration, raise their own armies, support their own navies, negotiate their own treaties, coin their own money, and fly their own national flags. They are, in fact, "colonial nations."

Statute of Westminster, 1931. The position of virtual independence and full partnership which the Dominions now enjoy has been set forth definitely in the Statute of Westminster. The Dominions are described as self-governing communities, "equal in status, in no way subordinate one to another in any aspect of their domestic or foreign affairs, though united by a common allegiance to the Crown, and freely associated as members of the British Commonwealth of Nations." The relationship between the Dominions and

The World's Peoples 

795 Great Britain, as defined by the Statute of Westminster in 1931, is precisely the relationship which the American colonists asked for in their "Olive Branch Petition" to George III in 1775. Had it been favorably received by the king, the 

Declaration of Independence might never have been signed, and the Thirteen Colonies might have continued to be members of the British Empire. 

Greater Britain. The nineteenth century was well advanced before Great Britain learned the right policy to adopt toward the colonials in North America, Australasia, and South Africa. The rising tide of democratic sentiment, as seen in the reform of parliamentary representation (pp. 572582), more than anything else stirred the British people to extend full rights to their colonials. Canada first received self-government in the 'forties of the last century (p. 611). 

Since then Great Britain has bestowed the same precious gift upon her Australasian and South African colonies. The change of British colonial policy, which has converted so much of the empire into a commonwealth of free states, is one of the outstanding facts of modern history. The vast extent of the Dominions, their enormous resources, and their rapidly growing population give promise of unlimited development in the future. They form a Greater Britain for the perpetuation through the ages of the language, literature, laws, institutions, and customs of the mother country.

The world's religions. The relations between Europeans and non-Europeans will probably be influenced more and more by the factor of religion. We sometimes forget that 

Christianity has as yet made little impression on the civilized world outside of Europe and America. We do not always realize how numerous are the Moslems of Africa, Asia, and Oceania, the Brahmanists in India, and the Buddhists in China, Japan, and other Oriental countries.

The World's Peoples 

797 rulers or peoples, may assume political importance. Islam has always been feared in this respect, because Moslems are encouraged to convert unbelievers by force, as well as by peaceful persuasion. Every year it gains millions of new followers, not only among the crowded populations of Asia, but also among the Negroes of central Africa. The World 

War produced an immense stirring among Moslems. Spain had trouble in Morocco, France in Syria, and Great Britain in Egypt and India, while all the European powers have been faced by a modernized Turkey. There has even been a movement to bring together the many Moslem sects, so as to oppose a united front to Christendom. This movement is called Pan-Islamism. Pan-Islamism is not a menace to the peace of the world, but imperialist Christian states will find it increasingly necessary to adjust their colonial policy to the wishes, and perhaps also to the prejudices, of their 

Moslem subjects.

The world's races. The relations between Europeans and non-Europeans are also affected by race. Classified by races, the world's population may be roughly estimated as 875,000,000 for the Caucasian race; 875,000,000 for the 

Mongoloid race; and 225,000,000 for the Negroid race.

These figures are only approximate, but they do show that the yellows and the blacks together considerably outnumber the whites. 

White expansion. Europe, with northern Africa and southwestern Asia, lies in the temperate zone, where nature seems to favor the development of the highest civilization. 

When, only four centuries ago, the European whites began their wonderful expansion overseas, they went chiefly to other parts of the temperate zone. This was true, above all, of English-speaking peoples, who found in the United States and Canada, and later in South Africa, Australia, and New Zealand, vast regions with a climate and productions similar to those of the homeland and not too thickly populated by the native inhabitants. The few whites settling in the tropical and sub-tropical parts of Africa, Asia, and

Oceania go as soldiers, officials, and business men. They seek, not new homes, but the profits of trade or of rule over subject peoples. Even in the tropical regions of America the European element (Spanish and Portuguese) is numerically far inferior to the Indians, Negroes, and mixed breeds. 

Modern science has proved that tropical diseases may be conquered by the elimination of insect carriers, proper sanitation, and medical treatment. Nevertheless, much doubt exists whether white men can long thrive in the hot, moist climate of equatorial countries or perform hard, continuous labor under such conditions. In the light of our present experience, it seems probable that, while whites may continue to control tropical lands, they will not settle them in large numbers. The Caucasian race is a temperate-zone race. 

Expansion of other races. There has also been some expansion by the black and yellow races. Slavery carried the 

Negroes far from Africa, and various contract labor systems as well as voluntary emigration have taken the Chinese and other Asiatics to many countries. Since the World War, there has been an increase of racial consciousness, and black and yellow people are less willing to accept the idea of the white man's essential superiority.

Racial concord. Modern science tends, however, to stress the resemblances, rather than the differences, between the races. The physical traits separating them may be numerous, but these do not seem to go deep. So with mental traits. A close parallelism certainly exists between the languages, religions, arts, and general culture of all mankind. 

In short, man is now recognized as essentially one in physical and mental endowment. This conclusion, in the measure that it is accepted, involves the decline and disappearance of the racial prejudice that has so long kept the world's peoples apart. If the League of Nations or some similar organization is to be successful, white men, yellow men, and black men must coöperate in the task of making a better world. Not the popular refrain "East is East and

West is West," but the Golden Rule and the saying attrib-

The World's Peoples 

799 uted to the Chinese Confucius, "All men between the four seas are brothers," express the true spirit of internationalism today. More and more what St. Paul declared to be true of individuals becomes also true of nations: "For none of us liveth to himself, and none dieth to himself."

REVIEW QUESTIONS 

1. Name ten of the seventeen new republics in post-war Europe. 

2. List five examples of democratic institutions. 

3. Name and identify five dictators. 

4. Recount the events of the March and November (1917) revolutions in Russia. 

5. What were the principles of the Bolshevists as announced by Lenin? 

6. What were the provisions of the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk? 

7. Explain how the U.S.S.R. is organized. 

8. What do the Russian communists mean by a productive laborer? 

9. What is meant by nationalizing a railway? 

10. Explain the NEP and the Five-Year Plan. 

11. Trace the story of Mussolini's rise to power. 

12. Characterize Italy under Mussolini. 

13. What is meant by the Corporate State? 

14. What conditions in Germany gave rise to Hitlerism? 

15. What countries did Turkey lose by the war? 

16. Give some instances of the Westernization of Turkey. 

17. What is Gandhi's doctrine? 

18. What was the Sinn Fein? 

19. What are the four types of government within the British Empire? 

20. Explain Pan-Islamism. 

21. Identify the following: Stalin, Ebert, Hindenburg, il Duce, Hitler, Stresemann, Ulster.

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS 

1. Why were democracies replaced by dictatorships in so many European countries? 

2. Discuss national planning in some of the European countries. Should all countries adopt national planning?

3. Show how dictatorships are in fundamental opposition to democracy. 

4. Will the world profit by the Westernization of Turkey? 

5. Should the League of Nations use force to carry out its decisions? 

6. How do you account for the fact that Gandhi stirred the imagination and sympathy of so many people throughout the world, even in England?

1. Prepare a class report on a significant development in some foreign country, as told in the latest issue of the Current History magazine. 

2. Debate: Resolved, That Hitler is justified in his foreign policy. 

3. Prepare a biographical sketch of one of the following: Lenin, Trotsky, Stalin, Mussolini, Hitler, Gandhi. 

4. Read President Wilson's Fourteen Points. (They may be found in

Webster's Modern European Civilization.) Show how far each of these 

Points has governed the conduct of the nations in international affairs.

Appendix B SUGGESTIONS FOR FURTHER STUDY 

Periodicals. Students of history should have access to the 

American Historical Review (N. Y., 1895 to date, quarterly, $4.00 a year). This journal, the organ of the American Historical Association, contains articles by scholars, critical reviews of all important works, and notes and news. The Social Studies (formerly the 

Historical Outlook) is edited in coöperation with committees of the American Historical Association and the National Council for the 

Social Studies (Philadelphia, 1909 to date, monthly, $2.00 a year).

History, the organ of the Historical Association, is a British publication for teachers (London, 1916 to date, quarterly, 8s. 6d.).

Every well-equipped school library should contain the files of the National Geographic Magazine (Washington, 1890 to date, monthly, $3.00 a year) and of Art and Archæology (Washington, 1914 to date, monthly, $5.00 a year). These two periodicals make a special feature of illustrations. Current History (N. Y., 1914 to date, monthly, $3.00 a year) contains much matter of contemporary interest.

Professional books. Useful books for the teacher's library include Henry Johnson, The Teaching of History (N. Y., 1915, Macmillan, $1.80), R. M. Tryon, The Teaching of History in Junior and 

Senior High Schools (Boston, 1921, Ginn & Co., $1.48), the Publications and Yearbooks of the National Council for the Social Studies (membership, including the Yearbook and Social Studies, $3.00, McKinley Pub. Co., Philadelphia), Edgar B. Wesley, Bibliographies for Teachers of the Social Studies (Philadelphia, 1932, McKinley 

Pub. Co., 30 cents).

Dictionaries and encyclopedias. For chronology, genealogies, lists of sovereigns, and other data the most valuable works are Arthur Hassall, European History, 476-1920 (new ed., N. Y., 1920, Macmillan, $4.00), G. P. Putnam, Tabular Views of Universal 

History (new ed., N. Y., 1915, Putnam, $3.00), and K. J. Ploetz, 805

Appendix B A Handbook of Universal History, translated by W. H. Tillinghast 

(new ed., Boston, 1925, Houghton Mifflin Co., $3.75).

Atlases. An admirable collection of maps for school use is W. R. 

Shepherd, Historical Atlas (new ed., N. Y., 1923, Holt, $3.90), with about two hundred and fifty maps covering the historical field. 

Another excellent work is Putnam's Historical Atlas, Medieval and 

Modern, edited by Ramsay Muir, George Philip, and Robert 

McElroy (N. Y., 1927, Putnam, $4.50). Much use can be made of the Literary and Historical Atlas of Europe, by J. G. Bartholomew, in "Everyman's Library" (N. Y., 1910, Dutton, $1.00). Other atlases in the same collection are devoted to Asia, Africa and Australasia, and America, respectively. 

Wall maps and charts. The Webster- Knowlton-Hazen European 

History Maps, prepared by Hutton Webster, D. C. Knowlton, and

C. D. Hazen, include nineteen maps for ancient history and twentysix for medieval and modern history (Chicago, A. J. Nystrom & 

Co.). The maps in this series are on a very large scale, omit all irrelevant detail, present place names in the modern English form, and deal with cultural as well as with political subjects. They are accompanied by a Teacher's Manual for each of the two sections. 

A somewhat similar series of wall maps, forty-three in number, has been prepared by J. H. Breasted, C. F. Huth, and S. B. Harding (Chicago, Denoyer-Geppert Co.).

Outline maps. The Historical Outline Maps and Exercises, pre pared by Hutton Webster and W. P. Webb, consist of three books devoted, respectively, to early European history, modern European history, and world history (Boston, D. C. Heath & Co., each 60 cents).

Illustrations. Photographs of ancient works of art may be obtained from the foreign publishers in Naples, Florence, Rome, Munich, Paris, Athens, and London, or from their American agents. 

In addition to photographs and lantern slides, a collection of stereoscopic views is very helpful in giving vividness and interest to historical instruction. The Keystone stereographs, prepared by the 

Keystone View Company, Meadville, Penn., are cordially recommended. Notable collections include Lehmann's Geographical

Pictures, Historical Pictures, and Types of Nations, and Cybulski's Historical Pictures (Chicago, A. J. Nystrom & Co., and Denoyer- 

Geppert Co.; each picture separately mounted on rollers).

A more elaborate work, also edited by Hutton Webster, is Historical Selections (Heath, $2.96), containing five hundred and seventy-five extracts from the primary and contemporary documents of ancient, medieval, and modern history. Appendix C TABLE OF EVENTS AND DATES 

c. 3400 Written records first kept by the Egyptians. Beginning of history in Egypt. c. 2100 Code of Hammurabi at Babylon. The earliest known code of laws. 

776 First recorded celebration of the Olympic games. Greek chronology begins to be precise from this date. 

753 (?) Rome founded. Traditional date. 

700 (?) The prophet Zoroaster in Persia. The founder of a monotheistic religion. 

612 Destruction of Nineveh. End of the Assyrian Empire. c. 560-c. 477 Buddha 551-478 Confucius 

509 (?) Roman Republic established. Traditional date. 

490 Marathon, 480 Salamis, and 479 Platæa and Mycale. The four battles which preserved Greece from Persian domination. 

461-429 Age of Pericles. Athens at this time the "school of Hellas." 

451-449 Laws of the Twelve Tables published. The basis of all later 

Roman law. 

431-404 The Peloponnesian War. Resulted in the downfall of the 

Athenian Empire. 

338 Battle of Charonea. The triumph of Macedonia over the disunited city-states of Greece. 

333 Issus and 331 Arbela. The two battles which overthrew the Persian

Empire and established Macedonian supremacy throughout the 

Near East. 

202 Battle of Zama. Ended the Second Punic War and left Rome without a rival in the western Mediterranean. 

146 Destruction of Carthage and Corinth. 

44 Death of Cæsar. 

31 Battle of Actium. Ended civil war between Antony and Octavian, leaving the latter supreme at Rome. 

31-180 A.D. Roman Peace. 

4 (?) Birth of Christ. Probable date. A.D. 

70 Capture of Jerusalem. 

98-117 Reign of Trajan. 814

Table of Events and Dates 

815 A.D. 

284 Reorganization of the Roman Empire by Diocletian. The imperial government henceforth became an absolutism of the Oriental type. 

313 "Edict of Milan." Placed Christianity on a legal equality with other religions of the Roman world. 

325 Council of Nicæa. Framed the Creed of Nicæa, which is still the accepted summary of Christian doctrine in Roman Catholic, Greek, and most Protestant Churches. 

330 Constantinople (New Rome) made the capital of the Roman Empire. 

It remained the capital for more than eleven centuries thereafter. 

378 Battle of Adrianople. The defeat of the Romans permitted the 

Germans to begin their inroads and settlements. 

395 Final division of the Roman Empire. Henceforth there were two lines of Roman emperors. 

451 Battle of Châlons. Saved western Europe from being conquered by the barbarous Huns. 

476 Deposition of Romulus Augustulus. Extinction of the line of Roman emperors in the West. 

496 Clovis accepted Catholic Christianity. Paved the way for intimate relations between the Franks and the papacy. 

529-534 Codification of Roman law under Justinian. The Corpus Juris 

Civilis formed a most important contribution of Rome to civilization. 

622 The Hegira (Flight) of Mohammed from Mecca to Medina. Marks the beginning of the Mohammedan era. 

732 Battle of Tours. The victory of the Franks under Charles Martel stemmed the advance of the Moslems into western Europe. 

800 Charlemagne crowned emperor of the Romans. Revival of the 

Roman Empire in the West. 

843 Treaty of Verdun. Marked important stage in the dissolution of 

Charlemagne's dominions. 

962 Otto I, the Great, crowned Roman emperor. Formation of the socalled Holy Roman Empire. 

1054 Final rupture of the Greek and Roman Churches. Destroyed the religious unity of European Christendom. 

1066 Battle of Hastings. Resulted in the Norman Conquest of England. 

1095 Council of Clermont. Beginning of the Crusades. 

1122 Concordat of Worms. A compromise arrangement between the papacy and the Holy Roman Empire. 

1215 Magna Carta. Defined the rights of Englishmen and inspired their later struggles for political liberty. 

1271-1295 Travels of Marco Polo. Polo's narrative of his travels greatly increased the interest of Europeans in the Far East.

Appendix C 

A.D. 66 1309-1377 'Babylonian Captivity" of the papacy. The removal of the popes to Avignon weakened their political authority. 

1337-1453 Hundred Years' War. Put an end to the Continental ambitions of England and made possible the complete unification of France. 

1348-1349 Black Death in Europe. Hastened the decline of serfdom and the emancipation of the peasantry. 

1378-1417 The "Great Schism." Weakened the spiritual supremacy of the popes over western Christendom. 

1453 Constantinople captured by the Ottoman Turks. End of the Byzantine Empire. 

1454 (?) First large book printed at Gutenberg's press in Mainz, Germany. Printing ranks among the most epochal of inventions. 

1487 Cape of Good Hope rounded by Díaz. Completed the Portuguese exploration of the western coast of Africa. 

1492 Discovery of America by Columbus. Revealed a New World and inaugurated the Atlantic period of European history. 

1498 India reached by Vasco da Gama. The Portuguese thus opened up an ocean passage from Europe around Africa to the Far East. 

1517 Luther's Ninety-five Theses posted. Beginning of the Protestant 

Reformation in Germany. 

1519-1522 Magellan's circumnavigation of the globe. A landmark in the history of geographical exploration. 

1545-1563 Council of Trent. 

Counter Reformation.

An important agency in the Catholic 

1555 Peace of Augsburg. Closed the first period of the Reformation in Germany. 

1558-1603 Reign of Elizabeth. A brilliant period of English history. 

1577-1580 Drake's voyage around the world. The first circumnavigation by an Englishman. 

1588 Defeat of the Spanish Armada. Gave to England control of the sea and made possible English colonization of North America. 

1598 Edict of Nantes issued by Henry IV of France. A noteworthy step in the direction of religious toleration. 

1607 Settlement of Jamestown. The first permanent English colony in America. 

1618-1648 The Thirty Years' War. A great international conflict, partly religious and partly political in character. 

1625 Grotius's "On the Law of War and Peace" published. Founded the study of international law. 

1642-1649 The Puritan Revolution. Arrested the growth of absolutism and divine right in England. 

1643-1715 Reign of Louis XIV. A brilliant period of French history.

Table of Events and Dates 

817 A.D. 

1688-1689 The "Glorious Revolution." Completed the work of the 

Puritan Revolution by overthrowing absolutism and divine right in England. 

1689 Bill of Rights. Renewed and expanded Magna Carta. 

1689-1725 Reign of Peter the Great. Europeanization of Russia began under this monarch. 

1713 Peace of Utrecht. Ended the War of the Spanish Succession. 

1740-1786 Reign of Frederick the Great. Prussia became a leading 

European power under this monarch. 

1762 Rousseau's "Social Contract" published. Its democratic teachings were put into effect by the French revolutionists. 

1763 Peace of Paris. Ended the Seven Years' War and gave to England a colonial empire in India and in North America at the expense of France. 

1769 Arkwright's "water frame," 1779 Crompton's "mule," and 1785

Cartwright's power loom. The great inventions ushering in the 

Industrial Revolution. 

1776 Declaration of Independence. The birth of a new nation in the 

New World. 

1783 Peace of Paris and Versailles. Ended the War of the American Revolution. 

1787 Constitution of the United States framed. A great and successful experiment in federation. 

1789 Meeting of the Estates-General in France. The first step toward the French Revolution. 

1794 Eli Whitney's cotton gin patented. Stimulated cotton production in the United States for British mills. 

1803 Louisiana Purchase. Made possible the expansion of the United States. 

1804 The Code Napoléon promulgated. The most lasting memorial of the Napoleonic era. 

1807 Fulton's steamboat, the "Clermont," in successful operation. Beginning of steam navigation. 

1814-1815 Congress of Vienna. Remade the map of Europe after the revolutionary and Napoleonic era. 

1815 Battle of Waterloo. Brought about the final overthrow of Napoleon Bonaparte. 

1823 Monroe Doctrine enunciated. Has prevented European interference in the affairs of the New World. 

1830-1831 The July Revolution in Europe. Overthrew absolutism and divine right in France and created modern Belgium. 

1832 Reform Act in Great Britain. The first step in democratizing the 

British government.

Appendix C 

A.D. 

1833 Abolition by Great Britain of slavery in the British West Indies. A triumph of modern humanitarianism. 

1839 Lord Durham's Report. Embodied liberal proposals for colonial self-government, which were subsequently adopted by Great Britain for Canada and other overseas possessions. 

1844 Morse's telegraph in successful operation. A revolutionary improvement in long-distance communication. 

1848-1849 The February Revolution in Europe. Made France again a republic and led to revolutionary upheavals in Italy, Germany, and the Austrian Empire. 

1851 Crystal Palace Exhibition at London. The first of the great inter national expositions. 

1854 Treaty between Japan and the United States. The first step in breaking down Japan's traditional isolation. 

1858-1861 Russian serfdom abolished by Alexander II. Another triumph of modern humanitarianism. 

1859 Darwin's "Origin of Species" published. Presentation of the evolutionary theory. 

1863 Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation. A third triumph of modern humanitarianism. 

1864 International Red Cross Society founded. Has become the greatest humanitarian organization in the world. 

1866 Atlantic Cable laid. The first of the many cables which now electrically bridge all the oceans. 

1869 Suez Canal opened. Created a new oceanic highway to the Far East. 

1870 Rome occupied by Italian troops. Unification of Italy completed. 

1871 German Empire proclaimed at Versailles. Unification of Germany completed. 

1874 Universal Postal Union established. An important agency in internationalization. 

1876 Bell's telephone in successful operation. Another revolutionary improvement in long-distance communication. 

1878 Treaty of Berlin. An attempted solution of the Eastern Question. 

1879 Incandescent electric lamp invented by Edison. 1890 Pan-American Union. Formed and maintained by the United 

States and the republics of Latin America. 

1896 Marconi's first patent for wireless telegraphy. A new method of long-distance communication inaugurated. 

1899 Meeting of the First International Peace Conference at The Hague. 

Resulted in agreements for the regulation of warfare. 

1903 S. P. Langley's airplane and Wright brothers' airplane. The conquest of the air begun.

1914-1918 World War. An international conflict on a scale unparalleled in history.

autocracy.

Condemnation of recourse to war for the solution of international controversies and renunciation of war as an instrument of national policy.
